## Day 1409

2026-01-02

[Z’s New Year address](https://www.president.gov.ua/en/news/novorichne-privitannya-prezidenta-ukrayini-volodimira-zelens-102261) commits what Judea Pearl would recognize as a fundamental error in causal reasoning: confusing correlation with causation, conflating wishful thinking with reality.

“90 percent ready” sounds wonderfully precise—the sort of number that implies scientific rigor. But what does it actually *cause*? In Pearl’s framework, we must ask: if we *make* Ukrainians believe peace is imminent, does that bring peace closer, or does it merely create what the psychoanalyst identifies as a “split”: people who *know* there is war but act *as if* there isn’t?

Z’s speech constructs an elaborate causal diagram where presidential rhetoric → hope → peace. But the arrows point the wrong way. The barometer doesn’t cause the atmospheric pressure. Moving the needle on public morale doesn’t generate electricty or end wars; it simply makes societies less prepared when reality—that stubborn thing—reasserts itself.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/05b9658d-e324-4163-9900-c306f476316f_931x760.png)  
*c/o CNN (January 2, 2026)*

Instead, Z could have told us what he is doing to turn the lights back on.

Contrast this with Zohran Mamdani’s inaugural address as New York City mayor. Where Z traffics in percentages plucked from ether, Mamdani identifies actual causal mechanisms: “universal child care for the many by taxing the wealthiest few.” One can disagree with the policy, but the causal arrow is brutally clear—*this* revenue stream funds *that* program. When Mamdani promises to “freeze the rent” or make “buses fast and free,” he’s not invoking magical thinking. He’s proposing interventions with traceable effects.

Pearl teaches us that causes precede effects in time. So what *actually* ends wars? Z’s speech admits it accidentally: “Russia will have to end the war—the moment they find one reason for peace more than for fighting.” Quite. And presidential speeches don’t typically register as reasons in Moscow’s causal calculus.

Mamdani understands something Z obscures: government is an *agent* with *power to intervene*, not merely a narrator shaping public sentiment. “No longer will City Hall hesitate to use its power to improve New Yorkers’ lives,” Mamdani declares—a statement that would be meaningless if power were purely performative.

When states abandon “the function of structuring reality,” the repressed eventually returns as rage—specifically, rage at those who mistook cheerleading for leadership. Ukrainians deserve what New Yorkers are being promised: not soothing fantasies about imminent peace, but leaders who understand that optimistic speeches don’t cause victories. Actions do.

## Day 1413

2026-01-06 · The Willing and the Unable

In Paris today, representatives from 35 countries—including 27 heads of state—gather for what the French presidency calls a meeting to demonstrate “alignment” between Washington, Kyiv, and European allies. The Coalition of the Willing, launched by France and the UK, convenes to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine as diplomatic efforts to broker a ceasefire, er, accelerate.

Among the attendees: Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, Emmanuel Macron, Keir Starmer, Friedrich Merz, Giorgia Meloni, Mark Carney, and Ireland’s own Helen McEntee, who will “emphasize that EU membership is an important security guarantee for Ukraine” and “underline Ireland’s strong support for progress on Ukraine’s EU accession path.” One can only marvel at the combined military might Ireland brings to such deliberations—a moral superpower unburdened by the vulgarity of actual power projection.

Meanwhile, the essentials remain unchanged:

Ukrainians have much to fear from the Golden Age of Ameriʞa we’ve just entered. So do Canadians, Venezuelans, Greenlanders, and maybe Colombians. If you don’t have nuclear weapons, you must sit in the back of the bus, which is currently being driven by superannuated would-be tough guys treating sovereignty like a timeshare presentation.

**Hasn’t it always been this way?**

Of course. That’s the whole sick joke.

The gang running things has always been the same—different uniforms, different flags, same business model. Power belongs to whoever can credibly threaten the most corpses. “When you’re not in the skin of a man, you can’t understand anything”—Céline knew this. The diplomat in his morning coat and the Zed in his unmarked fatigues are players in the same stupid game.

Shaw spotted it in 1914: every belligerent claimed God, civilization, and wounded innocence. The British condemned Prussian militarism while running the largest empire on earth. The Foreign Offices of Europe spent forty years preparing for war, then acted shocked—*shocked*—when it arrived. A massacre conducted by mutual agreement, dressed up as moral necessity.

Nothing’s changed except the technology. The nuclear club makes it explicit now: the hierarchy isn’t based on justice or democracy or any of that rot. It’s based on who can subjugate whom.

Canada, Venezuela, Ukraine, Greenland—they’re learning what smaller nations have always learned: there’s no international law, no balance of power, no cosmic juice. Just the eternal return of the same old squalor. The powerful do what they can, the weak suffer what they must. Thucydides wrote it down twenty-five centuries ago.

The old monsters hired poets to lie about their motives. Now they just send tweets—or dispatch special envoys to Paris hotels while the actual decisions get made elsewhere.

---

**This caught my eye:**

Longtime Liberal Chrystia Freeland announced she’ll step down as a member of Parliament in the “coming weeks” after accepting an unpaid role advising Ukrainian President Volodymyr Z. “Ukraine is at the forefront of today’s global fight for democracy,” she [wrote](https://x.com/cafreeland/status/2008288057414303956?s=20).

**Global fight for democracy?**

No. Z has spent the last six and a half years driving Ukraine into economic collapse while presiding over the grisly deaths of countless civilians. His recent “Mindichgate” scandal—where leaked recordings revealed his top lieutenants discussing how to embezzle as much as possible—suggests the democracy being fought for looks suspiciously like grand theft auto with better PR.

Freeland’s appointment is a perfect specimen of the genre: another Western politician converting proximity to carnage into post-political cachet. Call it what it is—a photo op in a flak jacket, dressed up as statecraft.

Meanwhile, if you’re an independent journalist in Ukraine, you don’t have an Achilles’ heel—you’re just another smear on the tracks waiting to happen. And when the train’s conductor is Z, derailment starts looking less like sabotage and more like public service.

Anent that, here’s an updated illustration of Thug Life.

## Day 1414

2026-01-07 · Black ice

Emerging from beneath a thick avalanche of shiny black-ice punditry and *L'Unifolié*-waving cockfighting in one's native land, one expects a certain sourness to follow—a hint of hauntedness, a kind of baggage clinging to one's heels. But bliss arrives in unexpected vessels: 120 seconds of tethered Ukrainian drones blowing invading Russian soldiers to smithereens.

The last thing you want during a war is to slip and break your hip. On days like today, traction is everything. Short, shuffling steps with your feet wider apart help with balance, and leaning slightly forward—counterintuitively—keeps you upright better than leaning back. But crampons are better.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fb833f33-4666-4ff7-b198-a57ebb3aee50_1042x695.jpeg)  
*Coalition of the Willing (c/o President’s Office , Paris, January 6, 2026)*

The joker on the far right is ex-convict Charlie Kushner, who in 2005 was sentenced to two years in prison for tax evasion, illegal campaign contributions, and witness tampering—he hired a prostitute to seduce his brother-in-law cooperating with federal investigators, arranged for the encounter to be recorded, and then sent the tape to his sister in an attempt to intimidate them and prevent their testimony against him. Charlie today is US ambassador to France. His as-yet-unconvicted son Jared and Z took part in a press conference following the Paris affair, along with Trump's idiot special envoy Steve Witkoff.

If you make the grave mistake of subjecting yourself to this 50-minute performance, within minutes your vagus nerve will stage a full revolt and your insula will light up, as if your brain’s disgust center is physically trying to reject what your ears are processing. It turns out there are two very different kinds of “coalitions of the willing”: one involves serious nations making legally binding commitments to defend sovereignty with multilateral forces, ceasefire monitoring mechanisms, and intelligence-sharing frameworks; the other involves whatever that was.

**On the difference between ice and ice**

There is the ice we navigate each morning on the downhill route to wherever we must go—treacherous, unforgiving, requiring careful attention and proper equipment. And then there is the ice we encounter in geopolitical theater: the slick surface of opportunism masquerading as diplomacy, the frozen moral landscape where grifters in expensive suits stand beside actual statesmen and pretend the temperature is the same. Our bodies, in their wisdom, recognize the difference before our conscious minds can fully articulate it. The crampons required for the latter do not yet exist, though we suspect a well-aimed tethered drone might serve a similar function. In the meantime, we shuffle forward, lean slightly into the wind, and take grim satisfaction where we can find it.

## Day 1415

2026-01-08 · The dice keep rolling

A thin coat of snow over ice makes running less slippery.

I spent six years in the US military, the last two unvoluntarily. Towards the end of my one and only *overseas* *tour,* Reagan thought it was a great idea to assault Grenada. [Operation Fury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Grenada) it was called. The farcical stunt killed 19 American invaders, at least three in a Blackhawk helicopter crash and others in friendly-fire incidents.

So: helicopters shot up over Caracas, tankers seized in international waters, Russian submarines playing escort, generals reshuffled in Kyiv, peacekeeping forces sketched on napkins in Paris, and Moscow forming divisions it can't properly staff or equip. The craps table's getting crowded, the dice keep rolling, and nobody's figured out yet that the house always wins. It's not entirely outside the arena of the possible that someone will notice before the next Chinook goes down, but I wouldn't bet the farm on it.

## Day 1416 (contd)

2026-01-09 · Welcome to the blockade

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/3c5ce12c-2237-4d5c-aed5-22c29ac3c5fc_1200x679.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o State Emergency Service (January 9, 2026)*

For elderly Kyivites and families with young kids—roughly 3 million souls in a city that once held 3.7 million—this is catastrophe. Ukraine’s population has hemorrhaged to 37-38 million from pre-war estimates of 41-43 million. We’re getting smaller, colder, and darker.

Russia’s gift? Ballistic missiles, IRBMs, including their Oreshnik toy that hit Lviv last night, and Shahed UAVs raining down on our infrastructure. The Kremlin loves its reflexive control campaigns—threaten the West, terrorize Ukrainians, rinse, repeat.

President Z—the one who didn’t warn us about the imminent inevitable invasion, who’s overseen corruption in state financing for energy facility protection and corrupt backoffices across the economy—reports: 242 drones last night, 13 ballistic missiles targeting energy and civilian infrastructure, one Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile, 22 cruise missiles. Four dead in Kyiv alone, including an ambulance worker. Dozens wounded. One residential building hit twice—the second strike landing while emergency services responded to the first. Twenty residential buildings damaged in Kyiv and the region. “The attack came precisely when significant cold weather arrived. Precisely against the ordinary lives of ordinary people.”

A Russian drone also damaged the Qatari Embassy—the very country that mediates with Russia to free Ukrainian POWs and civilians held in Russian prisons. Classy.

Z wants “a clear reaction from the world. First and foremost from the United States, which Russia actually pays attention to.” He’s calling the Energy Staff together for a meeting on restoration timelines, necessary equipment, and responsible parties. Maximum is being done to restore heat and electricity to people. Air defense support for Ukraine remains “a constant priority. Not a single day can be lost in deliveries, production, or agreements.”

Sound familiar? Welcome to Berlin, 1948. The Soviet blockade began June 24, 1948, cutting off all road, rail, and water access to West Berlin’s 2.5 million residents. The U.S. and UK organized a massive airlift—planes landing every few minutes at peak—supplying food and fuel for 15 months (462 days) until September 30, 1949. A defining Cold War moment. A major propaganda victory for the West.

Except this time there’s no airlift coming, just Britain dropping off a dozen air defense systems and two prototype Gravehawks. And even if planes were coming, Ukraine’s airports haven’t functioned since Day 1.

Mayor Klitschko: Half of Kyiv’s apartment buildings—nearly 6,000—are without heat. Water supply interrupted citywide. Utility workers have connected hospitals and maternity wards to mobile boilers. City services operating in emergency mode. The mayor urges residents who can temporarily leave to do so.

They’re draining the heating systems now. Without draining, pipes burst and the system is destroyed. The Kyiv City Military Administration helpfully notes this is “a standard technical measure at sub-zero temperatures and does not mean prolonged absence of heat.” They drain even for outages lasting hours—it’s safety protocol. So, nothing to worry about. Except everything.

Within days, hundreds of thousands won’t be able to stay in their apartments. Zeroing out Putin’s cold terror calculations is doable, but a gigantic pain in the ass.

Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Sybiha announces Z is ready to visit the U.S. next week to discuss security guarantees. If there’s a signal from the American side. The final decision depends on Washington’s position. Nothing says “allied solidarity” like waiting by the phone while your capital freezes.

Weather forecast: Snow through January 11, temperatures -6°C to 1°C. Mid-month “warming” to 7-12°C. Yellow warning for ice.

ISW reports Russia’s forming artillery brigades they can’t staff. The Kremlin rejected Western security guarantees—Zakharova called peacekeepers “legitimate targets.” Russia wants neutrality, demilitarization, puppet government. Their 2022 war aims, unchanged.

I didn’t shave this morning. We live on the 8th floor of a modern building in a swanky district. Doesn’t help.

Berlin held out for 462 days on planes landing every few minutes. We’re on day 1,416.

The difference? Truman, not Trump, was in charge and Berliners knew the world was watching.

## Day 1417

2026-01-10

So, now we have Valerie, “based in Moscow,” [writing from Berlin](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/09/world/europe/putin-russia-ukraine-oreshnik-europe.html), telling us about the latest IRBM adventure in Lviv.

Word on the street is that Drump and Z are penciled in for a tête-à-tête at Davos later this month—because nothing says "resolving existential conflict" like a Swiss mountain resort where champagne costs more than a Javelin missile. Two performers, one stage. Perhaps Val will materialize too, lurking in the background like a ventriloquist's dummy waiting for her cue.

Meanwhile, I’m preparing for my own dramatic production: dawn patrol at [Hryshko Botanical Garden](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Mo89gaDqC4Z61dramatically8) with the [Small Penis Running Club](https://www.strava.com/clubs/1317730) (yes, that’s what we’re calling ourselves—intimidation through radical honesty). We’re blazing trails through the [wolf-inhabited sections](https://www.google.com/maps/@50.4154135,30.5613775,3a,75y,249.35h,77.2t/data=!3m8!1e1!3m6!1sAF1QipO_033isse9cx7j4ym6vYqKeE-ytKOXuIxT9bRb!2e10!3e11!6shttps:%2F%2Flh5.googleusercontent.com%2Fp%2FAF1QipO_033isse9cx7j4ym6vYqKeE-ytKOXuIxT9bRb%3Dw900-h600-k-no-pi-10-ya150-ro-0-fo100!7i10240!8i5120?entry=ttu&g_ep=EgoyMDI1MDEwOC4wIKXMDSoASAFQAw%3D%3D) of the park, because apparently jogging past *Canis lupus* at 7 AM in sub-zero temperatures is my idea of reasonable life choices.

Sunrise isn’t until 8, but we start early—partially for the challenge, mostly because hypothermia waits for no one. If I survive, I’ll consider it a successful morning. ## Day 1421

2026-01-14 · Amplified wearing longjohns

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b962d659-a04a-4c26-9774-6d9d4fd850d5_2560x1755.jpeg)  
*Russian attack on January 13, 2026 (Graphic c/o Strategic Aviation )*

So, yesterday’s attack complicated an already bad situation. CHP-5, the central heating and electricity plant, isn’t pumping out enough heat and electricity to provide for Kyiv districts on the western side (Right Bank) of the Dnipro. This has led to unscheduled emergency blackouts, even for critical infrastructure, closure of supermarkets, suspension of electrified bus/trolley service, et cetera = misery for hundreds of thousands, what we whined about on Day 1416[1](#footnote-1).

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/373471bb-d7d1-442f-b6b5-a55bdf19e146_979x563.png)  
*Freezing our way to victory! (Photo c/o abdymok , made to look colder c/o ai. January 13, 2026)*

And I didn’t even mention the situation on the Left Bank, which is even worse. **The January 9th strikes knocked out power to 70% of Kyiv, with Moscow’s stated aim to “disconnect the city” entirely according to Ukrenergo.** Some neighborhoods on have been without reliable electricity for days now—emergency services have graciously set up warming tents with hot food stations, because apparently we’ve time-traveled back to the siege warfare era. Z calls them “Points of Invincibility”—complete with hot drinks, charging stations, and a warm welcome. Nothing says invincibility quite like huddling in a tent for basic human warmth. **In December, Kyiv residents averaged a delightful 9.5 hours without electricity per day.**

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5ce74bf7-c908-43ab-823c-83429068d0a1_4032x2268.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (January 12, 2026)*

**The timing is exquisite: daytime temperatures have dropped to -12°C, and as low as -19°C at night.** As Peter notes in his [Atlantic Council](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/) piece (presumably written from his own igloo), **the bombing campaign was deliberately timed to coincide with the coldest period in over a year, with temps plummeting to minus fifteen Celsius**[2](#footnote-2)**.** “They deliberately waited for freezing weather to make things worse,” Z observed. Strategic genius, really. People are sleeping in thermal underwear, ski clothes, and multiple layers, huddling together in the same bed like some dystopian camping trip nobody signed up for. Without electricity, there’s no water (pumps don’t work), no cooking (electric stoves), no heat in many buildings. Elevators are dead, trapping elderly residents in their apartments. **Some villages on the outskirts have been without power for four days straight and have blocked roads in protest.**

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/002f9932-3948-4be4-817b-b41451683f1e_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Combined Heat and Power Plant #5 (Photo c/o abdymok , January 12, 2026)*

It’s warmer if you keep moving, but being in perpetual motion burns a lot of calories and people get tired. **Over 700,000 consumers lost power in the past week before it was gradually restored.** The attacks on January 9th were described as “one of the most massive attacks on the capital’s energy infrastructure,” with Deputy Energy Minister Mykola Kolisnyk helpfully noting that **Russia is “going all in” to destroy Ukraine’s power system, launching attacks just five days apart.** The intention is crystal clear—as one resident cheerfully noted, “they’re trying to freeze us.” At least they waited for the cold snap.

**The buzz of generators has become the background noise of winter**—that is, for those lucky enough to afford them. Portable gas stoves are the hot new accessory. Mayor Klitschko has already urged residents who can leave to do so, presumably to less-affected areas where “power and heating are more readily available,” which is a delightfully optimistic way of describing “anywhere else.” Peter notes fears are mounting over a possible winter exodus to neighboring EU countries, which may be exactly what Putin has in mind. **A recent UN probe concluded Moscow’s actions amount to crimes against humanity: “murder and forcible transfer of population.”** But sure, let’s keep calling it a “special military operation.”

The last message as of this writing from [DTEK](https://t.me/dtek_ua/3740), our beloved monopoly energy supplier:

> *“The damage is serious, so emergency blackouts continue throughout Kyiv, as well as in the Brovary and Boryspil districts of the region. ‼️Remember, during emergency blackouts, schedules don’t apply. It’s hard for us and we’re very tired. But the work doesn’t stop for a minute. 629 DTEK crews are working around the clock. Thank you to everyone who supports energy workers in these difficult times. The lights are holding!”*

Well, “holding” is certainly one way to describe it. As building manager Oleksandr Matienko put it with admirable clarity: **“They are trying to kill us.”**

But as another resident told [The Guardian](http://theguardian.com), this just makes us tougher and more determined[3](#footnote-3). War amplifies who you are, and we’ve seen massive volunteering to help neighbors. So here we are, in our longjohns, being amplified.

### Weakness Demands Annexation

*mysteries of an atom / looking into the abyss / seeing all the infinite fun*

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explains that America needs Greenland because Europeans “project weakness.” Not minerals, not Arctic routes—weakness itself demands annexation. We’re the strongest country in the world, which settles matters. The dragon lived over the town for four hundred years, and they gave him maidens without so much as a meow. Good deeds you don’t forget—he boiled the lake once to prevent cholera[2](#footnote-2).

Compare Trump’s Greenland script with Putin’s Ukraine justifications. Same text, different accent, identical grammar: The territory’s been weaponized by hostile forces. Both are historical accidents begging for correction. International law? Cobwebs. What matters is positioning justified by Pechenegs and Vikings. Occupation becomes response, refusal justifies force. Look what you made me do, now with tariffs.

*do you trust yourself, babe? / theory of random walks*

This is peace through strength: so peaceful it threatens military force against Denmark to acquire 57,000 people who’ve made clear they’re not interested.

What’s alarming isn’t one administration. It’s simultaneous emergence in multiple former superpowers. MAGA and the Russian World both dismiss universal values as liberal fairy tales, treat ultra-conservative principles as uniquely legitimate, view alternatives as threats requiring eradication, understand democracy as dictatorship of the clan, worship force itself.

Americans think they’re entering splendid isolation. They’re entering the world before 1945—multiple great powers, metastasizing conflict, no reliable friends. The American order is over not because the United States proved incapable, but because it decided it no longer wishes to. American might that upheld eighty years of order will now destroy it.

*diving into instinct / micro dosing ego death / soon it will be later*

What does Europe do facing hostile powers on eastern and western flanks? If Germany, Britain, France, Poland arm to full capacity—including nuclear weapons—they’ll deter Russia and make an American president think twice. A rearmed Germany without American guarantee will take nationalist views. France is one election from nationalist victory. Imagine rearmed nationalist France facing rearmed nationalist Germany. They fought three major wars in seventy years before the United States established peace.

Japanese rearmament heightens nervousness in South Korea, facing hostile nuclear North Korea and possibly nuclear Japan, which invaded Korea three times.

*& you need to show up babe / even if you feel like a storm*

China and Russia aren’t satiated status quo powers. They’re dissatisfied have-nots seeking to restore regional dominance. Russia’s only in early stages of rebuilding its sphere. Ukraine isn’t the end but the beginning. Xi speaks of “great changes unseen in a century.” For Putin, Trump’s destruction of the transatlantic alliance is such a change. Why shouldn’t he seize it?

The first years won’t be marked by adroit diplomacy but intense confrontation. More like the brutal multipolar early twentieth century than the orderly nineteenth.

*as I feel I’m watching you change / & I know I will do the same*

Bessent believes Europeans will “come around.” Serene confidence of someone who cannot imagine weaker parties might have interests differing from his assessment. The burgomaster kept saying: we’ve learned to understand each other from ancient times here. The entire town shall look at you with dread and rejoice at your downfall.

Trump’s managed in one year to destroy the order and weaken America’s ability to protect interests in what comes next. We built international order because we were strong enough to remember what unchecked strength produces. We’ve forgotten. The monsters wake, stretch, prepare to teach us again. The dragon crippled them exactly as required—souls with no hands, souls with no legs, mute souls, chained souls, dead souls.

*oh it’s another blessed day*

Their training will have to be shattered and reassembled into a destructive version of itself—everything they’ve prepared to do for years applied backwards, against the people they trained to protect.

The dragon crippled them exactly as required: souls with no hands, souls with no legs, mute souls, chained souls, dead souls.

In Kyiv, the “patriotic consensus” exhausts itself. In Europe, capitals grasp that capitulation leads dragons to demand more. The transatlantic alliance transforms into a relationship on the dragon’s terms alone.

What happens when your protector becomes your threat? When mid-level functionaries in shining livery believe their uniforms make them masters? When the Board of Peace seats war criminals?

The dragon thinks he’s simply changing heads—swapping the diplomatic one for the military one, the reasonable face for the howling beast. But each transformation just reveals more of what he already is. The town watches, learns, adapts. Some put on uniforms and shine brass. Others write “L” on walls.

Is the endless still unbound, or are we just different now?

The brass fittings won’t shine themselves.

## Day 1427

2026-01-21 · The sleep of gadgets

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/629651e1-cfcc-4887-8458-24f7215f9041_1536x1024.png)  
*Illustration by abdymok w/ ai (January 21, 2026)*

Running water returned this morning. Heating too. Electricity. I took a long shower—the kind you take when you’re not sure when the next one might be—then made the catastrophic decision to set up a Xiaomi Smart Electric Hot Water Dispenser via Wi-Fi at 5:00 a.m.

The app cheerfully informed me the water was “ready.” What followed was a half cup of triumph, a thoughtful hum, then a dramatic geyser of steam scalding my fingertips. I deleted the app while my hand was still burning.

---

Standing there, fingertips throbbing, I skimmed four texts on my phone with my other hand. In my headphones, [Stewart Brand told Sean Carroll](https://www.preposterousuniverse.com/podcast/2026/01/19/341-stewart-brand-on-maintenance-as-an-organizing-principle/): “There’s way more ways a thing can go wrong than can go right.” The Xiaomi demonstrated this on my skin.

**[Trump’s press conference](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-conference-briefing-room-january-20-2026/)** scrolling past: Nearly two hours of rambling. Mug shots of migrants. Minnesota won three times (lost three times). Greenland. “You’ll find out.” Markets down 800 points. “Markets no longer have a better sense of what’s real and what’s theater.”

Brand: “When the makers of things are paying close attention to the maintainers of those things, all goes well. And if not, not.”

**[Russian strikes on Kyiv](https://understandingwar.org/research/russia-ukraine/russian-offensive-campaign-assessment-january-20-2026/)**: 470 drones, 47 missiles. Minus 18°C. Half the city without power. Chornobyl substations hit—second time in a week. “Minor power outages.” “Zero nuclear threat.” Training missiles with live warheads bolted on. Russia running low on actual stockpiles.

Brand explaining Arab militaries losing wars because they lack NCOs—the sergeants who maintain things, who overlap, who take responsibility. “That is a recipe for losing a war.”

**[Pastukhov’s essay](https://t.me/v_pastukhov/1791)**: The “striking similarity” between MAGA and the Russian World. Trump on Greenland, Putin on Ukraine—identical justifications. Predicate offense. Artificial states. Natural right older than international law. Victim’s stubbornness “provokes” the great power.

Carroll asking about solo sailors. Knox-Johnston improvising repairs. Crowhurst hating maintenance, running out of rum, going mad. “He would reward himself with a drink after completing an unpleasant piece of maintenance. Pretty soon he ran out of rum and wine and then went crazy instead.”

The Xiaomi beeped cheerfully. Still ready. Still confident.

---

Then **[Lavrov’s press conference](https://mid.ru/en/foreign_policy/news/2073858/)** yesterday in Moscow, where he quoted Marco Rubio quoting *The Godfather*: “Women and children can be careless, but not men.” Nuclear powers must maintain dialogue.

Lavrov said Rubio told him in Riyadh that Trump’s foreign policy is “guided by national interests and common sense,” which “implies recognition of the national interests of the United States’ leading partners.” When interests align, pursue them. When they diverge, “it would be a crime to allow such differences to escalate into confrontation.”

“I responded that I fully share this philosophy and logic,” Lavrov said.

This while Russia strikes Chornobyl. While Trump threatens Greenland with military force. While Pastukhov writes about “the simultaneous dominance, in two former superpowers, of ideologies with such an obviously similar nature.”

Lavrov also noted that Trump, “responding to a related question just a few days ago, stated that he has no interest in international law and that norms of behavior in the international arena are determined by his own moral judgment.”

---

5:20 a.m. Fingertips still tender. Four tabs open. Brand still talking about Pete Seeger at 85, watching hippies forget to maintain a Hudson River sloop: “You have to consider that one of the major arcs of civilization is maintenance.”

Systems designed without humility fail in predictable ways. A water dispenser announcing “ready” with aggressive LED confidence while having no idea what it’s doing. A two-hour press conference about Greenland seizures while markets crater. An ideology that treats maintenance—of alliances, of international law, of the distinction between truth and theater—as weakness. As *sailorizing*. Something to get through, reward yourself with a drink after, run out of rum, go crazy.

Brand: “We don’t have a backup. With a global civilization with no backup, does that mean it’s extra fragile or extra robust? I’m pretty sure it’s extra resilient, partly because so many parts are quite different from each other.”

But what if the parts start copying each other’s worst maintenance failures? What if “national interests and common sense” means two nuclear powers simultaneously deciding international law is for women and children?

Pastukhov: “This is too systemic, too deep, to dissolve on its own like a bad midnight dream. Rather, this is precisely the case when the sleep of reason produces monsters.”

The sleep of reason *wearing the mask of reason*. The algorithm. The “philosophy and logic.” The smart device confidently announcing it knows what you need while scalding your hand. Democracy as the dictatorship of one’s clan. Maintenance as something careless people do. Real men just take what they want.

I deleted the app. Turned off the dispenser. Ran my fingers under cold water.

I can’t delete the rest.

But at least the water’s running.

For now.

## Day 1429

2026-01-23 · Groundhog Day must end—starting with Z

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/25050180-30b5-4d84-913d-d93868284a04_1536x1024.png)

As on Day 1, on the Ukrainian jacket, it’s all in your face, famous tongues just a-snakin’ away, badass chains nestled in luxurious chest hair. But on the Russian jacket, lots of bullshit, and all that supermacho chest growth continues to recede.

The fried eggs and wine diet has obviously not worked for Z, and it was a bit rich for him to [lecture European leaders](https://www.president.gov.ua/news/zvernennya-prezidenta-do-uchasnikiv-specialnogo-zasidannya-v-102517) about anything yesterday at Davos.

Z closed his performance by insisting “Groundhog Day must end.” He’s right, but not in the way he thinks.

The real loop isn’t Europe’s—it’s Z’s. Another forum, another speech, another round of lecturing others about failures that mirror his own. Europe lacks courage? Z ignored explicit, detailed warnings and failed to prepare for invasion. Europe can’t act independently? Z admits “no security guarantees work without the United States.” Europe suffers from corrupt leadership? Almost every top official Z appointed—from SBU to Energy to Justice to Border Service—faces embezzlement charges.

The man who couldn’t defend his own coastline offers to patrol Greenland’s waters. The president who presided over strategic autophage—the state literally consuming itself through corruption while fighting for survival—lectures Europe on institutional development. The leader who botched conscription, approved faulty fortifications, and funneled defense contracts to cronies demands others demonstrate competence.

Z wants Europe to seize Russian assets while his officials seized everything not bolted down. He wants Europe to act on Iran while ignoring warnings about his own country. He wants a Special Tribunal for Russian aggression while neutering Ukraine’s anti-corruption prosecutors. He questions whether NATO would defend Lithuania while desperately seeking membership in an alliance he suggests is worthless.

This isn’t analysis—it’s performance art. Z emerged from a sham democracy where legitimacy comes from popular uprisings, not institutional competence, where reality isn’t expressed in rational categories, where sovereignty means theatrical defiance rather than state capacity. He never prepared to govern, never developed policy expertise, never built functional institutions. Why would he start now?

The French historian Ernest Renan said a nation is a daily plebiscite. Ukrainians vote daily by risking their lives. Their heroism is real and profound. But they are poorly led by a man who confuses his presence with governance, his eloquence with strategy, his moral clarity with institutional development.

Churchill understood the difference between sovereignty and subjectiveness. Z cosplays Churchill while exemplifying the opposite: not fortitude sending eloquence into battle, but eloquence substituting for strategy.

Europe has real failures—frozen assets, phantom tribunals, inadequate defense spending. But lectures from a leader whose top lieutenants loot during wartime, whose military interference costs lives, whose pre-war incompetence enabled catastrophe? That’s not critique. That’s projection from the stage of a primitive post-Soviet feudal autocracy.

Groundhog Day must indeed end. Perhaps Z could start by looking in the mirror—assuming he’d recognize what he sees after years of performing someone else.

**Slava Ukraini**—to the people paying the price for this magnificent resistance to reason.

## Day 1430

2026-01-24 · Unmentioned urbicide

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/ef98026e-81a4-45ff-9be8-946fe5e4c723_1280x931.jpeg)

*International Law’s Greatest Hits* Jan 24, 2026

Systematic destruction of urban environments without genuine military necessity - urbicide - is not allowed under international law. The legal prohibition exists through the [Hague Convention](https://www.unesco.org/en/legal-affairs/convention-protection-cultural-property-event-armed-conflict-regulations-execution-convention) protecting cultural property, the [Geneva Conventions](https://www.icrc.org/en/war-and-law/treaties-customary-law/geneva-conventions) prohibiting attacks on civilian objects, and the [Rome Statute](https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/2024-05/Rome-Statute-eng.pdf) criminalizing such destruction as war crimes. The [Helsinki Final Act](https://www.osce.org/files/f/documents/5/c/39501.pdf) provides additional philosophical grounding for protecting urban heritage.

Yet the post-WWII international legal order - designed to prevent exactly these atrocities - has proven powerless when permanent Security Council members like Russia choose to violate it.

Which brings us to tonight.

Russia launched 396 aerial weapons at Ukraine - 2 Zircon anti-ship missiles, 12 Kh-22/Kh-32 cruise missiles, 6 Iskander-M/S-300 ballistic missiles, 1 Kh-59/69 guided aviation missile, and 375 attack drones. The main target was Kyiv, with strategic aviation deploying Kh-22/Kh-32 missiles against the capital.

Between 1:47 a.m. and 3:59 a.m., as peace talks were underway in Abu Dhabi, the attacks rolled through eight districts - Holosiivsky, Desnyansk, Solomiansky, Dniprovsky, Darnytsky. Two missiles and 18 drones struck 17 locations. Debris from intercepted drones hit 12 more. Office buildings struck, residential windows blown out, garages and a fuel truck set ablaze, a private medical clinic damaged.

I documented some of the strikes from my building, located in the middle of Kyiv’s mystic triangle, shuffling back and forth from under the covers of my bed down the dark hallway to the balcony. A view of the fireworks. I marveled at the precisionless destruction - the randomness of what gets hit, what doesn’t, who lives, who dies. I can’t publish the pictures. The images might be incorporated into Team Russia’s dataset to target future strikes. Even documentation becomes weaponizable intelligence.

One person killed, at least four injured and hospitalized in Kyiv. In Kharkiv, a maternity ward, a dormitory housing internally displaced persons, and a medical college were hit - 19 people wounded, including a child. Energy infrastructure destroyed again, leaving 1,200 apartment buildings without heat and entire neighborhoods without water in freezing temperatures.

The documents say this should never happen. But it does, and it keeps happening.

Z’s [Telegram response](https://t.me/V_Zelenskiy_official/12642) was characteristically data-driven: “Russia massively attacked our regions overnight - launching over 370 strike drones and 21 missiles of various types... In the capital and region, the main target for the Russians was energy infrastructure. Unfortunately, this attack took one person’s life. My condolences to relatives and loved ones.”

He thanked rescue workers, medics, utilities, and air defense forces, then pivoted: “We count on the reaction and assistance of all our partners. Every Patriot, NASAMS missile helps protect critical infrastructure and helps people get through the cold winter. We must definitely implement everything agreed upon with President Trump in Davos regarding air defense.”

This is Ukraine’s data-point commander-in-chief - the man who presided over back-office corruption in the very ministries tasked with protecting the population, who failed to prepare for Russia’s invasion despite explicit warnings, now reducing civilian casualties to talking points about partner assistance and Davos agreements. One person killed becomes a segue to weapons deliveries. Nineteen wounded in Kharkiv becomes leverage for Trump negotiations.

**Meanwhile, at Davos**

The word “urbicide” appeared nowhere. Neither did “war crimes.” Neither did “Geneva Conventions.”

Instead, Davos offered visions of AI “rehumanizing work,” land deals, and investment opportunities. [Palantir’s Louis Mosley](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VLLm9vFIdWo) waxed philosophical about how artificial intelligence would allow us to “refine meaning in what we do professionally.” Washington Post columnist [David Ignatius](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VLLm9vFIdWo) nodded approvingly.

[Mosley recounted](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VLLm9vFIdWo) how it all began: in May 2022, barely ten weeks after the invasion, Z invited Palantir’s CEO to Kyiv and made “a very compelling offer.” The “very charismatic” Z painted a picture of Ukraine becoming “the Israel of Europe” - surrounded by enemies, locked in “a long generational struggle,” dependent on military technology partnerships with industrial partners like Palantir.

In exchange for Palantir’s software, Z offered access to Ukraine’s “very very talented bench of engineering” - young men and women in uniform who could “build on our software and begin to wield it in ways that perhaps our other military customers around the world had not.”

Mosley gushed that they encountered engineers Palantir would be “thrilled to hire” working with “an ethic that can only come from an existential situation” where “building a new feature might make the difference between saving a friend’s life.” What began as a “philanthropic endeavor” quickly became a business relationship built on Ukraine’s desperation and “extraordinary data asset.”

Puhleaze.

Fast forward to Davos 2026, and [Z used his platform](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mQdmb7fxz-E) not to confront this grotesque circus with the reality of what his country faces, but to lecture Europe about its failures - as if the man who ignored explicit warnings, presided over strategic autophagé where officials looted during wartime, and botched defense preparations has earned the moral authority to scold others.

He closed by insisting “Groundhog Day must end,” apparently unaware that the real loop is his own: another forum, another speech, another performance substituting eloquence for strategy while his people freeze in warming centers.

Meanwhile, [Palantir CEO Alex Karp sat down with BlackRock CEO Larry Fink](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aWCrw2wa3ls) for a cozy chat about how AI “will destroy humanities jobs” but create exciting opportunities for “vocational technicians” - people who “went to high school” and can now manage complex military systems. Karp praised his company’s Ukraine operations, claiming that “advanced algorithmic warfare systems” are equivalent to “tactical nuclear weapons.”

**The Data Asset**

As [Mosley celebrated](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VLLm9vFIdWo) Ukraine’s “extraordinary data asset” - “thousands, tens of thousands, even millions of hours of footage from drones” that is “completely unique in the world” - and Z delivered his latest theatrical critique of European resolve, the missiles kept falling on Kyiv.

The 1,200 apartment buildings without heat became a data point. The people who died became training sets. The wounded child in Kharkiv became a talking point for Patriot deliveries. The systematic destruction of a nation became a business opportunity and a stage for moral posturing.

**The Demographic Catastrophe**

Beyond the immediate violence lies something worse. In 2025, deaths in Ukraine exceeded births by 2.9 times - 485,300 deaths against only 168,780 births. In the worst-hit regions like Donetsk and Kherson oblasts, deaths outnumber births by over 11 to 1.

Ukraine’s population has collapsed from 48.5 million in 2001 to an estimated 35.8 million in mid-2024, with projections suggesting it could fall to 25.2 million by 2051.

This echoes the demographic hemorrhaging of early 20th century Ireland, when waves of emigration drained the country of its people. Like Ireland then, Ukraine faces not just immediate violence but the systematic destruction of its future - a people scattered across continents, their homeland deliberately made unlivable through the targeting of the very infrastructure that sustains life in winter.

**The Documents**

The international legal instruments designed to prevent exactly this - the Hague Convention, the Geneva Conventions, the Rome Statute, the Helsinki Final Act - gathered dust as reminders that law only matters when the powerful choose to enforce it.

For more about what that means:

- [Hague Convention](https://www.unesco.org/en/legal-affairs/convention-protection-cultural-property-event-armed-conflict-regulations-execution-convention)
- [Geneva Conventions](https://www.icrc.org/en/war-and-law/treaties-customary-law/geneva-conventions)
- [Rome Statute](https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/2024-05/Rome-Statute-eng.pdf)
- [Helsinki Final Act](https://www.osce.org/files/f/documents/5/c/39501.pdf)
- [Ministry of Justice of Ukraine - Statistical Information](https://minjust.gov.ua/actual-info/stat_info)

Which brings us back to Davos. It’s a grotesque circus where the systematic destruction of cities becomes an “attractive investment opportunity,” where war crimes become “data assets,” and where the word “urbicide” is never mentioned at all.

## Day 1433

2026-01-27 · The big melt

Depending on the robustness of your cardiovascular system, Kyiv is practically balmy this week—despite foreign media solemnly informing the world that we are all freezing to death[1](#footnote-1)[2](#footnote-2)[3](#footnote-3). The city sits on the ragged edge of the great purplish low-pressure blob smothering European Russia, which means temperatures may flirt with 0°C today and tomorrow.

The ground hasn’t gotten the memo. Pavements and streets remain brutally cold, so every bout of half-rain, half-snow mist instantly flash-freezes into a delicate, treacherous glaze. Uncleared sidewalks are coated in a good half-inch of it, growing slicker by the minute as everything turns to slush. Lots of people walking around with broken arms after slipping.

Janine’s article for [The Guardian](http://theguardian.com) uses the same pic as Viktor Yuschcenko’s [Instagram post](https://www.instagram.com/p/DT9u_FLDB7h/). The comparison between Troieshchyna and Sarajevo is inapt. The siege began in April 1992 and caught the city unprepared. Ukraine had the entire 2022-2023 winter as a preview, then 2023-2024, then all of 2024 and 2025 watching Russia methodically target energy infrastructure. The pattern was obvious. The response should have been systematic hardening of the grid, distributed generation capacity, underground facilities, redundancy built into heating systems.

Instead, we get tents pitched in living rooms and bricks heated on gas stoves—the same improvised desperation that characterized Sarajevo’s siege. Except Sarajevo had an excuse: they were caught off-guard. What’s Z’s excuse after three years of this playbook? [Operation Midas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Midas).

Di Giovanni writes that “no statistic can capture what it means to live in a city where winter has been deliberately turned into a tool of terror,” but there’s a statistic that matters enormously: how much money and effort went into preparing for exactly this scenario between 2023 and 2025? Because if the answer is “not nearly enough,” then the Yushchenko-style rhetoric about “altars of freedom” and “light that cannot be extinguished” starts to sound less like defiance and more like unnecessary pathos—a substitute for competent governance.

The heroism is real—the divers in the Dnipro River, Brekht dying at the substation. But heroism shouldn’t be necessary on this scale when the threat was telegraphed years in advance. We want less heroism, more competence.

We’re all about maintenance these days, having realized that the only way to make our Krebs Cycle go forward, is to eat less and run more. In the end, it’s all thermodynamics, as [Nick Lane](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vBiIDwBOqQA) would say. We definitely don't want our Krebs Cycle running in reverse because instead of producing the energy our cells need to function, it begins generating harmful byproducts and consuming resources—essentially working against us rather than for us.

*Cautionary Tale from Odesa*

Look, we’ve all been there. The alarm goes off. You think, “Five more minutes won’t hurt.” But here’s a pro tip: if you’re in a war zone and the alarm is an air raid siren, those five minutes absolutely *will* hurt.

Our sleeping beauty special correspondent, Askold (*Nom de guerre*: The Turtle, for his confabulatory reporting about the Melnychenko recordings[1](#footnote-1)), demonstrating the kind of commitment to unconscious reverie that would impress even the most dedicated teenager, managed to remain unconscious through multiple warnings that explosive death was literally flying toward him. Admirable dedication to rest, truly.

In Ukraine when sirens designed specifically to wake you up before you become part of the debris field start wailing, perhaps consider relocating. Your sleep schedule will recover. Your ceiling, as demonstrated at the [Hotel Alarus](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g295368-d12713777-Reviews-Hotel_Alarus_Luxe-Odesa_Odesa_Oblast.html) at approximately 2:20am, may not.

## Day 1435

2026-01-29 · Endless

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1ee6bc28-f9ee-4920-938b-633cf4bea49c_802x1489.jpeg)

One war, begun in 2014 and massively escalated in 2022, still confounds Marco Rubio, who at the two hours and forty-second minute of his testimony before the [US Senate Foreign Affairs Committee](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OkfwTrcNYsI&t=7187s) yesterday described the situation as “very fluid.”

There is one issue remaining: “The territorial claim on Donetsk,” Rubio said, adding the situation is “so fluid it could change in 72 hours.”

Look, we’ve all experienced fluid situations. Coffee spills. Market volatility. The gelatinous state of Trump’s promises. When someone describes an active genocide as “fluid,” they’re either catastrophically unqualified or practicing a very specific art form called **diplomatic cowardice**.

What’s fluid, apparently, is Trump’s willingness to demand Ukraine withdraw from all of Donetsk region as a precondition for “security guarantees.” [Reuters](http://reuters.com) and [The Financial Times](http://ft.com) confirmed what was an open secret: Trump’s “deal” mirrors Putin’s demands, a framework likely sketched in earlier understanding between the two leaders who understand each other “at half a word.”

*“Round and round and round we go.”*

> There’s a small legal complication. Since 2014, the United States has enacted multiple binding federal laws—the [Support for the Sovereignty, Integrity, Democracy, and Economic Stability of Ukraine Act of 2014](https://www.congress.gov/bill/113th-congress/house-bill/4152) and the [Ukraine Freedom Support Act of 2014](https://www.congress.gov/bill/113th-congress/house-bill/5859)—that explicitly affirm Ukraine’s sovereignty within its internationally recognized borders. U.S. policy recognizing Ukraine’s territorial integrity is embedded in [federal law](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title22-section8921&num=0&edition=prelim). The U.S. executive branch cannot legally recognize Russian claims to occupied Ukrainian territory without violating existing U.S. law.

One might think this matters. But we're watching the fragility of our institutions in real time. Even knowing the playbook of a demagogue doesn't mean we can successfully battle it. The gains we thought were permanent—rule of law, human rights, territorial sovereignty—turn out to be profoundly vulnerable when there are perceptions (real or manufactured) of scarcity, intergroup competition, or predation.

*“When will it end?”*

Rubio said earlier he’s in constant touch with Trump’s special envoys—including his son-in-law and golf partner—tasked with ending what the [Center for Strategic and International Studies](http://csis.org) estimates has killed two million people, mostly Russian soldiers[1](#footnote-1).

Recall that Trump pledged at least 83 times to end the Russia-Ukraine war within 24 hours of returning to the White House. Day 1435 suggests the timeline was optimistic.

*“But I can see no end.”*

Don’t call genocide fluid. Don’t pretend laws don’t matter. Don’t expect 72 hours to change what 1,435 days couldn’t.

*“Round and round and round we go / When will it end?”*

Stay un-gaslit. Stay furious. Watch out for falling icicles!

## Day 1436

I woke up very early this Friday and accidentally bumped into a [Washington Post](http://washingtonpost.com/world/2026/01/29/ukraine-russia-trump-zelensky-negotiations/?itid=sr_0_8ee7bf68-4d46-4de7-bd0f-969fa8686bec) article co-authored by David Stern, who in January 2017 wrote for [Politico](https://www.politico.com/story/2017/01/ukraine-sabotage-trump-backfire-233446) that Ukraine tried to “sabotage Trump” and that Poroshenko “actively worked for Secretary Clinton”—conspiracy theories that fueled Trump’s worldview for years[1](#footnote-1).

Now David writes:

> “Trump remarked Thursday that he had personally asked Russian President Vladimir Putin ‘not to fire into Kyiv and the various towns for a week, and he agreed to do that.’ Z responded to Trump’s comments on social media, thanking him.”

My immediate thought: Words have no meaning, only uses[2](#footnote-2). The same article describes “an insurgency in eastern Ukraine” in early 2014. You don’t have to be best buddies with [Evhen “Marshall” Zhukov](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%96%D1%83%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B2,_%D0%95%D0%B2%D0%B3%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%90%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B4%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87_(%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%B4%D0%B5%D1%8F%D1%82%D0%B5%D0%BB%D1%8C)) to know: there was no insurgency. It was a Russian invasion.

I next switched on the light and checked if the inner tube I patched last night for Bad Boy was still holding air. Yes. Success.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4fc4a81d-1bb9-478f-9e7e-ca45f86a4eda_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (January 30, 2026)*

---

**Which Stance Are They Taking Now?**

My favorite professional philosopher Daniel Dennett argued we adopt different “stances” to understand systems. The physical stance uses laws of nature. The design stance assumes functional purpose. The intentional stance treats systems as rational agents with beliefs and desires.

The intentional stance asks: What does this agent want? What does it believe? What will it rationally do next?

In evolutionary biology, there’s a parallel debate. Does life converge on similar solutions—eyes in arthropods, vertebrates, cephalopods—suggesting law-like patterns? Or is history radically contingent, dependent on accidents that could easily have gone differently? Stephen Jay Gould, Dennett’s co-panelist in [Wim Kayser](https://www.librarything.com/author/kayzerwim)’s 1993 documentary “[A Glorious Accident](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RVrnn7QW6Jg),” argued for contingency. Rewind the tape, let it play again, you get something completely different.

On Day 1436 of Russia’s war against Ukraine, observers are taking their stances.

Western diplomats adopt the design stance. They see a negotiation designed to produce equilibrium. Rubio calls the situation “very fluid.” Trump asks Putin not to bomb us for one week. The design assumes: enough pressure → enough incentives → deal.

Some Russian emigré aspiring philosophers adopt a version of the physical stance. They observe historical patterns—Europe’s weakness, Russia’s survival wars, the spirit of Anchorage—and predict outcomes as if they follow physical laws. Europe has no agency. Ukraine will fold. The final episode was written before it began.

Both are treating us as systems to be predicted, not agents with beliefs, desires, and the capacity to intervene.

But here’s what Judea Pearl understood about causality that these observers don’t: Observation is not intervention[3](#footnote-3).

You can observe that negotiations correlate with reduced bombing. You can observe European statements correlating with inaction. You can observe historical patterns. But correlation isn’t causation. The intentional stance matters precisely when agents decide to do something different.

Almost thirteen years ago this February, hours before the massacre, politicians and diplomats agreed to a truce. The design stance predicted: negotiation → agreement → stability. The physical stance might have predicted: people disperse, regime consolidates.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/cb2732c9-be7a-4e5a-8810-f36de02ffe80_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok c/o ai (February 21, 2014)*

But the people on Independence Square took the intentional stance toward themselves. They had beliefs about dignity. Desires for sovereignty. And they decided—rationally, given those beliefs and desires—to refuse the deal opposition leaders had just accepted.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/38b358e8-2296-440f-825c-dfb7c97f27de_800x1200.jpeg)  
*Ibidem*

There are many photos I took on the square at the exact moment this was happening[4](#footnote-4). I tried using AI to enhance some of them—to clarify what was actually visible through the fog of borrowed lenses and burning tires. ChatGPT refused: “We’re so sorry, but the image we created may violate our guardrails around violence.”

The AI won’t enhance the images because they show violence. But these *are* the images. This is what intervention looks like when you stop being observed and start acting. The guardrails aren’t there to protect us—they’re there to protect observers from having to see clearly what they’re watching.

The tape rewound itself that morning. Not because of physical laws or functional design, but because agents intervened—kids in helmets carrying hatchets, hunting rifles manning homemade mortars. And people taking their pictures.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a2c40010-16e4-4043-95ff-24d9c5f7e2fa_1536x1024.png)  
*Ibidem*

The algorithm hates gushing blood. It won’t clarify violence even when clarification is precisely what’s needed. It’s the perfect metaphor for how David, emigré fatalists and Trump’s negotiators approach Ukraine: observe from a safe distance, refuse to see clearly, impose guardrails that prevent understanding.

This is what they miss from their comfortable observation posts. They weren’t there then. They’ve adopted a stance that denies agency—theirs, ours, everyone’s. Europe has no “subjectivity” (their word). Ukraine lacks “internal guarantees” beyond the will to fight. Russia always wins survival wars. It’s all so predictable when you refuse to take the intentional stance toward the people you’re observing.

The irony: they’re right that Ukraine’s security depends on Ukrainians’ willingness to fight. They’re just wrong about what follows. It doesn’t mean inevitable defeat observed from afar. It means we’re the agents. We hold the beliefs. We have the desires. We make the decisions.

In “A Glorious Accident,” the final episode asked: “We wonder, ever wonder why we found us here?” Gould’s answer was contingency—a glorious accident of history. Dennett’s was the intentional stance—we’re here because we’re rational agents pursuing goals.

On Day 1436, we know why we’re here. Not as variables in someone else’s equation. Not as systems following physical laws or functional designs. But as agents who refuse the stances others are taking toward us.

Trump’s one-week “pause” isn’t convergence. Europe’s weakness isn’t physical law. Russia’s patterns aren’t destiny. These are observations from stances that deny our agency.

David still thinks there was an insurgency in eastern Ukraine. The AI won’t enhance images of violence. Russian emigré intellectuals won’t acknowledge Ukrainian agency. The diplomats won’t see intervention as different from observation.

The protesters on Independence Square understood this in 2014. They rejected being observed and chose to intervene.

We’re not taking your stance. We’re taking ours.

Have a great weekend!

Ladder of Causality

- Association (observation) - Seeing/observing correlations: P(Y|X) - “What if I *see* X?”
- Intervention - Actively doing something: P(Y|do(X)) - “What if I *do* X?”
- Counterfactuals - What would have happened: “What if I *had done* X instead?”

## Day 1441

2026-02-03 · Water from corpses

A woman will respond to her boyfriend’s anecdote about combined air attacks with unexpected fury, yelling that no, it’s not ‘amazing,’ it’s not even remotely ‘significant,’ and that no, it’s not ‘ironic’—it’s ‘inevitable.’ The distinction matters when you’re freezing to death.

For reasons that should have been glaringly obvious four years ago, we remain touchingly optimistic about Z and Trump, both of whom continue to believe that talking with Putin is the best prophylactic against gruesome death. Evidence to the contrary accumulates hourly, but why let reality spoil a good diplomatic photo-op?

## Day 1443

2026-02-04 · How the Cold Was Made: A Kyiv Resident’s Guide to the Arctic Squid Game

Simon Shuster’s *Atlantic* piece opens with Kyiv freezing and closes with inevitability[1](#footnote-1). Putin is relentless, winter is weaponized, Ukrainians endure. It’s polished, moving—and useless. If you’re walking on ice blocks because the mayor clears streets while presidentially-appointed district heads ignore sidewalks, you don’t need atmosphere. You need to know why the system guaranteeing your misery was designed exactly this way.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/87c5f21b-b2f0-474f-a30d-4c815868486b_2801x3513.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (February 4, 2026)*

This is the dogfooding loop Kyiv perfected: municipal workers reinstall bicycle barriers monthly while infrastructure decays. Activity signals competence; repetition guarantees contracts. Nothing improves because improvement ends the game.

Scale that to your apartment building. Darnytsia district contracted insulation for 119 buildings at UAH 254 million in 2025. Investigators found 20% price inflation—UAH 46 million siphoned. Inflate contracts, pocket margins, leave you freezing, repeat. You’re not cold because Putin is relentless. You’re cold because someone made 46 million while you waited for insulation[2](#footnote-2).

The energy sector runs bigger numbers. Operation Midas audio from September 2025 captured participants discussing kickbacks on protective structures for facilities Russia would destroy months later. $100 million gone while Russia prepared winter strikes. Investigation went public November 2025. Shuster filed February 2026. He mentions none of this.

Instead meet Maksym Bakhmatov, Darnytsia head, described as “former TV producer” from “the same comedy circuit as Z.” Omitted: Z’s Presidential Office appointed him May 2024. District heads serve presidential pleasure, not voters. When Bakhmatov admits “zero generators, zero food,” he’s describing his own chain of command’s performance. You got a comedian managing quarter-million people through winter war. Athletic prowess, comedic timing—essential qualifications for heating infrastructure, apparently.

Desniansky district relies on one thermal power plant. Fourth winter of war. Everyone knew Russia targets energy infrastructure. Instead of redundancy: CHP-6 and hope. Instead of protective structures: kickback negotiations. Instead of experienced administrators: loyalty appointments managing your frozen pipes.

Here’s your Squid Game: the elected mayor clears streets, Z’s appointed district heads clear sidewalks. Coordination fails, you walk on ice, nobody’s accountable because authority splits between democratic and appointed structures. When gaps freeze over literally, officials shrug. System works perfectly assuming the point was never heat but contract flow.

Key Operation Midas player: Timur Mindich, Kvartal 95 co-owner, Z’s close friend. Audio recordings caught him (call sign: “Karlsson”) discussing percentages with Energy Minister Halushchenko (”Professor”)—debating whether 10% or 15% was appropriate for protective structure contracts while Russia positioned for winter offensive. Infrastructure protection funds became commission structures.

You freeze, they debate margins[3](#footnote-3).

War explains the missile. It doesn’t explain why hardening funds became repair contracts, why protective structures weren’t built, why redundancy never materialized, why accountability froze before pipes did. None of this appears in Shuster, [NBC’s Kyiv coverage](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/ukraine/kyiv-freezing-dark-russian-strikes-leave-ukraines-capital-powerless-rcna254359), [Tim Mak’s humane reporting](https://www.counteroffensive.news/p/how-ukraines-homeless-are-faring), or Euronews’ [empathy quiz](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/02/02/watch-the-video-kyiv-is-freezing-would-you-survive-in-20c-without-heating) asking viewers whether they could survive −20°C without heating—governance failure repackaged as resilience porn.

You don’t need proof winter is cruel or civilians resilient. You need journalists explaining how known risks went unmitigated, how money moved, how appointments were made, why failure wasn’t just predictable but profitable.

Freezing isn’t fate.

Running water, electricity and heat at the apartment again this morning. I played around with the Xaomi hot water pump on Wi-Fi and listened to a podcast with Anne and Preet, titled *America is in Rupture Under Trump*[2](#footnote-2)**.**

Near the end, Anne said she has “a lot of sympathy with the people of the 1990s, because they had experiences that led them to believe that economic ties would lead to better political ties, and they thought that if you connected the world economically you would have a more peaceful world because no one would want to go to war with their trading partners… That was kind of the dominant theory of the 1990s”—globalization as a pathway to democracy.

She’s right to defend that generation’s reasoning, even if the outcome disappointed. The premise wasn’t naive: interdependence *does* raise the cost of conflict. What failed wasn’t the theory but the execution—the refusal to enforce conditionality, the tolerance for kleptocracy dressed as market reform, the unwillingness to defend the rules that made openness possible.

Now an American president has finished what autocrats started. Anne apologizes—as an American?—for the economic chaos Trump has unleashed on Europe and the world. But the damage isn’t just economic uncertainty. Trump has **obliterated** the foundational principles of the postwar order: Most Favoured Nation status, the rules-based trading system, international economic law, the very idea that agreements matter. What took eighty years to build—imperfectly, yes, but deliberately—has been gutted in eight years of contempt for institutions, allies, and the notion that open societies require defense, not just declaration.

The 1990s generation believed connectivity would make war costly. They were right. What they underestimated was how profitable dismantling that connectivity could be—for strongmen, for opportunists, for anyone who confused the *benefits* of the open system with permission to loot it. Trump didn’t inherit a failed experiment. He **destroyed a functioning one**, and what comes next won’t be a more peaceful multipolar world. It will be a return to the logic of blocs, spheres, and the kind of transactional brutality that globalization was supposed to make obsolete.

The principles of open society haven’t failed. They’ve been **abandoned**—by those who benefited most from them.

## Day 1447

2026-02-09 · Nine Megawatts of Victory

So Kyiv celebrated yesterday. Prime Minister Shmyhal convened the Emergency Situation Headquarters for Energy and [announced](https://t.me/Denys_Smyhal/12279) the capital would receive an *extra* nine megawatts of power.

Nine.

At current wholesale rates, we’re talking about €765 per hour. For a capital city of three million people.

But wait, there’s more: Ukraine has also received 27,000 tons of humanitarian aid since the invasion began. Of which 25,100 tons has already been distributed to the regions. In just the last two weeks, 17 humanitarian shipments arrived from 11 partners. Including 774 generators. And 40 units of modular boiler rooms, cogeneration plants, boilers, and other equipment.

Victory these days looks like press releases itemizing donated generators while announcing additional electrical capacity worth less than a Tesla Model 3 per hour.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/116ebccc-2590-40b6-9bd1-32a50fc08aed_750x1244.png)  
*Sunday’s electricity schedule (February 8, 2026)*

---

**On Social Cohesion**

What happens when the people in charge of defending the motherland are too busy dividing kickbacks “by three” to actually defend anything? Frostbite. You get a society that needs both external enemies *and* internal enforcers to remain intact.

---

**On Corruption as Strategy**

Those nine megawatts arrive courtesy of an energy infrastructure systematically pillaged by the heroic leaders in charge of defending it. The resignations last November of top bureaucrats—caught on tape dividing kickbacks in the Energoatom scandal—came just in time for winter.

The alleged ringleader? Z and his top lieutenants.

Two years ago, Z replaced the commander-in-chief and sacked a bunch of generals. It’s been downhill ever since—though the trajectory was already set by defense procurement and fall-back fortification schemes that treated Russia’s invasion as primarily a business opportunity.

When your energy-turned-justice minister is codenamed “Professor” on wiretaps discussing how to split the take, you’re running a very particular kind of wartime government.

Trump opened the door, Putin walked through it, and Ukraine’s leadership spent the intervening years ensuring the house was already half-looted before the demolition began.

---

**On Narrative as Strategy**

*“Narrative is strategy in story form.”* —Peter Pomerantsev, at 2,600 words. [TLDR](https://archive.ph/5GN8i).

Or so we’re told, at exhaustive length, by someone who has confused word count with insight.

For Ukraine’s most prominent expat champions who have built careers on narrative warfare, acknowledging Ukrainian malfeasance would complicate the story.

Better to write thousands of words about “medium-sized democracies” and “predator states” than to mention Z and his closest associates allegedly running wartime corruption schemes.

Better to theorize about “narrative escalation dominance” than to note that replacing your most competent military commander mid-war for reasons of ego might have strategic consequences.

The problem with treating narrative as strategy: eventually someone has to keep the lights on.

When your actual strategy has been to loot the energy infrastructure while opining about about resilience, you end up celebrating €765 worth of electricity as if it were the Marshall Plan.

---

**On Historical Memory**

There will be a reckoning. The residue left in Europe’s historical memory by the systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure will not wash away.

Sooner or later, a price will have to be paid—either by those responsible or by their children. Perhaps the children will ask their fathers: what was that about back then?

But Ukraine, freezing in the dark, counting its nine megawatts and 774 generators, cannot wait for history’s judgment.

It can only endure the present—a present where Trump’s strength delivered the conditions for civilizational collapse, one demolished power plant at a time, while Z’s inner circle divided the proceeds by three.

---

**On Presidential Messaging**

Z’s Sunday evening address: a masterclass in saying nothing while appearing to say something.

*“Air defense missiles are needed every day.”* That’s what air defense means.

*“The coming weeks will be active in working with our partners. As always, results are needed. There must be results.”* Three sentences to say: we will do things and hope they work.

*“Sunday was almost entirely devoted to restoration in the regions.”* Almost entirely. One wonders what the other portion was devoted to.

Best of all: the statistics. More than 200 heating points in Kyiv! Almost 9,000 people applied! Almost 40,000 heat packages issued!

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/166e63e8-4b88-4274-8029-5011f8f3706d_948x630.jpeg)  
*Heat package*

A capital of three million reduced to celebrating emergency blankets like hurricane relief.

Meanwhile: “Currently the necessary logistics are being maintained everywhere”—this after noting the Russian army has been striking the railway “almost every day this week.”

Logistics maintained everywhere. Almost entirely devoted to restoration. Results are needed. There must be results.

Leadership as word salad, postponing accountability until Monday’s meeting with partners who can be blamed when the results do not materialize.
