## Day 1448

2026-02-10 · Socks for Spring

On my Iphone as I write is a screenshot from [Vatican News](http://vaticannews.va). It shows Pope Leo XIV’s “solidarity amid Ukraine’s freezing winter”—three lorries carrying 80 electricity generators, along with medicine and food supplies, from Rome to Ukraine.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/0de1f6c9-fd3d-4516-a8cc-9ba4ecaed726_1148x802.png)  
*The Pope’s solidarity amid Ukraine’s freezing winter . Pope Leo has arranged for the delivery of 80 electricity generators, along with medicine and food supplies, to Ukraine ( Vatican News , February 10, 2026)*

Eighty generators. For a country of 37 million people. That’s one generator per 462,500 people.

The photograph also shows the Dicastery for the Service of Charity preparing “thousands of antibiotics, anti-inflammatories, antihypertensive medicines and various food supplies” for distribution through parish networks. An outpouring of generosity made possible, Cardinal Krajewski emphasizes—expressing thanks on behalf of the Pope—by “all people of goodwill who continue to support those who suffer.”

People of goodwill sending generators and sleep aids (”melatonin is especially in demand as it helps people sleep amid ongoing fear and constant stress”) while the people responsible for infrastructure send information pamphlets on energy efficiency.

This reminds me of walking around with the chief urologist at a dilapidated state hospital outside Bishkek in the early 1990s. The wards were full of men who had just been operated on for [Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/benign-prostatic-hyperplasia/symptoms-causes/syc-20370087). MSD’s wonder drug [Proscar](https://mozdocs.kiev.ua/likiview.php?id=12539)—which reduces prostate volume, improves urine flow, and can prevent the need for surgery—would have been invaluable to these men. Six months earlier. Before they needed the knife.

But there we were, discussing pharmaceutical donations for post-operative patients. Pills that prevent surgery, arriving after the surgery has already happened.

The Pope responding to appeals from Ukrainian bishops “aware of the suffering caused by the war.” Night-time temperatures falling to minus 25 degrees Celsius. People forced to leave their homes for heated shelters where, thanks to the generators, they can receive a cup of tea.

At least His Holiness acknowledges the actual problem: people need electricity and heat, not tips on how to conserve power.

Though one suspects even he might consider addressing the alleged corruption at Energoatom before blessing another shipment.

Meanwhile, here in Kyiv, winter is over—so Ukraine has decided to dole out heat packages (пакунки тепла) to immiserated citizens.

The kits include warm blankets, plaids, thermal blankets, energy-saving lamps, hygiene products, information materials on energy efficiency.

No, thank you.

Prime Minister Svyrydenko announced that 30,000 people have already received packages “in areas where the situation during frosts was most difficult.” Past tense. The frosts *were* difficult. They happened. We are now distributing comfort items.

President Z, in Monday’s meeting: “It’s important that people from each such building receive all necessary support.” Support. Not heat. Support.

Then: “The heat package program in Kyiv will also be expanded. In the near future, the program will reach a distribution volume of 40,000 such packages to people, with a significant portion specifically in Kyiv.”

Naftogaz, Energoatom, Ukrenergos, Ukrhydroenergo, and Lisy Ukrainy (Forests of Ukraine) have collectively pledged 70,000 additional packages. The initiative has “expanded.”

The heating has not.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/189a8559-9564-426b-a5fd-3ebbaaa8dbcb_2560x1483.webp)  
*Energoatom spends UAH 150 millon on heat packages*

Near future. After the worst has passed. After winter has broken.

This is crisis management calibrated not to the thermometer but to the news cycle. Scale up aid distribution precisely when the emergency is ending, ensuring maximum coverage of government action with minimum pressure to solve the underlying problem.

Absent from the packages: any timeline for heat restoration. Any acknowledgment of the procurement failures, the infrastructure corruption, the systematic looting that left Ukraine’s energy system so vulnerable that Russian strikes could reduce the capital to celebrating blanket distribution.

The packages contain “information materials on energy efficiency.” Tips on staying warm. How to conserve power. Make do with less.

Lady bountifuls of state enterprise, distributing wool socks to the deserving poor. Thermal underwear for pensioners. Candles for the disabled.

All very humane. All very photogenic. All very beside the point.

The point being: [we celebrated an extra nine megawatts yesterday](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1447). Today we’re celebrating thermoses and papal generators. Tomorrow perhaps we’ll celebrate the energy efficiency pamphlets.

Blankets that keep you warm, arriving after winter ends. Pills that prevent surgery, arriving after the operation. Generators for a crisis, arriving as temperatures rise.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/15ee4976-ea17-4925-b4b0-08200470a8b9_1512x999.webp)

But at least the vulnerable categories—properly registered, properly documented, properly grateful—will have a pair of new socks for the spring.

## Day 1449

2026-02-11 · Overnight oats in a blanket

The electricity went off at 0300. The mother of the woman claiming to be [KonMarie](https://konmari.com/?srsltid=AfmBOoqVMqMBXia7zvpDLpuWWF3LgDNYB3aGs7qDE52AQl8HucYS_XSF) wrapped up porridge in a blanket for when I got up at 0500. So yesterday’s oats would at least be warm.

That’s the actual story of Kyiv’s freeze—practical, unglamorous, the kind of detail that doesn’t make it into atmospheric retrospectives about “defiant ingenuity.” But it’s what happens when someone steals from the defense budget and calls it innovation.

After accompanying police on welfare checks in neighborhoods on the left (eastern) bank of the Dnipro. [The New York Times](http://nyt.com) ran a print story about our adventure, with weeks-old video, headlining the suffering of residents freezing in their apartments[1](#footnote-1). The convoy of suffering tableaux was accompanied by a [105-second video](https://www.nytimes.com/video/world/europe/100000010689521/how-ukrainians-are-coping-without-heat.html?searchResultPosition=3) of Andrew — NYT’s bureau chief— saying that he “really has a sense of Kyiv unravelling.”

Meanwhile, Simon dropped dropped his Atlantic [tech-optimism fantasy](https://archive.ph/qwOZx#selection-611.0-617.68) about laser cannons. Both stories arrived precisely on February 10, 2026, when investigation would be awkward and atmosphere would be safe[2](#footnote-2). Access for deference.

What else happened February 10th? US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker—former Iowa toilet-scam lawyer turned Trump loyalist—declared peace in Ukraine "as close as it's ever been." "I think we should continue to pray for peace," Whitaker said, "but at the same time, make sure Ukraine continues to have … all they need to defend themselves."

Whitaker is America's Pavlo Yelizarov, the protagonist in Shuster's fantasy: unqualified, inexperienced, appointed for loyalty not competence, now managing something important. The parallel is perfect. Unfortunately, the journalism covering both the cold snap and Yelizarov's innovations is identically worthless.

##### The Evasion Pattern

Kramer opens with Svitlana Zinovieva watching a Russian missile hit her heating plant. “It was like fireworks. But I knew it would soon be cold.” Beautiful. Haunting. Completely beside the point.

What Kramer doesn’t give you: Wine bottles in tents aren’t defiant ingenuity—they’re evidence someone stole the heating plant protection and building insulation budget.

Instead: outdoor rave, people in penguin suits, Zinovieva crossing fingers while watching her smokestack for steam. The kind of atmospheric drivel that makes editors weep and readers feel informed while learning nothing. Kramer gets his sense of Kyiv “unravelling” without explaining why the unravelling was profitable for specific people with names and bank accounts.

##### The Tech Theater

Shuster transforms Z’s catastrophic decision to put a TV producer in charge of air defense into startup hero story. Pavlo Yelizarov: former political talk show producer, “same comedy circuit as Z,” spearfishing enthusiast. Now he runs Ukraine’s air defenses.

This is the same patronage pattern that put Maksym Bakhmatov (TV producer, Kvartal 95 circuit) in charge of Darnytsia district. Year four of infrastructure war, and critical positions are staffed like a comedy troupe reunion. Loyalty over competence, entertainment connections over expertise, accountability flowing only upward to Presidential Office.

Shuster doesn’t investigate this. He tours drone factories, watches laser demos, learns about 3D-printed interceptors nicknamed “Pisun” (dick). He writes: “Ukrainian technology has caught up faster than expected.” The kind of breathless innovation coverage that reads like a TechCrunch press release crossed with war tourism.

##### The Access Economy

Shuster maintains Kyiv access. The Atlantic wants exclusive interviews, factory tours, commander sit-downs. Z’s Presidential Office controls that access like the velvet rope at [Tootsie Club](https://en.tootsie.kiev.ua/).

The transaction: access for deference. Ask hard questions about Operation Midas, Kvartal 95 cronyism, how UAH billions were mispent? Your factory tour invite gets revoked. Next access request gets slow-walked by the doucherockets in Z’s PR machine who’ve apparently learned media manipulation from watching Fox News Chief Correspondent Trey Yingst balance water bottles on door handles and prepare his mind through cold plunges.

##### What Gets Protected

Both filed February 10th when winter broke. Crisis retrospective arriving precisely when investigation is safe because urgency has passed.

The story isn’t P1-Sun interceptors or penguin-suited ravers.

It’s why TV producers run air defense and district heating during year four of infrastructure war. It’s why no foreign flak will write those sentences. Instead we get piffle.

Kramer gets his sense of Kyiv unravelling. Shuster gets his laser demos. Whitaker gets his prayer-for-peace soundbite.

The winter *was* cold. It is over. It's so warm today I'm wearing sneakers. The oatmeal wrapped in a blanket is room temperature now. And nobody's going to explain why it needed wrapping in the first place.

## Day 1450

2026-02-12 · P→Q,¬P⇏¬Q—and perhaps no story.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a4aa4fb3-b41c-49f1-82c2-cdd0f6d7e0ff_1024x1024.png)  
*Enchanted c/o ai (February 12, 2026)*

In an ideal world, the three journalists who co-authored yesterday’s piece in the *Financial Times* would resign. But we don’t live in an ideal world.

Consider the backdrop to their fantasy: in the early hours of February 12, Russia unleashed one of its largest barrages yet on Ukraine—24 Iskander-M/S-300 ballistic missiles from Bryansk, Voronezh, Rostov, and occupied Crimea; one Kh-59/69 guided missile from Donetsk; and 219 strike drones (around 150 Shaheds) from multiple Russian sites and Crimea, zeroing in on Kyiv, Kharkiv, Dnipro, and Odesa. Ukrainian air defenses downed or jammed 213 targets (15 ballistic missiles, 1 guided missile, 197 drones), but 9 missiles and 19 drones hit 13 locations, with debris at 14 more—amid Abu Dhabi "talks."

The chances that Ukraine will hold presidential elections and a referendum on an as-yet-unagreed peace plan by June 2026 are zero. Not slim. Not vanishingly small. Zero. That anyone anywhere is treating the suggestion with anything other than derisive laughter is a cause for concern. So why file the story[1](#footnote-1)?

Cognitive scientists talk about the “laws of thought” — the principles that govern rational inference. Chief among them: when new evidence arrives, you update your beliefs accordingly. You do not, as George Boole might have put it, simply reproduce the output with the highest prior probability. You do not stenograph what sources feed you and dress it up as analysis. And you are certainly not supposed to let three years in a Moscow bureau calcify your inductive bias to the point where you can no longer tell a peace process from a performance.

Permit us to introduce the FT’s three co-authors, each a distinguished violator of the above.

Henry Foy, the statement sock guy of Moscow correspondence, gained a certain notoriety in July 2019 for a profile of Putin so oleaginous it left grease stains on the reader’s screen. If P is “Putin says he wants a deal” and Q is “Putin wants a deal,” Foy’s career has been a sustained refusal to examine the conditional. Max Seddon is cut from similar cloth — another Moscow alumnus whose priors have, to put it charitably, not been updated since the Kremlin was a more congenial beat. The third, Christopher Miller, is perhaps most remarkable for having been based in Kyiv while for years failing to distinguish a Russian invasion from a separatist uprising аs it happened. Modus ponens, gentlemen: *if* there is a war, *and* you are the war correspondent, *therefore* you report the war. The logic is not difficult.

Together, this trio has produced a piece that injects not even a tiny droplet of political reality into the clear waters of our imagination.

Here is the reality. The Abu Dhabi talks — currently the designated venue for this diplomatic theatre — are not negotiations in any meaningful sense. Russia is there to discuss ending the war on its terms; Ukraine is there to discuss a ceasefire on its terms. The two conversations barely overlap. When negotiators start swapping prisoner lists, it generally means they have run out of anything else to discuss. They have run out of anything else to discuss.

The FT piece presents Z’s election gambit as a serious political pivot — a bold concession to American pressure. It is nothing of the sort. It is an attempt to convert the endgame into a show: proposing a personal meeting with Putin that everyone knows is a non-starter, thereby blocking substantive discussions from happening elsewhere. Whether you read this as clownish or strategically rational depends on your priors. The trouble is, the FT’s priors — shaped by years of Kremlin briefings, Brussels lunch circuits and the peculiar epistemology of the statement sock — are exactly the wrong tool for the job. Like a large language model trained on the wrong corpus, these journalists have become very good at producing fluent, high-probability output that sounds authoritative and explains nothing.

Meanwhile, this weekend Munich plays host to its annual Security Conference — this year more aptly described as the Insecurity Conference, a gathering of the anxious and the bewildered, convening to marvel collectively at the hole where Western strategic coherence used to be. The old order is not coming back, Washington has left its allies very little room for manoeuvre, and every deadline is performative. The dog-and-pony show will feature the usual procession of ministers affirming their commitment to things they are visibly not committed to, flanked by think-tankers who will explain, at considerable length, why everything is very complicated. Somewhere in a side room, someone will brief the FT. If both parties are merely imitating readiness for peace, then a dispatch treating a wartime election timeline as a workable proposition is not journalism. It is Boole without the algebra — the appearance of logical structure with none of the content.

The will to negotiate is the black cat in a dark room — and it isn’t there, on either side. No amount of Munich speechifying or FT sources “familiar with the matter” will conjure it into existence. You cannot reason your way to a conclusion your premises do not support. If P, then Q. But there is no P. Therefore, no Q. Therefore, perhaps, no story.

Perhaps, gentlemen, fewer sources. More thought.

Ukraine@War (February 7–12, 2026) highlights the widening chasm between high-level diplomatic “talk” and the freezing, kinetic reality for three million residents in Kyiv.

##### **The “Good Talks” vs. Kinetic Reality**

The week began and ended with massive Russian air strikes that stood in stark contrast to political rhetoric. On February 7, shortly after President Trump mentioned **“very, very good talks”** between Russia and Ukraine, cruise missiles targeted the **Rivne atomic power station**, aiming to sever Kyiv’s remaining energy supplies. By February 12, despite ongoing talks in **Abu Dhabi**, Russia unleashed one of its largest barrages yet, including **219 strike drones** and **24 ballistic missiles**.

##### **The Infrastructure Crisis & “Nine Megawatts of Victory”**

While leadership celebrated the restoration of **nine megawatts of power**—an amount worth less than a Tesla Model 3 per hour—Kyiv remained crippled by a lack of central heating. The sources suggest this vulnerability is not just due to Russian strikes, but also **systematic corruption** within agencies like Energoatom, where top officials were allegedly caught dividing kickbacks.

The government’s response has been criticized as “crisis management calibrated to the news cycle” rather than the thermometer. This included:

- **The Pope’s Solidarity:** Sending **80 generators** for a country of 37 million.
- **Heat Packages:** Distributing **wool socks, blankets, and energy efficiency pamphlets** to citizens just as the worst of the winter frost began to break.

##### **The Narrative War and Media Critique**

The week also saw a sharp critique of international media coverage. Reports from the *New York Times* and *The Atlantic* were slammed for focusing on **“defiant ingenuity”** and laser-cannon “tech-optimism” while ignoring structural failures. A key point of contention is the **staffing of critical defense roles** with former TV producers and “comedy troupe” associates of the President, such as Pavlo Yelizarov, who now runs air defense.

##### **Diplomatic Illusions**

As the **Munich Security Conference** (dubbed the “Insecurity Conference” by the sources) approached, reports surfaced of a potential **June 2026 election** and peace referendum. However, the sources dismiss these as a “dog-and-pony show,” noting that the **will to negotiate** is a “black cat in a dark room” that simply isn’t there on either side.

## Day 1454

2026-02-16 · Parabiosis of war

Munich, February 14th. Z tells Viktor Orbán he’s growing a belly instead of an army. The room laughs. Orbán responds, calmly, that Ukraine will not be joining the European Union. The comedian lands the joke. The statesman lands the punch.

The next morning, February 15th, NABU — Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau — [detained former Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko at the border](https://censor.net/ua/n3600670). On a train. Trying to leave the country. [NABU’s own Telegram channel](https://t.me/nab_ukraine/3712) was characteristically spare: “Today, while crossing the state border, NABU detectives detained the former Minister of Energy in the Midas case. Primary investigative actions are underway in accordance with legal requirements. Details to follow.” Halushchenko was Z’s appointee. He is a figure in [Operation Midas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Midas), the ongoing investigation into a $100 million kickback scheme at Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear energy operator. On NABU’s audio recordings he appears under the call sign “Professor.” Z had publicly demanded his resignation in November 2025, performing outrage. The Professor remained mobile enough to attempt a border crossing three months later. He did not get the memo about the Munich optics.

This is what happens when you let the stand-up instinct run the foreign policy desk while the back office runs itself. But the Munich moment and the morning-after arrest are symptoms of something the aging science describes with unusual precision.

When researchers connected the circulatory systems of an old mouse and a young mouse — sharing blood between them — the old mouse benefited modestly. The young mouse deteriorated rapidly. The more precise finding: it is not that young blood is powerfully restorative. It is that old blood is actively toxic. The exchange harms the young organism more than it helps the old one.

Putin is the old mouse. Z is the young one. The war is the shared circulatory system. Three years of this exchange have aged Z at double his chronological rate, hollowed out Ukraine’s institutions, exhausted its demographic reserves, and corrupted its procurement apparatus under the pressure of wartime urgency. Putin, meanwhile, has not been meaningfully rejuvenated — his economy battered but holding, his strategic position frozen rather than advanced. The parabiosis is not working for either organism. It is working fastest against the younger one.

---

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/bd05264a-a1a9-4c75-825c-96832c731575_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (February 16, 2026)*

The science of aging — actual science, not the supplement-hawking longevity-industrial complex — describes something called senescent cells. Cells that can no longer divide or regenerate. Cells that don’t die cleanly but instead linger, secreting inflammatory molecules, poisoning the tissue around them, blocking repair. The immune system, when young and functional, clears them efficiently. As the organism ages, the clearance mechanisms degrade. Senescent cells accumulate. Inflammation becomes systemic. The organism declines faster than the external damage alone would explain.

Orbán is a senescent cell with a Twitter account. This is not a controversial observation. He collects EU structural funds while blocking EU aid to Ukraine. He flies to Moscow. He vetoes. He does not regenerate anything. He secretes inflammatory signals — press releases, accusations, strategic ambiguity — and dares the immune system to clear him. The immune system, being the EU, cannot. So he accumulates.

Which is also why Merz’s Munich declaration — that Russia must reach the brink of economic and military collapse before peace is possible — lands as Captain Obvious rather than strategy. Everyone has been repeating this mantra since the invasion began. The question, entering year four of full-scale war, is not whether Russian collapse would end things but how you get there without American participation, without sanctioning India for buying Russian oil, without supplying Taurus missiles, and with China continuing to backstop Moscow’s war economy. Europe has no leverage yet. Merz knows it. So he buys time — using Ukraine as the buffer — while Europe prepares, slowly, to negotiate from something resembling strength. Z understands this too, which is what he actually means when he says Ukraine is holding the European front. The senescent cell and the time-buyer are, in their different ways, running the same play.

Putin is 72 and has been in power for 25 years. The aging literature is clear on what happens to decision-making under those conditions: accumulated cognitive bias, reduced capacity to hold competing facts simultaneously, creative output concentrated in earlier decades. His strategic imagination calcified around 1991. He is running on legacy programming in a threat environment that has completely changed. This is not a metaphor. This is what aging does to brains.

Which makes the Geneva talks this week — US, Russia, Ukrainian delegations — easier to read than the coverage suggests. Appointing Medinsky as Russia’s lead negotiator is not a diplomatic signal. It is a séance: summoning the spirit of the Istanbul/Anchorage framework, the gangster sit-down where Ukraine was divided like a St. Petersburg port — you keep what you grabbed, take two more terminals, leave the rest in the European common fund. Putin’s formula has not changed: he took Crimea and Donbas, wants the process blessed by the right people, and expects Trump to deliver Z and Europe in accordance with what Moscow understands as a gentleman’s agreement reached at the top. In Russian political culture, a tsar’s word is law. That Trump gives his word easily and retracts it just as easily is not read in Moscow as flexibility. It is read as a violation of the code — the same incomprehension Ivan the Terrible expressed toward Elizabeth I when she allowed her merchants to override her commitments. Kremlin patience is running out. Geneva is not a negotiation. It is a debt collection.

These are the people managing a land war in Europe’s largest country.

---

The accelerated aging has a dietary footnote. Z’s own hagiographer, Time correspondent Simon Shuster — the same Shuster who filed the [Atlantic laser cannon puff piece](https://archive.ph/qwOZx) on February 10th — documented in his 2024 book that during the early months of the invasion Z subsisted in the government bunker on tinned food, fried eggs, and wine. This is not a diet. It is a cortisol delivery system with garnish. The aging science is explicit: poor nutrition combined with maximum stress and sleep deprivation hits the mitochondria, accelerates oxidative damage, and degrades the cellular recycling mechanisms central to healthy aging. Shuster meant it as testament to austere dedication. The biology reads it as accelerant.

The less comfortable observation is that the aging literature distinguishes between damage from external assault and damage from internal system failure. The two produce identical symptoms. Ukraine’s parliament: dysfunctional. Constitutional court: dysfunctional. Judiciary: dysfunctional. These are the repair mechanisms. The organism’s capacity for self-correction does not degrade spontaneously — it degrades when the cells nominally responsible for maintenance are doing something else with the resources.

The belly line, in this light, is not a statesman’s joke. It is misdirection. Keep the audience’s eyes on Orbán’s midriff. Don’t let them look at the energy sector accounts — or the train schedules of departing ministers.

Orbán’s response was cold and surgical: *that’s precisely why you can’t become a member of the European Union.* He didn’t defend himself. He didn’t need to. He pivoted to consequences. The comedian got the laugh; the machine politician got the outcome.

There were other tells in Munich. Z referred to “my people” from the podium. Leaders of democracies say “the Ukrainian people” or “our people.” The possessive signals ownership, not stewardship. Dictators say “my people.” Tribal chiefs say “my people.” It is the language Pete Hegseth uses about soldiers and Kristi Noem uses about agents — the possessive of a patron, not a president. It is not a translation artifact. It is a tell.

His [chief PR handler was more explicit](https://www.facebook.com/1plus1.NataliaMoseichuk/posts/pfbid0xH8WkSCREx5k7xgmr8bwafKcq2G2LpiVXTuUYPHD1RmsiXvkxonGXyCgS4dhRwZ3l?locale=uk_UA). On January 22nd, in Ukrainian: *“The First is truly FIRST. We are witnesses to a phenomenon. When he is the Leader of the World. And his tribe holds the world.”* Плем’я — tribe — in the pre-state, anthropological sense. Not citizens. Not compatriots. His tribe. Defined by its relationship to him, existing as an extension of him.

Note what Orbán, for all his 15 years of systematic democratic dismantling in Hungary, does not do. He does not talk about his tribe. He talks about Hungary, Hungarians, the Hungarian nation. The referent, however cynically deployed, remains the people and the state rather than his personal dominion over them. The man Z fat-shamed in Munich has not yet reached the vocabulary of a personality cult. The man doing the fat-shaming has.

---

The aging science also describes what actually works: not the young blood transfusions, not the $2 million-a-year supplement regimes, not the rapamycin evangelism. The answer is unglamorous — moderate diet, exercise, sleep — plus functional repair mechanisms. Institutions that can detect damage and correct it. Quality control that isn’t subordinated to loyalty networks.

The lesson for Ukraine is not that Z should be nicer to Orbán. It is that a state organism with compromised internal repair mechanisms, no matter how heroically it performs under external assault, is running an autocatalytic decline. The damage accelerates because the systems that would fix it have been redirected.

Meanwhile Geneva convenes. Trump is stalling — domestic resistance, European revolt, Z refusing to read the room. Putin is losing patience in the specific way aging autocrats lose patience: not with anger but with a cold, calcified certainty that the terms were agreed and the other party is simply being difficult. The question Moscow is now asking is binary: either Trump delivers on the понятийка — the thieves’ code agreement — and brings Z to heel, or Putin begins dismantling the entire European common fund. Medinsky will channel the spirit of Anchorage. The delegations will exchange prisoner lists. The press will file dispatches about progress.

None of this appears in the foreign press coverage. The [Atlantic files laser cannon tourism](https://archive.ph/qwOZx). The [Financial Times runs a peace process fantasy](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1449?utm_source=publication-search) — elections and a referendum by June 2026, zero chance, treated as serious political pivot — sourced from the same briefing rooms that produced the statement sock school of Moscow correspondence. The [New York Times files atmospheric freeze coverage](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/10/world/europe/ukraine-war-russia-power-cold.html?searchResultPosition=3) — penguin suits, defiant ingenuity, a smokestack watched for steam — without explaining why the heating plant protection budget needed explaining.

The journalists embedded with Z’s Presidential Office are not reporting on Ukraine’s leadership. They are stenographing it. This does their readers a profound disservice: the war enters its thirteenth year overall, its fourth of full-scale invasion, and the people nominally leading Ukraine’s defense are not incidental to the outcome. Incompetent and compromised leadership during an existential war is not background color. It is the story. The Professor’s train was sitting at the border while Munich was still being applauded. Nobody filed that connection. The connections were [legible a year before the Russia’s all-out invasion](https://abdymok.substack.com/publish/post/33067615) to anyone not dependent on Presidential Office briefings — linking Z, Lukashenko, Crimea, and Donbas into a coherent pattern of post-Soviet strongman pathology. The war didn’t create the problem. It just made it more tragic to ignore.

The oatmeal wrapped in a blanket is room temperature now. Nobody’s explaining why it needed wrapping.

## Day 1455

2026-02-17 · The art of the non-deal

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d4d6dba9-7f55-4301-8be9-93444a17345a_3024x4032.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (February 16, 2026)*

*On Napoleon cakes, fitness-studio snipers and a capitulation with custard on top.*

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7fe3b26e-d2bd-43c4-868f-3f42cfaf72b3_912x1080.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (February 17, 2026)*

On Valentine’s Day morning in Kyiv, the mother of a woman known online as KonMari baked two Napoleon cakes. The first, full-sized, was for us. The second — smaller, a gesture of winter warmth toward a guest — was for a young man with nice muscles who was rumored to be a sniper with the Armed Forces of Ukraine, apparently toning those muscles at her downtown fitness studio. It should be noted that she baked both cakes with equal care, because that is the kind of woman she is, and also because a Napoleon cake, if it is worth making at all, is worth making properly, regardless of the recipient’s relationship to the truth.

The extended family had been laughing about this young man for months, and for two reasons, not one. The first: snipers do not spend their Valentine’s Day mornings in downtown Kyiv working on their physique. The second, more fundamental, and this is the kind of thing that separates those who understand war from those who merely discuss it at fitness studios: an actual Ukrainian army sniper would never, under any circumstances, tell a fitness instructor that he is a Ukrainian army sniper. If the young man with the nice muscles had somehow learned that people were calling him a sniper, he would have switched fitness studios immediately or killed the rumor on the spot — because in this war, operational security is not a bureaucratic courtesy but the precise distance between a man and his grave. The fact that the rumor circulated freely, warmly, cheerfully, all the way to a Valentine’s Day Napoleon cake, tells you everything about its relationship to reality. The family’s actual breadwinner — an officer who has been fighting on the zero line in eastern Ukraine since early 2022 — has never discussed what he does with anyone at a fitness studio. He did not receive a Napoleon cake, or a Valentine’s Day card, or indeed any of the pleasant accessories of a Kyiv winter Sunday. He received the zero line, which is its own kind of education.

This small domestic scene — the two cakes, the young man with the muscles, the officer who is elsewhere — contains, if one looks at it carefully and without sentimentality, everything that is wrong with how this war is being discussed, managed, and now supposedly ended.

✦

Standing beside Viktor Orbán in Budapest — and one must pause here to appreciate the choice of companion, a man whose relationship to Ukrainian sovereignty resembles the young man’s relationship to military service — Secretary [Rubio framed American abdication as American leadership](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/02/secretary-of-state-marco-rubioand-hungarian-prime-minister-viktor-orban-at-a-joint-press-availability).

> *“We’re the only nation on Earth that apparently can get both sides to the table to talk,” he declared, with the quiet satisfaction of a man who has confused the act of pushing someone toward a door with the act of opening it.*

The United States did not bring Russia to the table. It handed Russia the table, expressed admiration for the craftsmanship, and walked away from ours.

Trump had promised, more than eighty times on the campaign trail, to end the war in a single day. We are now deep into year four, which suggests either that the promise was somewhat optimistic or that the single day in question has not yet arrived. The [Kiel Institute data](https://www.ifw-kiel.de/topics/war-against-ukraine/ukraine-support-tracker/) is unsparing on the consequences: American withdrawal meant total military aid to Ukraine in 2025 ran 13 percent below the 2022–2024 average. Europe heroically surged 67 percent to compensate, because Europe, whatever its many faults, was paying attention. But the gap could not be fully closed. People died into that gap. Real soldiers, not fitness-studio snipers.

Which brings us to [Trump’s Air Force One remarks](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-gaggle-air-force-one-february-16-2026/), delivered the day after Valentine’s Day with the breezy authority of a man who has never personally experienced the zero line.

> *“Ukraine better come to the table fast, it’s all I’m telling you,” he said — about the victim, it must be noted, not the aggressor, a distinction that apparently no longer commands the attention it once did in Washington.*

Meanwhile [Rubio expressed bewilderment](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/02/secretary-of-state-marco-rubioand-hungarian-prime-minister-viktor-orban-at-a-joint-press-availability) that anyone would “criticize a President trying to end a war,” as though the criticism were of the goal rather than the method — as though a doctor who prescribed the wrong medicine to the wrong patient deserved applause simply for having entered the room. The criticism is of the method: cut support to the victim, legitimize the aggressor’s territorial gains, conduct the diplomacy from the capital of NATO’s most enthusiastic Kremlin apologist, and present the resulting document as a peace agreement.

Some European analysts, surveying this situation with the philosophical detachment available only to those not currently living in Kyiv, counsel patience. Outlast Trump, they suggest, the way one outlasts a pandemic — wait for immunity to develop, return to normal, open the bars again, order the pumpkin latte. It is a tempting prescription, and it has the considerable advantage of requiring nothing. But the old normal, one suspects, is not waiting. The retreat from Atlantic solidarity may be less Trump’s personal eccentricity than a genuine shift in American mass consciousness — a shift that subsequent administrations may soften, as a good custard softens a brittle pastry layer, but cannot reverse. On this diagnosis, the analysts are probably correct. On the therapy — patience, watchful waiting, the strategic doing of nothing — they are as mistaken as a doctor who charges sixty sheep per day while sleeping under a walnut tree.

✦

The Napoleon cake, by the way, tastes better on day two. The cream penetrates the layers overnight, softening what was brittle into something that holds together under its own weight. It is patient work, but the patience must be preceded by the work — someone must have rolled the layers thin, baked them one by one, prepared the custard, assembled the whole careful edifice. It does not improve on its own simply by being left alone.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2c6f8294-e7e7-4c5a-9fe4-12c6fef920c9_3024x4032.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (February 14, 2026)*

There were two cakes on Valentine’s Day morning. One for us — full-sized, the real thing, made with butter and time and the knowledge that it would be eaten by people who would appreciate it. One smaller one for the young man who was rumored to be a sniper and who, if he ever heard that rumor, certainly took no steps to discourage it. [Witkoff and Kushner flew to Geneva](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-gaggle-air-force-one-february-16-2026/) the following day, carrying terms that nobody on the zero line had been consulted about, which is perhaps appropriate, since the zero line is not currently accessible by private jet. And in a Carmelite monastery in Budapest, [Rubio assured Orbán](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/02/secretary-of-state-marco-rubioand-hungarian-prime-minister-viktor-orban-at-a-joint-press-availability) that this — all of this — is what ending a war looks like.

*It is a capitulation with custard on top. One cake for those doing the fighting. A smaller, more decorative one for those who merely claim to — and who, if they ever suspected people had noticed the difference, would have long since found somewhere else to be.*

---

**Letters to the Editor** *Foreign Affairs*

**The Border They Cannot See**

Slezkine and Shifrinson have written [a careful article](https://archive.ph/dlzn1) about a country that does not exist.

Their argument is internally coherent. De jure recognition of Russia’s territorial gains would clarify tripwires, attract investment, ease EU accession, and reduce escalation risk. The logic is sound. The premise is not.

The premise is Ukraine as rational unitary actor — a government capable of correctly assessing strategic tradeoffs, negotiating binding commitments, and administering a credible postwar state behind a newly recognised line. This Ukraine appears regularly in [Foreign Affairs](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/russia/price-peace-ukraine). It does not appear in Kyiv.

Consider the evidentiary record the authors decline to consult. On January 19, 2022 — thirty-six days before the full-scale invasion, after explicit warnings from the CIA, MI6, and Ukrainian military intelligence had been delivered repeatedly — President Zelenskyy told the nation to plan its Easter celebrations, its May holidays, its spring barbecues. A leader who could not process unambiguous invasion intelligence at thirty-six days’ remove is not a leader who will correctly model the consequences of de jure border recognition or credibly commit to anything Brussels or Moscow requires.

The morning after Zelenskyy’s Munich performance, Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau detained the former Energy Minister at the border. On a train. The formal suspicion notice — including a schematic of the financial architecture — is [publicly available](https://nabu.gov.ua/news/sprava-midas-pidozriuyet-sia-eksministr-energetyky/) and worth reading carefully.

> In February 2021, a fund was registered on Anguilla by members of a criminal organisation operating inside the energy ministry, headed by a professional money launderer from the Seychelles. Shell companies in the Marshall Islands named the minister’s ex-wife and four children as beneficiaries. Over $112 million in cash from criminal activity in the energy sector was laundered through three Swiss banks. The children’s tuition at prestigious Swiss schools was paid from these accounts.

The fund on Anguilla—located approximately 9,000 kilometers from Kyiv—was registered thirteen months *before* the invasion — while the West was already funnelling support premised on Ukraine being a reforming democracy worth defending.

The authors argue that legal certainty over borders would attract the private investment essential for reconstruction. But the uncertainty deterring capital is not primarily about where the eastern border sits. It is about whether the minister overseeing the energy sector your capital would flow into was simultaneously running Marshall Islands shells into Swiss accounts through a man called Rocket. The border is not the variable. The Professor is the variable.

A correct prescription administered to a patient whose institutions have been redirected into loyalty networks does not produce the expected outcome. Slezkine and Shifrinson have identified the right border. They have simply written the wrong country into the treaty.

## Day 1456

2026-02-18 · A view from three windows

[Kim Barker’s dispatch](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/17/world/europe/trump-ukraine-war-civilians.html) in this morning’s *New York Times* informs us, with the careful precision of a coroner’s report, that more Ukrainian civilians were killed in 2025 than in any year since the full-scale invasion began, that Russia sent five times as many drones at civilian targets as the year before, and that a café in Kyiv which had briefly called itself Trump Pizza Station has now closed its doors for good. The owner had renamed it Nolan — meaning noble, meaning one who does not embellish reality — and then reality, declining to be flattered, extinguished it anyway.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d710147d-c821-43b6-b94e-dc56e1f79d81_2973x1698.jpeg)  
*Trump Pizza Station, aka Nolan r.i.p. (Photo c/o abdymok )*

At approximately the same hour, [the chat window](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JFUtzDPo0YA) of a Ukrainian-language broadcast was in full philosophical session. Pany Renata was welcoming arrivals with small hug emojis and reminding the assembly that Z-symbols were not permitted. Ihor Cherepanya was proposing Roman Chervinsky for Minister of Defense. Someone from Kryvyi Rih announced himself. Flowers were distributed.

On [another broadcast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JFUtzDPo0YA), former minister Volodymyr Omelyan explained—with the systematic patience of a man who has said all of this before and expects to say it again—that:

- **Systemic Corruption:** The country was being run by a mafia whose sole purpose was personal enrichment.
- **Superstition and Flight:** Yermak had left his voodoo dolls behind when he fled because he trusted them to protect him.
- **Initial Response:** Z’s first instruction on the morning of the invasion had been to stay home and remain calm.
- **Performative Oversight:** The anti-corruption infrastructure was merely a performance.
- **Sabotaged Defense:** The rocket program had been undermined by appointing officials whose prior experience was limited to selecting filming locations and pouring concrete curbs.
- **Public Perception:** Despite this, two-thirds of Ukrainians, by the latest polling, still believed in the people responsible.

Omelyan added, with the tone of a man trying on optimism like an ill-fitting coat, that his glasses were not quite rose-colored—merely that the rose tint had not yet fully blackened, though the process was ongoing.

In Geneva on Tuesday and today, delegations from Russia, Ukraine, and the United States are scheduled to hold the next round of negotiations. Putin has signaled no retreat from his goals. Trump has called his relationship with Putin “fantastic.” The peace plan looked to Ukraine, in the words of those who read it, like a demand for surrender.

The café that did not embellish reality is closed. The chat window continues distributing flowers. The drones — fifty-three thousand last year, nearly five times the number of the year before — continue arriving at city centers, power plants, and apartment buildings where men like Oleksandr Polishchuk are trying to remember what it was like to feel heat.

Toward the end of his broadcast, Omelyan reached for two classics. The first was the Hegelian aphorism — circulating now without a fixed address, like so many displaced persons — that the main lesson of history is that people do not learn from the lessons of history[1](#footnote-1).

The second was [Volodymyr Vynnychenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volodymyr_Vynnychenko), the Ukrainian writer and politician, who observed that Ukrainian history cannot be read without bromide. Omelyan noted the irony that Vynnychenko himself then proceeded to illustrate the point: having pledged with Petliura not to move against Hetman Skoropadsky, he immediately went behind the scenes to negotiate with the Bolsheviks, helped overthrow the Hetman anyway, and spent the next thirty years on a comfortable estate in the south of France — not far, Omelyan noted with quiet satisfaction, from where the Ukrainian Monaco Battalion is currently stationed.

The more interesting citation, in other words, was also the more painful one. As it generally is.

In other news, I finished drafting the Belarusian chapter of a memoir, leaving out a lot of gruesome stuff I’ll prob include later.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/024faa4a-8de0-4cac-9618-93f3f263f40e_1024x1024.png)  
*Ties enchanted with AI (Photo taken in Minsk by Sergei Grits sometime in 1996)*

##### *Zaijchik and the Tsar*

---

I should say at the outset that the zajchik — the little rabbit, as the Belarusian ruble was affectionately known — was not, by any reasonable standard, a strong currency. Its name alone was a kind of confession. Other countries named their money after eagles, lions, crowns, the abstract solemnity of the pound sterling. Belarus named its money after a small woodland creature that survives primarily by being fast and not drawing attention to itself. This was, in retrospect, an omen.

I arrived in Minsk in the mid-1990s as the director of the Belarus Soros Foundation, which is to say I arrived as a man whose purpose was to give money to people who wanted to build schools, newspapers, libraries, and civic organizations in a country that was, at that particular historical moment, developing a strong institutional allergy to schools, newspapers, libraries, and civic organizations. I had, in other words, chosen an interesting line of work.

The president of Belarus at the time was Alyaksandr Lukashenka, a former collective farm director who had arrived in office in 1994 on a wave of sincere anti-corruption populism and was now spending the proceeds of that sincerity on something he found more personally satisfying: the consolidation of absolute power. He was a compact, ruddy man of the sort that Abkhazian villagers would have recognized immediately — the man at the feast who always wants to make a toast, who speaks a little too loudly of his love for the people, and who, if you watch carefully, is always counting the room.

What Lukashenka wanted, it became clear to me over the course of 1996, was not so much power in the sophisticated sense that politicians of other countries pursue it — through influence, alliances, the slow accumulation of institutional leverage — but rather power in the more elemental sense that a man wants the sun to rise on his schedule. He wanted the newspapers to say what he said. He wanted the economists to confirm that his economy was performing well even as it was visibly not performing well. He wanted the judges, the generals, the television announcers, and the foreign foundations to all work in the same direction, which was his direction, and he was genuinely puzzled and somewhat hurt when they did not.

He had, you see, what I can only describe as a very sincere relationship with reality. That is, he sincerely believed that reality was what he said it was, and sincerely could not understand why reality kept sending delegations to disagree.

---

In the early months of 1996, Lukashenka announced that the goal of his economic policy was “market socialism.” He delivered this announcement with great confidence, as a man delivers a piece of news he has been saving. I remember reading the transcript and sitting for some time with it, turning it over, looking for the definition. The definition, I eventually concluded, did not exist. What the phrase meant, as best I could reconstruct from the subsequent months of evidence, was the following: that the state would control all significant economic activity, fix all significant prices, and periodically announce that this was the market at work.

The economy, not having read the announcements, continued to collapse.

The dollar-to-zajchik exchange rate — which the central bank was controlling with the gentle touch of a man gripping a steering wheel over a cliff — shot from thirteen thousand little rabbits to fifteen thousand little rabbits over the course of a single week in June, after two decrees increasing state regulation of commercial activity went into effect and every bank in the country simultaneously decided this was an excellent moment to suspend hard currency operations. Account holders, displaying the kind of practical economic reasoning that no university had taught them but life had, began withdrawing their savings in whatever currency they could find, which further depleted the reserves, which accelerated the devaluation, which increased the inflation, which meant that by autumn prices would be twenty to forty percent higher than they had been in spring. This is what economists call a feedback loop and what the rest of us call a disaster.

No one was getting paid. This too was a problem, though it received somewhat less theoretical attention.

What was remarkable — and I say this not in criticism but in something closer to genuine wonder — was how thoroughly the president maintained his equanimity throughout all of this. He had concluded that the economists were wrong, that the journalists who reported on the economists were enemies of the state, and that the state, properly governed, meaning governed by him, would eventually prove everyone incorrect. There is a type of confidence so complete that it becomes, paradoxically, a source of stability — not economic stability, but the more personal kind, the stability of a man who has decided that doubt is for other people.

He was, and I want to be fair about this, genuinely beloved. Not by the intellectuals, who despised him with an intensity that was itself a kind of tribute, but by the broader population, who found in him something they had not found in the reformers and the technocrats and the pro-Western democrats: the sense that he was one of them, that he understood what they wanted, that he would say plainly what they felt. He spoke badly — not in the diplomatic way politicians sometimes speak badly on purpose, but in the authentic way of a man who has never cared much for precision — and this too they loved, because it sounded like themselves.

In January of 1996, during the visit of Chinese Premier Li Peng, Lukashenka praised his guest as “a great leader of the European mold, notwithstanding his Asian origin.” This remark, which managed in a single sentence to be both complimentary and catastrophically condescending, was reported in the foreign press with the fascination that people bring to the observation of rare natural phenomena. Earlier, he had declared publicly that it was impossible to say anything elegant in Belarusian, and that there were only two great languages in the world: English and Russian. The Belarusian nationalists and educated patriots received this observation with the kind of silence that comes before a decision.

I had, by this point, taped to the wall above my desk a quote from his interview with *Nezavisimaya Gazeta* in which he had said: *“The fourth estate is financed from abroad — by the Soros Foundation. The fourth estate is the fourth estate. But I am the first estate, and they better remember it.”* I kept it there partly as a reminder of what we were dealing with, and partly because I found it, in the way that a man in a lifeboat finds a good view of the storm, genuinely clarifying.[^1]

---

The libel case came in March. A Mr. Shkolnikov, representing his Party for Democracy, Social Fairness, and Justice — a party whose name contained so many admirable nouns that one began to suspect the nouns were compensating for something — had brought suit against me for remarks made on a television program, on the grounds that I had slandered both the communist party and Mr. Shkolnikov personally. Our lawyer presented the judge with materials documenting what Mr. Shkolnikov’s party had been publishing about the Foundation, as well as a recording of the television program in question, which, when played, demonstrated primarily that I had been on television and that Mr. Shkolnikov had feelings about this.

The case, as I explained in dispatches to colleagues at the Open Society Institute at the time, was not really about the libel. The libel was a genre, a form the pressure could take. The actual pressure was coming from the presidential administration, and it was coming from several directions simultaneously: forced polling of universities and scholars who had received Foundation grants, interrogations of faculty by security officials asking in great detail what the money had been used for, visits from the Presidential Office of Economic Crime to examine our accounting — which was, I should note, in excellent order, partly out of principle and partly because we had always understood that our accounting would eventually be examined by the Presidential Office of Economic Crime.

There is a technique that authoritarians use when they wish to destroy an organization without the inconvenience of a specific accusation: they audit. They audit thoroughly, patiently, repeatedly, and with the evident conviction that if they look long enough they will find something, and if they find nothing they will look again. The audits are not really about the accounts. They are about the hours spent responding to the audits, the staff whose work is disrupted, the donors who grow nervous, the partner organizations that begin to wonder whether their relationship with you has made them visible in ways they would prefer not to be. An audit, in the hands of a determined government, is not a financial instrument. It is a form of weather.

---

By June the weather had become remarkable.

Deputy Viktar Honchar — a member of the civil opposition, a careful man who chose his words with the attention that the times demanded — was shot at by a police patrol attached to the president’s security apparatus at three o’clock in the morning on June 13th. He was not hurt. His secretary was shot in the buttocks. The official explanation, delivered without apparent irony by the relevant authorities, was that the patrol had mistaken Honchar for a Chechen bandit. This explanation required the acceptance of several subsidiary propositions: that Chechen bandits were a known hazard of the Minsk streetscape at three in the morning; that the patrol had been patrolling specifically for them; and that their response upon spotting a Chechen bandit was to shoot at him once and then retreat when he turned out to be a parliamentary deputy. The explanation was not, in the technical sense, believed by anyone. It was offered and received in the spirit of a formality, like an invoice for a transaction both parties know has already occurred.

The same week, three large men visited the home of Halina Drakakhrust, wife of a journalist who had written a rebuttal of a state newspaper’s attack on George Soros and the Foundation. They beat her and told her to pass along their regards to her husband, who was, as it happened, in Poland at the time. I include this detail — the husband being in Poland — not because it changes the moral character of the event, which is not subject to revision, but because there is something about it that clarifies the nature of the communication. They had not come for him. They had come to leave a message. The violence was, in the technical vocabulary of the state, informational.

On Saturday of that same week, President Lukashenka delivered his state of the union address, during which he stated publicly that he did not suffer from schizophrenia and was not sick, and that if anyone didn’t believe him they could have it out man to man. A president’s insistence that he is sane is, as a rhetorical category, somewhat unusual, and I found myself wondering, in an idle way, what the occasion had been. No one had publicly questioned his health in terms he would have seen — which meant the comment was either a response to private information he had received about what people were saying, or it was a response to nothing, which raised different questions. Either way, the offer to settle the matter physically was, I think, sincere.

He also announced that beginning July first, controls would be tightened on the movements of all Belarusians leaving the country and on all foreigners traveling within the republic. This was accompanied by a cabinet edict requiring all non-governmental organizations and foundations to provide detailed monthly financial reports to the central tax inspectorate.[^6] We understood these measures as a system, which is what they were: a slow tightening of the space in which independent life could be conducted, applied with the patience of someone who is not in a hurry because they have no deadline.

I wrote to my colleagues at the time that events were proceeding as expected and that I did not want anyone to panic. This was true. It was also the kind of true that requires some maintenance.

---

In late July, approximately fifteen thousand people attended the Independence Day rally. The police behaved themselves and there were no incidents. I noted this in my dispatches with a lightness I did not entirely feel, because what I was noting was essentially: they did not shoot anyone today, and this seemed worth recording.

Lukashenka announced shortly thereafter that he would be employing a new tactic for dealing with pickets, marches, demonstrations, and strikes.

He would ban them by decree.

I had been, up to this point, maintaining a kind of professional equilibrium about the situation — the equilibrium of a man who understands that his job is to continue working and that continuing to work requires not catastrophizing, even when there is material available for catastrophizing. But there is something about the simplicity of that decree — the sheer unornamented directness of it, the willingness to say out loud, in the form of law, *you may not gather* — that broke through the professional equilibrium for a moment and left me sitting at my desk with a feeling I can only describe as clarified. Not surprised. Clarified.

---

The August press conference, in which Lukashenka had been reflecting on his two years in office, produced a statement I have turned over many times in the years since. He said: *“There is nothing wrong if the people vote on four or five questions every two years, because a referendum is the highest form of democracy. And how can it be that someone who comes to power democratically can be a dictator? It is impossible.”*

The question was not a rhetorical question. He appeared to mean it genuinely. He had arrived at his position through an election — a real election, the results of which were not contested — and he could not see how the word that came after an election could be anything other than its opposite. The logic, if you follow it charitably, has a certain coherence. What it leaves out is the interval between the election and the present, what happens in that interval, and what kinds of power one may accumulate during it while remaining, technically, elected.

Lukashenka may or may not have been familiar with the way Hitler consolidated power using national plebiscites in 1933, 1934, and 1935. I noted this in my dispatches at the time, and I note it again now not to perform a comparison but because the mechanism is genuinely instructive: a plebiscite, stripped of the institutional context that makes it meaningful, is not democracy. It is the performance of democracy in the service of its destruction. The audience is the people, who are also the material.

The president reaffirmed his intention to hold a referendum on November 7th — the anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution, which was either a coincidence or an aesthetic choice I found difficult to admire — during a two-and-a-half-hour nationally televised address from Hrodna, during which he cancelled parliamentary elections scheduled for November 29th. A mass media campaign of Orwellian proportions had been underway for approximately ten days. A later analysis by the European Institute for Media would find that of the two thousand minutes devoted to referendum reporting on state television, ninety percent openly supported the president’s position, and the remaining ten percent was considered non-biased. Radio coverage contained no opposition viewpoints whatsoever.[^1]

On the economic front, nothing had changed. We remained in a state of collapse. Everybody to the fields.

---

The tax inspectorate arrived in August, acting on instructions from Colonel Uladzimir Zamyatalin — who held the title of ideology chief of the presidential administration and had recently been elevated to deputy prime minister, a promotion that contained within it a certain editorial comment on how the administration understood the relationship between ideology and governance. The inspectors descended simultaneously on every significant non-governmental newspaper in the country: *Belorusskaya Gazeta*, *Belorusskaya Delovaya Gazeta*, *Imya*, *Narodnaya Volya*, *Svaboda*. Inspectors told people privately, in the way that inspectors sometimes confide in you when they feel a small human sympathy for the situation they have been sent to create, that they had been instructed from above to find something, anything.[^6]

At the same time, the deputy minister of communications sent a fax to Radio Station 101.2 informing it that programming would not be aired after midnight on August 31st, due to “technical reasons.”

Radio 101.2 was the only non-governmental station broadcasting in Belarusian to Minsk. It was the only station that broadcast objective news, including the BBC and Polish Radio. It had been born out of a Foundation grant of one hundred thousand dollars in 1994, had survived two years of bureaucratic obstruction with the stubborn vitality of something that knows it is needed, and had built the second-largest listening audience in Minsk — particularly popular among young people, who were at that moment being rounded up and sent to the countryside to pick potatoes, which was a separate policy.

The “technical reasons” were not specified and did not need to be. A fax is a fax. The station went dark. The young people continued, presumably, to pick potatoes, now in silence.

---

In September the parliament voted to schedule the referendum for November 24th in conjunction with parliamentary elections, and added three questions of their own to the ballot, including one supporting a proposed alternative constitution in which there was no president at all. The absence of a president, as a constitutional category, has a certain elegance — it is a solution with the directness of a folk tale. Cut off the head and the body will sort itself out. The president, predictably, did not appreciate the elegance.

Colonel Zamyatalin appeared on television to announce that parliament had committed a constitutional coup d’état. A loyalist member of the presidium declared that Lukashenka was now “free to act as he wishes.” This statement was offered as a kind of comfort to supporters but had, for those of us listening on the other side, the ring of something more like a threat — the announcement that a constraint had been removed, which is only reassuring if you trusted the constraint.

If Lukashenka held his referendum regardless, the sequence of events seemed fairly obvious: decree issued, parliament initiates impeachment, president dissolves parliament, and after that anything was possible, which is another way of saying nothing was guaranteed.

---

By the first week of October I had, in my dispatches, drafted three scenarios for the coming months. I do not reproduce them here to demonstrate prescience — I was wrong in the particulars, as one generally is — but because the act of writing them down was itself a kind of discipline, a way of imposing narrative order on what felt, from inside, like pure contingency.

In the best case: a falsified referendum passes, the parliament is disbanded, and Lukashenka’s regime receives a temporary respite until the next crisis, which I estimated would arrive within six months.

In the middle case: mass demonstrations, more than a hundred thousand people, clashes near the Palace of Sports, a human chain around the Supreme Soviet building, a referendum that fails, a military that refuses to crush the demonstrators, a president who flies out of Belarus toward an unknown destination.

In the worst case: the opposition dispersed, organizers arrested, deputies taken to unknown locations, a state of emergency, a referendum held under occupation, and then whatever came after, which depended on whether the opposition could regroup and on what Russia would decide to do, which was, as it always was, the real question.

We were trying, I wrote to my colleagues in New York, not to cry wolf. The desire to howl a little was, I confessed, irrepressible.

---

What actually happened was closer to the worst case than the middle case, as such things tend to be — the optimistic scenario requires many things to go right simultaneously, while the pessimistic scenario requires only a sustained application of will, which authoritarian governments are generally better positioned to supply.

Lukashenka held his referendum on November 24th. The results were falsified. A new constitution granting the president near-total power was adopted. The Supreme Soviet was replaced with a rubber-stamp National Assembly. The opposition was scattered. The independent media was extinguished, systematically, with the thoroughness of a man who understands that the light is the problem, not the specific lamps.[^3]

On a Friday evening in late March 1997, I returned to Minsk from a trip to Hungary and was arrested at the airport. I was held for more than twelve hours without access to anyone — made to sleep under guard, given nothing to eat. Officials from the United States Embassy were denied access until a few minutes before I was placed on a plane to Frankfurt.[^8][^9][^10]

A state television newscast that evening described how I had organized opposition rallies and shown footage from November as evidence. The footage showed me standing at a demonstration. I had been at the demonstration. The commentator presented my presence as the proof. I was also accused of having bought people, and a promise was made that a list of the purchased would shortly be released to the public. It was not released. Lists of the purchased, in my experience, are rarely released, because the accusation is not about the list. It is about the word *bought*, which sticks to the people it names and cannot be unstuck by the absence of a list.

President Lukashenka repeated the charges the following day. “We will not allow foreign citizens to finance the opposition or take part in disturbances,” he said, adding that he would not like the American government to regard my detention and deportation as “a deliberate act.”[^2][^11]

It was, of course, a deliberate act. Matthew Brzezinski, a journalist who visited the Foundation’s Minsk office during this period, captured something of the atmosphere in his book *Casino Moscow*. He described the Russian-language broadcasts of Radio Liberty — the only alternative to domestic state channels — experiencing frequent “technical difficulties,” and recorded the sardonic verdict making the rounds among the foreign community: “Welcome to Europe’s North Korea.” Byrne managed a weak smile.[^17] “It is no accident, diplomats say, that the first person expelled from Belarus was Peter G. Byrne, an American who directed the Belarus Soros Foundation, which finances about 80 percent of the country’s tiny independent sector,” Judith Miller reported in the *New York Times* that July.[^16] The choice of target was the message. It was also — as an anonymous source in the law-enforcement agencies told the Russian news agency Interfax — a warning shot, not against me personally but against the Foundation itself, which had by that point distributed thirteen million dollars in Belarus toward education, health, and environmental programs. Within weeks, the authorities levied a three-million-dollar fine for alleged currency violations and seized the Foundation’s bank account.[^4][^12][^13]

The Foundation continued working for several more months, with the equanimity of an organization that has decided that the work is the work regardless of the conditions, and then closed its Minsk office in September 1997. The State Department issued a statement calling the closure a very negative message about the intentions of the Belarusian government regarding democracy and human rights, which was accurate, and also somewhat beside the point, in the way that autopsies are accurate and beside the point. Belarus was the first country in the former Communist bloc to expel the Soros Foundation. George Soros said the campaign was an effort to destroy independent society.[^5][^14]

Radio 101.2 never came back on the air.

*Belorusskaya Delovaya Gazeta* was eventually shuttered.

Viktar Honchar — the deputy who had been shot at in June 1996, who had continued his work with the careful stubbornness of a man who has decided that stopping is not an option — disappeared in September 1999, along with former Interior Minister Yury Zakharenko, who had chaired the anti-dictatorship council. Their bodies have never been found.[^6][^15]

The zajchik, the little rabbit, survived in various forms for many years, continuing its primary adaptive strategy: running, not drawing attention, hoping for the best.

Alyaksandr Lukashenka is still president of Belarus.

*—P.B.*

---
