## Day 1457

2026-02-19 · Tactical athletics

You know how the intelligence analysts and geopolitical whiz kids have been bouncing around these ideas of hybrid warfare and fifth column infiltration: they write long threads about bad actors and institutional rot, about the structured paranoia of identifying traitors within one’s own ranks while scrolling through Telegram channels at 2am. Well of course it’s galling. It’s irritating that anyone anywhere can quantify/qualify the loyalty of a sitting general when it’s so freaking hard just to make up your mind about who’s actually running whom when presented with a cascade of burned documents, detained spooks, suspiciously timed explosions and backoffice shenanigans.

Even more galling is when it kind of lands. The allegations against Kyrylo Budanov — until recently head of Ukrainian military intelligence, now as of January 2nd 2026 Head of the Office of the President, a job that came with the previous occupant’s resignation still warm — teem with grey zones and burned files and classified materials that all interlock beautifully and make perfect sense to the upstart armchair analyst. Budanov, the claim goes, reportedly oversaw a procurement structure that failed to fulfill 83% of its arms contracts and left the army short of ammunition through 2022 and 2023.

Quite the résumé.

Most of this is, by design, impossible to verify. But one thing isn’t. Fourteen days after his appointment in August 2020, Budanov went on camera with a Putin flunkie employed by the President’s Office and said flatly that Wagnergate — the elaborate Ukrainian sting operation that lured 33 Wagner mercenaries to Belarus, where they were to board a flight to Istanbul that would have made a convenient emergency landing in Kyiv — was not a Ukrainian operation but an FSB-orchestrated one.

The [Bellingcat investigation](https://www.bellingcat.com/news/uk-and-europe/2021/11/17/inside-wagnergate-ukraines-brazen-sting-operation-to-snare-russian-mercenaries/), published fifteen months later and built on hundreds of verified documents, audio recordings, and interviews with participants on both sides, demolishes that claim with the kind of thoroughness usually reserved for war crimes tribunals. All of it Ukrainian, all of it documented. We covered Wagnergate in [September 2021](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/scale-free-wagner-pmc?utm_source=publication-search) and twice in November 2021 — [here](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/i-an-actor?utm_source=publication-search) and [here](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/pants-on-fire?utm_source=publication-search) — and have asked the woman claiming to be KonMarie running the backoffice of this Substack to make all of it available to non-paying subscribers, who should become founding members and paying subscribers anyway, for the hell of it.

Worth noting that the man Budanov replaced at the Office of the President is Andriy Yermak — the same Yermak who, per Bellingcat, requested the last-minute postponement that handed the Wagner mercenaries to Belarusian security services rather than Ukrainian ones, reportedly to protect a Donbas ceasefire announcement. One Wagnergate figure out, another in. The circle of life, Kyiv-style. And worth noting too that shortly after his appointment as chief of military intelligence, Budanov was found to be sharing a private estate in Khotiv, outside Kyiv, with the family of one [Oleksandr Hohilashvili](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/oleksandr-hohilashvili-busted) — a deputy interior minister whose story is best described as a greatest hits of the Z era: filmed berating police at a checkpoint in eastern Ukraine, reportedly a Russian citizen from Rostov with a criminal record, husband of Z’s personal aide and body woman Maria Levchenko, and a man whose appointment to shape state drug policy had been secured, apparently, by virtue of his wife’s proximity to the president. The estate itself belonged to the wife of Vyacheslav Strelkovsky, whom Ukrainian media identified as the organizer of large-scale cash conversion schemes. Budanov told Bihus.info he was only staying there temporarily while his apartment was being renovated. Naturally.

These are certainly not issues Piers Morgan asked Z about the other day during his 80-minute [uncensored interview](https://www.instagram.com/p/DU5w4CuCNS9/).

Instead, Z told him: “I want to say that I try to be as honest as possible in everything and with everyone. Cases of corruption exist, yes, but we are building a major anti-corruption infrastructure.” He is, as anyone can see, making excellent progress. On the subject of elections, Z noted that when Russians tell Americans that Ukraine can hold elections in one or two weeks, “they always forget that we are not Russia.” — which is, all things considered, a stupid thing to say.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/28608d64-c462-4670-9e1c-88ab144f82c9_1280x853.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o President’s Office (February 18, 2026)*

Meanwhile, in his wood-paneled office at the Ukrainian Embassy in London — walls hung with military aircraft posters and children’s drawings of battle scenes, toy drones on the mahogany table, live drone feeds from eastern Ukraine flickering on screens behind his desk, the whole aesthetic suggesting a man who has given the matter of his own legend considerable thought — Valeriy Zaluzhny is watching all of this from a careful distance. The general Z fired in February 2024 and packed off to Britain leads Z by three points in hypothetical presidential polling, turned down Paul Manafort who came calling in spring 2025, and says he’s not doing politics until the war is over. He also, in a [recent AP feature](https://apnews.com/article/ukraine-war-zaluzhnyi-zelenskyy-raid-5ff9e5e2054e0b17c10daf58d7eab63e), described for the first time how dozens of SBU agents raided his command center in September 2022 — hours after a tense meeting at Z’s headquarters — ostensibly searching for a strip club that had closed at that address before the full-scale invasion even began.

That strip club, almost certainly, was Tootsie — a venue near and dear to this vlog’s heart, covered [here](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-469?utm_source=publication-search), [here](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/stay-out-of-doorways?utm_source=publication-search), [here](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/imposter-syndrome?utm_source=publication-search), and [here](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-767-59a?utm_source=publication-search), the last of which explores the dizzying connection between Wagnergate, Tootsie, and Ukraine’s subjectivity. Tootsie occupied the ground floor of Samsonov’s House, a Neo-Renaissance architectural monument at 30/10 Bohdan Khmelnytsky Street — built in 1900-1901, beloved of Kyiv’s early 20th century intelligentsia, damaged in the war, restored, and since 2000 popularly known as Klitschko’s House, its beneficial owner being one Volodymyr Klitschko, Ukrainian citizen registered in Monaco. The premises had housed, in sequence: a celebrated deli privatized after the Soviet collapse by the family of Vitali Klitschko’s godfather; a casino; and then, once gambling was banned, Tootsie — a strip club that became a favorite of Lev Parnas, former New York City mayor Rudy Giuliani, Hunter Biden, and this correspondent, back when Kyiv was Kyiv. In January 2022 police raided Tootsie in a human trafficking investigation and found an underground brothel, drugs, weapons, and evidence the club had been secretly filming visitors for blackmail purposes. Tootsie has reportedly since closed, its sign removed from the facade — though we have our doubts.

Zaluzhny called Yermak and told him he was prepared to call in military reinforcements to repel the search. The SBU says no search was carried out.

Kyrylo Budanov is currently a member of the Ukrainian delegation negotiating peace with Russia.

## Day 1458

2026-02-20 · Week in Review

*There is a lot I did not write about this week, and I have made my peace with this. The unwritten things accumulate quietly, like mold spreading on the damp, unheated walls of a Stalinist-era apartment, and they have their own dignity. The Vibe One projector, for instance, which we set up with the particular combination of triumph and humiliation that all technology eventually produces. The return, briefly, of electricity, which deserves its own small ceremony and received none. And no — not the Epstein files. Some silences are principled.*

*Oatmeal in a blanket evolved, as things do when left to their own devices, into borshch in a blanket. Twice, insulated by tin foil and a towel. There is a whole philosophy of civilization in that sentence, if you are willing to look for it, and I am, on day 1458, willing to look for almost anything.*

*Z appeared on screen this morning in yesterday evening’s pep talk looking, as my hookup might have said,* **very awake for the hour***. He did not mention the anniversary. Thirteen years. The kind of number that should stop a man mid-sentence, that should make the teleprompter itself pause out of respect. It did not. Instead, Z talked about a big drug bust. He will mention the anniversary today, maybe, in that smooth AI-curated fashion where the grief has been optimized and the pauses inserted by his fuckpig PR staff. A wreath-laying ceremony.*

*What Z was doing on February 18th, 19th, and 20th of 2014 remains, as they say, a mystery. History is full of such useful mysteries. They are almost always the most important part.*

Which photo is *enchanted*? Some look the same to me.

The *week in review* is here:

The guards, it turns out, were not briefed on drones. This is what the state offers its citizens: conscription agents at the gate, shrapnel on the carpet. A poignant love story, and it illustrates the craziness of the moment rather well.

## Day 1460

2026-02-22 · What the Square Knew

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/76b7dc1b-9d44-4d6e-9517-3e8a3cbde48d_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo enchanted with AI (c/o abdymok , February 21, 2014, taken from the 13th floor of the Hotel Ukraine)*

It is 05:30 on Sunday morning in Kyiv and Russia has already launched at least 16 rockets at the city. CNN’s Clarissa Ward, who told *[Politico](http://politico.com)*’s Dasha Burns this week that Ukrainians no longer feel superhuman — that they feel broken, exhausted, barely able to get out of bed — is somewhere in the city on assignment. If she can get to the Motherland monument in Park Slava before sunrise, the lighting over the Dnipro will be perfect. So will the drones. It would make rather better television than the [soggy toast anniversary package](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/02/20/world/zelensky-ukraine-war-last-four-years-intl) filed on Friday and sourced entirely from Z’s own circle. The real story is elsewhere. It has been elsewhere for some time.

Two of the most significant works of long-form journalism published in the past two months — Adam Entous’s 12,500-word investigation in the *[New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/12/30/world/europe/ukraine-war-us-russia.html)* and Shaun Walker’s 6,700-word account in the *[Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/feb/20/a-war-foretold-how-the-cia-and-mi6-got-hold-of-putins-ukraine-plans-and-why-nobody-believed-them)*, produced by 19 journalists, drawing on over 400 interviews across 22 countries and naming 81 officials — arrive at the same quietly devastating conclusion: that Z knew Russia would invade, did nothing, and pretended otherwise.

Team USA does not emerge clean. The Entous piece — ten named sections, seventy-seven individuals, a cast large enough to populate a middling Russian novel — documents a parallel performance: aid described as flowing when it wasn’t, negotiations described as progressing when they weren’t, and a man who promised peace in twenty-four hours treated as a serious student of the problem.

Germany, too, earns its place. Walker includes what may be the most perfectly Teutonic detail of the saga: Bruno Kahl, head of the BND, flew into Kyiv on February 23rd, 2022, declined a seat in the midnight evacuation convoy because he had meetings the next morning, and had to be extracted in confusion by Polish intelligence when those meetings failed to materialise — because a war had begun. A man whose profession was to know things, in the one city where the only relevant fact was already known by everyone except him.

Then there was the shared assumption that Ukrainians would absorb the invasion and submit. Eighty-one named officials. Four hundred interviews. Centuries of combined experience in the dark arts of knowing things about people. Apparently not one serious reckoning with Ukrainians themselves.

The failure surfaced bluntly in a [Senate Armed Services Committee hearing](https://www.king.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/on-ukraine-a-significant-issue-that-we-missed_king-urges-intelligence-community-to-better-assess-will-to-fight) on May 10th, 2022, when Senator Angus King pressed Lieutenant General Scott Berrier, director of the Defense Intelligence Agency. Berrier insisted there had been no assessment that Ukrainians lacked the will to fight — only that their capacity was insufficient. King replied: if you assess that a country will be overrun in weeks, you are making a judgment about will. Berrier had no real answer. The failure, as both articles now make clear, was not technical. No satellite missed anything. No signal went unintercepted. The failure was human.

It was human because Western intelligence had spent three decades not truly studying Ukrainians — not their language, not their political memory, not the accumulated fury of a society repeatedly occupied, starved, Russified, and deceived. Anyone present on Independence Square in 2014, when ordinary Kyivans forced Yanukovych’s Berkut from the streets with their bodies and their rage, understood something fundamental had shifted. Western services were not in the kitchens and courtyards where the temperature of a people is taken. They were speaking to one another, mistaking consensus for insight, carousing at [Tootsie Club](https://uk.tootsie.kiev.ua/).

Z was also absent. Weeks earlier he had co-hosted Russia-1’s New Year’s Eve special alongside Maxim Galkin, while Vladimir Solovyov — later a daily advocate of Ukraine’s destruction — applauded in the audience. He was professionally and financially embedded in [Russia’s entertainment ecosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kvartal_95_Studio) as Ukrainians were dismantling it with their bodies. In March he said Russians and Ukrainians were one people. In May he was standing outside Red Square.

That context illuminates what followed: Russian-adjacent entertainer in 2014, insurgent president in 2019, unprepared wartime leader in 2022 — surrounded, in emergency, by people who saw chaos not only as crisis but as opportunity. Yermak’s office became the centre of gravity. Z held the podium; the back office ran the accounts.

A word about the millions who crossed westward with children and suitcases in 2022. That was not cowardice. It was parenthood. It must be kept distinct from the conduct of the elite class that remained. As refugees queued in the cold, defense contracts found cronies, fortifications went unbuilt, fallback lines existed on paper, conscription bit unevenly, and soldiers’ wages were insufficient. What should have been a war of attrition hardened into stalemate — not solely because of Russian resilience, but because of domestic corrosion.

And there was another Ukraine — the one neither article fully confronts. Alongside the heroism ran a quieter architecture of extraction. Yermak — who reassured Z that full-scale invasion was impossible and then became indispensable — presided over an office that functioned less as a centre of government than as a gravitational hub for patronage. Deputies investigated. Deputies charged. Energy-sector schemes recorded by [NABU](https://nabu.gov.ua/en). An energy minister detained at the border in February 2026, attempting to leave the country hours after Z made jokes in Munich.

Biology supplies a metaphor: parabiosis. Connect an old circulatory system to a young one and the old blood does not rejuvenate — it toxifies. Three years of war fused a young administration to the oldest post-Soviet pathologies, and the exchange ran in one direction. The decisive moment came in February 2024, when Z dismissed General Valerii Zaluzhny — the one commander broadly trusted, the one willing to say the front had stabilized into stalemate and that political decisions now prolonged it. Zaluzhny was replaced. The stalemate remained.

Moscow estimated ten percent would fight. Washington planned for a government in exile. Berlin sent its intelligence chief to book a hotel room. Z, meanwhile, confused a country with a population, a population with a mood, and a mood with a forecast.

## Day 1462

2026-02-24 · Intact from the outside

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/906c9379-2dbd-4b8b-80c4-7aa2b1c03de3_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo enchanted with AI (c/o abdymok , February 23, 2026)*

I deliberately wrote nothing yesterday for the occasion. There is something false in anniversary grief, the way there is something false in free bliny at the local Selpo on Masnytsya — the appetite is real enough, but the calendar has pre-emptied it, formatted it, made it available at the checkout counter. Sympathy that arrives on schedule is sympathy that has made other arrangements.

There is an engineering principle about hollow structures. A column can look intact — the facade smooth, the surface unbroken — while the interior has been systematically removed. It bears weight until it doesn’t. The failure, when it comes, looks sudden. I keep returning to this principle because it describes not just infrastructure but the specific texture of how Ukraine entered this war: a state whose exterior held press conferences and signed procurement contracts while the load-bearing interior had either been removed or, in some cases, never actually built.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/00cd4b5e-ae9c-436f-aa60-7a802ebedab7_1536x931.webp)  
*Team USA under Trump has been less than helpful*

And what would I have written about? The causes and consequences? That subject has been through the wringer so many times it has lost its original formatting. Every argument has been shared, debunked, reinstated, and shared again until the dirty suits are indistinguishable from the warcore chic outfits that replaced them.

---

So far, Zaluzhny’s [column](https://www.pravda.com.ua/columns/2026/02/23/8022301/) is the right counterweight to everything else said on the fourth anniversary of all-out war. It does something none of the other anniversary sources manage: it describes the war Ukraine is actually fighting rather than the war being narrated. The roboticized kill zone now 25 kilometers deep. Logistics impossible to 50 kilometers. The battlefield completely transparent. These are not rhetorical devices. They are the operational dimensions that explain why the hollow structure — present long before the first missile — became catastrophic rather than merely corrupt.

The three tasks at the end — preserve partners, stabilize the line, maintain sanctions — are the sober answer to everything [Chervinsky](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OajFd-3PF3M&t=1132s) and [Krivonos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ecYMAhmDu2Y&t=2226s) have identified as having gone wrong in the first place. Zaluzhny writes as a strategist. Chervinsky and Krivonos speak as men who were removed for saying inconvenient things. These are not the same war, narrated differently. They are the same war, witnessed from opposite ends of the accountability it never had.

The AFP [interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OajFd-3PF3M&t=1132s) is gold precisely because Z offers it without apparent self-awareness. Two years in a bunker. Hasn’t been to a cafe once. Doesn’t run outside anymore. Reads about the Caribbean Crisis to understand how a country becomes a bargaining chip. These details don’t humanize him so much as they illuminate the architecture of the situation — a man who withdrew from the surface of his own country while that surface was being managed by people with other priorities.

The bunker detail was the biggest tell. While kickbacks were being negotiated, the president was underground. While thermal power plants were left unprotected, Z, by his own account, was sleeping in a bunker and texting Kryvonizhka about air defense through the night. The bunker is not a metaphor. It is a fact the president volunteered, cheerfully, in an anniversary interview.

Meanwhile, Clarissa Ward’s interview with Z — CNN is rolling out [excerpts](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/02/23/europe/zelensky-trump-ukraine-russia-war-intl-latam) now, the full broadcast coming in hours — is framed around *resilience fatigue*. It will be atmospherically accurate. It will find, in the appropriate pauses, a man of improbable endurance. It will not ask about the bunker. Or about the *Z fatigue* we all experience.

---

Trypilska Thermal Power Plant, 45 kilometers south of Kyiv — owned by Centrenergo, a state company “in the process” of privatization since the 1990s.

On April 11, 2024, Russia fired 82 missiles and drones, including six Kinzhal missiles. The turbine hall burned. By morning, Centrenergo had lost 100 percent of its generation.

“The scale of the destruction is terrible,” the company said. “Money can’t estimate it.”

We know now that money had already estimated quite a few things. This year’s freezing of Kyiv has a paper trail.

The plant wasn’t merely underfunded — it was architecturally obsolete, a centralized Soviet-era node in a war that has made centralized nodes existentially vulnerable. Ali Baba, Karlsson, Professor *Сигізмунд*and Rocket — heroes of [Operation Midas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Midas) — weren’t only stealing. They were stealing from a system that needed to be redesigned anyway, which made their theft both more mundane and more catastrophic. Russian missiles found Trypilska because the money that should have hardened it had already left the country. The hollow structure principle again: the facade holds, Z plays musical chairs, the pep talks are delivered on schedule. Then the turbine halls burn, and people freeze.

---

Chervinsky would mention the hearth.

The decorated intelligence officer, now under house arrest, has argued that warnings of invasion were submitted daily, in writing — and suppressed. That troops were withdrawn from the Kyiv approaches and the Crimean corridor not from confusion but from design. That the 172nd Brigade reached the Irpin in darkness and held because a river happened to be there. That Russia sent Rosgvardiya — crowd control units — not an occupation army, but a political instrument meant to reinstall Yanukovych, whose removal in 2014 was still being contested in administrative courts.

Full-scale war followed the failure of that political operation.

In the first days of the invasion, Kyiv was saturated with warnings of saboteur groups and Chechen assassination squads. The atmosphere was real. The specific claims were unsubstantiated and almost always bogus. Years later, Z volunteered that his deputy Tatarov and intelligence chief Maliuk had been [out and about killing Chechens in Kyiv](https://en.interfax.com.ua/news/general/1010070.html#:~:text=50%2027.08.2024-,Zelenskyy:%20Tatarov%20takes%20part%20in%20liquidation%20of%20Chechen%20saboteurs%20in,in%20first%20days%20of%20war&text=Deputy%20Head%20of%20the%20Presidential,including%20in%20the%20United%20States.) during those early days. Complete bullshit. Manufacture the threat. Claim credit for defeating it.

Meanwhile: Serhiy Shefir — Kvartal 95 co-founder and longtime Z aide, reportedly overseeing the energy sector as early as 2021 — was photographed at Warsaw airport bound for Geneva. It was the day after Ukraine’s former Justice Minister and Energy Minister Halushchenko, Professor *Сигізмунд*, was removed from a train from Ukraine bound for Poland. The circle is small. The flights are real. The coincidences are geometric.

---

There is an old story — perhaps Trypillian, perhaps invented — about a village that burned every winter. Not from enemy torches. From its own hearths, untended by men who decided tending hearths was beneath their dignity.

The women carried water. The children carried water. The men carried the memory of carrying water — which they agreed was heavier.

Foreign correspondents would have filmed the flames beautifully. Essayists would have found, in the ashes, a woman of improbable resilience and a velvet dress representing civilization itself. Cable news would have sourced assassination counts to unnamed officials. All atmospherically true.

---

Winning requires that the men with call signs answer for their percentages. That warnings are not buried. That the hearth is tended. That the scream — heard perfectly well inside the bunker — wakes the man who has been texting about air defense all night, long enough for him to put down the phone and carry some water.

Trypilska is named after Trypillia — a civilization known largely through what the earth preserved after burning.

## Day 1463

2026-02-25 · The Peacemakers

*February 24–25, 2026*

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a9fe9bde-befb-4b50-b39c-49eb7f0c9d1c_1935x1048.jpeg)  
*Overlooking Semihory (Photo c/o abdymok )*

There is an old saying in Semihory — though perhaps I am inventing it just now, which is a Ukrainian tradition too — that the man who arrives after the fire to explain how he would have put it out deserves a certain kind of respect. Not admiration, you understand. A certain kind of respect.

[Semihory](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Semyhory,+Kyiv+Oblast,+09723/@49.5732085,30.9865577,3172m/data=!3m2!1e3!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40d393cbe77e1d3b:0x2720223a94661a02!8m2!3d49.57436!4d31.0007059!16s%2Fg%2F1215cnqx?entry=ttu&g_ep=EgoyMDI2MDIyMi4wIKXMDSoASAFQAw%3D%3D) is a small village near Bohuslav, where the ravine winds like a snake between green terraces and the millpond willows have been old for three centuries. It sits near the Ros River, in that part of the Kyiv region where the land remembers things longer than people do. The village is also where Nechui-Levytsky set his great comic novel of a family at war with itself — because the real Kaidash family prototype was known throughout the district for its nearly daily quarrels, brawls, and disorders. In the novel, the family fights for years over a pear tree on the property line. They fight until the tree withers and dies. Then they find something else to fight about[1](#footnote-1).

Hours ago, the President of the United States stood before his Congress and explained how he has ended eight wars, with Ukraine to be the ninth — the easiest one, he once said, though it has turned out to be the toughest. He has also ended eight and a quarter wars, he has said on other occasions, because Thailand and Cambodia briefly resumed fighting. A fractional war. One imagines the paperwork.

Yesterday, on this same fourth anniversary of the invasion, the President of Ukraine stood before his foreign guests in Kyiv and explained how reliably he is trying to end the bloodbath he did not prepare for.

A philosopher named Roger White has a useful thought about this. When an instrument reports on its own reliability — when the X-ray machine turns to face its own innards and announces that everything looks fine — the rational response is not to believe it, and not entirely to disbelieve it either[2](#footnote-2). It is simply to weight the report very lightly. Instruments that are truly reliable do not usually need to work so hard to seem so. Yesterday and today, on the same anniversary, we have been given two such reports from two such instruments. The attentive observer will apply the discount twice.

But let us be fair, in the way that fairness requires discomfort. Equal skepticism does not produce equal conclusions. The fact of invasion is not contested. The core of Z’s claim — we were attacked, we are being killed, we need help — have survived the discount, but just barely.

Trump’s core claim — I am bringing peace — does not survive contact with the calendar. Eight wars ended. Eight and a quarter. And the ninth, the easiest one, now in its thirteenth year.

In Semihory the Kaidash family once fought for years over a pear tree until the tree died. Then the fighting continued. The land along the Ros remembers this, the way it remembers everything — quietly, without comment, for longer than any of the parties to the dispute.

*Tonight the snow is melting there.*

A couple of days ago I mentioned two of the longer articles about the war — Adam Entous in [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/12/30/world/europe/ukraine-war-us-russia.html) and Shaun Walker in [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-interactive/2026/feb/20/a-war-foretold-cia-mi6-putin-ukraine-plans-russia)[1](#footnote-1). Neither thinks to mention the sequence of events without which the prelude to the mess makes no sense: the Paris summit with Putin in December 2019; the secret trip to Oman and the meeting with Patrushev in January 2020; the dismissal of the chief of staff and the installation of Yermak in February; Honcharuk ousted in March; the [criminal case opened against Poroshenko](https://www.unian.ua/politics/peregovori-poroshenka-i-baydena-genprokuror-zareyestruvala-kriminalne-provadzhennya-shchodo-oprilyudnenih-zapisiv-novini-ukrajina-11003834.html) in May, piggybacking on phone recordings released by Derkach, a Russian spy masquerading as a member of parliament; and then, in July, Wagnergate — the botched sting operation to capture Wagner mercenaries in Minsk, derailed at the last minute, per Bellingcat, on Yermak’s orders. That’s a pity.

Z’s vaca to Oman changed everything.

---

Read an article in [Foreign Affairs](http://foreignaffairs.com) about the war[2](#footnote-2).

Desch’s piece is a competent realist argument — Ukraine is losing, the numbers don’t lie, take the deal. But it is also a case study in what happens when you try to resolve a question of dignity with a stoplight chart.

The entire analysis operates in the register of measurable things: tank ratios, GDP, troops per mile, casualty rates. Within that register, the argument is coherent enough. But the war was never only — or even primarily — about material and rational indicators. It is about dignity. And dignity, as any Ukrainian could tell you, is not something that yields to a cost-benefit analysis.

Desch acknowledges this only to dismiss it: “the loss of the rest of Donetsk, although assuredly a blow to Ukrainian self-esteem...” — *self-esteem*, as if it were a psychological inconvenience rather than the animating force of the entire resistance. The Ukrainians are not fighting because they miscalculated the tank ratios. They are fighting because someone broke into their house.

There are also specific empirical weaknesses worth flagging. His casualty figures rely on Mediazona for Russian losses and UA Losses for Ukrainian ones, but he draws symmetrical conclusions that the methodologies don’t quite support. And his breezy “30 years to conquer Ukraine” reassurance to Europeans sits awkwardly alongside his simultaneous argument that Ukraine cannot hold on for another year.

But the deeper problem is this: Desch’s piece is addressed, implicitly, to Western policymakers — it is an argument for why *they* should pressure Kyiv to settle. It never seriously engages with the question that actually matters, which is not *can* Ukraine keep fighting, but *what is it fighting for*, and whether that is worth the price. That is a question Ukrainians themselves are increasingly, and agonizingly, debating. Desch doesn’t seem to know the debate is happening.

## Day 1468

2026-03-02 · The Golden Age of Hegemony

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1da1e13c-3cfd-4832-9ec8-357df5e9b608_1024x559.jpeg)  
*Illustration c/o Illustration: Created with Gemini using Nano Banana 2*

On the final day of diplomacy in Geneva, February 26, two men had a full calendar. In the morning, at the residence of the Omani ambassador in Cologny, they discussed Iran’s nuclear program. After lunch, a short drive across the city, at the Hôtel des Bergues on the Rhône, they discussed Ukraine’s survival. The conference rooms were close together. Efficiency is underrated.

The same men. The same city. The same smiles for photographers. One file concerned uranium enrichment; the other concerned the continued existence of a European state. Both were treated as negotiable.

Serious people observed this calmly. It is considered unhelpful to appear alarmed while history is being itemized.

While the morning talks were still running, a senior Iranian official said that an immediate agreement was within reach. Iran had tabled its first written proposal. The Omani foreign minister reported that both sides had exchanged creative and positive ideas. Talks were set to resume at six in the evening.

Meanwhile, the USS Gerald Ford had left port near Crete, bound for waters off Haifa. A dozen F-22s had been quietly deployed to Israel — the first American combat aircraft sent there for potential wartime operations. Several Western embassies had begun withdrawing non-essential staff from the Middle East.

The transitions in Geneva were seamless. Centrifuges before lunch. Borders after. By evening the word “peace” had been used often enough to feel procedural.

Witkoff and Kushner left Geneva without a deal in either file. But, at the very least, no collapse either.

The war — and it is a war, the President said so himself, in capital letters — required no congressional authorization and no defined end state. It required confidence. The President had promised, fifty-three documented times, to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. He had also promised not to begin new wars. These commitments were not contradictory. They simply belonged to different audiences.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2187f3bb-495a-4859-acff-ed8f75ec7b94_1056x687.png)  
*Former US Special Envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg praises Team USA’s attack on Iran ( Fox News , March 1, 2026)*

Meanwhile, Persian-language broadcasters were defunded. VPN access programs were cut. Civil-society tools were dismantled. Then bombs were dropped. The Iranian people were encouraged to reclaim their institutions.

“Surrender,” the President said.

The recipient was unspecified. Power, apparently, would organize itself.

Khamenei ruled for thirty-seven years by blood, fire, and tears. Weeks before the bombs fell, thousands of protesters were shot in the streets by his regime. His victims are entitled to feel relief at his absence. That is not a political position. It is a human one.

Relief is not the same as vindication. As Lebanese journalist Diana Moukalled [wrote](https://x.com/dianamoukalled/status/2027989281176698920): what happened was not a clash between right and wrong. It was a collision of domination projects. Khamenei was not a project of resistance. He was a project of control confronting another project of control. To transform him into a martyr — especially by those who remained silent as the grave on his crimes — is not a moral stance. It is a falsification of memory. And to celebrate the men who killed him is to replace one logic of glorification with another.

In the struggle for hegemony, the strongest wins. The problem is that we continue to count the losses.

Z, a serious man in an impossible situation, responded that American resolve was important. When America acts decisively, criminals weaken. He does not mention what follows it.

Seventy percent of Ukrainians do not believe the negotiations will produce lasting peace. They were not asked.

Elsewhere — in a small northern community in British Columbia — a fabric shop posted a call for help. Quilters across Canada answered. The goal: 2,700 quilts, one for every resident of Tumbler Ridge after a senseless tragedy. Each quilt is stitched by hand. Each one meant to feel like a hug.

They may produce too many. There is already a plan for the extras.

It is a modest ambition: one quilt per person. No red lines. No ultimatums. No airstrikes. Just warmth distributed evenly.

In the Kremlin, Putin watched the bombing of Tehran with professional interest. From Belgrade to Baghdad, from Kabul to Tehran, the pattern has been educational. Power arrives dramatically. Responsibility departs quietly.

He indicated the burning city.

*That could have been us*, he said.

He was not wrong.

## Day 1469

2026-03-03 · Clown show vs death cult

This morning, during my constitutional — a modest act of civic maintenance — I surrendered my thoughts to Huxe’s algorithm. It is a modern habit: instead of consulting sages, we consult the feed.

Around mile four it queued up U.S. War Secretary Pete briefing journalists with John about the [Iran operation](https://example.com). One imagines maps, acronyms, firm nods. Then came little [Marco Rubio’s press spray](https://example.com) — a phrase that suggests either light rain or industrial solvent. After him, [Sean Hannity chatting with Benjamin Netanyahu](https://example.com), both sounding as though history were something that could be arranged with sufficient confidence.

Next was [Trey Yingst reporting from Israel](https://example.com) — the chief foreign correspondent of [Fox News](https://example.com), who balances water bottles on door handles and prepares his mind through cold plunges. The ancients had ascetics. We have idiot correspondents.

When I returned home, I opened a quieter document.

The Constitution of the United States. Specifically, Article I, Section 8.

Clause 11 reads:

> “The Congress shall have Power… To declare War, grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal, and make Rules concerning Captures on Land and Water.”

Article I enumerates the powers of Congress.  
Article II defines the President as “Commander in Chief” of the armed forces.

The framers divided authority with deliberate suspicion:

The power to start war → Congress.  
The power to conduct war → President.

The framers separated ignition from steering because they understood momentum. Once something is set in motion, it does not pause to reconsider the fine print.

Below is a photograph of the result. Drones do not argue constitutional theory. They simply arrive.

## Day 1470

2026-03-04

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1bfefc10-b46f-47cb-8749-3ff0b6d3f24a_1536x1024.png)  
*Illustration created by ChatGPT (March 4, 2026)*

If you’re as exhausted as we are by the metastasizing genre of strategy document — those careful monuments to institutional self-regard, produced with the confidence of men who have confused the writing of plans with the execution of them, and whose principal function is to provide, in the event of catastrophe, a paper trail demonstrating that someone, somewhere, said the right words before the bombs fell — then the [National Security Strategy](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/National-Security-Strategy.pdf) and [National Defense Strategy](https://media.defense.gov/2026/Jan/27/2003398550/-1/-1/1/2026-NATIONAL-DEFENSE-STRATEGY.PDF), published in November 2025 and January 2026 respectively, will not disappoint.

Key message: No more interventionism. No more endless wars. No more regime change.

Six weeks later, Iran.

---

Yesterday in the Senate, Tim Kaine read the NDS back to one of its authors with the patience of a man holding a receipt. If you arrest one foreign leader and assassinate another, is that not regime change? US Deputy Secretary of War Elbridge Colby — whom we have pillaged repeatedly — would not say. This is strategy’s first and most reliable instinct when pressed by reality: renegotiate the definitions. When language softens, missions expand. When missions expand, the documents are archived — diet plans tucked beneath a takeout menu.

Mark Warner, fresh from classified briefings, reported no imminent threat from Iran. Only a succession of rationales: nuclear sites, then missiles, then naval assets, then regime change, now recast as necessity. A war of choice, he called it. Someone chose. It was not Congress.

---

[Iran’s foreign minister spoke to Al Jazeera](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TAUOeoLqzUE) and did something rarer than outrage: he drafted the afterword before the chapter had closed. The assassination unprecedented. A violation of international law. Dangerous. The Supreme Leader not merely a head of state but a transnational religious figure for tens of millions beyond Iran’s borders — damage measured carefully, almost tenderly. Americans, he added, deserve better.

Inside the condemnation was architecture. America entered this war on behalf of Israel, he implied. The blood is on Israeli hands. If this is not groundwork for future reconciliation — we were never truly at war, we were maneuvered — then what is it? A new leader will be elected. Everything constitutional. Everything orderly. The exit drafted before the entrance seals.

---

We have seen this structure before. In July 2025, we examined Colby’s wager that Moscow could be peeled from Beijing — a clean pivot to Asia, Europe demoted to distraction — a theory that presumed a Putin shopping for alignment[1](#footnote-1). The Putin who exists shops for survival. Moscow sank deeper into Beijing’s orbit. China acquired a dependent, not a weapon.

The flaw, in Iran as in Russia, is identical: abstraction over agency. Pivot to Asia, wage war in the Middle East. Avoid regime change, remove regimes. The theory is always cleaner than the autocrat.

---

Separately, Trump referred to Z yesterday as [P.T. Barnum](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/116165640188665672) — for the second time. Barnum was a 19th-century circus pioneer and professional hoaxer; the reference requires a specific cultural literacy that Kyiv does not possess, which may be the point. Trump has previously called Z “the greatest salesman on Earth.” The escalation in contempt tracks the escalation in strategic irrelevance. Ukraine was always the thing Colby’s Asia pivot needed to leave behind. It is being left behind. The salesman has become the clown.

---

Iran can be degraded militarily. That is not the question. The question is whether a republic that generates polarization without algorithms and wages war without authorization can sustain the discipline great-power competition requires.

Colby wanted to husband resources. The resources are definitely not in Ukraine.

The strategies promised limits. The limits reside in the archive, filed under lessons learned, beside the previous lessons learned, beside the ones before those.

The current catastrophe will produce more documents. They will be very clear. They will promise restraint.

## Day 1472

2026-03-06 · Children and coordinates

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5cdb5918-b30f-46af-936d-d2df7eb323d2_2400x1200.webp)  
*This photo, released by the Iranian government's foreign media department and distributed by the AP without changes, shows graves being prepared for the victims, mostly children, of a Feb. 28 Israeli–U.S. strike at a girls’ elementary school in Minab, Iran, seen on March 2, 2026. Photo: Iranian Foreign Media Department via AP*

Tomas, the surgeon in *The Unbearable Lightness of Being*, knew from the resistance of tissue under the knife exactly where he was. This knowledge was not innate. It was the residue of ten thousand operations — ten thousand moments in which the hand learned what the eye could not see.

When Tomas was certain, it was because he had spent years being unsure.

This is one kind of confidence. *Einmal ist keinmal*.

There is another kind — the confidence of the man who has read about surgery and found it straightforward. This kind is not diminished by failure. If anything, failure improves it, because failure is always someone else’s instrument.

Pete Hegseth stood before the cameras at U.S. Central Command headquarters in Tampa — six days into Operation Epic Fury — and [explained that America was winning decisively](https://www.timesofisrael.com/hegseth-iran-is-toast-and-the-us-and-israel-will-rain-down-death-and-destruction/).

Iran is toast.

Its navy rested at the bottom of the Persian Gulf. Its air force, built for 1996, had been destroyed in 2026. Its ballistic missiles — the ones not yet buried deep enough — were being hunted by B-2 bombers dropping 2,000-pound penetrator bombs. The next phase, he said, would raze the missile industrial base entirely.

The throttle was going up.

Pick your adjective: violent, decimated, most-lethal, savage.

We are punching them while they’re down, which is exactly how it should be.

Our timeline, he said, is ours and ours alone to control.

It was, by any measure, a confident briefing.

Werner Heisenberg, who was a better pianist than a prose stylist, understood something about instruments that Hegseth has not yet had occasion to consider.

If you wish to observe an electron, you might bounce a photon off it and detect what returns. But the photon, in striking, imparts momentum to the electron and changes the path of the thing you were trying to measure. Or the electron, moving as quantum particles do, is no longer where it was when the photon first bounced.

Either way, the act of observation alters what was being observed.

You cannot know both where the particle is and where it is going. This is not a failure of technology. It is not a problem better instruments will eventually solve.

It is a condition of reality.

Kant saw this before quantum mechanics gave it a name. The thing-in-itself — the *Ding an sich* — is not available to us directly. We know only what our instruments can reach. Heisenberg formalized it: measurement disturbs the thing measured. Borges turned it into a fable — a map so detailed it becomes the same size as the territory, and therefore useless.

Three centuries, three disciplines, one problem.

The distance between the knower and the known is not an inconvenience to be engineered away. It is the condition that makes knowledge possible in the first place.

Erase it entirely — let the map become the territory — and you do not achieve perfect knowledge.

You achieve the blindness of the man who has confused his picture for the world.

Hegseth’s briefing contained thousands of words. Humility occupied none of them.

*The most-lethal, most-precise aerial operation in history. Our timeline is ours and ours alone to control.*

These are not the words of a man who has considered the gap between the picture and the thing. They are the words of a man who has not been asked to.

**The map is never the territory.**

Coordinates programmed in 2013 do not know that a sports field was added in 2014, that recreational areas appeared over time, that children were sitting at desks on a Saturday morning — which in Iran is the first day of the working week.

[On February 28, a precision strike hit the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/05/world/middleeast/iran-school-us-strikes-naval-base.html), near the Strait of Hormuz. At least 175 people were killed, many of them children.

The school had once been part of the Revolutionary Guards’ naval base. By September 2016 it had been partitioned off, no longer connected by road, bearing by then all the hallmarks of a school — a sports field, recreational areas added over time.

A former Pentagon adviser, reviewing the satellite imagery, called the strike picture perfect.

Asked about the school, Hegseth said: we’re investigating that. We of course never target civilian targets.

The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, was more precise: not that we know of.

U.S. military investigators now believe it is likely that American forces were responsible, though they have not reached a final conclusion. The investigation has largely answered itself while Hegseth is still calling it an investigation.

This is not exactly a lie.

It is the genuine belief of a man whose instrument does not include, in its field of measurement, the possibility that the picture might be wrong.

Tomas knew the picture could be wrong. That knowledge is what made him a surgeon rather than simply a man holding a knife.

I am writing from Kyiv, where we have some experience with picture-perfect strikes and the investigations that follow them.

On July 8, 2024, a Kh-101 cruise missile struck the Okhmatdyt National Children’s Hospital. The missile was programmed using predetermined coordinates, which the Ukrainian Prosecutor General says indicates the deliberate nature of the strike.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/73446ed5-0ddf-4576-b0c7-6d239f8cdc44_1280x853.jpeg)  
*Okhmadyt Hospital, Kyiv Ukraine (July 8, 2024, photo c/o State Emergency Service)*

A thirty-year-old doctor named Svitlana Lukianchyk was killed. The dialysis ward, where children received treatment, was obliterated.

It cannot be rebuilt.

This week Ukrainian law enforcement served Russian Major General Sergei Kuvaldin with [a notice of suspicion in absentia](https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/03/04/8023813/). He issued the combat order. He is currently in Russia.

Measures are being taken.

Measures are always being taken.

Milan Kundera’s great theme was the weight of the irreversible. *Once is never*, because what happens once might as well not have happened at all.

But the heavy things cannot be taken back.

The coordinates cannot be unprogrammed. The school cannot be unstruck. The dialysis ward cannot be unbuilt from rubble.

The Minab instrument was working from old imagery. Kuvaldin’s instrument was working from malice.

The origins were different.

The children were the same.

Outside Minab, excavators dug nearly a hundred small graves before the funerals.

There is a notice of suspicion. There is an investigation. There is a press secretary who said *not that we know of*.

These are the instruments that arrive after the picture-perfect strike — when the picture is examined and found, with some embarrassment, to have been taken ten years ago.

Heisenberg would have recognized the situation.

The electron was no longer where the photon expected it to be. The school was no longer what the coordinates remembered.

The observation changed nothing about the thing observed, because the thing observed was already gone — replaced, over years, by children and a sports field and a Saturday morning the instrument did not know about and did not ask.

The uncertainty principle does not excuse the measurement.

It demands more care in the taking of it.

The strike was picture perfect.

The picture was ten years old.

Somewhere, a general is in Russia.

Somewhere, a secretary of war is returning to the cameras.

Our timeline, he will tell us, is ours and ours alone to control.

## Week in Review

2026-03-07 · Day 1468 to Day 1472

The problem:

The last piece I published this week began with a surgeon and ended with a general in Russia. In between, I tried to trace what happens when the instrument of knowledge loses contact with the thing it claims to know — and what it costs when no one in the room notices, or cares.

Borges and Kundera arrived in that piece not as decoration but as diagnosis. They are part of the same tradition — Central European and Latin American literary thought — that took epistemological humility as its central moral commitment. The idea that the gap between what we know and what is actually there is not a technical problem to be solved but a condition to be honored. Both wrote from positions of political precarity. Both understood, from direct experience, what happens when power decides it has closed that gap.

The filiation between them is not often traced explicitly, but it runs deep. Borges came first. His fable of the map that becomes the territory appeared in 1946, in a story barely longer than a paragraph. The empire that builds the perfect map is not made wiser by it. It is made helpless. The map rots in the desert alongside the territory it claimed to describe.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f3b8726b-5eb6-4543-9e37-f883040658ef_673x408.png)

Kundera, writing three decades later from the ruins of the Prague Spring, was working a related seam. His great theme — lightness versus weight, the irreversibility of the real against the consoling fiction that things might have been otherwise — is in some sense an extension of the Borgesian problem into lived political history. For Borges, the danger was the map that replaced the territory. For Kundera, the danger was the ideological certainty that replaced the ambiguous, irreducible particular — the individual life, the specific body, the child in the dialysis ward.

Kundera had another word for it: kitsch. **The aesthetic of certainty.** The refusal of ambiguity. The brass band that plays over the graves. Kitsch, he wrote, is the absolute denial of shit — by which he meant the irreducible remainder, the thing that does not fit the picture, the dialysis machine in the rubble, the sports field that appeared on the satellite image too late. The briefing room is a kitsch environment. It is designed to be. The maps are clean, the arrows are decisive, the adjectives are superlative. Most-lethal. Most-precise. Picture perfect.

I should have included Vasyl Bykov in the piece, and I didn’t. I knew him in Belarus — the last of the great Soviet-era writers who refused the Soviet consolation, who kept returning to the particular weight of the particular man in the particular frozen field. Bykov’s soldiers do not die for abstractions. They die in the mud, in the dark, having made a wrong turn or trusted the wrong person or simply run out of time. *Sign of Misfortune* (1982) and *To Live Till Sunrise* (1973) are not war novels in the heroic sense. They are novels about the catastrophic distance between the map — the order, the objective, the ideological justification — and the territory, which is cold and does not care about justifications.

Bykov belongs in the same line of filiation as Borges and Kundera, though the three never occupied the same literary conversation and would have made awkward dinner companions. What they share is the insistence that the irreducible particular — the body, the face, the specific moment of dying — cannot be abstracted away without moral catastrophe. For Borges the catastrophe is epistemological. For Kundera it is political. For Bykov it is military, and the mud is real, and he knew because he was in it, along with Valentyn Taras, [whose recollections of the underground](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sgfy9lans1s), documented by Alexander rounded out my understanding of the mess. Alexander, as I recall, [got the boot right](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/russian/reports/belarus/1997/august/topic2a.html) after me.

Had my favorite philosopher Daniel Dennett still been alive, I would have brought him in as well. His framework of physical, design, and intentional stances maps cleanly onto the problem. A targeting system takes the intentional stance toward a building: it treats the structure as having a function, a purpose, a place in a military design. That stance is what makes it targetable. What it cannot do, by definition, is take the physical stance toward the children inside — to see them as particular bodies, with particular weights, in particular seats, on a particular Saturday morning. The targeting system is not evil. It is something more dangerous: correct within its own framework and blind outside it.

I thought about all of this talking to an old friend from Minsk this week — Sergei Grits, the AP photographer, who materialized in Kyiv recently. We talked about the briefings, about the satellite imagery, about picture-perfect strikes. He told me about Basrah in 2003, shooting on streets so hot the air bent. His local fixer kept fifty meters of distance from him at all times. Not because he didn’t trust Sergei. Because he understood, with a precision that no targeting system has yet replicated, that the man with the AP camera was a different kind of coordinate — one that attracted a different kind of attention — and that fifty meters might be the difference between the map and the territory, between the picture and the thing.

That fixer was doing applied epistemology in real time. He understood, with the clarity that comes only from skin in the game, the difference between the picture and the thing.

Between the picture and the thing: a bullet between his eyes.

---

Which brings me to Russia’s strikes on Ukrainian cities, and the difference — important, clarifying, and finally irrelevant to the dead — between the American precision I wrote about this week and what I have watched from Kyiv’s streets.

The American strikes on Minab were, in the technical sense, precise. The school was hit because the instrument said it was a target. The instrument was wrong, but the aim was accurate. That is the Borgesian pathology: the map was perfect; the territory had moved on.

Russia’s strikes on Ukrainian cities are not precise. They are deliberately, programmatically, almost aesthetically imprecise. I know this because I have watched them from what locals call the mystic triangle — a stretch of Kyiv that has absorbed more than its share of incoming, for reasons that remain, to put it generously, unclear. The Kh-101 that hit Okhmatdyt did not go astray. The Shahed drones that circle in the dark over residential blocks are not malfunctioning. The pattern, observed over months and years, is not the pattern of a military force trying to hit military targets and occasionally missing. It is the pattern of a force that has decided the civilian is the target, and is working outward from there.

This is the inversion of the American problem. Hegseth’s instrument is too confident in an outdated picture. Kuvaldin’s instrument knows exactly what it is looking at and strikes anyway.

Bykov understood both failure modes. His officers are sometimes incompetent and sometimes malicious, and the men under them die either way. What he never allowed his readers was the comfort of clean categories — this death was a mistake, that one was a crime. The mud does not organize itself into legal distinctions. The mothers of Minab and the mothers of Kyiv are not waiting for the relevant jurisdiction to reach a finding.

Vasyl Bykov died in June 2003 — the same year Sergei Grits’s fixer was keeping his careful fifty meters on the streets of Basrah.

The mud, as always, did not care about the timing.

---

I subjected myself to considerable C-SPAN, Fox News, and Trey Yingst this week in the service of understanding the current grammar of American military jingoism. It is a specific dialect — confident, present-tense, passive when convenient. Mistakes are investigated. Responsibility is pending. The throttle is always going up.

Next week I will turn back to Ukraine’s ruling elites, who have their own complicated relationship with the gap between the map and the territory — less bellicose than Tampa, more Byzantine, and in some ways more dispiriting for being so close to home.

## Day 1475

2026-03-09 · Deus Vult (contd)

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/48909d6c-672d-4c0d-8110-e7cceaa3a930_4192x947.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (March 9, 2026)*

There is a famous problem in the science of causality. A rooster crows every morning just before sunrise. Day after day the correlation is perfect — more reliable, frankly, than most things in this world.

And yet we do not say the rooster causes the sun to rise.

We understand, somehow, that the rooster is merely listening to the light gathering on the horizon. He is downstream of events he did not author.

Judea Pearl, who has spent much of his life teaching machines how to reason about cause and effect, says the real question is not what correlates with what. The real question is: **what listens to what[1](#footnote-1)**.

It sounds simple. It is not simple. Most of the world’s institutions — governments, militaries, morning television — are organized around the confusion between these two things.

Which brings us, naturally, to Pete Hegseth.

Here is a man who observed, over many years, a reliable correlation: appearing on Fox News in a state of theatrical agitation produced, reliably, the approval of one particular viewer in Florida.

The rooster crowed.  
The sun rose.  
The rooster concluded he was in command of the heavens.

Now this rooster commands the heavens.

What has gone wrong with Team USA’s adventure in Iran is precisely a failure of causal reasoning at the highest level. There is a difference, Pearl would remind us, between observing that something happens and understanding what will happen if you intervene.

The second is harder.

It requires a diagram — arrows pointing from causes to effects — and the humility to ask: if I do this thing, what will the world look like afterward? Not in my imagination. In the world.

The performance at the Pentagon podium — “toast,” “punching them while they’re down,” the social-media reel scored with music from Gladiator — this is not strategic communication.

It is a man who learned that a certain kind of noise produces a certain kind of applause, and who has not yet discovered that the variables have changed.

He is running an old experiment in a new laboratory.

The barometer has been moved indoors, but he is still predicting rain.

Hegseth’s tattoos say *Deus vult* — God wills it[2](#footnote-2).

This is, in its way, the oldest and most confident causal claim in human history: the outcome is predetermined, the arrow points only forward, the diagram needs no revision.

The crusaders believed this too.

The diagram did not go especially well for them either — though the end took a long time, which is the other problem with confident causal diagrams.

Pearl also tells us that babies in their cribs are not pacified until they understand **why** the toy makes noise. They shake it, drop it, throw it. They are running experiments.

Human beings, he argues, are born with a craving for causal understanding. It is what distinguishes us from other animals, which are driven more simply by reward.

It is a charming theory.

Looking at Washington this week, one wonders about the sample size.

##### The Ukraine Jacket

The temptation to confuse correlation with causation is not confined to Washington.

Z has spent years discovering a reliable correlation: blunt public appeals and chest thumping are often followed, sooner or later, by weapons shipments and financial aid.

It is an understandable inference.

Last week, addressing the slow movement of a European support package reportedly worth around EUR 90 billion, Z warned that if a certain obstruction in Europe continued — widely understood to mean Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán — Ukrainian soldiers might be given the man’s address and encouraged to “call him and speak in their own language.[3](#footnote-3)”

It was meant as pressure.

But here again the arrows matter.

European aid is not produced by rhetoric alone. It emerges from a system of parliaments, coalitions, vetoes, and domestic politics — a machine considerably more complicated than a television audience.

When the rooster crows at the sun, the sun does not feel threatened.

Diplomacy is a slightly more delicate causal system.

Sometimes the rooster crows and the dawn arrives.

And sometimes the rooster discovers he was only ever listening.

## Day 1477

2026-03-11 · The Boys Who Ate the Mirror

Sigh.

---

I once heard about a man in Vilkhivets — though perhaps it was not Vilkhivets; perhaps it was Yakhny; my neighbor from Semihory told the story, and he had the habit of knowing everyone — who spent several years in his youth stealing goats.

He was not, by temperament, a thief.

My neighbor from Semihory said he was simply a young man with an unusual amount of moral energy and nowhere particular to put it. The goats, in this sense, were incidental.

When he stopped stealing goats, he did not simply stop. He became, with the same enormous energy, a passionate opponent of goat theft.

He gave speeches.  
He wrote pamphlets.  
He visited schools.

He could describe, in devastating detail, the psychology of the goat thief, the social conditions that produce such a person, the algorithmic pathways by which an impressionable youth encounters his first stolen goat and discovers — to his surprise — that it feels like solidarity.

The schools found him very impressive. He had, after all, been there.

My neighbor from Semihory observed that this man knew more about goat theft than anyone alive, and understood it less than almost anyone — and that these two facts were not unconnected.

---

#### I. On the Interview as Genre

I raise this man only because I have been watching, with the mild fascination one gives a persistent weather system, the career of a young Irish influencer and vlogger who works in Ukraine and interviews presidents on camera while air raid sirens sound tastefully in the background.

The interview in question lasts approximately twenty-two minutes.

In the first two of these minutes the influencer explains to us — and incidentally to Z, who is present — what the interview will be about, why it matters, and what the world is currently experiencing.

Z, who has been experiencing the world rather intensively for several years, waits with the patience of a man who has learned to wait for many things.

It is a feature of a certain kind of vlogging that the vlogger’s presence in a place becomes the news.

Not: what is happening here.  
But rather: I am here, observing what is happening, and I have feelings about it.

The war becomes a backdrop.  
The backdrop becomes atmosphere.  
The atmosphere becomes — and here a small alchemy occurs — a credential.

“How does that feel?” the vlogger asks, when the siren sounds.

It is a question of some metaphysical ambition.

One imagines Z briefly considering the entire catalogue of what he feels: the particular weight of responsibility, the calculus of acceptable losses, the memory of his children’s faces when he last saw them, the specific texture of fatigue that is not tiredness but something older.

Then he says, with the brevity of a man who has learned that honesty and completeness are not the same thing:

“I don’t have too much time to feel.”

It is, as answers go, a complete essay.

The influencer moves on to the next question.

---

#### II. On the Redemption Arc, and Its Maintenance Costs

The influencer’s story, which he tells with practiced fluency, is genuinely interesting.

A gay boy from Kilkenny.  
A Catholic school.  
A migration to London in search of tolerance.  
An encounter instead with men who preferred him out of their neighborhood.  
A mass shooting in Orlando.  
A YouTube search.

And then — the particular horror of the modern world — a recommendation engine that knows what you are looking for before you know it yourself.

He spent three years making videos for people who were, by his later account, building toward real-world violence.

He left.  
He recovered.

He now makes videos about those people, explaining how they work.

Which is to say: he makes videos with the same urgency, the same production values, the same millions of views, the same essential grammar of civilizational threat — only the villain has changed.

The villain is now more straightforwardly villainous, which makes everything much more comfortable.

A man who has changed his cause has not necessarily changed his method.  
He has merely found better material.

He received, recently, an award: the Honorary Ambassador of Ukraine Award for Digital Diplomacy, issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and supported by the president’s wife.

“I’m so proud,” he said while accepting it, “to be able to show the resilience of Ukraine and tell the truth about what this incredible country represents.”

I do not mock this sentiment.

I mock only its texture, which is the texture of a press release rearranged into the first person.

“Show the resilience.”  
“Tell the truth.”  
“This incredible country.”

These phrases mean everything in general and refer to nothing in particular. They are the verbal equivalent of a flag — all color and flutter, the flag itself never explaining what it is planted in.

There is a Ukrainian word, or so I am told by people who know Ukrainian, for the feeling of hospitality that persists even in terrible circumstances.

Z speaks of it at the end of the interview, haltingly, with the grammar of a man translating from a language that does not translate.

It is the most alive moment in twenty-two minutes of footage.

The influencer thanks him and calls it amazing.

---

#### III. On the Comfortable Comparison

Around the sixteenth minute, as reliably as a clock striking the hour, the vlogger raises Hitler.

Fascists use sport to cover up their crimes.  
The 1936 Olympics.  
We know the end of Hitler.  
We understand the end of Putin.

Z agrees, as he must.

The influencer agrees with Z agreeing with him.

One has the impression of two men standing before a mirror, each gesturing toward the reflection of the other.

The Hitler comparison is not wrong, exactly.

It is something more troubling than wrong: it is correct in ways that make thinking unnecessary.

Once you have said Hitler, the thinking stops.  
The emotion begins.  
The camera — which has been waiting for this — leans in.

And the influencer, who has spent years studying how extremist videos achieve their emotional effects, deploys those effects with the confidence of a man who has discovered that a technique is not made innocent by its new employer.

*My neighbor from Semihory would probably have said that the only real difference between a former propagandist and a current one is the direction in which the wind happens to be blowing.*

---

#### IV. What My Neighbor from Semihory Would Have Said

My neighbor from Semihory, who distrusted anyone with a clean conscience, would have liked the influencer well enough.

He would have noted that the vlogger is not stupid, not cynical in any simple way, not indifferent to the suffering he films.

He would have noted that the war is real, the drones are real, the dead are real, and that any camera pointed honestly at any of it performs a service.

But he would also have noted — pouring a second glass and settling back — that there exists a type of person for whom belief is not a position but a metabolism.

Such a person does not choose causes.  
He processes them.

The far-right was a cause.  
Ukraine is a cause.

Both causes produce the same heat, the same output, the same sensation of being — at last — on the right side of something enormous.

The only difference is that one cause was monstrous and the other is just.

Justice, my neighbor from Semihory would have said, does not automatically improve the character of those who are enthusiastic about it.

The goat thief, after all, was genuinely against goat theft.

This was not the problem.

The problem was that he loved the feeling of being against something more than he loved the goats.

The influencer, to his credit, is in Ukraine. He is not filing from a hotel bar in Warsaw or a comfortable desk in West London.

He has been sanctioned by the Russian government and issued with a warrant for his arrest, which is, in its way, an honest review.

He has done things that are difficult and some things that are brave.

And yet — here my neighbor from Semihory would pause, tilting his glass toward the light — the camera follows him through all of it, and the camera’s eye is always, at some angle, admiring.

Not the war.  
Not even Z, who is — if you read the transcript carefully — a genuinely complex and melancholy man trying to explain something true in a second language to someone who has already written the caption.

The camera admires the vlogger admiring the war.

This is a small thing.  
Perhaps even a forgivable thing.

But it is not quite journalism.

My neighbor from Semihory would have said that it resembles something else: the man who travels very far to visit a holy place and then spends the rest of the evening explaining the journey.
