## Day 1478

2026-03-12 · Cards. Chess. Clowns. But Never Wrestling.

*A digression on open cards, closed minds, and the peculiar confidence of people in rooms.*

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/583b7530-58b6-4e8a-8262-961a83beb9af_1408x768.jpeg)  
*Illustration by Gemini 3 Flash / Nano Banana 2*

Yesterday I wrote about a man who looks into a mirror and sees, reflected back, the precise image of himself he had always hoped to find. The mirror, in this case, happened to be a camera[1](#footnote-1).

Today I want to write about another kind of mirror — the one that appears in rooms with mild hallucinogens and people of, as they say, *unlimited capabilities*, where everyone agrees so completely that the agreement itself becomes the most frightening thing in the room.

These rooms are full of metaphors. Cards are common. Drones buzz around oil barrels.

What almost never appears is wrestling.

I was told about such a gathering recently. The topic was the war in the Middle East. The consensus, reached with what my informant described as *paradoxical and alarming unanimity*, was this: Trump does not want a long war, therefore the war will end quickly. Two weeks, perhaps. Two months at the outside. Probably two weeks.

What struck me was not the conclusion but the reasoning. Everyone in the room had decided that Trump holds the situation like a deck of cards — that he can play them or withhold them at will, and that the game ends when he chooses to end it. The only debate concerned what he would settle for when he laid down his hand: an actual deal, or what my informant beautifully called **“self-declaration of victory”** — the art of pointing at rubble and announcing that the rubble was the plan all along.

Cards are useful instruments — in card games.

Over a lifetime of watching powerful men make confident predictions, I have noticed that the metaphor most often invoked in these rooms is always the one that flatters the man holding it.

There is, it seems to me, a better metaphor. It has been hiding in plain sight in the Oval Office.

The president, it was reported last week, has developed a habit of gifting close advisers pairs of his favourite loafers — a brown Florsheim, $145, paid for from his own pocket[2](#footnote-2). The ritual proceeds as follows: the president guesses the recipient’s shoe size out loud, in front of them. A week later, a brown box arrives. Sometimes the president has signed it. The recipient wears the shoes. Everyone, as one White House official put it, is afraid not to.

The Vice President wears them. The Secretary of State wears them. The Secretary of the Treasury, Commerce, Energy, the Special Envoy to the Middle East — all of them in matching loafers, in Davos, discussing the fate of nations.

A photograph of Secretary Rubio has been circulating. In it, his heel floats visibly above the back of the shoe. The president guessed wrong. The shoes are being worn anyway.

This is not mockery. The loafers are decent shoes. The generosity appears genuine.

But the ritual contains, in miniature, the logic of the moment: the strong man names the size, the box arrives, and the question of whether it fits is not one the recipient is in a position to raise.

This works well enough when the recipient is the Secretary of State. It works less well when the recipient is Iran, which did not apply for the position, has not accepted the box, and has been forming its own views about shoe sizes since 1979.

Z has solved the costume problem differently. Since the early days of the invasion he has worn, almost without variation, black tactical clothing — the costume of a man who has decided what the story is and intends to remain inside it. It is a clever solution. The clothing makes the argument so the man does not have to.

Interviewers arrive — our vlogger among them, air-raid siren on cue — and find themselves already inside a frame Z has built. The clothing says: this is a war, I am a soldier, you are a visitor. Most interviewers accept the premise.

Trump’s people wear whatever shoes they are given. Z wears the same thing every day. Both are costumes. Both make claims about who controls the story. The difference is that Z chose his own.

The deeper problem is that everyone is still speaking inside Trump’s metaphor.

Trump once declared that Z had **no cards** to play against Russia. It was a bully’s metaphor: the strong man naming the game, setting the table, deciding what counts as a hand. Z eventually adopted it himself. Analysts adopted it as well, because once a metaphor enters circulation the mind reaches for it automatically.

But what is happening in the Gulf is not poker.

It is wrestling.

More precisely: **Greco-Roman wrestling.**

The version where you may not attack the legs. Only the upper body. Only the clinch. Points accumulate slowly — throws, exposures, turns. A match ends either by pin or by **technical superiority**: an eight-point lead and the referee stops the contest immediately.

Between serious wrestlers the pin is rare. What is common is the grind — the patience of someone who knows the clock runs when the clock runs.

There is no bluffing in Greco-Roman wrestling. Only who lets go first.

Which is why the men in that room were also wrong about the clock.

A Greco-Roman match runs two periods of three minutes each. The analysts assumed the war would follow a similar format: short periods, predictable ending.

But the Iranians never agreed to the format.

They have not signed the scorecard. They are not entirely sure they received the memo about the three-minute periods. Iran also happens to be one of the great wrestling nations on earth — Olympic champions, a sport woven into national identity.

If you are going to set a wrestling clock against Iran, it is worth asking whether your opponent has done this before.

The Americans are not winning by eight points. The match has not ended early. The periods are still running.

The Iranians — and beside them, quietly, the Russians and Chinese — can see Trump’s hand perfectly well. They know he is time-limited. They know the American electoral calendar the way a chess player knows the edge of the board.

Their counter-move is simple.

Wait.  
Endure.  
Let the clock run out.

Because the wrestling-clock theory assumes the other side has agreed to wrestle.

But a regime that has survived forty years of sanctions, assassinations, proxy wars, and repeated American attention is not a three-minute-period operation. The ayatollahs are not running a quarterly earnings call. They are running — or believe themselves to be running — something considerably longer.

Which means that if the clock theory is wrong — if the buzzer does not sound when expected — then the men in the room with unlimited capabilities have mistaken the story they prefer for the story that is actually happening.

My informant wrote his assessment on day eleven of the American invasion[3](#footnote-3). He did not hedge. Trump, he wrote, cannot leave the Gulf gracefully without Iranian help.

That same week, Bill Clinton said almost exactly the same thing into a microphone[4](#footnote-4).

Clinton, who once kept the Fifth Fleet in Bahrain specifically to keep the Strait of Hormuz open, explained the mechanism. Iran did not close the Strait with a blockade. They launched a handful of drone strikes nearby, and the global insurance industry withdrew coverage. Tankers do not sail without insurance. An insurance crisis shut down the most important energy corridor on earth.

Every serious strategist in Washington, Clinton said, knew this was the lever Iran would pull.

Which raises a simple question: if everyone knew it, why does it look so much like nobody planned for it?

Clinton mentioned the Development Finance Corporation’s proposed insurance workaround. It has a limited budget, slow approvals, and legal constraints never designed to insure maritime commerce through a war zone.

As one analyst put it — a line Clinton quoted with some appreciation — *boats are going to sink.*

That is not a strategy. It is an afterthought.

My informant saw the problem from London. Clinton saw it from the vantage point of a former president watching events unfold. Two men, two rooms, same week, same conclusion.

The wrestling clock, it turns out, had no buzzer.

Or rather: the buzzer exists, but the Iranians are not listening for it, because they never agreed to the format.

I am not a man of unlimited capabilities, and I was not in the room. I am simply reading two texts — one written in London by the Russian legal scholar Volodymyr Pastukhov and one spoken in America by Bill Clinton — and noticing that they arrive at identical conclusions by entirely different routes.

The men in the room reached their consensus the usual way. They began with what they wanted to be true — the war will be short, Trump will find an exit, the clock will buzz — and then constructed the reasoning that supports it.

The mistake was simple: assuming everyone else had agreed to the same rules.

The rules of the shoe box.  
The rules of the card game.  
The rules of the wrestling format.

Their unanimity was not the unanimity of evidence. It was the unanimity of preference dressed as analysis.

This is not unusual. It is how political thinking works in most rooms.

The difference is that the preferred stories of powerful people have larger consequences when they turn out to be wrong.

Clinton knows this.  
Pastukhov knows this.  
The Iranians, one suspects, have known it longest of all.

My neighbour from Semihory, had he been present, would have repacked his pipe, inhaled thoughtfully, and asked a single question.

**What if the Iranians never agreed to the format?**

It occurred to me later that nobody in that room had ever wrestled an Iranian.

This may not seem important, but in certain contests nothing else matters as much.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

[Yesterday's piece](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1477) — on the Irish vlogger, the air raid siren, the twenty-two minutes — was apparently also reviewed by a Ukrainian commentator named [Viktor Bobyrenko](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9tzQxcNn0j4&t=62s), who reached the same conclusion by shorter means. Z, Bobyrenko observed, cannot face his own press, which asks inconvenient questions. So he gives interviews to vloggers. To this vlogger specifically. The interview was strange, wild, and frightening: large alarming claims about Russia sending weapons to Iran, none connected to reality. The main achievement was distraction — the Hungarian scandal, the generals who moonlight as couriers, the price of petrol. For this, a sufficiently large cloud of nonsense will do. The interviewer was not a journalist. He was a weather system. One raises this because there is something clarifying about two people — one writing in English from some distance, one speaking in Ukrainian from inside the thing — arriving independently at the same image. The cloud was the point. The vlogger made the cloud. Z next sat down with [a proctologist from Politico](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c4kLBTVudSM&t=373s). Equally moronic. I don’t have the energy to write about it.

## Day 1479

2026-03-13 · Maintained incapacity

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/08dc4797-fc8e-4248-8e28-abfcd98c3657_960x1280.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o Veronika (March 13, 2026)*

It is Friday again, and there is a great deal I did not write about this week. I did not write about mitochondrial function, about what twenty-five years of regular running does to the cell, about the inner membrane folds that multiply with training until the surface area for generating energy is, in the language of the researchers, dramatically enhanced. I did not write about Kilian Jornet, who posted [a short video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EXjH3nG8hJU) last week announcing his racing plans for 2026 — Western States, Sierre-Zinal, UTMB — from what appears to be a very old house with a leaking roof, which he likes precisely because it leaks. *If everything is easy,* he said, standing in it, *you get too comfortable. Making things not comfortable is important.* He is forty-one years old. His mitochondria, the researchers would tell you, are in better condition than those of most men half his age.

The running season started two weeks ago. I have been wondering, as I do each year, how long it will take the organelle to snap back into shape — how many weeks of patient z1 work before the machinery remembers what it is for. This is a small and private preoccupation, familiar to readers of this newsletter who have followed my perhaps excessive interest in becoming, if not a better person, at least a better athlete. How one pursues this in a genocidal war, with interrupted sleep and a diet governed by what the shops have and what the power allows one to cook, is a subject for another Friday.

Today I am less concerned with my own mitochondria than with those of the men currently directing Ukraine’s war and American foreign policy.

---

The mitochondrion — to briefly inconvenience the reader with biology — is the organelle responsible for converting oxygen and fuel into energy. [Nick Lane](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zn7bCggQCtQ), professor of evolutionary biochemistry at University College London and author of *Transformer: The Deep Chemistry of Life and Death*, describes what is happening inside it with a precision that is also, somehow, a kind of poetry: we are stripping the electrons out of food, passing them into respiration, passing them on to oxygen to produce water as a waste product. We are, in his phrase, burning hydrogen in oxygen. That is what is powering us. The Krebs cycle — the strange loop of reactions at the heart of this process — is what makes it possible. And what ageing does, Lane notes, is make that cycle slow. The respiration runs down. Instead of burning hydrogen to generate energy, the cycle loses its spin. The intermediates that once built the molecules of life begin to behave differently. The cell, still nominally alive, is running on something closer to memory than metabolism.

*One thinks, in this context, of several people.*

Long-term endurance training counteracts this. It increases both the number and the density of mitochondria in muscle cells. It stimulates the removal of damaged mitochondria and the growth of new ones. Master athletes — older runners with decades of consistent training — carry unique mitochondrial proteins not observed in sedentary people of the same age. The researchers call this maintained capacity. The rest of us call it being able to do hard things without falling apart.

Secretary Hegseth, who has been conducting press briefings on Operation Epic Fury with the confidence of a man who has never had occasion to doubt his instruments, does not appear to be a man who has spent twenty-five years doing hard things in order to find out what he is made of. He appears to be a man who has spent twenty-five years telling us what he is made of, which is a different kind of fitness entirely.

It produces a certain fluency.  
A certain ease in front of cameras.  
A certain capacity for the declarative sentence.

It does not, as far as the available evidence suggests, produce many mitochondria.

> *[A related data point](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/03/11/hegseth-press-briefings-photos-iran/), for those keeping records. On March 2nd, Hegseth appeared at the Pentagon briefing room podium for the first time since June — days after the joint strike on Iran that killed Ayatollah Khamenei. Press photographers from the Associated Press, Reuters, and Getty Images were present. They published their photographs, as photographers do. Members of Hegseth’s staff reviewed the images and found them, in the language of two people familiar with the decision, “unflattering.” Photographers were barred from the two subsequent briefings, on March 4th and March 10th. Only the Defense Department’s own staff photographers have been permitted in since. The Pentagon press secretary explained that the department was “using space effectively.” The National Press Photographers Association noted that excluding photographers because officials disliked how they looked in published images was, for a public servant, “not a good look.” One raises this not to mock the secretary’s vanity, exactly, but to observe: a man who has genuinely found out what he is made of tends, over time, to become less concerned with how he appears in photographs. The mitochondria, if maintained, provide a certain equanimity about these things.*

Z is a more complicated case.

Two years into the war, performing at a festival in Jūrmala, Latvia, he stood on a stage and described Ukraine’s condition with the unsentimental accuracy of a man who had not yet decided to be its president:

> *«Україна, якщо чесно, між нами, нагадує актрису з німецьких фільмів для дорослих. Тобто, готова прийняти в будь-якій кількості з будь-якого боку. Якщо вам не шкода.»*

Ukraine, honestly, between us, resembles an actress from German adult films: ready to accept, in any quantity, from any side. If you don’t mind.

He later clarified that the joke was about financial dependence — the IMF, the creditors, the structural condition of a country that cannot say no because it cannot afford to. He was not wrong. He was merely, as it turned out, describing the metabolism he would one day inherit.

The black tactical gear arrived six years later. The condition did not depart with it.

The cell is still running. One watches the briefings, the summits, the appeals, and thinks: this is a man who once named the thing clearly, from the outside, and has since moved inside it — and cannot, from inside, name it anymore.

That is not cowardice. It may simply be what the costume costs.

Both men are in their mid-forties. Both are, by any observable measure, men of considerable output — press conferences, summits, appeals, declarations, briefings, tours of allied capitals in matching outfits. What neither of them appears to have is maintained capacity: the kind that comes not from being inside the story, but from having asked something genuinely hard of the body and the mind, repeatedly, over many years, without an audience. Hegseth has the cameras. Z has the gear. Between them, they have produced an extraordinary quantity of declarative sentences. The mitochondria, one suspects, are another matter.

---

> *A note, for completeness: the most-lethal, most-precise aerial operation in history, which Hegseth described from Tampa on day six with the composure of a man reading good news, has since been found by its own preliminary investigation to have directed a Tomahawk missile into an elementary school. The walls were blue and pink. The picture was ten years old. There are, officials emphasize, important unanswered questions.*

Kilian Jornet, in his leaking house, chose this year’s race calendar not because it was easy but because it was where the best competition was. He was sick at Western States last year and the execution wasn’t perfect. He intends to go back. This is what twenty-five years of accumulated mitochondrial adaptation looks like as a decision-making framework: you return to the hard thing, you find out what went wrong, and you try again. You do not hold a press conference announcing that the previous attempt was picture perfect.

*The organelle does not care about your confidence.  
It cares about what you have asked of it,  
and for how long.*

My neighbor from Semihory, who ran every morning until he was seventy-three and who distrusted all men who had never been seriously cold, would have had one question about the current leadership of the American defense establishment. Not about the school. Not about the piano. Not about the ten-year-old picture. He would have asked, quietly, while repacking his pipe: when did any of these men last do something that required them to find out what they were made of?

And then he would have waited, patiently, like a man whose mitochondria were, all things considered, in excellent condition.

## Day 1483

2026-03-17 · Proximity-based Cheese Grinding

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/bfe8afe5-873a-437c-8e93-4c36789d07eb_1408x768.jpeg)  
*Illustration by Gemini 3 Flash / Nano Banana 2*

**What Are They Actually Optimizing For?**

This year at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Z explained Europe to itself.

This happens from time to time. Europe, being large and somewhat self-conscious, often appreciates an external perspective on its own deficiencies. Z spoke about courage, about competence, about the dangers of hesitation. Europe listened, as Europe does, with a look that combines interest with mild surprise at being addressed in this tone.

It was, all things considered, an unusual [lecture](https://www.president.gov.ua/en/news/zvernennya-prezidenta-do-uchasnikiv-specialnogo-zasidannya-v-102517).

Ukraine, at that very moment, remained a country in which institutions functioned the way old houses do during a storm: they hold, but they creak. Top officials appeared in corruption investigations with a regularity that suggested not scandal so much as scheduling. Mobilization worked, though visibly. Procurement existed, though not always in a way that invited inspection.

But Davos is not a place for creaking houses. It is a place for clean sentences.

And so the sentences were clean.

Another forum. Another audience. Another careful redirection outward — toward people who cannot vote in Ukrainian elections but can influence the flow of weapons and money. Z rarely speaks to Ukrainian journalists. He speaks to fawning ones and foreign actors. The conversation inside the country — the one conducted under sirens, in kitchens, on Telegram channels of uncertain origin — proceeds largely without him.

This, too, is a kind of policy.

---

---

There is a certain type of man — one meets him in provincial theaters, occasionally in politics — who steps onto the stage and, for a moment, becomes indistinguishable from the role he is playing. He speaks clearly. He gestures well. The audience understands him immediately, which is not a small achievement.

The difficulty begins later, when the set must be dismantled and something real must be built in its place.

Trump is this kind of performer. Z, in a different register, is also this kind of performer.

One lectures allies about loyalty while loosening the threads that make loyalty possible. The other lectures partners about competence while presiding over institutions that visibly struggle to produce it.

The circumstances are not the same. The stakes are not the same.

The method, however, has a family resemblance.

Performance.

Performance is efficient. It travels. It compresses complexity into something that fits between advertisements. It produces applause, which is measurable, and headlines, which are even more so.

Reality does not travel as well. It prefers to remain where it is, accumulating consequences.

---

There is, in machine learning, a concept that would have been appreciated by certain Soviet administrators, had they encountered it at the right moment: the objective function.

It is not what the system claims to do. It is what the system, when observed patiently, actually does.

A factory may claim to produce shoes. If, over time, it produces only reports about shoes, then reports are its true output, and the rest is decoration.

Politics, too, produces outputs.

In Ukraine, official news is not optimized for the reader’s understanding. It is optimized for something simpler: the continued stability of Z’s position. Often these goals align, which allows everyone to proceed without discomfort. But alignment is not identity. When they diverge, one notices small absences. Then larger ones. Eventually one notices that certain questions no longer quite form in the mind.

This is not censorship in the theatrical sense. No one storms the stage. The script simply narrows.

---

It is a useful exercise, then, to ask — of any system, in any country:

What is it actually optimizing for?

Not what it says. What does it produce?

This week, the answer became easier to observe.

It did not flatter anyone.

---

Three weeks ago, the United States began striking Iran.

The operation was described, depending on the speaker, as limited, open-ended, decisive, precautionary, and, on one occasion, a “little excursion,” which has the advantage of sounding both temporary and optional.

Language, in such moments, becomes a kind of scaffolding. It allows one to move around the structure without quite touching it.

Money, however, has less patience for language. In two weeks, approximately $12 billion was spent. The Strait of Hormuz — that narrow, inconvenient fact of geography — became less navigable. Oil prices, obedient to physics rather than rhetoric, began to rise.

To calm the markets, sanctions on Russian oil were briefly lifted.

This produced an elegant arrangement: a war partially financed by the alleviation of pressure on the same system funding another war, which the same administration was attempting, in parallel, to conclude.

It is possible to describe this as contradiction. It is perhaps more accurate to describe it as consistency of a different kind.

---

At a certain point, one must listen not only to what is said, but to how often it changes.

Iran wants a deal. Iran does not want a deal. The terms are insufficient. The terms are unspecified. The leader may be alive. If he is alive, he should surrender.

Allies are invited to participate. Allies decline.

Officials promise timelines. Other officials, with the air of men who have seen timelines before, gently withdraw the promise.

At a press briefing, the defense secretary — a man who has spent years insisting on the primacy of war as both language and identity — described a particularly successful day of strikes. In the same conversation, he expressed a hope that a news network covering the war might soon come under more congenial ownership.

Not a complaint.

A preference.

In certain systems, preferences are more informative than statements.

---

A few days earlier, Z had offered a different kind of statement.

Ukraine, he said, had definitive proof that Russia had transferred drone technology and targeting intelligence to Iran — the same drones now shaping the conflict in the Gulf.

This was not entirely new information. It had, as they say, circulated. But it had not been placed, so directly, into the American conversation.

Russia is helping to kill your soldiers.

With familiar tools.

In a familiar way.

The response, from Washington, was that this detail was not, at present, a focus of attention.

Focus, like language, is an allocation problem.

---

Z went further. Ukraine, having spent several years learning how not to be destroyed by these drones, offered its expertise. Teams were dispatched. Techniques were demonstrated. The proposal was not dressed in sentiment.

Technology, in exchange for funding.

Experience, in exchange for relevance.

It was, in its way, refreshingly clear.

The response was also clear.

“We don’t need help.”

---

If one were inclined toward geometry, one might sketch the situation.

A country under attack develops a method of survival. Another country, newly engaged with the same method of attack, declines the offered solution. Meanwhile, the source of the method receives temporary economic relief to stabilize a third variable affected by the second country’s actions.

The lines do not intersect.

They run, neatly, in parallel.

---

This is not a disagreement in policy. It is not even, strictly speaking, a disagreement in priorities.

It is a set of systems, each pursuing its own objective function, producing outcomes that appear contradictory only if one assumes a shared goal.

Remove that assumption, and the contradictions resolve themselves.

---

Once one begins to look in this way, certain symmetries emerge.

Trump, for instance, does not optimize for strategy in the classical sense. Strategy implies subordination to an external objective. He optimizes for dominance within the immediate frame. The conversation itself is the territory. To concede dependence is to lose ground. To acknowledge assistance is to redraw the map in someone else’s favor.

And so assistance becomes unnecessary. Reporting becomes hostile. Ownership becomes a solution.

The system is internally coherent.

---

Now consider the other system.

While Z was explaining competence to Europe, Ukraine’s anti-corruption bureau was investigating a scheme inside Energoatom. Percentages were discussed. Contracts were arranged. Money moved with the quiet efficiency that money often displays when unobserved.

At the center of the network was a familiar figure: a longtime associate, a business partner, a man without formal office and therefore without formal constraints.

And, incidentally, a man connected to the structure that produces the national broadcast through which a significant portion of the country understands the war.

This is not, strictly speaking, unusual. Power tends to concentrate. Information tends to follow it.

Z responded correctly: support for investigators, dismissals, sanctions.

Correct responses, however, do not dismantle systems. They adjust them.

The broadcast continues. The access remains limited. The message retains its shape.

One might say: the house still creaks, but the facade has been repainted.

---

It is important, here, to resist the temptation of symmetry carried too far.

These situations are not equivalent. One country is fighting for survival. Another is managing its image of strength. The moral weight is not distributed evenly.

But methods have a way of resembling one another, even when purposes diverge.

And resemblance, once noticed, is difficult to unsee.

---

A recent study in Ukraine found something quietly interesting[1](#footnote-1).

People have become better at recognizing falsehood. They check sources more often. They identify manipulation with increasing skill.

At the same time, they trust less.

Fewer believe that the media reports what matters. Fewer believe it serves the public. Many assume, with a certain resignation, that it serves those who control it.

This is not confusion.

It is adaptation.

When the environment produces conflicting signals, the rational response is not certainty. It is caution.

---

There is a tendency to attribute this condition entirely to external influence. And external influence exists. It is persistent, well-funded, and often effective.

But one should not overlook the contribution of internal design.

If a system rewards alignment with power, it will produce alignment. If it constrains certain questions, those questions will diminish. Over time, the absence becomes normal.

The fog, in other words, does not require a single author.

It can be the collective output of many small decisions, each of which appears reasonable in isolation.

---

Democracy, like certain delicate mechanical devices, depends on tolerances.

Not agreement. Not harmony. Simply the shared assumption that reality exists independently of the mechanisms used to describe it.

When that assumption weakens, the device continues to function — for a time. The dials move. The readings change. But the connection to the underlying system becomes, gradually, unreliable.

At that point, performance becomes not merely an addition to governance, but a substitute for it.

---

And so we return, as these things often do, to the question of the objective function.

Observe long enough, and patterns emerge.

Not alliances. Not institutions. Not even, reliably, outcomes.

Presence.

Visibility.

Control of the frame.

---

Once this becomes apparent, a small shift occurs.

One stops asking whether the performance is persuasive.

One begins to ask what it is designed to obscure.

This is a less entertaining question.

It is also a more useful one.

---

There is, however, a modest consolation.

Under pressure, people learn. The proportion of those who accept information without question has declined. Verification, once a habit of specialists, becomes a general practice.

This does not solve the problem.

It changes the conditions under which the problem is experienced.

---

In the end, the prescription is neither technical nor novel.

Do not outsource your judgment. Not to systems. Not to narratives. Not even to those with whom you agree — especially not to those with whom you agree.

Thinking is uncomfortable. It always has been. But we now live in an age engineered to fill every pause, every idle moment, with something frictionless and immediate. The scroll doesn’t ask you to think. It thinks for you — confidently, at scale, in fifteen seconds.

So the competition isn’t really between good ideas and bad ones. It’s between ideas and the path of least resistance.

Ask a simple question: what are they actually optimizing for?

Then watch what they do. Not between notifications — just watch, for long enough that the answer becomes obvious.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

[Індекс медіаграмотності українців-2025](https://detector.media/infospace/article/248338/2026-03-15-indeks-mediagramotnosti-ukraintsiv-2025-korotka-prezentatsiya/) (*коротка презентація*, March 15, 2026)

## Day 1484

2026-03-18 · The Tube

*A digression on maps, boys, and the distance between Chernihiv and the Maidan*

———

On Monday morning, the air raid sirens over Kyiv did what they always do — they arrived before the understanding did. I was a couple blocks away when the debris began to fall on the Maidan, wreckage from drones that had traveled, in some cases, from as far as Chernihiv, strung out across the sky at 1,500 meters like a slow, determined procession. The Ukrainian air defense, which has grown very good at this, knocked most of them down. Many shots were fired. A few pieces made it through. No one was killed.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/43169873-c3d8-4665-8651-096a56fb6c31_1000x611.png)  
*Zala Lancet drone (Photo c/o Wikipedia )*

What made this attack weird — and strangely instructive — was what the drones were not. At least one was a Lancet, a weapon designed for close frontline work, with a combat range of 30 to 80 kilometers. EW expert Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov—appointed advisor to Ukraine’s new Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in January—[posited](https://t.me/serhii_flash/7118) that to reach Kyiv, the Russians had stripped out the warheads and replaced them with extra batteries, launching from the nearest possible point, waiting for a favorable wind. They were not, in any meaningful sense, trying to destroy anything. They were trying to produce a photograph, he said. A fragment on the Maidan. Something to show Putin. Something to show the Russian people. The whole elaborate operation — forty Lancets, a swarm of accompanying Shaheds carrying planted Lancet debris — was, at its core, a content strategy.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/78f68a6c-65ba-4418-a7bc-25c208ab08e9_1024x683.webp)  
*Fedorov and Flash (Photo c/o Defense Ministry of Ukraine )*

Wut? I thought about Serhiy’s dubious unsubstantiated wacko explanation for a long time afterward. About the distance between the weapon and its purpose. About a military that will spend enormously, and sacrifice real capability, for the appearance of a result.

And then I read about an American general, Antonio Aguto, who traveled here with a tube of maps, concluding that the explanation looks less like a reconstruction of events than an attempt to impose narrative order on uncertainty.

---

In a certain ministry, long before the war it would later explain, there was a briefing about small, cheap drones that did not return. They flew one way, like determined swallows, and ended their journey by exploding. The Ukrainians, who had already been living with such birds for years, spoke at length about them—about their cost, their numbers, their habit of arriving in flocks, and the curious arithmetic by which a machine worth $30,000 could compel the launch of a missile worth a hundred times more. The ministry listened carefully, thanked the Ukrainians, filed the presentation, and then prepared for a different war. When, some years later, those same one-way drones began to [visit American bases in the desert,](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/03/17/politics/drones-us-iran-war) the ministry was surprised—not by the drones themselves, which it had seen, but by their persistence, which it had not believed.

It is a particular habit of institutions to learn in detail and forget in practice, to study the future as if it were a foreign country whose customs need not be adopted at home.

General Aguto traveled to Kyiv [with a tube of maps so large they could not be folded](https://www.militarytimes.com/news/your-military/2026/03/16/army-general-left-classified-maps-on-a-train-in-poland-watchdog-finds/), only carried like a minor piece of artillery. Somewhere between [Kyiv and Wiesbaden](https://news.liga.net/en/society/news/pentagon-us-army-general-brought-classified-maps-to-ukraine-then-forgot-them-on-train), the tube remained behind on a train, as if it had decided, quite sensibly, to stay closer to the war than its owner. For twenty-four hours the maps belonged to no one, which is to say they belonged to everyone.

They were later returned—untouched, we are told. This word, *untouched*, is a comforting one. It suggests a kind of moral hygiene, as if secrets, like porcelain, can be inspected for fingerprints and declared intact. But a secret is not a teacup. It is more like a rumor: once it has had the opportunity to travel, it is already changed, even if it returns to you looking exactly as before.

The Americans, being practical people, opened an investigation. They discovered that no courier had been assigned, that responsibility had been diffused in the democratic manner of all modern bureaucracies, and that the general, being the senior man, accepted responsibility in the ceremonial sense—like a toast, or a wreath. The investigation also noted the general’s fatigue, including a night of overindulgence at [Tootsie Club](https://uk.tootsie.kiev.ua/) in Kyiv that left him disoriented for a meeting with the Secretary of State the following morning.

This might have been the whole story, a small parable about a tube and a train, if not for another story, earlier, and in its way more instructive.

In 2023, a young man named [Jack Teixeira, who served in the Massachusetts Air National Guard](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/former-air-national-guardsman-sentenced-15-years-prison-unlawfully-disclosing-classified), discovered that secrets, when photographed carefully and shared among friends, acquire a new and lively existence. The documents he released—briefings on the war in Ukraine, assessments, fragments of the great machine of knowing—traveled much farther than any tube on a train. They crossed continents in seconds, were examined in Discord chats, argued over, denied, confirmed, and finally absorbed into that vast modern archive where everything is both known and disbelieved.

The boy did not leave the documents behind. He carried them with him, in his pockets, in his phone, in that peculiar space where loneliness and performance meet. If the general’s error was one of fatigue and procedure, the boy’s was one of appetite—the desire to be, for a moment, at the center of a story larger than himself.

Between the general and the boy lies the entire structure of modern secrecy.

On one end, a tube: physical, heavy, governed by rules written for a world in which distance was an ally. On the other, a chatroom: weightless, immediate, governed by the much older rules of vanity and belonging.

The institution, confronted with these two failures, asks the same question twice: What lessons were learned?

It is a serious question, and like all serious questions, it invites unserious answers.

The first lesson, we are told, is procedural. Assign the courier. Track the object. Log the movement. Ensure that the tube is never without a guardian, like a minor prince who cannot be trusted to be left alone.

The second lesson is technical. Restrict access. Monitor downloads. Watch the watchers. Build systems in which a 21-year-old cannot so easily carry the state home in his pocket.

These are sensible lessons. They are also incomplete.

Because both stories share a quieter assumption: that secrets fail at the edges—through negligence, through youth, through the occasional lapse in discipline. But the truth is that secrets fail at the center, where human beings remain stubbornly human.

The general drinks too much in a city at war, because the war is long and the evenings are longer. The boy shares documents with his friends, because to possess a secret and not share it is, at twenty-one, an almost unnatural act.

And now, a third figure enters the story, attempting to bridge the gap between the heavy tube and the weightless chatroom. [In an interview with the New York Post](https://nypost.com/2026/03/16/world-news/ukraine-ready-to-jump-in-to-help-us-as-other-american-allies-drag-feet-zelensky-tells-post/), Z proposes a “drone deal” to Donald Trump, offering to turn Ukraine into the world’s laboratory—a factory where American finance meets Ukrainian scar tissue. He speaks of a world where missiles are ending and thousands of drones are beginning, where the distance of 1,000 kilometers is crossed tomorrow by a machine made for the price of a used car. Yesterday he [presented King Charles an Ipad](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Go_iRIs-7qc) to keep track of combined air attacks on Ukraine. “Flash” [posted](https://t.me/serhii_flash/7120) a picture of it on his Telegram page.

Z offers to train American troops in the art of this new, cheap war, noting with a certain grim politeness that despite their previous wars, they have not experienced this one. What he may not have fully accounted for is that [the drone market he is pitching into is already being carved up](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/military-drone-company-tied-trump-195629023.html). Donald Trump Jr. sits on the board of drone maker Unusual Machines, holds a major stake in Anduril through his investment firm 1789 Capital, and has received Army orders connected to his position—orders whose price, charged to U.S. taxpayers, was not disclosed. Eric Trump, meanwhile, promotes Israeli drone maker Xtend to his followers on X. A drone company counting both brothers as “notable investors” has just announced a merger with a Florida golf course operator, the combined entity promising to support “American drone industry dominance” through “strategic defense partnerships.” The golf courses, the press release notes, may serve as proving grounds. Elon Musk [announced](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/tesla-could-become-major-player-105417517.html) drone manufacturing plans last summer..

Z is not merely asking America to learn from Ukraine. He is, perhaps without quite realizing it, competing with the president’s sons and the richest man in the world, who also happens to be Trump’s biggest campaign donor. I’ll leave out the bits about Palantir, whose reps are also regulars at Tootsie Club.

The response from the center, however, remains consistent. Trump, speaking to Fox News, demurs. *We don’t need help*, he says. *We have the best drones in the world.*

It is the peculiar confidence of those entrusted with secrets, and those who possess the most expensive systems, to believe they cannot be tutored by the cheap, the small, or the young. Yet, as [David Petraeus observes](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/middle-east/autonomous-battlefield), the era of autonomous warfare is already emerging, quietly and inexorably, in the skies of eastern Ukraine. The advantage will not go to the side with the largest fleet, but to the side that first develops the operational concepts to employ them.

The US military, Petraeus warns, risks fielding “autonomous trinkets” instead of mastering autonomous warfare if it fails to grasp the stakes. While Ukraine updates its software every two weeks, the NATO doctrine revision cycle takes 15 to 20 months.

In this gap between the speed of the front and the weight of the ministry, a new and stranger kind of ownership has emerged: the [Danish Model](https://en.interfax.com.ua/news/general/1110185.html). It is a system of direct financing where foreign allies bypass the traditional, slow-moving donation of old stockpiles and instead send cash directly to Ukrainian manufacturers. It is a quiet revolution in how a state survives when its own pockets are empty but its factories are humming. While the physical drones are delivered to the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the intellectual property is increasingly being anchored in European hubs to give Western investors the legal comfort they require while the actual combat-testing remains in the hands of the engineers in Kyiv. It is ownership by osmosis: the knowledge flows west to be protected, while the hardware stays in the east to be used.

But where the Danish model is polished, [the business model of the Trump family](https://english.elpais.com/international/2026-03-16/the-persian-gulf-a-booming-business-for-the-trump-family.html) is more visceral. As the President urges allies to help unblock the Strait of Hormuz, his sons, Donald Jr. and Eric, have assumed control of an empire that has extended its reach to Dubai, Riyadh, and Jeddah. Here, ownership is a franchise—a name lent to luxury resorts and digital assets for hefty fees. The family has found generous allies in Gulf sheikhs, investing in bitcoin mining and AI data centers like the $20 billion project announced with Hussain Sajwani. Even Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners has raised billions, primarily from the Saudi public investment fund.

In this landscape, the lines between statecraft and private interest become as thin as a drone’s wing. Steve Witkoff, a business partner and Special Envoy to the Middle East, leads negotiations in Gaza while his sons partner with the Trumps in cryptocurrency ventures. The “Art of the Deal” has moved from Manhattan skyscrapers to the geopolitics of the Gulf, where secrets and investments are traded in the same breath.

Against this gold-plated backdrop, [the story of FirePoint](https://babel.ua/en/news/120997-kyiv-independent-nabu-investigates-the-activities-of-the-manufacturer-of-the-flamingo-missile-they-suspect-price-gouging) is the dark reflection of what happens when “flat organizational culture” meets the old habits of patronage. FirePoint, once a casting agency, now claims to build long-range drones from YouTube tutorials. This “Cinderella story” has curdled into a disaster of quality and corruption, with investigations by NABU into inflated pricing and quality failures, including a production run of drones that came out pink.

The burning question remains: who, specifically, owns Ukraine’s drone interceptor technology and how is ownership stipulated? It is a legal and bureaucratic gray zone. Ownership is stipulated not by patent law, but by access. In the FirePoint case, technology is a commodity of the connected. It is “owned” by those who can navigate the corridors of power in Kyiv to secure the contracts, even if the machines themselves are duds.

Even the high-gloss promises of Silicon Valley have stumbled when they hit the dirt. Anduril Industries arrived with the confidence of a “disruptive” alternative, yet in the intense electronic fog of Ukraine, the hype met a brutal reality check. State Security Service of Ukraine found that the Altius loitering drones repeatedly failed, leading the Ukrainians to abandon them entirely. Despite these frontline failures, the ministry’s faith remains unshaken; [in mid-March 2026, the U.S. Army awarded Anduril a monumental enterprise contract worth up to $20 billion](https://www.jpost.com/defense-and-tech/article-889950). While Anduril suggests these failures are merely the “messy” but necessary iterations of their development cycle, the Ukrainian operators see it differently.

The ministry returns to its conclusions. It writes them down carefully. It files them.

Meanwhile, the Dnipro river registers its objections in a more direct form—  
a meter-thick granite section of wall, neatly removed by an errant drone.

## Day 1485

2026-03-19 · An efficient division of labor

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c264db1e-dfc5-4116-8de2-6ad9d00ed4a1_852x1280.jpeg)  
*c/o 157th Mechanized Brigade (March 18, 2026)*

When Sean Penn skipped the Academy Awards and flew to Ukraine, it suggested seriousness. A man declining applause in favor of history. One imagines a quiet decision, the sort that improves in the retelling.

History, however, has its own casting director.

The photographs appeared. Penn near Sloviansk — close enough to borrow the front’s authority, not so close as to require its obligations. Soldiers arranged themselves with the courtesy reserved for guests and funerals. Beside him, positioned with the ease of long practice, sat Andriy Yermak: recently dismissed, recently investigated, recently in need of different lighting.

Yermak had, before his departure from office, attempted to weaken the institutions investigating him. This produced protests — not the theatrical kind, but the stubborn kind, where people insist on remembering what happened and who did it. The EU weighed in. Eventually even the system he had tried to rearrange found it necessary to rearrange him.

There was also the smaller matter, noted with restraint by Ukrainian outlets, that Yermak had shown little enthusiasm for military service. Yet here he was at the front, demonstrating sudden precision of movement. He did not come to fight. He came to stand beside someone who had come to witness fighting. An efficient division of labor.

Penn has made several such journeys. In 2023 he released *Superpower*, a documentary about Z that premiered at the Berlinale, where Penn introduced a live video address by the Ukrainian president with the solemnity of a man who has recently discovered that solemnity suits him. At a press conference, Penn described the film as “the idiot’s guide” to the conflict — an admission of such frank self-awareness that one wishes it had extended further. He also acknowledged making “an unapologetically biased film, because that is the truth we found.” The truth, in this case, arriving pre-packaged and camera-ready.

The film largely follows Penn following the story — cigarette-and-vodka-filled scenes, advocacy work, a shallow American’s journey to base-level understanding. Those expecting insight were advised to adjust expectations. What they received instead was Penn, convinced, after a brief bunker interview on the first day of the invasion, that Z possessed a superpower. “I believe with everything in my heart,” he told a journalist shortly afterward, “that this is a man of love, of intelligence and courage.” One notes that everything in Penn’s heart was formed over the course of a single afternoon, under conditions not optimally suited to biographical assessment.

He is not alone in this habit. Bernard-Henri Lévy, writing today in the [Wall Street Journal](https://archive.ph/YiVNL#selection-569.0-853.187), informs us that Z now “holds aces.” The metaphor arrives already worn smooth. Lévy’s Ukraine is the dealer, the Middle East the table, history a sequence of hands changing possession at decisive moments. What is less clear is where, in this well-lit arrangement, one places the dismissed official, the resisted investigation, the small persistent facts that decline to be dealt away. They do not appear — not because they are denied, but because they are unnecessary to the game being described.

This style of thinking prefers large metaphors to small realities. It does not stumble, because there is nothing on the floor.

It reminds me of a certain season of confident explanations in post-Soviet hotel lobbies — beneath soft lighting, among expatriates still uncertain to which story they belonged, grand interpretations offered with ease. The conclusions were large. The setting did not interfere — until you wandered outside to the nearest railway underpass, populated by people the metaphors had forgotten to account for.

Near Sloviansk, the setting is less accommodating. Mud has no interest in metaphors. The soldiers there understand something visitors often do not: reality is not arranged in advance and does not improve when described at altitude.

They pose for photographs nonetheless. This too is part of the work — to provide images that others will interpret later, in cleaner rooms, with better lighting.

In one version, a famous actor stands with a nation. In another, a compromised insider stands with a famous actor. In a third, less circulated version, both stand briefly with men who will remain after the image has moved on.

The soldier is not using anyone. He is being used — politely, almost imperceptibly — as part of a composition that requires his presence but not his circumstances.

The photograph tells the truth, as photographs do.

It shows who was there.

It does not show who is holding what.

---

Another photo op for Z, meanwhile, in Spain:

---

I watched this yesterday evening.

The hearing proceeded with admirable thoroughness. Senators pressed Tulsi on what was imminent, what was omitted, what was truncated and why. She answered carefully, which is to say she answered other questions than the ones posed.

Questions asked, but not answered: how Russian targeting intelligence reaches Iranian operators. How Chinese components find their way into the weapons currently killing American servicemen. These would have required a different kind of hearing — one where the answers were not already known in advance and deemed inconvenient.

## Day 1486

2026-03-20 · Lost in translation, again

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/98f87d3c-f8b6-4713-8959-2e674527957b_3958x876.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (Alley of Friends, March 20, 2026)*

*Imminence in America’s underpants*

More than four years ago — exactly 20 days before Russia launched its campaign to decapitate Kyiv — we tried to draw a line between *imminent* and *inevitable*. It was a modest effort, and it failed. But thousands of people read that post, which the woman claiming to be [KonMari](https://konmari.com/?srsltid=AfmBOorz-J2dvxb0GuJZBtiSHAcmoXnooeMRHeZKxCczqJu_eevt2zcT) later placed behind a paywall, hoping to draw more founding members into this Substack experiment[1](#footnote-1).

Running early this morning down the *Alley of Friends* along Kyiv's western embankment of the Dnipro River, I thought: *We are back.* New country, new war, same two words. A leader ignoring his intelligence community. The result, again, is literal. A third word has now joined them.

A small observation. Words do not contain meaning; they trigger it. *Imminent* is especially excitable. It has now triggered, in sequence: the invasion of Ukraine, a war with Iran, and a certain unease in the crossed eyes of Kash, Tulsi, John and “Rainman,” DIA’s new [clueless](https://greydynamics.com/dia-director-james-adams-iii-new-era-for-us-intelligence/) boss.

In February 2022, the White House warned publicly that Russia’s invasion was *imminent*—that is, soon, very soon, possibly before you finish this sentence. Z, advised by men who treated translation as a decorative art, heard *inevitable*—which is to say, abstract, negotiable, not necessarily Tuesday. He waved off the warning as one waves off an elderly relative who has mistaken the weather for prophecy. The intelligence was good. The judgment was not. The invasion, when it came, declined to be metaphorical.

Now Iran. Donald Trump, who Anne Applebaum [suggests](https://archive.ph/wQqVh) does not think strategically, historically, or with sustained care, launched strikes on a country his own intelligence community assessed as not building a nuclear weapon. He explained this with a “good feeling.” One hesitates to file this under methodology.

On Wednesday, his Director of National Intelligence was asked whether Iran posed an imminent threat. She replied, with admirable economy, that defining *imminent* is not her job. It is the president’s. She supervises some 80,000 people who produce judgments. One must respect the division of labor.

Her written testimony said Iran had made “no efforts” to rebuild its nuclear infrastructure. Her oral testimony suggested it was “trying to recover” that same infrastructure. Mark Warner noted the discrepancy. She did not contest him with enthusiasm.

John, more practiced in Washington’s bilingualism, offered that Iran has been a *constant* threat, long watered and carefully tended by previous administrations. This is the analytical equivalent of explaining that the fire predated one’s arrival with gasoline.

Let us pause on *constant*. We now have three words: *imminent*, *inevitable*, *constant*. They are not synonyms. A constant threat is durable, familiar, almost comforting in its predictability. It was there last year, and the year before, and on [Day 1465](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1465) of Russia’s war, when American envoys discussed Iran in the morning and Ukraine after lunch. The rooms were nearby. Efficiency has its moments.

A constant threat is neither new nor urgent. It does not, by itself, justify a war begun on a feeling. Ratcliffe’s statement, read slowly, argues against the war while appearing to support it. His analysts knew this. They were spared the inconvenience of saying so.

The Strait of Hormuz is now obstructed. Oil rises. The Navy recalculates. NATO allies—tariffed, mocked, and periodically threatened with annexation—decline to assist. In the Kremlin, Vladimir Putin observes events with professional curiosity and notes, correctly, that burning cities are transferable.

The symmetry is plain. Z discounted good intelligence because he preferred his judgment. Donald Trump discounted it because he prefers his feelings. One was overconfident, the other, less encumbered. Both paid. Others paid more.

In both cases, we are told only the leader can decide what is *imminent*. Not the analysts. Not the professionals. Not the 80,000 employees nominally employed for that purpose. Only the leader—then and now. This has been stated plainly, even under oath.

It is, in a modest, technical sense, insane.

[Fazil Iskander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fazil_Iskander) wrote that real humor requires approaching the edge of pessimism, peering into the abyss, convincing oneself there is nothing there, and then walking back. The footsteps on the return journey are the joke.

I have looked. The labeling is accurate.

Not imminent. Not constant. Inevitable. Stupid.

## Day 1489

2026-03-23 · The drone was Iranian

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/bd578d8f-9817-4cc5-86c5-46456c82ba10_4032x2268.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (March 21, 2026)*

[George Bernard Shaw](https://www.epedagogia.com.br/materialbibliotecaonine/2874Common-Sense-About-the-War.pdf), writing in November 1914 while the mud at Mons was still fresh, noticed something that has not stopped being true. Both nations, he observed, had been duped — but not quite unwillingly duped — by their militarists into fighting a war that served neither of them. He was considered impolite for saying so. He said so anyway. This is the first thing to understand about Shaw: he treated impoliteness as a civic duty, and performed it with considerable pleasure.

The second thing to understand is that he was right.

The photograph above this piece was taken on Saturday, directly opposite to a café once called Trump Pizza Station. The café has since changed its name, then closed entirely. The building in the photograph has not been renamed. It simply stands, or most of it does, in the way that things stand when they have been partially disaggregated by a Shahed drone — Iranian, as it happens, now that Iran is on the other end of a different war’s paperwork. The street is otherwise unremarkable. This is the thirteenth year of the war, and remarkability has been rationed.

At the [Imperial War Museum](https://www.iwm.org.uk/) in London, the exhibits are arranged chronologically. The arguments are not. Walk through the galleries and you will find that each war arrives with fresh justifications and familiar shapes — necessary, limited, preventive, decisive. [David Kaye, writing in the Times this week](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/22/opinion/trump-iran-war-memes.html), notices that the purposes of the Iran war multiply precisely where clarity is absent. The war, like a well-trained actor, adjusts its role to the audience. This too is a tradition with deep institutional support.

[Bertrand Russell](https://users.drew.edu/~jlenz/br-ethics-of-war.html) had a category for what follows: the war of prestige. It begins in abstraction — credibility, resolve, the necessity of being seen to act — and ends in arithmetic. The dead. The displaced. The quietly surprised. Nations, he wrote, rarely ask what good a war will actually produce. They ask only whether it can be made to look proper. The paperwork is not a reason for war but a decoration. Nations go to war and then, in the hours after, discover their reasons, the way a man who has already jumped from a window discovers, on the way down, that he was pushed.

Shaw would have found this insufficiently comic. He preferred the version in which everyone knew perfectly well what they were doing and chose, collectively, to pretend otherwise. His militarists — English and German alike — had been drinking to The Day for a generation. When The Day arrived, they expressed shock. Shaw found this shock rather difficult to take seriously. His remedy was recrimination, which he considered not only appropriate but practical: you cannot negotiate what you will not name.

[Valerii Zaluzhny](https://english.nv.ua/opinion/zaluzhnyi-why-wars-repeat-and-global-leaders-fail-to-stop-them-50593006.html), writing over the weekend with the patience of a man who has used up his patience, adds the operational dimension. Wars repeat, he argues, not from passion or miscalculation, but from the systematic failure to close one unresolved conflict before opening the next. He does not use Shaw’s language, but he is describing Shaw’s mechanism. The war of prestige generates its own continuation. Each inconclusive end becomes the beginning of something that has not yet been named, and will not be named until it is too late to matter.

Outside, Kyiv is managing. This is what Kyiv does — it manages. Russia sent more than 60,000 drones at Ukrainian civilians last year, nearly five times the number of the year before, which was itself a record. The negotiations [continue](https://x.com/SEPeaceMissions/status/2035794441861259293) in Miami. The purposes multiply.

What Shaw asked for in 1914 — what Russell asked for, what Zaluzhny is asking for now, with considerably less patience for irony — is modest enough to be embarrassing: that we decide what a war is for before it begins, rather than after it ends. That the purposes survive contact with reality. That the language retain some memory of what killing is.

The museum in London is prepared for our failure to manage this. It has been quietly expanding its collection for a hundred and twelve years.

The building opposite Trump Pizza Station is also, in its way, prepared. It has stopped waiting to be repaired.

## Day 1490

2026-03-24 · Me and the Ayatollah

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/551ee741-0c0e-4db4-97e2-e23951cf89af_1100x844.jpeg)  
*Belarusian strongman Alexander Lukashenko chats up Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran, Iran (Photo c/o Office of the Supreme Leader , November 7, 2006)*

My old friend [Valentyn](https://knihi.com/Valancin_Taras/Na_vyspie_uspaminau_mp3.zip.html) knew nothing about physics but lots about tyrants, despots and their flunkies—the kind that entangled eastern Europe after the World War II—used to say: the information is in the correlations, not in the parts.

He meant this about people. John Preskill means it about the universe.

"[The] era of fault-tolerant quantum computing," [he writes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.00862), "may still be rather distant. No one really knows how long it will take to get there."

A quantum system cannot be read sequentially. Page by page, there is nothing. The signal is in the relations.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/692c0f8f-f823-457a-9319-245a23ee774c_1474x704.jpeg)  
*Photo by abdymok enchanted with AI (March 24, 2026)*

Last month two men spent a day in Geneva moving between crises as though they were meetings. Before lunch: uranium. After lunch: Ukraine.

They were Trump’s son-in-law and golf partner[1](#footnote-1).

A third element has since been introduced.

Alexander Lukashenko—in office since 1994—[is being discussed](https://www.ft.com/content/69675c86-d1ff-4bbf-a55a-a480421bd165?syn-25a6b1a6=1) as a White House guest.

He released 250 prisoners. Then 500. An opening number, not a conclusion.

“Tell Donald Trump I agree to work out this big deal.”

No deal specified.

In quantum terms, a superposition: all outcomes held in reserve until observation collapses them.

Valentyn’s version was simpler. Despots and their auxiliaries form a system. You can adjust individual elements. The system remains.

Consider the pages together.

Iran: negotiations offered after bombing.  
Ukraine: a settlement proposed without terms that hold.  
Belarus: a meeting floated in exchange for the staged release of prisoners.

Individually, these are positions. Together, they describe a method.

In Moscow, Putin watches Tehran with interest. That could have been us.

He reads the system, not the page.

Valentyn understood this. The flunky manages the page. The tyrant reads the book.

Preskill, writing about qubits, notes that fault tolerance remains distant. The system cannot yet hold its state under stress.

He is describing a machine. The description applies.

Most Ukrainians do not expect a durable outcome. They are not participants in the design.

Valentyn would not have been surprised.

A sequence of pages produced without reference to what precedes them. No mechanism for reconciling the whole.

The structure persists.

The correlations, as always, outlast the parts.

## Day 1491

2026-03-25 · Walking to Dodo Socks

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6c8e813e-385f-4d17-a24c-25d69577bc46_1152x864.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (March 25, 2026)*

Yesterday morning we wrote about Valentyn, who knew nothing about physics but everything about how power operates in the shadow of empire[1](#footnote-1). His insight — that information lives in the correlations, not the parts — rhymes, as we noted, with John Preskill’s description of quantum systems: you cannot read them sequentially. Page by page, there is nothing. The signal is in the relations. ([Gerardus ‘t Hooft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_%27t_Hooft), it should be said, would find this entire framing irritating — his cellular automaton interpretation holds that quantum mechanics is *deterministic* at depth, that the probabilism is ours, not nature’s. The metaphor is contested even among the physicists. We are using it anyway.)

We meant it about memory and entanglement. But it applies, with grim directness, to the negotiations currently determining whether Ukraine survives as a state.

I thought about this after a cup of coffee at ZigZag with Ruslan, who told me that a printing house in Salerno, Italy had agreed to print a limited edition anthology of his works, a compilation, as it were, of five books, including Wartime Sketches[2](#footnote-2)[3](#footnote-3).

The picture is not readable part by part. Each element — a broken Rada vote, a stalled IMF benchmark, a deputy muttering that “there are no votes” in a presidential meeting — looks like noise in isolation. The correlation is the signal. And the correlation says: the system is closer to collapse than the probabilistic language of Ukraine experts is willing to admit. (This thought arrived, with some force, while walking past [Puncher Fight Club](https://puncher.kiev.ua/pechersk) on the way to [Dodo Socks](https://dodosocks.com/en/)’ flagship store in central Kyiv. The city has a way of concentrating the mind.)

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/30ee1a78-8489-4249-8b90-e73d9858ea71_3520x2856.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (March 25, 2026)*

The negotiations have calcified around a single question: will Ukraine withdraw from the portions of Donetsk oblast it still holds. Everything else — energy deals, humanitarian corridors, ceasefire geometry — exists primarily to generate the appearance of momentum. Trump’s golf partner returns to this point regardless of what else is raised. The Russians barely need to show up. The golf partner is doing their arguing for them.

Z is not passive in this. On Sunday he announced that Ukrainian military intelligence holds irrefutable evidence of Russia supplying Iran with signals data — effectively telling Washington: we are useful to you in the Iran adventure, too. It is a desperate move. Though one should note that neither man has distinguished himself as an astute consumer of military intelligence. Z spent six months in 2022 dismissing American warnings of an imminent invasion as destabilizing noise. Trump’s relationship with his own intelligence services has been, to put it generously, transactional. Two leaders who have each, in their own way, looked at the signal and seen static.

The fuzziness here is not fundamental. It is epistemic. The American model has too few variables: it excludes the military logic (commanders holding high ground in Donetsk cannot be told that open steppe is strategically equivalent), the political logic (a parliament that cannot pass IMF benchmarks will not ratify a territorial referendum), and the economic logic (European unity on EUR 90 billion in credit is, to be charitable, unverified).

Z is already planning for three more years of war. Not as ambition. As contingency. The parliament is being quietly restructured for what one insider recently called, with exhausted irony, “survival mode.”

The stalemate is not a stable equilibrium. It only looks like one read part by part. Read the correlations and the position is already determined.

Someone in Kyiv knows which way. They just can’t say it yet.

On the Ukraine jacket, desert arithmetic (with guarantees).

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/ccaf6015-b8fb-4caf-ac73-c67ff912372a_663x217.png)  
*c/o Interfax-Ukraine (March 25, 2026)*

Z says Europe may block him, so he looks to the Gulf. It sounds like initiative. It is, in fact, subtraction.

The February note from [Carnegie Politika](https://carnegieendowment.org/russia-eurasia/politika/2026/02/arab-world-russia-support) reads like a quiet audit: the Arab states have already adjusted—to Moscow. Trade grows. Mediation flatters everyone. No one chooses.

Now the arithmetic sharpens. In his [interview with Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/us-links-security-guarantees-ukraine-giving-up-donbas-zelenskiy-says-2026-03-25/), Z describes an American offer: guarantees, in exchange for Donbas. Security, priced as territory. He calls it risk. He is right. But he is already negotiating inside the price.

He thanks Donald Trump for Patriots while explaining that Patriots are not enough. Gratitude and insufficiency, in the same breath. This is not strategy. It is exposure.

Z arrives in the Gulf with urgency, offering alignment to partners who prefer options. He speaks in war; they answer in margins. Iran has rearranged the language. Moral clarity now travels at a discount.

So the Middle East becomes a “prospect.” A polite word for a market where your adversary already has better terms.

There is no vacuum there. Only pricing.

And Z, increasingly, is the asset being priced.

---

Jonathan Chait has written an interesting piece in *[The Atlantic](https://archive.ph/Z3AEm#selection-691.0-1071.431)* about Joe Kent[1](#footnote-1). We wrote about Joe Kent exactly one year ago[2](#footnote-2). We mention this not out of vanity — well, not *entirely* out of vanity — but because the gap between these two dates is itself the story.

On March 27, 2025, in a newsletter with a paid subscriber list considerably smaller than *The Atlantic*‘s readership, we called the Gabbard-Kent-Witkoff arrangement what it was: a jamboree of jackasses sharing time-sensitive US attack plans on a commercial app while regurgitating Kremlin narratives about Russia’s war. We noted that Joe Kent’s posts on Twitter mirrored content from Ukraine Watch, a Telegram channel endorsed by the Russian government. We noted that Kent had described Putin’s territorial demands as “very reasonable.” We noted that his failure to shut down the Houthi Signal group was borderline dereliction of duty. We called his boss’s boss, Steven Witkoff, the reincarnation of unwitting idiot Carter Page. We did all of this, we should add, while Kharkiv was being hit by UAV attacks and the Associated Press was filing credulous dispatches about a ceasefire that did not exist.

Chait, writing a full year later, calls Kent’s opinions “strange.” This is generous. Strange is your uncle at Thanksgiving insisting the moon landing was filmed in New Jersey. Kent was the chief of staff of the Director of National Intelligence, pending confirmation to lead the National Counterterrorism Center, while mirroring Kremlin Telegram channels and blaming the CIA or Ukraine for a Moscow terror attack. The word Chait is looking for is not strange. The word is *installed*.

This is the distinction *The Atlantic* essay, for all its analytical elegance, cannot quite bring itself to make. Chait sees a faction — hawks versus populists, a coalitional struggle playing out on podcasts and op-ed pages, a rhetorical war over who truly speaks for MAGA. What he misses is the personnel operation running underneath it. Kent was not merely voicing heterodox opinions about Ukraine. He was Gabbard’s chief of staff. Gabbard’s colleague Nicholas Kass, whose resume suggests intelligence work as a recreational hobby, was installed atop the National Intelligence Council, which produces the assessments on which policy is built. The faction wasn’t just talking. It was redecorating the building.

Chait’s framing — Republican hawks versus populist anti-interventionists, with Trump as the weathervane — is not wrong. But it treats the problem as essentially ideological, a battle over ideas that will be won or lost depending on whether the Iran war succeeds. Our diagnosis, offered from the cheaper seats a year earlier, was structural: you cannot perform incomplete defenestration and call it a solution. It does not matter whether you throw the body from the 29th floor or the 9th floor. What matters is whether it hits the pavement. Kass, for his part, spent seven months atop the National Intelligence Council — seven months producing or overseeing the assessments that shape how America understands the world — before quietly stepping down in early 2026. No hearing. No reckoning. No *Atlantic* essay. He did not hit the pavement so much as drift gently to street level and walk away. The building remains redecorated.

We do not begrudge Chait his platform or his prose, which is considerably more elegant than ours. We only note that the watchtower of prestige journalism has a peculiar relationship with time — it confirms what the smaller, more exposed outposts reported long ago, and it does so with the calm authority of a man who has just discovered fire and would like to explain combustion to you. By all means, read *The Atlantic*. But consider also that somewhere in the Substack wilderness, amid the paid tiers and the Ukrainian jacket updates and the digressive notes about the Queen of the Netherlands, someone was already telling you this. They were telling you when it still might have mattered.

There is no truce. There is no ceasefire. There is only the photograph of Donald, standing next to Putin in Anchorage, hanging in the White House — and a year’s worth of Sunday magazine prose catching up to what the jackasses were doing all along.

## Day 1493

2026-03-27 · Dr. Strangelove

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2f33e5dc-cfb0-4132-99b7-433d29f97f20_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo by abdymok enchanted by AI (March 27, 2026)*

We thought about *Dr. Strangelove* this morning at dawn celebrating the end of the first month of this year’s running season. *Dr. Strangelove*, or *Red Alert*, because I fell asleep last night listening to Trump’s inane Cabinet meeting. The movie bubbled up this morning, specifically the War Room scene where Dr. Strangelove himself keeps losing control of his own arm. His right hand, apparently with a will of its own, keeps lurching toward a Nazi salute, which he has to wrestle back down with his left hand — at one point nearly strangling himself in the process.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d5d05208-8577-42c4-85fc-148dbd9a4302_1408x768.png)  
*Image generated by Gemini 3 Flash (Nano Banana 2) based on a prompt by abdymok (March 27, 2026)*

Before setting out I listened to two [old white aspiring Russian philosophers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQsQ3lTz2lA&t=504s) invoke Strugatsky’s *Hard to be a God* describing Team USA’s Iran folly, but the interlocutors have zero stake in the outcome of the disaster beyond moral discomfort.

Where the Strugatskys gave us the paralysis of the witness — the observer from a more advanced civilization, watching catastrophe accumulate, forbidden to act — *Red Alert* — and especially its Kubrick incarnation — is about what happens when the machinery of intervention runs ahead of the humans nominally in charge of it. Trump’s golf buddy Witkoff saying "it all smelled fishy" and Trump launching the strike the next morning sits uncomfortably close to the Strangelove universe[1](#footnote-1).

A *New York Times* [dispatch](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/26/us/politics/trump-iran-talks.html) from Washington, dated the day after our Thursday broadcast, fills in the details with a specificity that is almost novelistic in its bleakness. We learn that a senior American official attended the critical Geneva meeting — the last chance, apparently, to avoid war — without technical experts, and emerged surprised to discover that Iran considered uranium enrichment a sovereign right it had been publicly asserting for decades. We learn that this same official repeatedly mispronounced the name of the international agency that has monitored Iranian nuclear activity for years. The president launched his attack the following night. General Ripper, one feels, would have recognized the epistemology.
