## Day 1496

2026-03-30 · Despite their leaders

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d9758637-1c6a-4088-970b-9909f62fd0fa_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (March 30, 2026)*

Yesterday, at Pechersky Market, I paid 300 hryvnia — about seven dollars — for a haircut.

The woman who cut my hair did not hurry. She was middle-aged, precise, and entirely indifferent to the idea that anything in the world might be urgent. Around us, the market moved in its usual way: vegetables arranged with quiet optimism, meat displayed with a kind of resigned honesty, people buying what they could and not what they wanted. War, like the weather, had been incorporated into the price of things.

She asked me, without curiosity, how short I wanted it. I told her. She nodded, as if confirming not a preference but a fact about the world that had always been true.

At some point, the conversation turned — not toward the war itself, which would have been too large and therefore impolite — but toward electricity, prices, the small arithmetic of survival. She spoke about outages the way one speaks about an unreliable relative: with irritation, but without surprise. There was no drama in it. Only adjustment.

When she finished, she brushed the hair from my shoulders with a quick, almost affectionate motion, as though correcting a minor administrative error. Then, as an afterthought — though in fact it was the final act — she trimmed my eyebrows with careful attention, restoring a kind of order that no larger authority seemed capable of providing.

I paid. She gave change. Neither of us mentioned that somewhere not very far away, men were attempting to alter the map of Europe with artillery.

Outside, the market continued. It occurred to me that whatever else this country lacks, it does not lack for systems that function in the absence of permission.

This is a detail that does not travel well.

---

There is a species of Washington analysis that resembles an expensive suit worn without shoes. [A recent Washington Post editorial](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/03/29/trump-iran-russia-ukraine-united-states/) attempts such tailoring: Russia’s war in Ukraine, it argues, resembles America’s war with Iran. Missiles, proxies, waterways — the parallels align neatly from altitude, where detail disappears and everything resembles everything else.

A single sentence notes that Iran is not Ukraine. The sentence is correct and immediately abandoned.

It is worth not abandoning it.

Iran is not an unfinished state navigating its sovereignty between great powers. It is Persia — a civilization that has buried Greeks, Arabs, Mongols, and British imperialists without ceremony, and with something approaching aristocratic indifference. Ukraine is a state still learning which parts of itself are permanent. The comparison works only from very high up, and the author has clearly never been lower.

Then there is leadership, which the piece dispenses with in one exonerating clause and never revisits.

Ukraine is governed by a former entertainer who confuses visibility with control. Around him, the state developed a parallel economy of extraction. Operation Midas — named with an irony that would have delighted Gogol — revealed that Energoatom functioned less as national infrastructure than as personal resource. Timur Mindich, Z’s old comedy partner, call sign “Karlsson,” allegedly collected percentages while missiles fell on the power grid above. Ministers were fired. One fled on the Kyiv-Warsaw train.

More instructive is Andriy Yermak — “Ali Baba” in NABU recordings — Z’s former chief of staff, who allegedly instructed law enforcement to obstruct the anti-corruption bodies investigating his associates. He was eventually dismissed, publicly thanked for his patriotic service, and replaced on 2 January 2026.

He did not leave. He redistributed himself.

By February, Ukrainska Pravda had located Ali Baba in a private Kyiv office — “the Godfather working remotely.” Among his visitors: Oleksandr Kamyshin, former Minister of Strategic Industries, current strategic adviser to Z, who arrived carrying a notebook, stayed an hour, and subsequently told journalists he could not recall what they had discussed. This is not amnesia. It is a method.

While this was happening, the war itself quietly revealed something important.

Ukrainian drone manufacturers — funded by the state, distrustful of its procurement apparatus — built ten factories abroad in secret, exporting interceptors and keeping the core technology beyond administrative reach. Z [called this harmful](https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/03/28/8027604/) to Ukrainian exports. The manufacturers called it survival. Both were correct. Under Kamyshin’s ministerial watch, by his own admission, of 35 drone types developed with state funds, only three produced concrete results — the remainder existing primarily to extract grants, like sunflowers arranged to face the money.

---

[Simon Shuster, writing in The Atlantic](https://archive.ph/cM9kn#selection-607.0-1191.38), sees the innovation. He has heard the sirens; his prose carries their specific gravity. His portrait of Armin Papperger — Rheinmetall’s CEO, who dismisses Ukrainian drones as kitchen craft and “Legos” while his order backlog approaches 135 billion euros — is accurate and sharp. Papperger cannot perceive the revolution because it invalidates his scale. Fair enough. Industrialists are not required to welcome their own obsolescence.

But Shuster has a blindspot of his own, and it is not accidental. His celebrated book on Z presents the invasion as, among other things, a story of remarkable wartime leadership. This framing does not merely linger in his Atlantic piece — it selects his sources. Kamyshin explains strategy with elegance and forgets conversations with precision. He is a superb interview subject. Shuster quotes him admiringly and moves on. The factories built abroad in deliberate secrecy are not an anecdote in this telling. They are the conclusion — and they are omitted.

Shuster’s job, it seems, is to make Z and his managers look good. He performs it with considerable literary grace.

Meanwhile, as this piece goes to press, Z has completed a Gulf tour — Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Jordan — selling Ukrainian drone expertise to buyers who do not inquire about Ali Baba or Karlsson, and who understand perfectly well that outcomes are separable from the systems that produced them. At home, an increasing number of Ukrainians feel distinctly unwell whenever he boards a plane on their behalf. They have learned what it means when the showman goes on tour.

---

And here is what all three miss — Willick with his Washington frameworks, Papperger with his balance sheets, Shuster with his hagiographer’s brief.

In both Iran and Ukraine, the population has learned to route around its leadership. Not from ideology, but from experience. Civil networks in Iran. Autonomous war production in Ukraine. In both cases, resilience lives outside authority — because authority has repeatedly demonstrated what it does with the inside.

This is the similarity that matters. Not missiles. Not maps. Not metaphors.

Willick sees structure and misses agency. Papperger sees industry and misses revolution. Shuster sees revolution and misses betrayal. The Ukrainians, characteristically, see all of it — and get on with the work anyway.

They build accordingly. They always have.

---

*Footnote on method: the Washington Post piece reflects a familiar condition — analysis conducted at altitude. This is not automatically fatal. Tocqueville also wrote from partial distance. But Tocqueville traveled. He dirtied his boots. He sat with people whose lives were the subject of his sentences. There is a specific confidence that grows in clean rooms. It produces elegant prose, stable abstractions, and, at the edges, the serene blindness of a man explaining rain while remaining perfectly dry.*

## Day 1497

2026-03-31 · Tel Aviv, Monaco, Miami

The weather has grown warm, and winter — like an unpleasant relative who overstayed his welcome — has been shown to the door. People are sitting outside again. Children are eating ice cream without guilt. It is the season when a man naturally forgets that he was ever cold.

And it is precisely this season that T.J. of *[The New York Times](http://nyt.com)*chose to publish his great investigation into Russia’s use of cold as a weapon[1](#footnote-1).

The article ran to some four thousand five hundred words. I counted. Or rather, I felt them — the way you feel a long journey on a bad road. In all those words, there was no room — not a single comfortable paragraph, not even a footnote’s worth of space — for the observation that perhaps the pipes had burst not because of geopolitical cunning, but because of something more ancient and universal: the theft of the money meant to insulate them, and the profound human capacity to avoid thinking about 2026 when it was 2022.

But then, T.J. is an old acquaintance of ours. We knew him in 2014, when he was a younger man — or at least a man with younger ambitions — and he joined forces with colleagues (Noah, Sabrina and Andrew come to mind) to tell the world a very wacko, flawed story about eastern Ukraine. The rebels there, we were given to understand, had risen from the earth like mushrooms after rain, spontaneously, organically, full of local grievance and native passion. It was a beautiful story. The kind of story that a very talented person tells when he has already decided, in some quiet room before he sat down to write, what the story will be.

There is a certain kind of journalist — and I say this with the respect one reserves for a skilled craftsman — who approaches the truth the way a man approaches a large dog he does not own: carefully, from a specific angle, making no sudden movements, and always keeping the exit in view.

---

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/16fedc3a-f9ed-4b71-a80d-e7b01eebaaa8_1024x1536.png)  
*Illustration generated with ChatGPT (OpenAI image generation).*

On the Ukraine jacket, the big news is Z sucking up to Bibi, or trying to suck up, or vice versa.

Spring has arrived, and with it comes love. Or at least, the diplomatic approximation of love — which is to say, two men who have not spoken in two years discovering, simultaneously, that each possesses exactly what the other needs.

Z, returning from a tour of the Middle East with the satisfied air of a man who has just remembered he has friends, sat down with [Barak Ravid of Axios](https://archive.ph/pFNip#selection-659.0-659.182) — a journalist who has made something of a specialty of sitting down with Z — and spoke warmly of Bibi. He has not spoken to the man himself in two years, you understand. But he spoke warmly *about* him, which in diplomacy is considered a promising first step, like leaving flowers outside a door you are not yet certain will open.

“We have what he needs,” Z said, with the quiet confidence of a man at a bazaar who knows the other man’s pockets. “And he has what we need.” One searches, in this formulation, for any difference from an ordinary business transaction, and finds mostly that the goods in question are weapons, and the currency is the mutual company of powerful friends — which has always been the true currency of the Middle East.

Bibi, for his part, has spent these two years “balancing.” This is the word Z used, generously, for what a less diplomatic observer might describe as a man standing on a fence so long that he has begun to regard the fence as his natural habitat. Russia is helping Iran — this Z knows, has shared the intelligence, has presented the satellite images. And Bibi balances. One almost admires the athleticism of it.

What makes the courtship additionally fragrant is that Israel has not been merely a passive admirer from afar. It has, in the generous tradition of a country that takes hospitality seriously, been housing a remarkable collection of Z’s former associates. There is Tymur Mindich, Z’s old friend, a man of considerable ingenuity whose involvement in the affair known as Operation Midas has made him, shall we say, temporarily inconvenient to have around Kyiv. There is Kolomoisky and Boholiubov. There is Vadym Rabinovich. There are, by all accounts, dozens of others — a small colony of disgraced Ukrainian politicians, each one suspected of crimes that would require a separate and lengthy article to enumerate, most of them enjoying the Mediterranean climate and the certain comfort of knowing that extradition is a concept Israel has always approached with the same philosophical detachment that Bibi brings to fence-sitting. The residents of this colony are not, it should be said, sedentary by nature. They commute — between Tel Aviv, Monaco, and Miami, principally — with the easy frequency of men who have solved the problem of borders that so vexes ordinary people. One begins to understand that the relationship between the two countries, even during these two years of official silence, has never really been cold. It has simply been conducted at a different level.

The Passover season lends the whole affair a certain poignancy. Z, who did not visit Israel on his Middle Eastern tour — Israel, notably, did not ask — nonetheless wished all Jews worldwide “peace,” calling it the greatest deficit in the world, ahead of energy. This is a generous and also carefully sequenced hierarchy. A man who supplies air defense systems understands that the wish for peace and the trade in the instruments of war are not contradictions. They are, in fact, the same industry, viewed from different ends of the transaction. And a man whose friends are warmly received in a country he is publicly courting understands that diplomacy, like most human arrangements, operates on several floors simultaneously, not all of them visible from the street.

What is touching, in the manner of a story that knows it is being watched, is the courtship ritual itself. Ukraine has sent military experts to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the UAE — countries that did ask — to demonstrate the elegant Ukrainian system of combining defensive layers so that a sky full of Iranian drones becomes, eventually, a quieter sky. Israel observed this from a distance, as a reserved suitor observes a dance. It has not yet asked to be taught the steps.

But Z is patient. He is a man who has learned, over several years of war, the difference between those who call and those who need to be called. He waits. The deficit in air defense is real. The deficit in peace is larger. And somewhere in Jerusalem, a very experienced balancer is looking at his fence and quietly reconsidering his footing — while, in a nearby café, several of Kyiv’s most wanted are ordering their second coffee of the morning, unhurried, unextradited, and perfectly at ease.

## Day 1498

2026-04-01 · Thirty-Seven Thousand Targets

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2c157f88-d0d1-4497-be44-09b63642016f_2048x1365.webp)  
*Former US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo joins Fire Point’s press conference online on Nov. 21, 2025, after becoming a member of the company’s advisory board in November 2025. (Photo courtesy of Fire Point PR service)*

There is a particular kind of distance that cannot be measured in miles. Ukraine, in the past month, destroyed [37,804 targets](https://t.me/usf_army/1720) using unmanned systems — including, yesterday, 203 enemy personnel, 61 drone launch points, and 324 hostile drones, dispatched before lunch. The United States, in the same period, issued [a formal request](https://www.shephardmedia.com/news/air-warfare/us-air-force-automated-low-cost-cuas-expeditionary-solutions/#:~:text=small%20drone%20attacks.-,US%20Air%20Force%20is%20eyeing%20cost%2Deffective%20automated%20counter%2Ddrone,fixed%20and%20semi%2Dfixed%20sites.) asking contractors to please submit, by April 7th, any thoughts they might have about automated drone defense. The gap between these two sentences is not geographical. It is civilizational.

The list of requirements reads, with only mild exaggeration, like a description of what Ukraine has been cobbling together since 2022: acoustic sensors that hear before you see, cameras that see before you think, radios that listen to what should not be there, and software that ties it all together quickly enough that a man can still finish his cigarette before the engagement is over. Two operators. Seconds, not minutes. Cheap enough to buy in quantity.

“Current solutions,” the notice observes, in the tone of a man discovering that water is wet, “are often expensive, require significant operator training, or lack the automation needed to counter multiple simultaneous threats.”

Iran has launched more than two thousand drones since late February — at an estimated cost to Tehran of somewhere between $40 and $100 million. The United States, intercepting a fraction of them with missiles costing between $2 and $4 million each, has likely spent more doing so than the $820 million it has set aside this year to think about the problem. America says it already has the best drones in the world. One imagines Hegseth says this with a straight face.

Men have been leaving certain countries in a hurry and arriving in others at a leisurely pace. They travel lightly, but not without consequence. Their relationship to Ukrainian sovereignty resembles that of a landlord to a building he has insured and then, by coincidence, set on fire. They move between Tel Aviv and Monaco and Florida as men of means do — unhurried, untroubled, and, for the moment, uncollected by the law. Before leaving, one of them appears — on surveillance tapes, in the company of men with names like characters from a provincial comedy — to have taken an interest in a drone company called Fire Point.

Fire Point did not exist before the invasion. Its founder’s previous screen credit was a romantic comedy. By 2025 it had become the largest recipient of Ukraine’s drone procurement budget — about a billion dollars — without ever undergoing the price negotiations required by law, an audit found. The formal owner, known on NABU tapes by a nickname suggesting technical competence, had previously lived in Russia. The man whose name keeps appearing says he only wanted to buy shares and was refused. This may even be true. In this ecosystem, formal ownership is the least interesting detail. What matters is that Fire Point occupied space — space where faster, cheaper, less entangled companies might have grown. Each inflated invoice was not just money lost but something not built: a sensor not deployed, a network left theoretical, a pilot training on yesterday’s machine[1](#footnote-1).

Corruption, in this sense, is not merely theft. It is delay. And delay, eventually, presents its bill.

Between March 9 and 15, small groups of drones — twelve, fifteen at a time — flew over Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana. They stayed for hours. They varied their routes. They appeared to be testing responses, like a man gently pressing on a door to see if it is locked. Barksdale houses the B-52 fleet and the headquarters of Air Force Global Strike Command. The flight line was shut down. Analysts concluded, with professional calm, that the incursions would [likely continue](https://abcnews.com/International/multiple-waves-unauthorized-drones-spotted-strategic-us-air/story?id=131245527).

The good news, it is said, is that no military learns faster than the American one. There is even [a center dedicated to lessons learned](https://www.army.mil/call). One notes, without insisting on the point, that there are people who have already learned these lessons. They have offered to share them.

What America has, more precisely, are very expensive drones and very confident contracts. Donald Trump Jr. holds stakes in Unusual Machines and Anduril. Eric Trump promotes an Israeli drone maker to his followers. A company counting both brothers as notable investors has announced a merger with a golf course operator, the combined entity promising dominance through strategic defense partnerships — the courses, a press release notes, may serve as proving grounds. Anduril’s loitering drones, when exposed to real electronic warfare in Ukraine, failed and were abandoned. The Army then awarded Anduril a contract worth up to twenty billion dollars. The ministry writes its conclusions carefully and files them.

Into this comes the market. Erik Prince holds a position in Swarmer Inc. — SWMR closed Monday at $47.20, up nine percent, in a fifty-two week range running from $11 to $65, which is less a stock chart than a weather system. No earnings, no dividend, no PE ratio: pure expectation, trading on the idea that swarms are the future and that someone, somewhere, will pay for protection. A safe investment.

Ukraine updates its drone software every two weeks. The U.S. military's drone doctrine revision cycle runs fifteen to twenty months — and that is before the contract is awarded, the protest is filed, the oversight hearing is scheduled, and the press release is written. Between those two clocks — the fast one and the slow one — there is a gap.

In that gap sit many things: a base in Louisiana, a contract in Washington, a workshop in Dnipro, a man on a golf course in Boca Raton with time enough for a second coffee.

The deadline for responses is April 7th. There is, officially, urgency. In practice, there is still time.

Pompeo, formerly Secretary of State, in November 2025 joined the advisory board of Fire Point, [according to AP citing company leadership](https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-pompeo-missiles-drones-58d1ebcb1141c19c326ef05b3a03df63) — one of several new figures brought in as the firm presents itself as a maturing international defense contractor. Har, har.

## Day 1499

2026-04-02 · The sons also rise

There is a particular quality of ambition that only flourishes in warm climates. On the beaches of Boca Raton we used to say that a man who has everything will eventually want the thing he cannot name. At Mar-a-Lago, apparently, that thing is Ukrainian drone technology.

Alex and Zach Witkoff — sons of Steve, the special envoy, the man who negotiates with the world on behalf of his golf partner — have discovered what every war eventually produces besides casualties: an investment thesis. They call their approach “Peace Through Profit,” which is the kind of phrase that sounds better the less carefully you examine it.

The thesis is not foolish. In fact it is rather elegant, in the way that a well-designed weapon is elegant. The problem they have identified is real: expensive missiles chasing cheap drones is a losing arithmetic. A Sidewinder costs four hundred thousand dollars. The drone it intercepts costs eight hundred. Somewhere in that gap lives either catastrophe or opportunity, depending on which side of the transaction you occupy.

> *Their father negotiates peace. They invest in the infrastructure of the next war. This is not a contradiction. This is, in a certain light, a complete family portrait.*

They are not alone. This is, it turns out, also a map of people — and the people are worth naming.

Palmer Luckey, who sold one company to Facebook and built another to arm the Pentagon, is here. Donald Trump Jr. is here, attached to a drone manufacturer called Unusual Machines with the enthusiasm of a man who has discovered a new hobby. Erik Prince — who has always been here, in every room where private violence meets public money — is here, this time with something called Swarmer. Eric Schmidt, who left Google to become the invisible architect of American military technology, is present in two forms simultaneously: Istari and Rebellion Defense, the brain without the body. Eric Trump has attached himself to the Israeli drone sector, which requires less explanation than it receives. Elon Musk circles the entire enterprise from a greater altitude — SpaceX, xAI, Tesla — a one-man stack that could, if the mood struck him, collapse the cost of the entire kill chain before breakfast.

And then there is Selçuk Bayraktar, the Turkish engineer who married the president’s daughter and built the Bayraktar TB2, the drone that made the world pay attention. He is the only one in this room who has actually changed a war. He stands slightly apart, as people who have done the real thing tend to do.

What Ukraine learned from all of this is simple enough: the future of drone defense is not sophistication. It is inventory. It is the kill loop running in seconds. It is the $10,000 interceptor that can be manufactured in the same week it is designed, tested in the field, and redesigned by Tuesday.

Whether the Witkoff sons — or any of the men named above — have learned this lesson, or merely learned to describe it fluently at dinner parties in Palm Beach, remains a private matter. Their portfolios are not public. Their results are not public. Only the philosophy is public, which is itself a kind of investment strategy.

On the beaches of Boca Raton we had a saying about men who stood at the border between two worlds and called it a position. We admired them, a little. We also kept count of which side they ran to when the shooting started.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/85df17de-65e3-45a1-bda9-07e2e95cc7ed_912x1171.png)  
*c/o abdymok (April 2, 2026)*

I had intended to embed the full report here — all ten pages, properly formatted, with the fonts it deserves. The woman who manages this Substack has the instincts of a ruthless editor and the convictions of someone who has read too much [Marie Kondo](https://konmari.com/?srsltid=AfmBOoo_RYEbGdWr_vRfZlQT41jO1jyQzr-lQvwBcMfZL92YuSj1oapO). Iframes do not spark joy. She has disabled them, and suggested, not unkindly, that I charge for the privilege instead. We will reach an agreement when she visits Kyiv next week.

## Day 1500

2026-04-03 · The Corridor to Transdniester

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c73788cc-b8f4-421e-8913-9e3b0f3f8de9_2560x1755.jpeg)

As of this writing, around 0830, there’s a lot flying around. Not on the map are airborne Russian strategic bombers with cruise missiles, 2× Tu-160 (from Ukrainka airbase) 3× Tu-95MS (2 from Olenya, 1 from Engels-2).

---

Paid-up subscribers to this Substack will no doubt recall the scene in Kyiv on Orthodox Easter in 2022 and the wild wheels-up party at [Tootsie Club](https://uk.tootsie.kiev.ua/) after Randy George and our hungover American friends departed the capital by train.

The intro to that post went something like this:

> *There is no consecution* (последовательность) *in madness. We exit Ward No. 6 and make strides towards the office belonging to the landlord’s sister — when out of nowhere, the smell of a kitchen punches through the corridor. We spin around and plow directly towards it, bedpan in hand. Someone asks what we’re holding. A bedpan, we say. Don’t be absurd, they say. That’s a corridor to Transdniester.*

---

That was Day 59[1](#footnote-1).

The Americans had landed. Randy, Tony and Lloyd, disembarking in a city still blinking at itself in the mirror — monument-polished, swept, barricaded, braced. Z held his press conference from an undisclosed metro station, apologizing for the sound of wagons.

It was, briefly, a good day. If memory serves, I took [Triple C](https://www.magnumphotos.com/photographer/chien-chi-chang/) on a hike.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/cd4b86f6-1e27-4350-9994-91c2ab39544a_5674x3783.jpeg)  
*Randy opposite Valery in Kyiv, April 24, 2022 (Photo c/o US State Department )*

There is a particular American habit, visible in moments of institutional stress, of confusing motion with control. A man removes another man from his post and calls it strategy. The act itself becomes the argument. And so Pete Hegseth has decided to sack General Randy A. George, and in doing so has offered us not merely a personnel change, but a small window into how this war — the one we discussed yesterday, the one made of drones and arithmetic — is being misunderstood at the highest levels.[2](#footnote-2).

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/60f00e69-0dd5-4525-9ce5-d8cdb7cdd9e4_1231x848.png)  
*The Fast Clock and the Cheap Kill. How Ukraine solved the drone interceptor problem while everyone else held a meeting about it. (p. 8, c/o adymok , April 2, 2026)*

General George’s offense, if it can be called that, was not failure. It was attention. He had been looking, with increasing seriousness, at Ukraine.

Not Ukraine as metaphor, or talking point, or fundraising device — but Ukraine as laboratory. A place where the cost curve of war has broken in half. Where a quadcopter assembled in a garage can hunt a tank. Where the side that learns faster survives longer. He understood, perhaps too clearly, that the old grammar of force — armor, mass, time — is dissolving into something else: speed, iteration, and volume.

This is not a comfortable realization for a large institution. It is even less comfortable for men for whom a war, to be real, must be describable to a taxi driver.

Yesterday’s post made a simple claim: that the future of drone warfare is not brilliance, but scale. Not the exquisite system, but the abundant one. The $10,000 interceptor, not the $400,000 missile. We did not arrive at this conclusion through theory. We arrived there through necessity, which is the most persuasive teacher available to man.

George was listening to that teacher.

He spoke, repeatedly, about a battlefield that had become transparent. About units that could no longer hide. About the need to distribute drones down to the smallest formations, to accept that every soldier would operate within a mesh of sensors and signals. He was, in other words, attempting to translate a Ukrainian reality into an American doctrine.

This is not the same thing as winning a war. It is, however, the beginning of not losing the next one.

Hegseth’s decision suggests a different instinct. Not adaptation, but reassertion. Not learning from the periphery, but restoring the center. It is the belief — deeply American, deeply persistent — that complexity can be managed by replacing the man in charge of it.

But the problem George was describing does not belong to him. It does not disappear with his departure. The drone does not become less cheap because a general has been dismissed. The kill chain does not slow down out of respect for institutional hierarchy.

If anything, the timing is instructive. At the very moment when private capital — the Witkoffs, the Luckeys, the Princes, the Schmidts — is reorganizing itself around the economics of drone warfare, the man most responsible for executing war is demonstrating his discomfort with the same lesson.

There is, in this, a kind of symmetry.

Yesterday we wrote about men in warm climates discovering that war can be rendered as a balance sheet. Today we observe a colder reality: that institutions, when confronted with the implications of that balance sheet, may choose denial over adaptation.

On the beaches of Boca Raton, we used to say that a man who cannot change his environment will change the subject. In Washington, the method is more direct. You change the general.

The environment remains.

Have a great weekend!

## Day 1503

2026-04-06 · On naming things plainly and what follows

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b10a116d-0d09-43b9-9f3b-f646172aa79f_1024x1536.png)  
*Image generated c/o Gemini (April 6, 2026)*

America is preparing a special holiday.

Tuesday, the President of the United States announced, will be Power Plant Day. Also Bridge Day. All in one. A twofer. There will be nothing like it, he promised — and one believes him, because there has genuinely never been anything quite like this: a sitting American president posting in the early morning hours, signing off with *Praise be to Allah*, and threatening to destroy the civilian infrastructure of a country of ninety million people, the way one might text an ex-girlfriend at 2 a.m., except the ex-girlfriend has no electricity afterward, and the children in the neonatal ward are on backup generators that run for six hours.

> Tuesday will be Power Plant Day, and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one, in Iran. There will be nothing like it!!! Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH! Praise be to Allah.  
> — @realDonaldTrump, Truth Social, Apr 05 2026, 8:03 AM ET

One recalls, not so long ago — three years, give or take an eternity — when General Mark Milley, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the United States Armed Forces, stood before the cameras and said of Russia: *indiscriminate and deliberate attacks on civilian targets is a war crime in the international rules of war.* ([Ukraine Defense Contact Group press conference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w1lOq6VjDwM), October 2022.)

Russia had been hitting power stations. Bridges. The things that keep the lights on and the old women warm and the dialysis machines cycling. The general was grave. The world nodded. Evil was being named.

We wrote about this as it unfolded — [Day 1005](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1005?utm_source=publication-search), [Day 1006](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1006?utm_source=publication-search), [Day 1017](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1017?utm_source=publication-search), [Day 1149](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1449?utm_source=publication-search) — when the pattern was still being explained, when the words still felt like they might matter if repeated often enough and with sufficient clarity.

That was then.

Now the President of the United States would like to do Power Plant Day.

The magnitude of what is being casually proposed deserves the kind of protracted, nauseating reckoning that the human mind resists, because it was not designed to hold it comfortably. We are not talking about a military strike on a radar installation. We are talking about the deliberate erasure of the infrastructure that keeps hospitals running, that pumps water to apartment buildings, that allows a city of millions to remain a city rather than a slow emergency.

People will die — not soldiers, mostly. The elderly man whose oxygen concentrator stops. The premature infant. The woman on the fourteenth floor who cannot carry water up the stairs. The ones who depend on a machine that depends on electricity that depends on the continued existence of a power plant that the President has decided to call a military target because the negotiators on the other side wanted to meet next Tuesday instead of next hour.

And here is the part that should make the room spin: the officers who would carry out these orders — whether they have been sufficiently hollowed out of conscience, whether the steady removal of anyone who raised an ethical concern over the past fourteen months has produced the desired result — this is no longer a theoretical question posed by historians imagining dark futures. It is an operational question.

The institution that was supposed to say no has been carefully, methodically prepared to say yes. This is what the firings were for. This is what the purges were for. History, which has seen this before, is not surprised. History is just tired.

There is a Fox News correspondent named Trey — we have met him before, and again, and again — going back at least to February 20, 2022, when he was standing in a field somewhere in eastern Ukraine, narrating the opening phase of a war he did not understand:

He has not changed.

On Sunday morning, Trey called the President and learned that Power Plant Day is coming, that the Kurds may or may not have kept some guns intended for Iranian protesters, and that there is a good chance a deal gets done by tomorrow. He reported all of this as though it were fascinating rather than terrible. There were, he noted, fifteen points. The President sounded optimistic. Trey sounded optimistic. The anchor said: incredible reporting.

Ninety million Iranians were not consulted.

There are moments in history when language begins to fail — not because the events are complex, but because they are simple in a way that resists interpretation. A thing is said plainly. A threat is issued plainly. The machinery that would carry it out stands ready.

No metaphor is required. No parable will improve it.

A day has been named.

Tuesday will come.

The spring in Tehran is said to be beautiful.

*Praise be to Allah*, the President wrote.

One assumes He is taking it under advisement. One assumes He has seen this before. One assumes, even now, He is not entirely sure what happens next.

## Day 1504

2026-04-07 · Surrender dressed for dinner

We’re on day four of an AI-assisted experiment to rewire how I run — specifically, to bring the glutes back online, reduce the over-reliance on quads, and find what has been sitting there unused. Not more training, not more force. Just a small shift: push behind, stop reaching in front. The glutes wake up, the stride opens, more space, more flow. Same body, working differently.

And it is not comfortable. It is, in fact, surprisingly painful. Not because it is harder in the muscular sense, but because it requires attention. You have to unlearn what your body has been quietly doing for years and ask it to do something more honest.

I think ageing can feel like this. Not only losing things, but discovering that many of them were never gone — just misfiled. Strength that was still there, but no longer accessed. Movement that still exists, but needs to be reintroduced, carefully, patiently. The work is not to go back. It is to reconnect. To adjust small details. And in doing so, to find that “same body, working differently” is not a loss of identity, but a form of progress.

Not everyone, of course, is interested in reconnecting. Some prefer the soreness to simply go unnoticed — the kind that makes contradiction feel normal because it persists long enough. The kind that stops noticing when the lines connect.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/ab163682-d6bb-4a30-892d-8e20936e93af_4192x819.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok*

Let us notice, then. Briefly. With whatever alertness remains.

Pete Hegseth stood before cameras on Easter Sunday and noted, with evident satisfaction, that the rescued airman’s plane had been shot down on a Friday, that he had hidden through Saturday in a cave, and had been flown home as the sun rose on Sunday. A pilot reborn. God is good. Tattooed on Mr. Hegseth’s bicep is *Deus vult* — “God wills it” — the battle cry of the Crusades[1](#footnote-1). He is now directing a bombing campaign against a majority-Shiite nation. The Pope has called this use of Christianity to justify warfare “entirely foreign to the way of Jesus Christ.” Mr. Hegseth has not appeared troubled by the disagreement.

The war itself offers no good exits. Destroy Iran’s energy infrastructure, and Iran destroys the Gulf’s — global recession as party favor. Walk away without a deal, and Iran becomes king of the strait, extracting tribute from passing vessels. Launch a ground operation, and as empires periodically rediscover, occupying territory is not the same as solving a problem. Each path leads, with differing elegance, to the same destination: economic damage, political ruin, and the particular humiliation of a man who believed he was winning.

Meanwhile, J.D. Vance has flown to Budapest to campaign for Viktor Orbán six days before the Hungarian election. The same Russia that arms Iran and shields it diplomatically is the country whose preferred candidate Mr. Vance has traveled to endorse in person. Hungary’s foreign minister, recorded telling Sergey Lavrov “I am always at your disposal,” has the manner of a man comfortable with his geometry. The billboards in Budapest show the opposition candidate beside a shadowy Z: *They are dangerous. Let’s stop them.* In one circulating image, Hungarian police wear Cyrillic insignia. The correction will arrive eventually.

I remember Budapest in the 1990s. Dilapidated restaurants and very good steak tartare. Lounge bars and hours-long conversations about open society and what it might become. Serbian refugees. City squares later reconstructed with Gazprom funds. Running laps around Margaret Island, then the Palatinus Baths, hot summers — and once, in a thunderstorm, a potted plant falling from a balcony high overhead, missing my head by not very much.

The people had a direction. Imperfect, uneven, occasionally dangerous in the literal sense. You could feel it in the conversations, in the scaffolding.

That feeling is gone. Not because history reversed, but because the people entrusted with its direction found, to their evident relief, that cynicism required so much less of them.

The lines connect. They have been connecting for some time. The soreness that stops you seeing it is not wisdom, not experience, not the hard-won equanimity of someone who has watched the world long enough to know its habits.

It is simply surrender, dressed for dinner.

## Day 1505

2026-04-08 · Even a stopped clock

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b8c71c5b-aa49-4949-a5d2-8e741d8bf68a_1407x768.png)

Let’s go back to yesterday’s flower pot[1](#footnote-1).

Budapest, summer 1998. A day so hot the city seems to stall — air thick enough to lean on, the Danube barely moving. By late afternoon the sky gives up pretending. Wind first, like a bailiff clearing the room. Then rain.

We had just come from dinner — avocado, tequila, the confidence that accompanies both — and were walking through the old city when, ten floors up, on the façade of one of those crumbling Habsburg buildings, a flower pot lets go.

It falls with authority. Not fast, exactly. Decisive. It misses us by what I will describe, generously, as inches.

The woman beside me that evening is the mother of our daughter. Our daughter was born in Kyiv. None of that was visible from the pavement that night. But there it is.

I was in vacationing that summer, as I often was in previous years, following a 4-year stint at bootstrapping ground-floorism. It was also, that time, a honeymoon. Around us, the prelude to something else was forming — decisions that would end in Vienna and Belgrade.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8e804ae0-1dce-40aa-ad41-a33a3a9e1400_993x703.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (Vienna, 1998)*

Elsewhere that summer, in Ohio, JD Vance was fourteen, surviving a difficult household. No one holds this against him. Childhood is not a choice. But it is worth noting that his relationship with eastern and central Europe — its wounds, its liberation and reconstruction — begins, and ends, with this week’s visit to campaign for Viktor Orbán.

David Petraeus was doing something else. In the Pentagon, at the elbow of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, working through Bosnia, Kosovo, the slow arithmetic of force in Europe. Not a tourist. A participant.

Three men, one summer. One in the rain under a falling flower pot. One in Ohio. One in the Pentagon.

I have, on these pages, been unkind to David Petraeus. I placed him in the usual Washington circuitry — advisory boards, contractor-adjacent policy circles, the permanent anticipation of the next war. Later, in the reconstruction salons: London, conference rooms, presentations about Ukraine’s future while its present continued to burn.

The description is accurate. It is also incomplete.

He has now been to Ukraine ten times since the invasion. Last week again: frontlines, drones, manufacturers. What he says on return is simple. Drone warfare is not an addition to modern war. It is modern war. The United States is not built for it.

“Innovativeness,” he noted recently, “is not giving 50 drones to an armored battalion. It is replacing the armored battalion.”

A retired four-star general, former CIA director, and partner at KKR — a firm shaped by Henry Kravis and George Roberts, and now circling European infrastructure and Ukraine-adjacent capital — suggesting the obsolescence of the systems that sustained that world. One notes the moment.

What he describes is not hardware but integration: surveillance, targeting, strike — one system. Ukraine’s [Delta platform](https://cepa.org/article/the-heart-of-war-ukraines-key-battlefield-system/) renders the battlefield as a continuous surface. He recounts watching a soldier tracked by successive drones, then struck. Observation is now terminal.

Ukraine will produce millions of drones this year; the United States, a fraction. Ukraine updates software in weeks; NATO doctrine moves in years. No coherent U.S. doctrine for autonomous formations. Promises delivered in the hundreds.

By 2022 the break was already visible. This is not an evolution of twentieth-century war. It is a replacement.

It is now being said aloud in rooms that matter, by people formed in the old system. That is not nothing.

Which brings us back to Budapest.

This week JD Vance arrived there to campaign for Viktor Orbán. He spoke about energy, civilisation, Brussels. What he did not speak about — what did not appear to interest him — is the transformation of war now underway on the same continent.

For him, Ukraine is a negotiation. Possibly a nuisance. Possibly, as he suggested, a meddling presence in Central European democracy.

The country rewriting the terms of modern conflict becomes, in this telling, an irritant to be managed.

The Budapest of 1998 understood something about direction. You could hear it in conversation, see it in the scaffolding — literal and otherwise. The work was unfinished, but it was work.

That sense is gone. Not because history reversed, but because it became easier to stop asking what it required.

Petraeus, for all the company he keeps, has at least been looking at the war. He has stood close enough to see what it is.

Vance flew in to talk about something else.

The flower pot missed. We looked up, stood in the rain a moment, and moved on. Some people, given time, pay attention to what nearly happened. Others arrive later and speak as if it didn’t.

## Day 1506

2026-04-09 · Rat on a journey

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/00f6e2ef-cabb-433b-b85b-225619b9836c_1911x1314.png)  
*Rat on a journey . c/o Mariia Prymachenko (1963)*

To all my American friends, you are fucked — though you probably already knew that, which is, in its own way, a kind of wisdom. Citizens may not all be accountable. They remain responsible, however. This is the distinction that history, that most patient and least forgiving of schoolteachers, tends to enforce long after the classroom has emptied.

There is a particular kind of rat — not the flustered kind, not the cornered kind, not even the ambitious kind who at least has the decency to want something real — but the kind who lies the way a man lies when he has collapsed the distinction between lying and storytelling, which is to say: completely, and with flair. This rat told a television anchor, when asked directly whether he had fabricated a story, “Yes!” — with the breezy confidence of a man announcing that he takes his coffee without sugar. He considered this a feature. One must, in a way, admire the consistency.

On Tuesday morning, while this rat stood at the Mathias Corvinus Collegium in Budapest telling thousands of Hungarian students about America’s deep commitment to peace — a subject he has studied, one imagines, the way a cat studies swimming — the rat’s boss posted on Truth Social that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.” He was not speaking in metaphor. He was describing Iran. In the old stories of my country, the man who announces the death of a civilization before lunch is usually the villain. In the new stories, he is the president. Hours later, his flunkies did their taco Tuesday routine for the cameras, as men do when they have learned that the performance of normalcy is itself a form of power. The vice president, reached for comment, was unavailable. He was explaining sovereignty to students in Hungary. This rat is today in Islamabad, brokering peace with Iran — because the world, having run out of serious men, has begun hiring storytellers[1](#footnote-1).

We have written twice this week about almost being killed by a falling flower pot in Budapest — a city that has, it turns out, a talent for dropping things on people’s heads, a talent it shares, one notes, with its current government. The rat was there the same week. He stood before the students and described fourteen months of patient diplomacy, pieces of paper exchanged, positions converging, Viktor Orbán cast as an indispensable statesman of peace. The students applauded. It sounded wonderful. It was, in most of its meaningful particulars, a story — and if there is one thing the rat knows how to do, it is tell a story. A man who knows he is lying and says so on television has achieved a kind of terrible freedom. He is no longer constrained by the facts, which are, he has discovered, much slower than he is.

What the rat did not say — could not say, standing next to a man whose government has blocked EU aid to Ukraine and whose intelligence services have been credibly linked to Russian influence operations — is that the boss rat’s administration has spent those same fourteen months dismantling every piece of leverage the United States ever held over Moscow. Sanctions relief floated. Military aid suspended. Intelligence sharing paused. American negotiators told the Ukrainians, in front of the Russians, that they would never get Crimea back. This is not what mediators do. This is what one party to a conflict does when it has already chosen a side and requires a story to make the choice look like wisdom.

Ukraine is not “haggling over a few square kilometers,” as the rat put it, with the warmth of a man describing a flea market dispute over a slightly damaged lamp. Russia invaded Ukraine. Russia has killed tens of thousands of civilians. It is, by any legal definition that has ever been applied to anyone other than the current friends of the United States government, a genocide. In the fables of my childhood, the man who omits this kind of context is not called a mediator. He is called something else. The students did not ask. Perhaps they were being polite. Perhaps they already knew.

Back in Washington that same morning, the rat’s boss — a man one sharp observer has called a malfunctioning LLM, a rat who would never have been hired to run a Fortune 500 company and yet is running the world, which tells you something about the world, though I am not entirely sure what — was announcing the death of a civilization. Not a metaphor. A statement of intent so unambiguous it functions, as any prosecutor would note, as evidence of motive. The men around him kept their heads down and kept working. This is what men do when they have decided that the alternative to complicity is inconvenience. They will tell their grandchildren they were at the agriculture department. Vance was in Budapest, warning students about foreign influence while conducting a foreign influence operation, describing a genocide as a haggling dispute, calling its enabler a peacemaker, and being an ocean away while the rat’s boss announced, cheerfully, the end of a civilization before lunch. There is a word, in several languages, for this. In English, the closest approximation is: shameless. In the language of fables, the word is: rat.

It is, at the moment, a roughly thirty-hour trip from Terminal 1 at John F. Kennedy International Airport to Kyiv — an overnight flight to Warsaw, an evening train out of Warszawa Wschodnia, and another night in motion, arriving the next morning. People make that trip every day. Journalists. Volunteers. Soldiers going back. It requires no act of imagination, only the decision to go. The rat has made no such decision. He is in Islamabad. The golf partner and son-in-law of the rat’s boss have been invited to Kyiv instead. If any of the three does show up, one suspects the reception will be less forgiving than the one the rat received in Budapest. The flower pot, after all, missed.

Western civilization may not be so lucky.

## Day 1507

2026-04-10 · Green eggs and ham

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/60abe721-14b5-4a73-b39a-3cda5f524670_1264x842.png)  
*Image generated by Nano Banana 2 (April 10, 2026)*

Z gave three performances this week — one to Alastair Campbell on *[The Rest Is Politics](https://linktr.ee/restispolitics)*, one to [RAI’s GR Radio](https://www.rainews.it/maratona/2026/04/raid-aereo-russo-su-zaporizhzhia-una-vittima-vance-in-ungheria-per-sostenere-orban-f3fd5224-d46e-4356-8030-c04bbc93b99a.html), and [one in Uzhhorod](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TqjlQiEbtg4), where the cherry trees were already in bloom and, miraculously, someone had not yet taken a selfie. This is how wars are fought now — one eye on the front, one eye on the flowering branch.

In Zakarpattia he spoke of many things, as men in his position must. About multiple citizenship — five countries first, then others, the way you test a bridge before trusting it with a truck. The journalist from Uzhhorod nodded, satisfied with something that wasn’t quite an answer but had been carefully carved into the shape of one. About JD Vance’s “piece of territory” remark, Z explained, with the patience of a man long resigned to repetition, that a piece of territory is not the same as a piece of bread. About Pokrovsk: the enemy wants it by the end of April; he does not have the strength; the situation is very difficult but stable. This is how mountain people describe an avalanche that has not yet reached the village. The sakura was still blooming when he left.

The RAI interview is the most revealing of the three, precisely because it is so monumentally boring. Ready to meet Vladimir Putin — not in Moscow, not in Kyiv, somewhere in the Middle East or Europe or America or anywhere — the kind of statement that sounds like news and contains absolutely nothing. The Donbas argument, by now a set piece, is delivered again with the same fortification timelines, the same Kharkiv threat, the same “societal fracture” warning. Giorgia Meloni is “a strong leader.” Donald Trump thinks he’s honest with him. The €90 billion must be unblocked. One reads it waiting for a verb that has not yet been used.

Then there is the question of what to do with material that genuinely isn’t boring. Z’s claim that Russian military satellites photographed U.S. bases and Gulf energy infrastructure and passed the intelligence to Tehran is, if true, significant. He said it in the Campbell interview. Luke Harding at The Guardian duly ran it as a story, attributed to a podcast, under the byline of a journalist who functions, with some regularity, as Z’s stenographer. The story is real. The sourcing — a podcast conversation — tells you something about the current condition of the information ecosystem around this war.

It also lands at a moment when the Russia–Iran–Ukraine triangle has become impossible to ignore: as [Day 1450](https://sidestack.io/directory/substack/abdymok?utm_source=chatgpt.com) noted back in February — the very day Benjamin Netanyahu was in the White House Situation Room pitching Donald Trump on Iran — Russia was simultaneously launching one of its largest barrages yet on Ukraine, with Shahed drones coordinated from multiple Russian sites and Crimea. The overlap between Moscow’s war in Europe and its partnership with Tehran is not a podcast talking point. It is the architecture of the problem. The White House was being briefed on Iran while the evidence of Russian-Iranian coordination sat, apparently unread, in whatever inbox Z had sent it to.

The Campbell conversation itself has texture, though much of that is Campbell’s doing. Z’s English, once serviceable, is now genuinely difficult in places — as if the language itself has begun to tire. And yet the charge of circular reasoning undersells what is, at moments, sharp analysis. His three-part test for whether Putin wants peace — a trilateral leaders’ summit, American troops on the contact line, the absurdity of a man with seventeen million square kilometres demanding six thousand more — is structured and, probably, correct. His reading of Putin’s real objective as time, not territory, is more sophisticated than much Western commentary, and certainly more so than the credulous stenography currently passing for analysis at certain distinguished mastheads.

The problem is not Z’s thinking. It is that Campbell is too much the admirer and too little the interrogator — ending by dreaming aloud about Ukraine, Britain, and Canada joining the EU on the same day. That is not an interview; it is a toast delivered before the first course. Meanwhile his mother calls twenty times before he picks up. One understands the impulse.

## Day 1510

2026-04-13 · Two images, one table

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/316bb0c6-7035-4525-8bfd-5d63627467f2_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (April 12, 2026)*

This is someone’s kitchen in Kyiv yesterday morning. An embroidered tablecloth. Tulips — pink and yellow, the determined colors of people who have decided, against considerable evidence, that spring is worth celebrating. Two paskas, freshly baked. A cat asleep in a patch of sunlight, with the complete moral indifference that cats bring to all human occasions, including historic ones. And in the window, hanging from a string of lights, a small wooden tag that says Paris.

Sellars would have loved that detail. [Wilfrid Sellars](https://conservancy.umn.edu/items/494b3d5f-7c7d-4fe9-afc2-6dc25544690f) — not widely read, which is a pity — was a philosopher who said that philosophy’s only real job was to explain how two images of the world hang together: the manifest image, which is the world of ceremony and meaning and embroidered tablecloths, and the scientific image, which is the world as careful inquiry reveals it, indifferent to tulips. Not to abolish one in favor of the other. To hold both, honestly, at once, stereoscopically.

This is harder than it sounds.

Yesterday Z addressed the nation from Saint Sophia Cathedral. He quoted the inscription above the altar — God is in the midst of the city, it shall not be moved — and spoke of Ukraine as one great family, of children’s laughter, of the first peaceful Easter that was surely coming. His voice was steady. The manifest image was, for six minutes, complete and luminous and — I want to be careful here — genuinely moving. The cathedral does stand. The children do laugh. Someone did bake those paskas.

On April 10th, two days before Easter, [Kyrylo Budanov](https://www.ukrinform.ua/rubric-ato/4111141-budanov-bez-ludej-vijni-ne-vigrautsa-droni-ne-zroblat-ce-za-nas.html) — who has headed the President’s Office since January 2nd, a promotion whose backstory [repays attention](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1457?utm_source=publication-search) — gave an interview to Ukrinform and Novyny.LIVE that read like a dispatch from a different country entirely. He called draft evasion a “terrible problem” — страшенна проблема — and named the central contradiction of Ukrainian public life with a bluntness rare in any senior official, let alone the head of the President’s Office: everyone says the war must be fought to victory, and everyone flees mobilization. But his sharpest observation was this: Ukraine has somehow produced two kinds of hero simultaneously. The soldier at the front, bleeding. And the man who films himself telling the recruitment officer where to go, or boasting about how he slipped across the border. Both are heroes at the same time, Budanov said. This is a terrible problem. It shows the absence of unity. He asked the only question that follows logically from that observation: if everyone evades, will Ukraine remain on the political map of the world? His answer was unambiguous. No. It will not.

The scientific image underneath his words is not comfortable. Two million Ukrainians wanted for violating military registration rules. Systemic violations documented during conscription — beatings, arbitrary seizures, men taken from streets. Support for a negotiated end to the war risen from twenty-seven percent in 2023 to sixty-nine percent in 2025. A practice called busification so common it has its own word, which is always the sign that something has become ordinary.

Z almost never discusses any of this publicly.

It would be tempting to read the distance between Z’s cathedral monologue and Budanov’s interview as a contrast between liturgy and honesty. It is not. Budanov is Z’s man — completely, structurally, from the beginning. His first public act after his 2020 appointment as head of military intelligence was to go on camera and deny that Wagnergate was a Ukrainian operation, a claim Bellingcat demolished fifteen months later with several hundred verified documents. He has been operating in the gap between the manifest and scientific image his entire career — not as a corrective to the presidency, but as its instrument. Z does the liturgy. Budanov gets deployed when the scientific image needs to be named without Z having to name it. The two monologues don’t come from opposing camps. They come from the same apparatus, performing different functions. Which makes the crack in the manifest image harder to repair, not easier. The divining rod and the icon are held by the same hand.

Here is what Sellars gives us to understand the distance between these two monologues. The difference is not that one is honest and the other dishonest. It is that one is doing what Sellars called philosophy — navigating between the two images, letting the scientific image correct the manifest one, naming the crack so that it might be repaired. Z is doing something older and in its proper place more dogmatic: liturgy. Liturgy sustains the community in the image it needs to hold. The cathedral, the inscription, the family, the first peaceful Easter — these are not lies. They are the image as icon, and icons have their purpose.

When the manifest image cracks down the middle, when a society makes heroes simultaneously of the man who bleeds at the front and the man who films himself evading the recruiter, liturgy alone cannot hold it. The image needs repair from within. Philosophy — honest, uncomfortable, blunt grammar and unanswerable questions — is what repair looks like.

Wartime leaders have always preferred liturgy to philosophy. Churchill did it. Lincoln did it. This is not a character flaw; it is a structural requirement of the role. But Sellars’ warning was precise: the manifest image becomes dangerous when sealed off from correction entirely. The ceremony must remain in contact with what it is sustaining people through — or it stops sustaining them and starts simply performing itself.

But there is a further complication now. When the scientific image is being managed by the same hand that holds the icon — when the divining rod and the liturgy are instruments of the same apparatus — the Sellarsian repair becomes structurally unavailable. Budanov naming the crack is not philosophy. It is pressure management. The crack is acknowledged so that it need not be addressed. We have written about this arrangement [before](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1457?utm_source=publication-search).

This is not the first time these questions have been worth asking about Z. In the early months of the COVID epidemic, writing about his government’s pandemic response, we invoked Rudolph Carnap — a logical positivist who, as it happens, was one of Sellars’ formative influences — and his observation that the classical theory of probability “puts a premium on ignorance.” The argument then was that Z’s mitigation thinking substituted comfortable assumptions for honest inquiry. The argument now is not so different. The philosopher changes; the premium on ignorance remains. (See: Plague Mitigation, June 2020)

The religious tradition Z invoked this morning knows something about this too. The Easter story does not skip the tomb. Христос воскрес is not a denial of what came before. It is an insistence that what came before was not the final word. The resurrection is a claim made on the far side of catastrophe, not instead of it.

That is the harder Easter — the one that holds both images at once. The embroidered tablecloth and the two million outstanding summonses. The cat asleep in the sun and the men hiding from their summons in apartments not entirely unlike this one, in buildings visible, perhaps, through that very window.

The Paris tag hangs in the light. The tulips are open. The paska is on the table.

Христос воскрес. Воістину воскрес.

## Day 1511

2026-04-14

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7fe5d4c9-72aa-456a-b4dc-9647d6c222e9_1407x768.png)  
*Illustration c/o Nano Banana 2 (April 14, 2026)*

There is a kind of promotion that is also a verdict. The man who fails upward has been judged, just not as he fears. The system has looked at him and said: yes. This one. He will do what is necessary and remember it differently afterward. A rare talent. Not to be wasted.

Someone baked paska in Kyiv on Sunday. Two paskas. Tulips — pink and yellow. A cat asleep in the sun. In the window, a small wooden tag: Paris. Why Paris, nobody explained.

Z spoke from Saint Sophia Cathedral. He spoke of children’s laughter and the first peaceful Easter that was surely coming. It was moving. The cathedral stands. The children laugh. The paskas were baked.

Also that morning: four hundred drones. And in a courtroom that receives less attention than the cathedral, a man named [Roman Chervinsky](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aKpGNiP7yp0&t=1s) prepared for another session of a trial now in its third year. The charges are fabricated. The people who fabricated them have been promoted. This is not a paradox. It is the system describing itself.

A retired American general said true things after visiting. Ukrainian forces have made greater incremental gains than the Russians over the past two months. Ukraine’s cruise missile now flies farther and carries a heavier payload than America’s. He was witnessing extraordinary innovation — a smaller force outthinking a larger one. He was right to be astonished.

He did not say why the innovation was necessary.

A country does not become ingenious because it wishes to. The soldiers are extraordinary the way a man pushed from a building is extraordinary for learning, on the way down, to fall correctly. The falling is real. The ingenuity is real. Who did the pushing is a different question. It is not asked at security forums. It was not asked when [Z presented the hardware](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Br_kdXR-sk&t=11s) yesterday, in what is its own kind of liturgy.

---

---

In Belgrade, Oleksandr Lytvynenko is settling in.

He was Ukraine’s chief of foreign intelligence from 2021 to 2024. By presidential decree, he is now ambassador to Serbia. Yesterday he gave his [first interview from Belgrade](https://interfax.com.ua/news/interview/1158835.html). It is a pleasant document.

He discusses Serbian bookshops: forty shelves of English titles for every one in Russian. Encouraging. The Orthodox connection. A future free trade zone. A direct train from Kyiv to Belgrade — someday, once Belgrade–Budapest is sorted. He notes that more than a hundred thousand Russians now live in Serbia, against two to three thousand Ukrainians. Worth noting.

The interview does not mention 2021 to 2024.

During that period, on detailed and sourced accounts that have not been refuted, Lytvynenko disbanded the directorate within foreign intelligence tasked with monitoring Russia. August 2021. Completed by December. His own officers were documenting invasion corridors, force concentrations, timelines. He reported to the president that no invasion was coming. The president said so publicly. The invasion came.

Lytvynenko was then appointed to lead the body whose archives contain the most complete record of what was known, and when.

He is now in Belgrade. The bookshops are well stocked. The train may run someday.

---

There is a word for the confession that protects. It is not confession. It is something older, more precise. Perhaps we lost it. Perhaps we never had it.

The man now heading the President’s Office [said recently](https://www.ukrinform.ua/rubric-ato/4111141-budanov-bez-ludej-vijni-ne-vigrautsa-droni-ne-zroblat-ce-za-nas.html) that draft evasion is a terrible problem. That Ukraine has made heroes of both the soldier who bleeds and the man who films himself evading the recruiter. If everyone evades, Ukraine will not remain on the political map. He asked the question and answered it: no, it will not.

This was reported as honesty.

One pauses here and asks a simple question: what have these two men — the one discussing Belgrade bookshops, the one naming the mobilization crisis — actually done to earn the platforms from which they now speak? The answer, if one consults the record rather than the title, is clarifying. The platform is not the reward for the achievement. The platform is the achievement. This is how the system pays its debts.

This is the same man who, in 2020, denied on the record that the Wagner operation had taken place — a claim demolished fifteen months later by hundreds of documents. The same man who, the morning Navalny died, told the public the opposition leader had not been poisoned. The same man whose directorate prepared daily intelligence briefings that should have named invasion routes. Did not name them.

When this man names the crack, he is not outside the wall. He is the wall. The alarm is raised so it can substitute for repair. The crack is acknowledged so it need not be fixed. This is not honesty. It is honesty’s uniform, worn by someone else.

The divining rod and the icon are held by the same hand. The hand now sits at the head of the President’s Office.

---

In the courtroom, the trial continues.

Chervinsky’s account — of who disbanded what, who reported what to whom, who was promoted, whose names were passed to foreign prosecutors through a man later designated by the U.S. Treasury as a Russian agent — is public record. It has not been answered. It will not be. Answering would require the system to look at itself from outside itself. It was built to prevent this.

The general admires the soldiers. He is right. The cathedral held the ceremony. The ceremony was not false. The ambassador discusses bookshops. The bookshops are real. The official names the crisis. The crisis is real.

Everything is real. That is the difficulty.

---

The tulips are still on the table. The cat likes to nibble on them. The small wooden tag still says Paris, in a city where four hundred drones came one morning, and a man goes to court for the third year for the crime of having been right.

The tomb was sealed by someone. It is worth knowing who. And where they are now. And what pleasant interviews they are giving. And what they choose not to mention.

## Day 1512

2026-04-15 · Everything rhymes

Yes. [This](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-04-14/ukraine-zelenskiy-s-new-chief-aide-budanov-is-on-the-rise?srnd=homepage-europe) is the piece that completes the picture[1](#footnote-1).

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/77445831-c7db-4b83-9f8e-46f7a73bc3bd_884x288.png)  
*Puhleaze*

Read it against [Day 1511](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1511) and the irony becomes almost architectural.

[Bloomberg](http://bloomberg.com) gives you Budanov admiring Napoleon at his tomb in Paris — his first international trip as chief of staff. The chess set. The katana. The frog named Petro. The sitcom Friends playing in reception. The adviser who profiles Russian negotiators psychologically. The man who “buries many people” and therefore understands the true cost of war.

It is a masterpiece of profile-writing in the service of myth-making. Every detail is chosen to produce a specific figure: the warrior-intellectual, the reluctant statesman, the realist who can end the war. The piece even provides its own disclaimer — “it’s too early to think about that now” — which is the oldest way of thinking about it.

What the piece does not contain: Wagner. Navalny. The invasion briefings. The daily intelligence reports that did not name the routes. None of it. Not one word.

And there, in the window of Budanov’s new office, if you look carefully at the Bloomberg piece: a pysanka behind the secretary’s desk. A painted Easter egg — the same icon that surfaces in every register of this war, for every audience, in every language.

The Paris tag. The paska. The cat. Everything rhymes. The Z system is very good at this. The details change. The omissions don’t.

---

On the Kyiv jacket:

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/ece13eb6-5c92-4b96-9514-fc5dd5a1af26_864x1010.png)  
*Not Norwegian violin music*

Veselka, Kyiv’s premier queer-techno collective, returns to Collider on May 2, 2026, for Pure Hard II. Curated by local favorite Polka, this high-velocity format strips away compromise, prioritizing a “dense and ruthless” sonic experience — the kind of density that does not negotiate. The event will be attended Eternity and Raven Cure, names that sound like they were chosen by someone who had been awake for several days and was no longer entirely joking.

Veselka remains a sanctuary of freedom with a strict “no casual” dress code — think leather, latex, and chrome, the armor of people who have decided that seriousness and pleasure are not opposites. Photography is forbidden to protect the space, whatever that means. Admission is free for military personnel, but requires registration on the spot with ID cards for everyone else.

---

Meanwhile, Z is zipping around Europen capitals signing bilateral drone framework agreements — the latest iteration of a habit that never quite became a strategy.

There was a time when nothing had a name yet, and therefore nothing was officially happening. Only the usual confusion of volunteers, engineers, and officers trying to explain to one another — across different languages of urgency — why paper maps were no longer sufficient for a war that had already become digital without permission.

In those early years, groups like Aerorozvidka appeared not as institutions but as habits of mind. They were what happened when people who knew how systems should behave met a system that did not yet agree. Drones were assembled in workshops that still smelled faintly of domestic life. Reconnaissance reports travelled faster than the bureaucracy could file objections. It was not revolution, exactly. It was improvisation that refused to stay temporary.

From this atmosphere, a new idea slowly formed: that the battlefield could be seen, not in fragments, but as a continuous field of information. The system later called Delta did not arrive like a discovery. It accreted. It passed through committees, field tests, wartime necessity, and institutional hesitation. It became official in the way things become official in wartime Ukraine — not by declaration, but by exhaustion of alternatives.

There was a moment when this accumulation crossed a threshold. Systems that had once lived in parallel — military, volunteer, experimental — began to align. Not perfectly, not cleanly, but sufficiently to function under pressure. NATO interoperability entered the vocabulary, not as aspiration, but as grammar. The language of war itself began to change its syntax.

Outside this process, or perhaps inside it in another form, the new defense economy began to take shape. Startups appeared with names that sounded like weather phenomena or birds that had forgotten migration routes. Brave1 became a kind of administrative greenhouse where ideas were no longer asked whether they were serious, only whether they could survive contact with reality.

Western partners entered this ecosystem not as architects, but as suppliers of cash and components — analytics systems, mapping tools, integration layers. Palantir was among those present in this landscape, offering structures for making sense of data that already existed in overwhelming quantity. But the architecture remained, stubbornly, Ukrainian in its orientation: fragmented, redundant, adaptive. Nothing truly centralized survived long without being forced to justify itself again.

And then there are the people who move between levels — between ministries, industries, and presidential corridors — trying to keep the system from separating into incompatible realities. Not controllers, not symbols, but something closer to translators under pressure. Their task is not to impose order, but to prevent different kinds of order from cancelling each other out.

What emerges from all this is not a clean story of ownership. It is something more awkward and more durable: a hybrid structure in which the state is everywhere and yet not alone, in which private actors build what the state cannot specify in advance, and in which foreign systems attach themselves like scaffolding that may or may not be removed later.

People sometimes describe this as a loss of control. It is more precise to call it redistribution of authorship. The map is no longer drawn by one hand. It is revised continuously by necessity.

Wars, in the end, do not only destroy. They also assign vocabulary. And once a new vocabulary takes hold, it becomes difficult to remember the exact moment when it stopped being improvised speech and started becoming the only language available.
