## Day 1513

2026-04-16 · Smoke over the sunrise

The young woman—tidy in the manner of [Marie Kondo](https://konmari.com/?srsltid=AfmBOopFDRjZdD6Ktl2eUK45epbKuqy-ldwETvKGpDarLTfjiaI8_7zv), and representing that organization in some professional capacity I didn’t entirely follow—remarked yesterday evening, over two lukewarm shots of Patrón Reposado in the kitchen, that JD Vance’s animosity toward Ukraine might trace back to his 2022 Senate campaign in Ohio. She lives in Washington, D.C., and is here on a week’s vacation; tomorrow she begins the journey back. His opponent, Tim Ryan, supported continued assistance. Vance did not. It wasn’t the central issue, but it was a live one—particularly for the American-Ukrainian community that Ohio, somewhat inconveniently for Vance, happens to contain.

Hours later, at around 2:30 a.m., Russia launched another ballistic missile attack on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Several explosions. As of this writing, civilians are reported dead, dozens wounded. The usual.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2c1f4fc6-30c3-4720-a7cd-deac8b9a7901_1280x823.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o State Emergency Service (April 16, 2026)*

Later, on the mat, moving through a set of propulsion exercises before heading downtown, I found myself thinking about Vance and what he represents: a small, thick cloud of black smoke blocking what could have been a very nice sunrise. Exactly the image in this video—looking east from Pechersky, down Lesi Ukrainky Boulevard toward the Motherland Monument and the museum of local wars. A clear morning, interrupted.

Earlier this week, Vice President Vance sat before a scattering of students in Georgia and described ending weapons transfers to Ukraine as one of the proudest achievements of his administration. It is worth noting—gently—that the transfers had already ended months earlier. That Europe had already assumed the burden. That the war, inattentive to these pronouncements, continues into its fifth year, despite promises to end it in twenty-four hours.

This is the achievement: not doing something, and doing it loudly enough that it registers as action.

A familiar form. The man who arrives late to the harvest and takes credit for the empty field. There is a certain cleanliness to it. Nothing touches you.

From this position of careful distance, Vance has also found time to advise the pope to concern himself with matters of morality and leave politics to others. An interesting division of labor, especially from a man for whom the safest moral act is abstention—provided it is announced with sufficient conviction.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2674f7c2-6fff-45a6-b0f2-ccda5f5bcd41_682x515.png)  
*Aid Allocation to Ukraine 2022-25 – Europe vs. US (c/o Kiel Institute, February 2026)*

By the end of 2025, Congress had already approved more than $188 billion in Ukraine-related spending. The shipments had gone out; the consequences were already unfolding far from Georgia lecture halls. Vance now celebrates the moment he chose not to continue. It is like congratulating oneself for not boarding a train that has already left the station.

The room, on this particular evening, did not quite cooperate. Too many empty seats. Too much space for the words to travel without resistance. This is a performance that depends on proximity—the warmth of bodies, the reassurance of applause. Without it, the claim has to stand on its own.

It doesn’t.

This is not hypocrisy. Hypocrisy requires tension between what is said and what is known. This is something looser, more accommodating. When a voice from the depleted crowd shouted that he was killing children, Vance replied that conservatives should stay engaged and take the country back. He did not specify from whom.

This, too, is part of the achievement: to mansplain in a half-empty auditorium, in a country your party fully controls, and speak of liberation[1](#footnote-1).

## Day 1517

2026-04-21 · The Director of Victories

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7251ff5f-1b8f-4bac-9fcd-5640be7058fd_1728x1243.jpeg)  
*c/o Oleh Smal*

**The Shooting**

On Saturday, April 18, a gunman opened fire in central Kyiv, killing at least seven people and wounding others. Body camera footage later revealed what happened when two patrol officers arrived at the scene: they saw wounded civilians including a child who was bleeding and pleading for help. Instead of engaging the shooter, the officers ran away. As Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko stated, the armed man “continued unimpeded to move down the street and shoot defenseless passersby.” The gunman was eventually killed by special forces, but not before the damage was done.

The officers faced charges of negligence with grave consequences—potentially five years imprisonment. The incident sparked immediate public outrage and raised urgent questions about accountability, training, and leadership.

---

You know, there’s a curious thing about watching a man respond to a crisis. You can tell everything about him by which crises he rushes to meet, and which ones he approaches as if they were invoices requiring a filing stamp.

President Z, when faced with the Kyiv shooting, demonstrated remarkable flexibility. On April 19—his first response—he was calm, measured, procedurally sound. An investigation was underway. Personnel decisions would be made. Protocols required review. Very sensible. He mentioned it the way one mentions a plumbing problem: real, requiring attention, but not something that demands you raise your voice.

Then came April 20. Overnight, something changed. The officers hadn’t merely failed to act; they “should have done everything to stop the killer” but instead “fled.” There must be accountability. Accountability! A word that had been oddly absent the day before, suddenly appeared, impossible to miss.

What happened in those twenty-four hours? Public outrage, certainly. But also something more revealing: Z discovered that condemning the officers cost him nothing politically. Everyone agreed. This was the rare moment when moral clarity and popular sentiment aligned perfectly. So he seized it.

**The Difficult Questions**

This is the pattern worth examining. Z can be decisive. What he avoids is the harder thing: taking positions when the cost is real.

Consider the questions that followed the shooting. Should Ukraine mobilize its police force to the front, despite domestic security needs? Should civilians be permitted to own handguns for self-defense? How should post-war demobilization work? On these matters, Z remains silent—not because he’s unclear about the facts, but because any answer alienates someone. Military commanders want police manpower. Police families want their relatives home. Gun control advocates oppose armed citizenry. Security hawks demand preparation.

Rather than navigate this tension, Z has perfected what might be called the “director of victories” approach. He claims credit for successes, distances himself from failures, and speaks with moral force precisely when speaking costs him nothing. When the bill comes due, he’s elsewhere.

This isn’t cowardice in the physical sense. It’s something more interesting: the spinelessness of a leader who avoids structural decisions to preserve popularity. A genuine statesman would accept the cost of unpopular positions. Z calculates the cost and moves on.

**The Baltic Misstep**

Recent events reinforce this pattern. In a Sunday interview, Z speculated that Russia is preparing a major attack on the Baltic states and used this to question NATO’s commitment to Article 5. Estonian officials [responded](https://news.liga.net/ua/politics/news/estonskyy-ministr-zaperechyv-zelenskomu-shcho-rosiia-mozhe-napasty) with the kind of patience one extends to an unreliable acquaintance. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Z’s claims don’t match their intelligence assessments and that Russia is actually weak militarily and economically.

More pointedly, Parliamentary commission chair Marko Mihkelson observed that Ukraine keeps “pointing fingers at Europe” with warnings that if Ukraine loses, the Baltics are next. This feeds Russian narratives, he noted, and should be discussed quietly between allies, not broadcast to the press like a cry for help.

Z’s apparent goal—to pressure allies for more aid by raising existential threats—backfired. Instead of rallying support, he generated friction with committed allies and gave ammunition to those who argue he weaponizes fear to extract resources.

**A Forced Reckoning**

There’s an irony worth noting: Z appears to have finally abandoned the pursuit of American favor. For over a year after Trump’s return, he played the long game with remarkable patience: participated in fruitless peace talks, agreed to mineral deals meant to enrich Americans, lavished praise on Trump himself. But as U.S. aid dried up and pressure mounted to cede Ukrainian territory, something shifted.

Now Z speaks with unusual candor about [American alignment with Russia](https://archive.ph/SULLP#selection-607.0-1050.0) and the need for Europe to build independent security architecture—language that would have been unthinkable a year ago. “Russia played the Americans again,” he said recently. He’s advocating for a European security framework independent of NATO, seeking new military partners, and attacking Russian oil infrastructure despite American objections.

But notice: this honesty emerged not from principle but from necessity. Ukraine’s improved military position—driven by homegrown drone innovation and battlefield success—gave Z the confidence to stop performing. He could finally afford to tell the truth.

Even this demonstrates the pattern. Z speaks honestly when circumstances eliminate the option of silence. When he has the luxury of deflection, he takes it. The moment the calculation changes, so does his rhetoric.

**The Question Remains**

Z can be decisive when it matters and costs him nothing. He can be honest when forced by circumstance. The question that lingers is whether he’ll ever take a genuinely difficult position—one where conviction matters more than calculation.

Based on the record, the answer appears to be no. And that, perhaps, tells us everything we need to know.

## Day 1518

2026-04-22 · Donnyland

There is an old saying in the Kyrvyi Rih — though perhaps I invented it just now — that that a man who perfects the art of kneeling will eventually forget how to stand..

Z is a practical man. He understands that dignity, like a good overcoat, must sometimes be pawned when winter is very cold. And the winter in the Dnipropetrovsk region has been very cold indeed, for many years now.

So Z’s people, being resourceful and not without humor, proposed naming a depopulated strip of adjacent coal country — fifty miles long, forty miles wide, populated mainly by soldiers and the shops that sell them flowers for their wives — after the most powerful man in the world. Donnyland, they called it[1](#footnote-1). A place that sounds like happiness, though it is not.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/be3a1897-2cca-4e98-ad49-adae74a2ba59_561x690.png)

One must admire the ingenuity. Trump, after all, has his name on towers, casinos, a university that was not quite a university, and now — if things go well — a small wounded piece of eastern Europe. Z’s people even prepared a flag. Green and gold. And a national anthem, composed with the assistance of a machine that has read everything and understood rather less.

The most poignant detail, to my mind, is this: it is not clear the Americans ever saw the flag.

This is the essence of the relationship. Z gestures grandly across a great distance. Trump looks the other way, occupied with other matters — Iran, perhaps, or a press conference.

Six years ago, a writer noticed this pattern and said: it will not end well[2](#footnote-2).

He was not wrong. He was simply early.

## Day 1519

2026-04-23 · A pattern that explains too much

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f7e938b2-72b7-4524-baeb-d5d91f925f33_1122x1402.png)  
*Photo enchanted with AI c/o abdymok*

The philosopher Daniel Dennett once proposed [a test for reality](https://ruccs.rutgers.edu/images/personal-zenon-pylyshyn/class-info/FP2012/FP2012_readings/Dennett_RealPatterns.pdf) that has the charm of a joke.

A checkerboard can be written down quickly. A field of flax, seen from above: hundreds of small blue and violet flowers, each slightly different, scattered without order, light catching some and losing others, and a dark human shadow cutting through the middle, takes longer to encrypt. There is nothing to say about it except itself.

From this he concluded: a pattern is real if it allows you to say less.

This is a comforting idea. It suggests the world, at least in places, can be shortened.

On April 18, a man with a gun killed seven people in Kyiv. Two police officers arrived and left.

The next day, there was a statement. It contained the usual things: procedures, reviews, the future tense.

A day later, the language improved. The officers had fled. There would be accountability.

Nothing essential had changed. The sentences had.

It is tempting to explain such shifts. One can speak of pressure, of advisors, of timing. These explanations are available in abundance, like confetti.

But there is a simpler approach, which requires a certain restraint.

Dennett suggested that, when faced with a system one does not understand, it is often useful to pretend it is rational. Not wise, not good—only consistent. Then one asks what it would want, and watches.

Z is a man who speaks well when speaking costs nothing.

This is not a rare talent.

He also prefers silence when speech would require him to choose between two things that both have consequences. This, too, is not rare, though it is less often noticed.

Between these two observations, a certain economy appears.

One begins to suspect that many details are unnecessary.

There was a [conversation with Amanpour](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=4509715932594959) about peace. It went well. It could hardly do otherwise.

There were later remarks about American behavior, sharper than before. They appeared at a moment when silence had begun to look like a decision rather than an absence.

Again, the sentences improved.

If one wished to be unkind, one could say that the man develops convictions precisely at the point where they become inexpensive.

But this would be to say too much, and also too early.

It is better to wait.

Elsewhere, other men speak.

Donald Tusk and Emmanuel Macron meet and discuss unity. The word appears several times. It does not seem to burden them.

At the same time, there are calculations. Not hidden exactly, but not emphasized. What is given, what is received, what is conditional.

The conversation proceeds without difficulty.

Empires, when they divide, usually do so more plainly. There is a certain relief in that.

A pattern, if it is real, should reduce effort.

In this case, one can ignore almost everything: the topic, the tone, the declared principles. A single question remains, modest but persistent:

what does this cost?

From it, much follows.

There is something faintly embarrassing about a person who can be understood in this way. Not because he is worse than others, but because he is clearer.

Clarity, in such matters, has a way of shifting from virtue to symptom.

One begins to wonder whether the man is leading events, or whether events have found in him their most economical expression.

Difficulties arise when the arithmetic stops working—when what is advantageous and what is necessary no longer coincide.

At such moments, patterns of this kind do not break. They pause.

This is also a form of consistency.

A real pattern allows you to say less.

It also leaves you with less to hope for.

## Day 1520

2026-04-24 · Heavy rotation

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4011718e-6bb4-42d6-8903-5ab9af333cdd_1536x1024.png)

A historian tried to explain onversations that don’t happen. He’d been asked what he’d say to people close to power—people who shape policy, not comment on it. His answer was simple: those conversations don’t happen.

Why?

Because they’re afraid.

Not physically afraid. The more specific fear: exposure. Having to defend a position that only works at a distance. Sitting across from someone who understands the system well enough to ask the one question you can’t evade.

I nodded along, because I’ve seen this dynamic before, just not in politics.

A godsend apartment in Lichterfelde, back when West Berlin still felt provisional: top floor, two rooms, bay window, roof garden. Rent was $250, half paid in liquor from the PX. One afternoon I came home to find a party blooming across the street on the balcony of a building that had been boarded up the day before—shoulder pads and glassy cocaine smiles, beer mugs raised to what was clearly a very good investment. A restaurant was opening. German classics. Currywurst, Kassler, the works.

That night the soundtrack arrived. Tinny outdoor speakers, one song in heavy rotation. It would stop—someone flipping the tape—and then start again: the same drum fill, the same chorus, over and over. You could leave the room, shut the window, drink yourself into indifference. It didn’t matter. You still had to listen.

That’s the part people underestimate: what you can’t tune out[1](#footnote-1).

---

The same historian won’t be having certain conversations about Ukraine. Not with critics. Not with people inside the system who can describe, in unglamorous detail, how it actually works.

The reason is the same. Fear, yes—but also cost.

Because if the conversation happens, something has to be named. And once it’s named, it doesn’t go back in the box.

---

---

There’s a pattern here, and it isn’t especially complicated.

It begins with the belief that narrative can substitute for system. Early scandals break; the response is cosmetic. Reset, move forward. The assumption holds: control the story, control reality.

Then the problem shifts. From optics to trust. Or rather, the absence of it. Internal fractures widen. Decisions narrow. Competence gives way to proximity.

Finally, the system learns what it’s for. Money moves the way authority has been structured to move—upward, inward. Funds misallocated, contracts feeding the same circle. At that point, calling it corruption misses the point. This is the system functioning as designed.

---

---

Now imagine the historian sitting across from someone who can lay this out cleanly, without rhetoric. The same framework he uses elsewhere, applied here without modification.

What does he say?

He can’t deny the pattern—he’s spent years describing it.

He can’t claim ignorance—the pieces were public.

He can’t defend the exception without weakening the rule.

So the conversation doesn’t happen.

---

He once said, about another political circle, that their refusal to engage was “entirely their fault.” He would have the conversation; they wouldn’t, because they’d have to defend the indefensible in real time.

Fair enough.

But frameworks don’t stay selective. Apply it here and it holds. Refuse to apply it and something else breaks—credibility, or the quieter sense that you’re curating rather than analyzing.

Neither is a stable position.

---

This isn’t cowardice, exactly. It’s self-preservation. If your authority rests on seeing patterns clearly, there are some patterns you can’t afford to acknowledge late.

Because lateness implies choice.

And choice implies that the silence wasn’t forced.

---

People inside the system don’t need metaphors anymore. They’re looking for recognition—someone to say: yes, this pattern is real, and it has consequences.

Instead, they get omission. Analysis that stops just short of application.

---

I learned, in that apartment, that you can tolerate almost any distraction.

But not everything.

If the same song plays long enough, it stops being background. It becomes the structure of your attention.

Some things, once heard, don’t fade.

Some patterns, once seen, don’t resolve into something nicer.

And some conversations, avoided long enough, don’t just remain undone.

They become impossible.

---

Have a great weekend!

## Hebdomada

2026-04-25

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c1be2a62-a1cc-4117-95bc-eb843d7e5762_1536x1024.png)  
*Illustration c/o ChatGPT*

**Introduction: The Pattern Beneath the Chaos**

On April 18, the relative stillness of central Kyiv was shattered by gunfire. Seven people died while two police officers, faced with the immediate choice to protect or preserve themselves, fled the scene. This tragic failure of duty provides more than just a case for a prosecutor; it offers a window into what the philosopher Daniel Dennett called “economical patterns.”

Dennett proposed a test for reality that has the charm of a joke. A checkerboard can be written down quickly, its logic easily encoded. But a field of flax, seen from above—hundreds of small blue and violet flowers, scattered without order, light catching some and losing others, a dark human shadow cutting through the middle—takes longer to encrypt. There is nothing to say about it except itself. From this, he concluded: a pattern is real if it allows you to say less.

In the wake of the shooting, the voice of President Z fluctuated with a telling frequency. By examining the shift from procedural calm to moral outrage, we can begin to see the underlying arithmetic of modern statesmanship: a system where a leader’s intensity is rarely a measure of conviction, but rather a calculation of political cost.

**Takeaway 1: Conviction as a Calculation**

The “Director of Victories” approach defines a leadership style that prioritizes optics over structural resolution. On April 19, President Z’s initial response to the Kyiv shooting was almost clinical. He spoke of investigations, personnel reviews, and protocols—the “plumbing problems” of governance. However, by April 20, as public fury mounted, his tone underwent a radical transformation. Suddenly, the officers hadn’t just failed; they had “fled,” and the word “accountability” became the centerpiece of his rhetoric.

This shift reveals a leader who seizes moral clarity only when it aligns perfectly with popular sentiment and carries zero political risk. He can be decisive when everyone already agrees, but he remains silent on the harder, more divisive structural questions. He avoids the “Difficult Questions” that follow such a tragedy: Should the police force be mobilized to the front despite domestic security needs? Should civilians be permitted to own handguns for self-defense? How should post-war demobilization work? On these matters, he is silent, because any answer would alienate a key constituency.

“You can tell everything about him by which crises he rushes to meet, and which ones he approaches as if they were invoices requiring a filing stamp.”

President Z calculates the cost of every position. He develops convictions precisely at the point where they become inexpensive. When the bill for a genuine, unpopular decision comes due, he is often found elsewhere, preserving his popularity by avoiding the friction of leadership.

**Takeaway 2: The “Donnyland” Strategy and the Pawned Overcoat of Dignity**

Pragmatism in a time of crisis often requires the sacrifice of pride. Z understands that dignity, like a good overcoat, must sometimes be pawned when the winter is very cold. This was never more evident than in the proposal to rename a fifty-mile strip of depopulated Donbas coal country “Donnyland.”

This was a blatant appeal to Donald Trump’s vanity—an attempt to trade a piece of geography for political momentum. The project carried a poignant level of detail: a fifty-mile-long strip of land populated mainly by soldiers and flower shops, a newly designed green and gold flag, and a national anthem composed by an AI that had read everything but understood nothing. It was a grand gesture across a great distance, made all the more absurd by the fact that the Americans likely never even saw the flag. It was the ultimate expression of a leadership willing to perform for an audience that wasn’t even looking.

“A man who perfects the art of kneeling will eventually forget how to stand.”

**Takeaway 3: The Baltic Misstep and the Weaponization of Fear**

In a recent Sunday interview, President Z attempted to pressure NATO by claiming Russia was preparing an imminent attack on the Baltic states. This was a tactical attempt to use fear as a lever for aid, but it resulted in rare public friction with his closest allies.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna was quick to push back, noting that Z’s claims did not match intelligence assessments and that Russia remains militarily and economically weak. More pointedly, Marko Mihkelson, chair of the Estonian parliamentary commission, critiqued the habit of “pointing fingers at Europe.” He argued that such public warnings actually strengthen Russia’s psychological warfare by feeding their narrative that the Baltics are inevitable victims. By broadcasting these warnings to the press instead of discussing them quietly between allies, Z risked his credibility and generated irritation rather than the intended surge of support.

**Takeaway 4: When Corruption is the System Functioning as Designed**

To understand how narrative eventually fails, one must understand the concept of “heavy rotation.” I recall a godsend apartment in Lichterfelde, back when West Berlin felt provisional. One afternoon, a party bloomed across the street on a boarded-up balcony—shoulder pads and glassy cocaine smiles, beer mugs raised to a new restaurant investment. That night, the soundtrack arrived. A single song played on tinny speakers in heavy rotation. It didn’t matter if you shut the window or drank yourself into indifference; the song became the structure of your attention.

In modern governance, there is a similar progression. It begins with the belief that narrative can substitute for system. Control the story, control reality. But eventually, the problem shifts from optics to an absence of trust. Internal fractures widen, and competence is replaced by proximity to power. Money begins to move exactly as authority is structured: upward and inward. Funds are misallocated, and contracts are funneled to a tight inner circle.

“At that point, calling it corruption misses the point. This is the system functioning as designed.”

Policy-shapers often avoid honest conversations about these mechanics because they fear exposure—having to defend a position that only works at a distance. When the “heavy rotation” of a narrative plays long enough, it stops being background noise and becomes a reality that can no longer be ignored.

**Conclusion: The Cost of the Impossible Conversation**

The patterns of leadership are real because they allow us to say less. If we apply Daniel Dennett’s test for reality, we see that President Z’s behavior is consistent: he speaks when it is inexpensive and remains silent when speech requires a difficult choice between two consequences. This clarity is not a virtue, but a diagnosis.

The arithmetic of leadership works as long as “advantageous” and “necessary” overlap. But eventually, the numbers stop adding up. When the narrative can no longer hide the absence of trust and when the “Donnylands” of the world go unnoticed, the conversation becomes impossible. It leaves the observer with a persistent, uncomfortable question: Is a leader truly guiding events toward a better future, or has he simply become the most economical expression of the chaos surrounding him?

---

I didn’t write this week about quietly **rewiring my propulsion system** in pursuit of a sub-six minute mile—a project that turns out to be less about lungs and more about teaching a reluctant posterior chain to behave like one.

This has involved a series of highly specific, faintly punitive interventions: slow-eccentric **Bulgarian split squats** that feel like negotiating a treaty with your hip stabilizers; isometric holds at end-range hip extension where the **gluteus medius muscle** begins to tremble like a small, overworked civil servant; and banded lateral walks designed to wake up fibers that have apparently been on administrative leave since 2019.

There are also **single-leg Romanian deadlifts**, performed slowly enough to expose every lie your balance system tells you, and hip thrusts that convert abstract anatomical diagrams into immediate, local pain. The **gluteus maximus muscle**—long accustomed to outsourcing its responsibilities to quads and lower back—has been recalled to active duty.

The technical goal is straightforward: restore clean hip extension, stabilize the pelvis under load, and eliminate energy leaks that show up, at pace, as inefficiency rather than drama. The lived experience is less elegant. It’s a steady accumulation of micro-failures: shaking holds, asymmetries you can’t unsee, and the distinct sensation that parts of your body are being introduced to each other for the first time.

Progress, if that’s what it is, comes in small, measurable shifts. A stride that feels marginally more elastic. Ground contact a fraction cleaner. The sense—brief, unreliable—that forward motion is being generated from somewhere behind you, rather than assembled awkwardly in front.

It’s technical. It’s tedious. It’s a little painful.

## Day 1524

2026-04-28 · The Inferior Play

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/03347e7a-4463-4b64-97c2-9ce14d56de9d_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (April 27, 2026)*

There are two narratives about Ukraine, and they cannot both be true.

The first is the one now routinely told in Western capitals and respectable opinion pages: [that Volodymyr Z has emerged as the standard-bearer of liberal democracy](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/26/opinion/zelensky-ukraine-trump-nato-leader.html), a Churchillian figure rallying not only his own country but the moral imagination of the West. The comparison to Cold War Berlin is popular. But let’s be honest about what that comparison actually is.

A Guardian podcast quoted someone saying Kyiv “feels like Berlin felt during the Cold War.” The problem: the person saying it was 13 years old when the Wall fell. He didn’t live through Cold War Berlin. His Berlin correspondent job started in 2003—a decade after the Wall came down. He’s invoking historical gravitas he never actually experienced, wandering around cardboard protests with a microphone, interviewing scene kids as atmospheric color. [This is a pattern.](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1252) Western journalists and analysts donning the costume of historical insight they didn’t earn.

The second story is less cinematic but rather more consistent with observable reality. Ukraine has indeed performed something extraordinary: it has resisted a full-scale Russian invasion. But this achievement belongs, in the main, to its soldiers, its junior officers, and a society capable of improvisation under extreme stress. It does not follow that the country’s political leadership has therefore exemplified the highest standards of democratic governance.

One must insist on a simple distinction that is being willfully blurred: military resilience is not the same thing as liberal democracy.

A liberal democracy is not defined by the eloquence of its wartime speeches or the sympathy it elicits abroad. It is defined by constraint: independent courts, a legislature that can obstruct as well as applaud, and a press permitted to ask questions leaders would prefer not to answer.

On these measures, the Ukrainian record under Z is, at best, ambiguous and, at worst, troubling.

Power has become concentrated. Media has been consolidated. Parliamentary dissent has narrowed to near-irrelevance. Access between the presidency and independent Ukrainian journalists has become selective in ways that would raise eyebrows in any democratic state.

Consider the rotation crisis. [Ukraine’s military ombudswoman has documented something stark](https://www.pravda.com.ua/articles/2026/04/27/8031931/): soldiers are spending 200, 300 days on position without rotation. The order mandates a 15-day maximum. No one follows it. Why? Because there’s no accountability. As she put it: “This is a dead norm that no one observes, which means there are no limits at all. Some commanders don’t feel responsible for the fact that their soldiers have been sitting in bunkers for a year or more.”

The ombudswoman’s research shows that after 40 days, soldiers develop complete apathy—they stop caring whether they survive. Beyond that is not effective. It’s torture by another name.

Mobilization is simultaneously failing. Ukraine has 1.6 million eligible citizens but cannot reach them. Why? Inadequate state communication about defense needs. Citizens evade service. Instead of building public consensus through transparent policy, the government relies on police enforcement and recruitment centers operating under opaque authority. This is Z leadership. This is administrative failure.

When the ombudswoman tried to implement systemic change—to establish clear term limits for service—she encountered resistance at every level. Commanders ignore written orders. Vague authority means zero accountability. She has written 10 formal requirements for compliance. There are no teeth. As she noted: “We lack instruments to punish commanders who don’t follow the ombudswoman’s lawful requirements.”

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/345c4188-c40c-486a-a0b1-334bc899831b_3024x3409.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (Escape the Labrynth, April 28, 2026)*

Consider, too, endemic corruption. [Operation Midas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Midas) documented substantial schemes in the energy sector, implicating networks close to the center of political power. Senior figures associated with the presidential administration found themselves dismissed, investigated, or removed. One may call this a purge, a reform, or coincidence. What one cannot call it is irrelevant.

More revealing still was what followed. As anti-corruption bodies pressed investigations, legislative efforts emerged to curtail their independence. The response was public: the 2025 anti-corruption protests in Ukraine, the first significant anti-government demonstrations since the full-scale invasion. Faced with public pressure, the government retreated.

This sequence deserves attention. It suggests not a system comfortably committed to accountability, but one in which accountability must be extracted, often against resistance.

Ukraine’s most impressive achievements in this war—its adaptation to drone warfare, its decentralized tactical innovations, its capacity for rapid learning—have not been products of centralized political control. They have emerged from below, from units and commanders operating where initiative is rewarded because it must be.

This creates an awkward but unavoidable conclusion: the success of Ukraine’s resistance does not, in itself, validate the structure of its governance.

To say this is not to diminish Ukraine’s struggle, nor to question the necessity of supporting it. It is to insist on a distinction that allies, of all people, are obliged to maintain: the difference between solidarity and myth-making.

If Ukraine prevails—and one hopes it does—it will face a second challenge. It will need to reconstruct the institutional safeguards that have been bent, suspended, or quietly eroded since Z was elected. Courts will need to reassert independence. Legislatures will need to recover the habit of resistance. Journalists will need to ask questions that no longer have the convenient excuse of national emergency.

At that point, the flattering fictions of wartime will become less useful. And the question of what, exactly, has been built in the meantime will no longer be avoidable.

## Day 1525

2026-04-29 · What the transcript cannot hear

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/16f3d8f6-b0dd-4ee2-acd3-87cfdb545038_1491x1055.png)

*Ukrainians have long understood that outsiders tend to hear less in conversation than those raised inside the language—not only fewer words, but fewer meanings. Still, few expected that the gap would become so visible at the precise moment when fragments of Russian-language speech, allegedly recorded in private exchanges among senior figures, begin to circulate as if they were documents of state.*

*The recently leaked material—purportedly drawn from conversations involving Z’s inner circle—has already produced a familiar spectacle. Foreign analysts, and even some local intermediaries, approach the transcripts as if they were technical puzzles: lines to decode, statements to verify, names to confirm. Meanwhile, those accustomed to how such conversations actually function hear something else entirely.*

*Consider the exchanges between Tymur Mindich and Rustem Umerov concerning the Kyiv-based defense firm Fire Point. On the surface, the discussion appears disjointed—shifting from personnel decisions to financing gaps, from foreign investors to warehouse delays. To the untrained ear, it may even seem unfocused.*

*But this impression arises precisely because so much is left unsaid.*

*The participants do not explain who depends on whom. They do not clarify why certain payments matter more than others, or why the timing of a ministerial reassignment might threaten an entire production chain. Instead, they proceed as if all relevant knowledge were already shared. And in a sense, it is.*

*Professional listeners—whether linguists, intelligence officers, or simply attentive citizens—recognize this pattern. Meaning does not reside in the words alone. It emerges from the interaction between speech and context, between what is spoken and what is merely implied. The words themselves serve as triggers, activating a network of assumptions that the speakers have no need to articulate.*

*Thus, when Mindich remarks that “tomorrow the factory will stop,” the informed listener does not hear a literal prediction of shutdown. Rather, he hears a compressed statement about liquidity, contract flow, bureaucratic blockage, and political dependency. When he suggests that a problem could be resolved with “one phone call,” the phrase does not describe a simple administrative act. It signals the existence of a hierarchy in which informal intervention outweighs formal procedure.*

*Likewise, Umerov’s responses—measured, at times noncommittal—contain more than they appear to say. His references to delayed funds, partner contributions, and upcoming decisions indicate constraints that are not fully named. Yet the businessman understands them immediately, because they are operating within the same frame of reference.*

*Foreign observers often attempt to compensate for missing clarity by focusing on the text itself: parsing phrases, comparing translations, searching for explicit admissions. But this strategy is limited. In spoken interaction, especially of this kind, the most consequential elements are frequently those that remain unspoken.*

*The discussion of a potential sale of a 33% stake in Fire Point illustrates this point. The numbers are clear enough. The structure—investment plus partial cashout—is stated directly. Yet the significance lies not in the figures, but in what they imply: a need for external support, a hedge against political uncertainty, and a tacit acknowledgment of who stands to benefit.*

*Similarly, references to foreign partners, described as engaging in a “spy game,” should not be taken as literal accusations. They reflect a shared understanding that information, like capital, is a commodity to be negotiated. The speakers do not elaborate because elaboration would be redundant.*

*In everyday life, Ukrainians—like people everywhere—rely on what psychologists have termed “analysis by synthesis”: the ability to reconstruct incomplete signals by drawing on prior knowledge. In these recordings, that ability becomes essential. Without it, the conversation dissolves into fragments. With it, a coherent picture emerges.*

*What one hears, then, depends less on the recording than on the listener. And until those examining such material learn to follow not only the words, but the assumptions that sustain them, much of what is being said will continue to pass unnoticed—clearly audible, yet effectively unheard.*

## Day 1526

2026-04-30 · The Birthday in the Mountains

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f88b18b4-0069-4241-872f-0744e5927767_1536x1024.jpeg)

There is a particular kind of friendship that does not need to be explained, because it explains everything around it. It is the kind that secures a helicopter from a state emergency service for a private occasion, because an emergency, after all, had arisen: a man was turning fifty, and the mountains were far away.

This happened in November 2021, in the Carpathians, at a state residence called Synohora — Blue Mountain — which is a beautiful name for a place where beautiful arrangements are made[1](#footnote-1). The guests arrived. Among them, the same faces that would later appear, like recurring characters in a novel whose author denies writing it, across defense contracts, land schemes, and recordings that were never meant to be heard.

Three years later, the same circle — older, richer, considerably more exposed — was still meeting. Still building. Four estates in a cooperative called *Dynasty*, which is a name that requires no translation. One for Yermak. One for Chernyshov. One for Mindich. One, according to those who listened, for a man referred to simply as “Vova,” which is a diminutive, and diminutives in the Ukrainian tradition are reserved for intimacy.

---

*I want to be precise about what I am and am not arguing here. I am not presenting a verdict. I am not constructing a prosecution. At a certain point, the question stops being whether any single fragment proves direct involvement and becomes whether the total pattern still allows for meaningful distance. When the same circle of long-time associates appears across state contracts, private ventures, and informal coordination — and when decisions affecting those flows consistently align with their interests — the space for plausible non-awareness narrows on its own. No single element settles the matter. But taken together, they make the idea of sustained detachment increasingly difficult to maintain. That is all I am saying. That, it turns out, is quite enough. (And I forgot to mention that ex-CIA chief/US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo [joined](https://thehill.com/policy/defense/5609334-ukraine-defense-firm-pompeo/) the Advisory Board of Fire Point in November 2025, making this tragic drama even more idiotic.)*

---

The transcripts arrived the way all important things eventually arrive in such stories: not through heroism, but through resentment. The investigators had distributed their evidence to the accused, as the law requires. Some of the accused were in detention. Others were in Israel, or the Canary Islands, or conducting meetings about foreign investment. Those who remained on the inside looked at those who remained on the outside, and felt the particular injustice that only the guilty can feel toward one another. And so the transcripts moved, from pocket to pocket, until they reached the journalists, who performed the unglamorous but necessary function of telling the public what it had already, in some sense, suspected.

What the tapes revealed, beyond the specific sums and favors, was a grammar. Mindich pressing the Defense Minister for hundreds of billions in contracts. Mindich asking for “one phone call” to clear a warehouse of bulletproof vests. The minister responding — that soft, affirmative sound that in Ukrainian carries the full weight of yes without the inconvenience of commitment. Chernyshov scolded not for corruption, which apparently required no comment, but for the graver sin of not sharing.

And at the end of all this: a missile. “Flamindich,” someone called it, with the specific cruelty of an accurate joke. A weapon built by a friend, procured by a friend, defended by a friend — and documented, by those who track such things, at two confirmed hits from twenty-six known launches.

There is an old understanding, common to all mountainous peoples, that a man who builds his house on a slope must be very certain of his foundations. The birthday guests built on friendship, on proximity, on the reasonable assumption that the institutions below them would remain, as institutions often do, politely inert.

They, including Mike, did not account for disclosure[2](#footnote-2).

Which is, perhaps, the only genuinely hopeful sentence in this entire story.

[2](#footnote-anchor-2)

#### [Statement by the Public Anti-Corruption Council at the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine Regarding the “Midas” Case](https://www.facebook.com/anticormou/posts/pfbid02nSnAanCGQ6TzdAJ2r2h7mZwvtGSJGYxofw49kS17KNqJvcmB2pnLnexaGA1Vjcuol)

❗️ In connection with the fact that society has received unverified but significant evidence of ties between former Minister of Defence of Ukraine Rustem Umerov, sanctioned businessman Tymur Mindich, and the company “Fire Point,” the Public Anti-Corruption Council at the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine announces the following:

Based on materials held by anti-corruption authorities, the former Minister of Defence is believed to consider Tymur Mindich the de facto owner of “Fire Point.” All available data unequivocally indicates that Tymur Mindich is either one of the company’s beneficiaries or its sole true beneficiary.

Once this is confirmed legally — for example, by a court ruling — “Fire Point” will lose all ability to supply its products to Ukraine’s Defence Forces, given that Tymur Mindich is listed under sanctions. It is already evident that “Fire Point” provided deliberately false information regarding its beneficiaries and should consequently be fined and designated as a high-risk supplier.

🔺 We are therefore faced with a complex, multi-layered problem. De jure, the sanctioned businessman still has no formal connection to the company in question and could theoretically remain in this legal limbo for years while court proceedings and appeals drag on. De facto, the entire public has become convinced of the ties between Mindich and “Fire Point” — a perception that will become firmly embedded in the minds of both Ukrainians and international partners alike.

The state must now choose the least damaging strategy for Ukraine’s Defence Forces, which are actively using “Fire Point” products. At the same time, while fulfilling all legal requirements, the moral dimension of this matter remains of paramount importance. The country’s leadership is obligated to completely distance itself from past and present friendly relations with individuals who have exploited their positions, posts, and connections for personal enrichment.

☑ We interpret the actions of Rustem Umerov as bearing the hallmarks of **abuse of power** (Article 364 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine); and, with regard to his promotion of Mindich’s interests in the cases involving the “Israeli body armour” and “Fire Point” — **disclosure of state secrets by a person to whom they were entrusted or became known in the course of official duties** (Article 328 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

☑ We interpret the actions of Tymur Mindich as bearing the hallmarks of **abuse of influence** (Article 369-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine); and **incitement to misappropriation of funds** (Article 27, Part 4; Article 210 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

In light of the above, the Public Anti-Corruption Council at the Ministry of Defence calls for the following:

📌 **The immediate removal of Rustem Umerov** from his position as Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine.

📌 **The President of Ukraine**, in his capacity as Chairman of the NSDC, to **initiate a process of selective (partial) nationalisation** of “Fire Point” from its Ukrainian resident owners — which would allow, subject to certain conditions, for the uninterrupted supply of products to the front to continue, without enriching those implicated in corrupt abuses.

📌 **The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine to establish a working group** comprising representatives of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the branches and services that use “Fire Point” products, as well as anti-corruption and investigative bodies — with a view to conducting a comprehensive audit of the company’s contracts and pricing, and to minimising the harmful consequences for Ukraine’s Defence Forces.

The Public Anti-Corruption Council at the Ministry of Defence stands ready to participate in the work of such a group in order to resolve the matter as swiftly as possible.

## Day 1527

2026-05-01 · Anonymous Imposter's Club

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2aac09ab-ffe2-4a74-85c7-1bbb83806554_1536x1024.png)

**Friday. Unshaven. Marginally operational.**

This week:  
– continued rewiring of the propulsion system (end of the beginning, I think)  
– asked AI to rewrite my [About](https://abdymok.substack.com/about) page (have not read it, already suspicious)  
– [dronedept](https://x.com/dronedept) Twitter account mysteriously unblocked  
– and the denouement of the Z thought experiment ([last four posts](https://abdymok.substack.com))

Logical positivist Rudolph Carnap might boil down our experiment down to this:

Imagine you design a system to turn inputs into outputs efficiently. Naturally, you include feedback loops—ways for the system to notice when it’s failing and correct itself.

Now imagine someone quietly disconnects the inconvenient feedback loops.

The system still runs. It produces outputs. From the outside, everything looks normal.

Only the outputs drift.

This is not a thought experiment.

---

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/38b3c9ef-a84b-4684-9da6-4617f6cda937_1402x1122.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (c/o Anonymous Impostor's Club , May 1, 2026)*

---

There is, for instance, a missile called the Flamingo. It has reportedly been used twenty-six times in combat. It has hit its target twice.

That’s a 7.7% success rate.

Pause on that. Not because the number is shocking—it isn’t, statistically—but because it’s informative. It’s a signal. The system, such as it is, is saying: *this isn’t working.*

The signal has been received and filed somewhere that does not influence procurement. The program continues. Contracts continue. By late 2025, a former CIA director has joined the advisory board.

From the outside: activity, continuity, seriousness.  
From the inside: no meaningful adjustment.

Philosophically, this is what you might call a zombie system—responsive in appearance, unresponsive in fact.

(One of the AI About-page lines, I’m told, says I have a habit of *mistaking persistence for functionality*. That seems… relevant.)

---

**The intentional stance problem, institutional edition**

When you look at a chess engine, you can describe it three ways: as hardware, as code, or as something that “wants” to control the center.

That last one—the intentional stance—is a shortcut. We use it on institutions all the time. The Defense Ministry *wants* to defend the country. Courts *want* to deliver justice.

Usually, that shorthand works.

It stops working when it becomes a kind of polite hallucination—when behavior consistently contradicts the supposed goal, and we keep the story anyway because updating it would be inconvenient.

So: what does the Ukrainian Defense Ministry actually *want*?

Not what it says. What does it *do*?

Leaked transcripts help. When a defense minister responds “it stands today” to a private individual’s procurement instruction, we’re no longer in the realm of intentions. We’re looking at mechanism.

And the mechanism is not arranged the way the story says it is.

---

**The thermostat problem**

A thermostat is honest. Too cold: heat on. Too hot: heat off. Feedback loop intact.

Now give your neighbor partial control. Sometimes their preference overrides the temperature reading.

You no longer have a thermostat. You have something else wearing a thermostat costume.

Current data points:

– 1.6 million mobilization-eligible citizens unreachable  
– legally mandated 15-day rotations stretching into 200–300 days  
– an ombudswoman documenting all this without the authority to enforce change

That’s not a flawed system. It’s a different system—one optimized for the appearance of responsiveness.

Daniel Kahneman would recognize it instantly: fast, intuitive, persuasive—and largely indifferent to correction.

---

**The birthday party**

The most interesting datapoint this week isn’t technical. It’s social.

November 2021: a private celebration at a state residence, reached by state helicopter. A small circle of men. The same names later show up in procurement flows, transcripts, adjacent real estate (Blue Mountain). The President is addressed by a nickname.

None of this is illegal, or even unusual. People have friends.

What matters is memetics—not conspiracy, but replication. Shared assumptions, habits, intuitions about how things work. Reinforced over dinners, favors, proximity. Over time, this becomes the operating system.

Operating systems are hard to dislodge. You don’t notice them until things start crashing.

(The AI About page, allegedly, describes me as “someone who lingers at the level below narrative, where systems quietly decide what stories are allowed to be true.” I wish I’d written that. I probably didn’t.)

---

**Two systems, running in parallel**

Ukraine’s military resilience is real. It’s emergent, distributed, adaptive—what you get when selection pressure does the design work.

The political infrastructure is something else. Parallel, not fully integrated, occasionally cooperative.

This is normal, biologically speaking. Systems coexist. They align when forced.

But clarity matters: the heroic narrative merges them. Reality doesn’t.

Which leads to reconstruction.

Rebuilding courts, a legislature, a functioning press—these aren’t “political reforms.” They’re system redesign.

And the first rule of redesign is simple: you don’t fix a system using only the parts that broke it.

The Blue Mountain circle will not dismantle Blue Mountain. Not because they’re bad people. Because that’s not how systems behave.

---

**The soldiers**

There’s a threshold, the ombudswoman suggests: around forty days.

After that, something shifts. Not cowardice—optimization. The brain stops modeling the future because the future no longer reliably exists.

This is what prolonged stress without feedback does to a system.

These are the people the Flamingo was meant to help.

7.7% is the answer they’re getting.

---

If we’re being honest—and clarity, not comfort, is the whole point here—that answer isn’t just immoral.

It’s diagnostic.

It tells you the system is failing.

And unlike moral failures, system failures are fixable.

But only if you stop calling the system “functional” just because it’s dramatic.

## Day 1528

2026-05-02 · The shortcut state

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/22fcf3a5-d4eb-4deb-ae97-02b407690d58_4032x2268.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 2, 2026)*

*This morning I had to jump a wall to get into Kyiv’s Hryshko Botanical Garden.*

*Normally, the gates open at five. Around seven-thirty, guards begin charging admission—one hundred hryvnias, or thereabouts. It is an orderly arrangement: first nature, then bureaucracy.*

*This morning the gates were locked.*

*No explanation was offered, which gave the situation a familiar administrative elegance. A few runners and people with dogs stood outside pretending to deliberate. I climbed over the wall.*

*On my walk home, I passed a man welding an iron staircase outside an apartment building. He wore a strange helmet to keep sparks from reaching his eyes. It looked ridiculous. It also worked.*

*States develop similar helmets.*

---

---

Somewhere in your body is a cell as long as you are tall[1](#footnote-1).

One end begins near your toe. The other reaches the base of your skull. A single neuron carries signals across that entire distance without relay stations, bureaucratic handoffs, or institutional review. It exists because speed matters more than elegance. If your nervous system required committee meetings between your foot and your brain, you would fall down every staircase you encountered.

Power often evolves the same way.

Formal institutions are slow. Ministries deliberate. Parliaments vote. Procurement systems generate paperwork. Regulators ask questions. In stable democracies, this friction is called accountability.

In unstable systems—especially wartime systems—that friction begins to look like an obstacle.

And so governments evolve informal neural pathways: private calls, trusted intermediaries, personal friendships, off-book meetings, conversations conducted in apartments and offices after midnight. These pathways are faster than formal institutions because they bypass them entirely.

Ukraine did not invent this phenomenon. Every state has versions of it.

What makes Ukraine unusual is that somebody recorded the signals moving through the nervous system.

And now the public can hear them.

---

Transcripts of conversations released over the past week—captured across 2025 and distributed in fragments throughout 2026—do not reveal a simple corruption scandal. Corruption is too primitive a word for what appears to be happening.

What they reveal is an operating system.

The recordings capture fragments:

Tymur Mindich telling Defense Minister Rustem Umerov that *“our factory will stop”* unless hundreds of billions begin flowing by the seventeenth.

Mindich asking for *“one phone call”* to force acceptance of bulletproof vests sitting in a warehouse.

Oleksandr Tsukerman and Vasyl Veselyi sitting in an apartment selecting the supervisory board of Sense Bank while calling candidates to verify loyalty.

The Ukrainian cabinet approving nearly that exact list forty days later.

Luxury estates being built through a cooperative called *Dynasty* for Mindich, Andriy Yermak, Oleksiy Chernyshov, and someone referred to simply as “Vova.”

Three conversations.

Three sectors.

Defense procurement.

State banking.

Political appointments.

One invisible network.

---

The most revealing detail is not the money.

It is the language.

These men conduct official state business in Ukrainian.

They conduct actual power in Russian.

This matters less as a nationalist observation than as a sociological one. Language reveals assumptions about intimacy. About belonging. About who is inside the room and who is not.

The *Dynasty* cooperative tells the same story in concrete form.

People do not build wartime palaces by accident.

They build them because they assume continuity.

They assume protection.

They assume the future belongs to them.

A mansion is simply political confidence made visible in stone.

And while this parallel state was constructing houses, much of the Western press remained hypnotized by the official performance of wartime heroism.

Timothy Snyder wrote moral epics.

Sean Penn filmed documentaries.

David Remnick polished narratives.

The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Financial Times largely repeated the visible story while Ukrainian investigative journalists did the dangerous work of following the hidden one.

Perhaps they did not see it.

Perhaps they preferred not to.

The distinction matters less than people think.

The result was the same: Western audiences were given a heroic screenplay while the real script was being written elsewhere.

---

The recordings reveal how this hidden circuitry functions.

Formal authority exists.

But informal authority dominates.

A businessman appears more powerful than ministers.

Ministers seek approval from men with no formal title.

Appointments are determined before formal competitions begin.

Contracts are distributed before tenders conclude.

Board seats are assigned before committees meet.

The visible state becomes little more than a ceremonial reenactment of decisions already made in private.

This is not the abolition of institutions.

It is worse.

It is their theatrical preservation.

Institutions continue existing precisely so they can legitimize outcomes generated elsewhere.

Like muscles receiving instructions from a hidden nervous system, they move without understanding why they are moving.

---

There is also something darkly comic in how these systems fail.

Not through morality.

Not through revolution.

Not through sudden democratic awakening.

They fail because insiders begin hating one another.

Investigators distributed evidence to suspects, as procedure required.

Some suspects were in detention.

Others were abroad.

Others remained protected.

Those still vulnerable developed the ancient resentment of unequal criminals.

And so the transcripts began moving from hand to hand until they reached journalists.

History often arrives not through idealism, but through wounded vanity.

---

Everyone in these recordings believes they are saving Ukraine.

Mindich speaks about weapons production.

Z speaks about defending civilization.

Umerov speaks about wartime necessity.

Everyone believes speed justifies bypassing process.

Everyone believes loyalty is more efficient than institutions.

Everyone believes emergency suspends ordinary rules.

And perhaps, in the short term, they are correct.

That is what makes systems like this so durable.

The shortcut works.

Until it becomes the road.

The recordings do not show cartoon villains twirling mustaches over stolen cash.

They show intelligent people making rational decisions inside a structure that rewards speed, secrecy, and loyalty over competence, law, and institutional trust.

And that is far more dangerous.

Because corruption can be prosecuted.

But rational systems that slowly consume the institutions meant to restrain them?

Those can survive for years.

Sometimes until the war ends.

Sometimes long after.

By then, the people who needed institutions most—those without access to informal networks—have already paid the price.

These are pseudounipolar neurons that have their cell bodies located in the Dorsal Root Ganglia (DRG) near the spinal cord.

## Day 1532

2026-05-05 · One midnight apart

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8ced9e71-f405-43c1-b679-e5755928cee2_1536x1024.png)

It is Tuesday, which already feels excessive.

Yesterday, Z was in Yerevan at the European Political Community summit, moving from one bilateral meeting to another with the endurance of a wedding guest who understands that leaving early would be noticed. Finland promised $300 million in defense support and discussed a drone partnership. Norway offered nearly $1 billion for air defense and natural gas for winter. Britain discussed sanctions on the shadow fleet and peace negotiations. The Czech Republic spoke again of Ukraine’s future in Europe.

And somewhere on the margins of all this respectable diplomacy, there was also a meeting with Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, who remains on Ukraine’s own sanctions list.

“There are unresolved issues between our countries,” Z said afterward. “It is important to maintain dialogue at all levels.”

He did not explain what kind of dialogue one conducts with a man one is simultaneously sanctioning. Perhaps this is what modern diplomacy looks like: everyone speaking earnestly while pretending not to notice the seating arrangements.

From Yerevan he flew to Bahrain, where officials confirmed he had arrived for talks on “security cooperation,” a phrase broad enough to include anything from missile defense to polite tea.

The summit circuit continues.

Meanwhile, the ceasefire situation has developed the sort of complexity that usually appears only in old imperial archives.

Russia announced a unilateral ceasefire for May 8–9, not through diplomatic channels but on a state-backed messaging app, while also warning that if Ukrainian drones appeared over Moscow during the Victory Day parade, central Kyiv could expect massive missile strikes. Residents and foreign diplomats were advised, with touching concern for their wellbeing, to leave the city.

Ukraine responded with its own unilateral ceasefire, beginning three days earlier — tonight at midnight.

Neither ceasefire was negotiated. Neither side appears especially committed to the concept. Yesterday, while both governments were drafting statements about peace, Russian strikes killed nine civilians across Ukraine.

Speaking in Yerevan, Z noted that Moscow’s parade this year will proceed without tanks or missile systems.

“They are afraid drones may buzz over Red Square,” he said. “This is telling.”

It is difficult to disagree.

According to a leaked European intelligence report, Vladimir Putin has been spending increasing amounts of time in underground bunkers in Krasnodar Krai and rarely visits his Moscow residences.

History has a vulgar sense of humor.

For two decades, Victory Day served as an annual demonstration of Russian power: tanks crossing Red Square, missiles rolling past reviewing stands, choreographed certainty presented as national destiny.

Now the missiles stay home and the president goes underground.

Such revisions are rarely planned.

And yet the week was not finished.

The Midas Operation recordings remain where they have been for days: on desks, in encrypted chats, in the nervous hands of people deciding whether to publish more names.

MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak says he has reviewed all 1,400 pages of transcripts. He describes three parallel financial ledgers: “Manhattan,” “Project 23,” and “Trading.”

Nuclear energy. Military procurement. Electricity trading.

Three separate compartments, arranged with the careful neatness of people who believed walls could hear but microphones could not.

On the morning of July 8, 2025, at 7:37 a.m., Timur Mindich allegedly called Defense Minister Rustem Umerov.

The factory was about to stop, he explained. Two thousand workers. Bulletproof vests sitting in a warehouse. One phone call from the minister could solve everything.

“Say you don’t want to hear about the vests anymore,” Mindich reportedly suggested, “and I’ll meet with you twice a week.”

They also discussed selling a 33 percent stake in drone manufacturer Fire Point to Emirati investors and the mechanics of structuring the sale.

Umerov has not been charged.

He was moved from the Defense Ministry to secretary of the National Security and Defense Council and remains involved in negotiations with both Russia and the United States.

Yesterday, in Yerevan, he was presumably somewhere nearby, walking through the same hallways as everyone else.

This is also modern governance: one man discussing ceasefires, another discussing parade routes, a third explaining offshore transactions, and all of them insisting these are separate conversations.

Meanwhile, much of the Western press prefers the cleaner narrative: the parade, the bunker, the ceasefires, the symbolism of May 8 and May 9.

It is, admittedly, a very convenient story.

Europe marks one date. Russia marks another. Eighty years of memory compressed into a midnight border between calendars.

Editors appreciate stories that can be illustrated cleanly.

The other story is less cooperative.

It is unfolding in Ukrainian.

And this week, that remains a language many foreign editors still do not read.

## Day 1533

2026-05-06 · Compliance report: 0

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/ea42534a-03d0-4c30-b477-221a340e3020_1536x1024.png)

There is a sophisticated form of cruelty that flourishes far from war.

It does not bomb apartment buildings or leave craters in playgrounds. It sits at a respectable desk, reviews the available suffering, and explains to people living under missile attacks that their survival is evidence of sound strategic thinking.

This week, Ross Douthat offered [a polished example](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/05/opinion/trump-ukraine-iran.html).

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fc4755ac-6ddd-417d-b8e3-cdd54e116e27_414x327.png)  
*c/o The New York Time s, May 5, 2026*

His argument, more or less, is that Donald Trump’s Ukraine policy has succeeded because America spends less, Europe spends more, and Ukraine continues fighting. Iran, meanwhile, is where things have become messy.

From a great distance, this probably looks very elegant.

One imagines arrows moving across maps. Budgets being rebalanced. Someone using the phrase “security architecture” over a good lunch.

The only inconvenience in this theory is Ukrainians themselves.

They keep appearing in hospitals without limbs, at funerals, in dark apartments during blackouts, in towns that no longer exist.

Still, even this can be absorbed into the framework. Their endurance becomes “resilience.” Their dead become proof that America has recalibrated successfully.

This is one of modern commentary’s more impressive tricks: converting another country’s catastrophe into evidence of responsible imperial bookkeeping.

We remain stubbornly unimpressed.

Missiles continue arriving without consulting columnists. Widows show little interest in burden-sharing debates. Children pulled from rubble rarely pause to admire geopolitical efficiency.

Analysis has its place. Countries have interests. Resources are finite.

But a person watching a city burn should be cautious before congratulating himself for discovering efficiency in the flames.

## Day 1534

2026-05-07

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a43993f8-af99-493a-92c2-d7cea3205061_1672x941.png)

I sit in Kyiv on May 7th reading and listening to pronouncements and announcements with the strange sensation of watching exhausted incompetent politicians argue over a future none of them can control.

This was not the future anyone designed.

It lacks grandeur. It lacks even strategic elegance.

It is simply what happens when the old arithmetic collapses and nobody has learned the new one yet.

---

---

On Wednesday, May 6th, Maria Zakharova appeared on Telegram—because of course she did, because this is how empires communicate now, through the apps of scam empires—to warn the diplomatic corps that they should evacuate Kyiv promptly. Not eventually. Promptly. She used the word “inevitability” in connection with a retaliatory strike. This is the language of physics, not politics. As if a bomb were a law of thermodynamics.

The irony, of course, is that the American embassy is already operating on fumes. Julie Davis, the acting ambassador, resigned in late April after less than a year in the job. The State Department denied that she had grown frustrated with Trump over his lack of support for Ukraine, which is exactly what you say when someone has grown frustrated with Trump over his lack of support for Ukraine. By June, she will be gone. What remains is a skeleton crew—a couple of Marines, perhaps an ISA team if we’re generous with our accounting. The Americans, it seems, had already begun their evacuation before Zakharova’s warning made it official.

The reasoning, you understand, was almost elegant in its circularity. Ukraine’s president, speaking in Armenia on Monday, had made what the Russian Foreign Ministry termed “aggressive and threatening statements” about disrupting Russia’s Victory Day parade. In response, Russia was announcing in advance that it would bomb the city where I live. This is not a paradox, exactly. It is bureaucracy achieving a kind of purity—the perfect expression of how modern states make threats. They announce them. They give you time to leave. They preserve, at the level of form, the notion that this is regrettable, that you have options, that you could have chosen differently.

Several EU countries were present at Z’s remarks in Armenia, Zakharova noted. None of them reprimanded him. You can hear her thinking: this is what happens when the grown-ups stop enforcing the rules. The children run wild. One child threatens a parade. Another child, having announced the rules, now announces the punishment in advance, like a schoolmaster who has lost all authority and retained only the capacity to document his own impotence.

But there is something genuinely revealing in this moment, something that the earlier pieces—the drone economics, the Witkoff boys calculating profit margins on the infrastructure of the next war—were circling around without quite naming it. We are watching the moment when military force stops being a tool and becomes a language game. Russia cannot actually prevent Ukraine from doing anything. Russia can only announce that it will respond. And then it responds, or it doesn’t, and either way the script continues.

What makes this particularly interesting is that the American president did not see this coming. Not because it was invisible—Ukraine has been teaching this lesson for years now, in real time, with actual casualties. But because he was not interested in learning it. One of his advisors noted, with the kind of careful understatement that suggests deep frustration, that Trump “stubbornly refused” to pay attention to what was happening in Ukraine. The nature of modern warfare was changing on the battlefield in front of him, and he was looking somewhere else.

And now, even as Russia announces the inevitability of strikes on Kyiv, the American attention is still elsewhere. Rustem Umerov, Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council secretary, is scheduled to meet Steve Witkoff—Trump’s special envoy, whose sons are busy calculating investment opportunities in drone technology—in Miami sometime this week. The meeting, the first high-level contact between Kyiv and Washington in weeks, comes as negotiations have stalled. No one will say what they’ll discuss. Ceasefire proposals? Peace terms? Military assistance? The vagueness is itself the message. Even the meeting itself feels provisional, uncertain, like something that might or might not happen depending on what the president decided to have for breakfast.

Meanwhile, Trump held a 90-minute phone call with Putin on April 29th, which he described as “very good.” One does not need to imagine what was discussed.

The Iranians began deploying Shahed drones—built by themselves, launched by the Russians—against Ukraine in 2022. Years before that, Nagorno-Karabakh had already made clear that drones were no longer supplementary to modern warfare but central to it. The lesson was available. It was public. It required only attention.

The American military still has not come to grips with it. When confronted with the reality, they discovered something alarming: cheap drones cost millions of dollars to shoot down. A ten-thousand-dollar aircraft, and you’re spending millions in missiles to neutralize it. A smaller nation can simply bleed a larger one dry, very easily, very cheaply.

So when Trump stood up in the White House and announced that the Strait of Hormuz wasn’t his problem—the Europeans could figure it out—he was making a statement based on a world that no longer existed. The Iranians, with their cheap drones, had already figured out how to hold the Americans hostage in that same strait. You cannot simply walk away from a problem when the problem has drones.

Z’s comment about the drones was almost offhand. The Russians, he noted, cannot afford military equipment. They fear drones buzzing over Red Square. This is telling, he said—and it is. Because what it tells us is that the expensive architecture of deterrence, the missiles and the doctrine and the carefully maintained threat, has been made obsolete by a ten-thousand-dollar aircraft that you can manufacture in a week. And the president of the United States spent months failing to notice.

So now we have this perfect inversion: Russia announces it will bomb Kyiv to prevent Ukraine from disrupting a parade. Ukraine notes that Russia cannot even protect its own parade.

The announcement stands. The threat is real. The drones are cheaper than the missiles. And all of us, it seems, are waiting to discover which laws of physics still apply.
