## Day 1535

2026-05-08 · Pies and poppies

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2c57c012-7713-4f84-bdf9-0fb08751597a_1734x907.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok*

I’m retiring a pair of sneakers today. Wore them out.

---

May 8 is recognized in the United States by proclamation as **Victory Day for World War II**, marking the end of the war in Europe. It is not a federal holiday. Government offices stay open. Banks stay open. Markets open on time.

Meanwhile, May 8 is also National Coconut Cream Pie Day.

There is a kind of honesty in this. Not admirable honesty — but honesty nonetheless.

Victory over fascism merits a proclamation and little else. No pause in ordinary life. No interruption of commerce. The machinery hums along. This is not exactly callousness. It is something more revealing: forgetfulness disguised as normalcy. The luxury of distance.

The war was won long ago, decisively, and at staggering cost — much of it borne elsewhere. Americans can afford to treat the day as historical background noise, something acknowledged if convenient, ignored if not.

Ukraine, where I happen to be, marks May 8 differently.

People lay red poppies at monuments to the dead. Quietly. No military spectacle. No triumphalist rhetoric. Maybe this year will be different. Probably not.

The arithmetic explains the difference. Around eight million Ukrainians died in World War II. Seven million were mobilized. Entire cities vanished. The war consumed not only soldiers, but the architecture of ordinary life.

When loss reaches that scale, celebration begins to feel obscene. You remember instead.

And remembrance here remains deliberately quiet because the dead have already been exploited once before.

That was the Soviet trick: take catastrophe, dress it in uniforms, march it through Red Square, and tell citizens their dead proved the eternal righteousness of the state.

Bertolt Brecht understood this instinctively.

While fleeing Nazi Germany, Brecht clipped wartime photographs from newspapers and assembled them into *[War Primer](https://www.e-skop.com/images/UserFiles/Documents/Editor/bertolt-brecht-war-primer.pdf)* — a brutal little archive of images paired with bitter poems. In one photograph, an American soldier stands over a dying Japanese soldier he has just shot. Brecht writes:

*And with their blood they were to colour red*  
*A shore that neither owned.*  
*I hear it said*  
*That they were forced to kill each other. True.*  
*My only question is: who forced them to?*

That question survives every victory parade.

Who forced them to?

Brecht understood that states turn the dead into arguments. They convert suffering into legitimacy. They take the young men who died terrified on beaches and in trenches and convert them into symbols of national virtue.

The Soviets perfected this.

Americans sanitized it.

Ukraine, perhaps because history has offered so little room for illusion, is trying something harder: memory without spectacle.

The flowers are quiet because the dead will not be conscripted again — not into empire, not into propaganda, not into someone else’s mythology of strength.

And this is where the comparison becomes more interesting than a simple contrast between two holidays.

Donald Trump speaks about freedom as something possessed — something won once and defended against outside threats. It is a comforting story: we defeated fascism, secured liberty, and now must protect what is ours.

Ukraine suggests something less comfortable and far more demanding.

Freedom is not something you possess.

It is something you choose.

Repeatedly. Daily. Sometimes at extraordinary cost.

The laying of flowers matters because it rejects triumph as the final meaning of history. It insists memory belongs to the dead, not the state.

Totalitarianism speaks in the language of inevitability. It tells you history has already rendered its verdict, that power has been justified, that obedience is rational.

Freedom sounds different.

It asks something of you every day: remember honestly. Resist mythology. Refuse the lie that history’s worst chapters stay safely in the past.

This is harder than pie.

## Day 1538

2026-05-11 · Other circular activities

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/60c7fa44-1d80-4a56-94dc-e8207159bb14_1672x941.png)  
*Photo enchanted w/ AI c/o abdymok (May 9, 2026)*

In May, the lilacs bloom in Kyiv and Moscow alike. The flower is indifferent to borders, to war, to political circumstance. It blooms because that is what lilacs do in spring—a cycle so regular, so predictable, that watching it feels like observing the only honest thing left in the world.

Donald Trump announced the latest ceasefire during this season: three days of suspended hostilities, prisoner swaps, the beginning of peace—timed to coincide with Russian Victory Day, as if the rhythm of diplomacy could somehow align with nature’s indifference.

One day later, Russians and Ukrainians were accusing one another of violating the ceasefire.

This was not surprising. A ceasefire, like a promise to let the lilacs bloom undisturbed, often contains within itself the seeds of its own failure.

In Moscow, Victory Day produced an unintentionally honest image. The parade meant to display imperial confidence looked nervous. Fewer tanks. Mobile internet shut down. Air defenses repositioned to protect a ritual of strength from very modern anxieties. Even nostalgia now requires drone protection.

At the front, meanwhile, mathematics remains cruel. Russia spent winter grinding forward at enormous human cost and appears to have exhausted the gains. Ukrainian drones now stalk supply routes, strike oil facilities, and make distant rear areas feel less distant. Russia continues feeding men into a machine that consumes them faster than it replaces them. Ukraine continues finding cheaper ways to destroy more expensive things.

The drones will return after every ceremonial pause because drones do not respect political theater.

But war is not the only repetitive system.

The leaked recordings now circulating in Kyiv—what local media calls the Mindich tapes—have given Ukrainians the unpleasant confirmation that powerful men often sound exactly as one imagined in private: discussing placements, inconvenient associates, investigations, and personal exposure with the calm of people reorganizing seating charts at a wedding.

Move this person here. Hide that problem there. Wait for public attention to wander elsewhere.

The conversations are striking not because they reveal criminal genius, but because they reveal banality. The old post-Soviet habit survives: rearrangement instead of reform.

And Ukrainians appear increasingly tired of it.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1ecab32b-8928-4dc4-ba81-b6b2b92d66cd_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 10, 2026)*

Military leaders remain widely trusted. Political leadership increasingly does not. More striking still: many Ukrainians now say corruption poses a greater threat than Russia itself.

Z’s response has been familiar—small cash payments, subsidies, temporary relief. Enough to dull anger, not restore trust.

And so the loops continue.

Russia repeats military failure.  
Ukraine’s elite repeats institutional habits.  
The public repeats its disappointment.  
Foreign observers repeat selective blindness.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/3b6f482b-efab-4290-9077-556ea7138533_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 10, 2026)*

Then someone announces a ceasefire, which is often what people do when they have run out of solutions but still possess microphones.

The war resumes. The corruption resumes. The explanations resume.

Only public trust, once exhausted, has a habit of not returning.

## Day 1539

2026-05-12 · Construction during wartime

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/70293aea-33e4-4624-8472-415ec962e125_1596x986.png)  
*R2’s mansion c/o National Anti-corruption Bureau of Ukraine (May 11, 2026)*

And here the international press begins to resemble reporters everywhere who spend their careers translating obvious absurdities into respectable prose.

When power behaves irrationally—or obscenely—the institutional instinct is often to impose coherence where none exists.

A leader rambles. Advisers reinterpret. Stenographers insist everything is under control. Reporters quote the stenographers because the stenographers sound sane.

The performance continues because everyone involved benefits from pretending there is still a script.

In Ukraine, the mechanism is quieter but recognizable[1](#footnote-1)[2](#footnote-2)[3](#footnote-3)[4](#footnote-4).

Officials urge patience. Allies murmur about stability. Foreign correspondents retreat into the familiar language of palace intrigue: who is rising, who is falling, who still has access to Z.

[The Financial Times](https://archive.ph/q0c9K#selection-1581.0-2031.240), [Politico](https://www.politico.eu/article/former-zelenskyy-chief-staff-charged-with-corruption-andriy-yermak/), and [the Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/world/ukraine-corruption-investigation-ensnares-zelenskys-ex-top-aide-f6298cec?mod=europe_news_article_pos3) reported yesterday that Andriy Yermak—once Z’s closest adviser—has been served with a notice of suspicion involving roughly $10 million in allegedly laundered state funds and participation in what investigators describe as a criminal group.

[The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/11/world/europe/ukraine-corruption-yermak-zelensky.html?searchResultPosition=2) offered the same facts with the same careful distance.

And then reality intrudes in embarrassingly specific ways.

Not anonymous whispers.

Not strategic leaks.

Actual transcripts.

Voice notes.

Construction schedules.

Architectural renderings.

Requests for roof tiles, window deliveries, wardrobe revisions, landscaping plans.

A communal spa complex.

Conversations about accelerating construction timelines while Russian missiles were landing on Ukrainian cities.

The material is almost too revealing because it requires so little interpretation.

While ordinary Ukrainians were buying generators, body armor, and one-way train tickets west, a small circle of powerful people was discussing heated floors, design revisions, and how quickly their private estates could be completed.

And still much of the coverage remains strangely procedural.

The charges.

The legal process.

The political implications.

The careful language of institutions trying not to look directly at what is in front of them.

But sometimes the most accurate form of reporting is simply refusing to sanitize what power openly reveals about itself.

The transcripts did that.

The videos did that.

And what they revealed was not merely corruption.

It was a governing class behaving as though war were an inconvenience happening to other people.

## Day 1540

2026-05-13 · The house burns

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/52d3b345-ca06-43d5-af99-1d69f960b95e_1536x1024.png)

February 2022 was a busy time for this Substack, at least judging by the titles of our posts. We were writing about separate realities, air drums over Kyiv, the roasting of chicken—topics that ping-ponged between the philosophical and the utterly trivial. Looking back now, I’m struck by how *precisely* we were capturing the moment: the acceleration of events, the way thought splinters under pressure, the comedy of people still discussing things that suddenly don’t matter.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6dde0c9f-d4ec-400c-9095-c332b666bc90_1219x840.png)  
*Specialized Anti-corruption Bureau and Specialized Anti-corruption Prosecutor’s Office - Investigation of R2 (allegedly Andriy Yermak) May 11, 2026*

What this convo, dated February 16, 2022, allegedly between Yermak (R2) and his house designer, sounded like in English:

> **Designer:** Good day. We have fresh visualizations of your house. Ready to meet during the week. Please let us know when and what time would be convenient for you to meet.
>
> [Later, during communication between R2 and the person he brought in to organize the construction process, there is an exchange of images of the design of R2’s residence.]

What we didn’t know then, or perhaps what we were trying not to know, was that Andriy Yermak—the head of the President’s Office, the man presumably orchestrating some kind of response to the gathering storm—was holding meetings about the first-floor layout of his mansion outside the city. **Before the invasion. During. After.** Scheduling design consultations and wardrobe sketches with the same methodical attention he presumably brought to, well, everything else. The way you might discuss paint colors while the house itself is burning—or, more precisely, while it’s already burning, has burned, and will continue burning.

---

Yesterday I [posted](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1539) the visualization of Yermak’s mansion and listened to the hours-long hearing at the High Anti-corruption Court selecting a measure of restraint (temporary confinement/bail) before the case goes to trial. The hearing resumes today. Yermak maintains he did nothing wrong. Z has no comment.

---

The moral vertigo of the moment keeps pulling me back to a specific image: Tarkovsky’s *[The Sacrifice](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sI5oM0cJ2l4)*, a house burning at the edge of apocalypse.

In Tarkovsky’s *The Sacrifice*, a house burns as redemption—the protagonist destroys what he loves most to transcend the material world and touch something divine. The fire is voluntary, meaningful, a prayer for salvation amid apocalypse.

Yermak’s mansion burns differently. It represents wealth extracted through corruption and money-laundering, its construction continuing even as the country ignites. When it finally burns—through investigation and seizure—there is no spiritual leap, no grace. Only exposure.

Both are houses consumed at the moment of apocalypse. But one man chooses to lose everything to transcend the material. The other desperately builds material monuments while apocalypse rages, then loses them anyway, without redemption.

Tarkovsky’s protagonist learns possessions mean nothing. Yermak seems to have learned nothing. He negotiated wardrobe sketches while Burns warned of decapitation strikes. The mansion was meant to prove arrival, power, victory. Instead it became evidence of complete disconnection from reality—a bureaucrat optimizing closet space while the country mobilized to survive.

## Day 1541

2026-05-14 · Wind-water

Russia is attacking Kyiv at the moment, so I will be brief. The text and images in this post may appear disjointed, perhaps bizarre.

As the rockets and drones and bombs came whistling in this morning I learned there exists a fortuneteller in Kyiv, a woman of fifty-one years, called Veronika Anikiyevich, though she prefers the title “astrology consultant”—which possesses a certain dignity that “fortuneteller” lacks, the way a man might insist he is a “beverage historian” rather than merely a drunkard. Her contact list presents her more frankly as “Veronika Fenshui ([Feng shui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_shui)?) Office” and “Veronika Anikiyevich/Fortuneteller Yermak.” She runs a Telegram channel called “Lunar Hours” and, since 2024, operates as a registered sole proprietor offering “other individual services”—a classification so vague it could encompass anything from tarot readings to the rewriting of history itself.

Her Russian father, named Fedor Anikiyevich, once headed some provincial political organization in a town called Henichsk, and one suspects the apple did not fall far from the tree, though it rolled in a different direction entirely. He is a Russian citizen who, judging by recent photographs, still resides there, posing with Russian flags and St. George ribbons.

This Veronika possessed a most curious talent: she could read the heavens like other people read newspapers. Her educational credentials—financial analysis and management from Kherson State Technical University—suggest she was once ambitious in more conventional ways. But apparently, a certain gentleman named Andriy Yermak—Z’s righthand man, the second most important politician in the country—would send her the birth dates of people he wished to appoint to important positions, much as a housewife might send a servant to market with a list of vegetables, asking only that they be fresh and properly portioned by the zodiac.

Yesterday prosecutors claimed—and here we must pause, as one does when hearing such things—that Yermak appointed a prosecutor general, a health minister, a deputy chief of the presidential office, and the head of state administration, all according to this woman’s celestial calculations. He would send her birthdates and ask for advice, the way medieval kings consulted astrologers before battle. One imagines the conversation: “But surely,” says the rational man, “you cannot run a government by the stars?” To which the fortuneteller presumably replied: “Why not? You are running it by something.”

When journalists from [Radio Free Europe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ng2x2eXg89o&t=943s) came to ask her about this arrangement, she hung up the telephone. She called the investigators “scoundrels” and the journalists “jackals” on social media, suggesting the entire affair was a “Trump-Putin special operation for Ukraine’s capitulation”—which suggests she understood perfectly well what was being said about her, and preferred not to elaborate. The rational world has its limits; beyond them lies only silence and contempt for those who ask impertinent questions.

```
Alex Karp was back in Kyiv this week, moving through the city with the curious ease of a man who knows he is both welcomed and distrusted. He met with Z, praised Ukrainian engineers, admired the improvisational genius of wartime coders, and offered Palantir’s software as a weapon in Ukraine’s survival kit. In his interview with UNITED24 Media, Karp sounded almost tender. Ukrainians smile at him on the street, he said. They understand what his software does.

Of course they do.

When Russian drones circle overhead at four in the morning, philosophical objections to predictive analytics lose their force. If software helps identify a Shahed drone faster, route an interceptor faster, clear a minefield faster, or spare a city block, people are not inclined to ask whether the algorithm has read Hannah Arendt.

Ukraine, in this sense, has become Palantir’s strongest moral argument.

And yet.

Meanwhile, The New York Times published a long profile of Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s 35-year-old defense minister, presenting him as the visionary architect of a new kind of warfare—autonomous weapons, algorithmic killing, the “mathematics of war.” The article notes, almost in passing, that Fedorov has met with Karp and is “working with Palantir to further integrate A.I. into warfare.” This is the distribution mechanism. The ideology arrives not as manifesto but as profile. As innovation. As inevitability.
```

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1349947a-ab86-48ec-b0cd-1c7853e52593_1280x853.jpeg)  
*Karp and Fedorov (c/o United24, May 12, 2026)*

```
Reading Karp’s 22-point manifesto is like overhearing a brilliant man mistake synthesis for wisdom. The document announces that “some cultures have produced vital advances; others remain dysfunctional and regressive.” It lunges from civilizational decline to technological destiny, from national service to cultural hierarchy. It reads as though Oswald Spengler, Ayn Rand, and a defense procurement officer were locked overnight in an airport lounge.

The manifesto has been called “an irredeemable mess”—not as insult but as diagnosis. Palantir is no longer content being a contractor. It wants to be a philosopher-king in fleece. Its stock trades at a P/E ratio over 230. Trump praised it on Truth Social. The company has made a simple calculation: there is money in American authoritarianism, and alignment with it.

That is where Ukraine complicates everyone’s moral geometry. It too is an irredeemable mess. 

Palantir’s critics in comfortable democracies have long described the company as a digital mercenary—embedded too deeply in ICE deportations, police surveillance, and the machinery of authoritarian governance. They are not wrong. Palantir’s software sits uncomfortably close to the mechanisms of state power. It routinely arrives wrapped in the language of efficiency and departs leaving behind questions about accountability the company has shown little interest in answering.

But then there is Ukraine—that impolite fact.

Ukraine did not summon Palantir because it was seduced by techno-messianism. Ukraine summoned everyone. Drone startups. Satellite companies. Hackers. Volunteers. Retired generals. Teenagers soldering components in garages. When a larger empire arrives with missiles, glide bombs, and mass graves, ideological purity becomes a luxury item.

The Ukrainians, as Karp himself admitted, may be the real story. They took foreign systems, broke them apart, rebuilt them under fire, and created a battlefield feedback loop that traditional militaries envy. Palantir supplied software. Ukrainians supplied the thing no Western consultant can manufacture: existential urgency.

This is the contradiction Karp cannot solve.

He may be right that democracies need sharper tools. He may be disastrously wrong in believing the men who build those tools should also be trusted to write manifestos about civilization—or worse, to believe their own.

Ukraine genuinely needs software, but this software comes packaged with an ideology about cultural hierarchy, and that's not accidental or separate from the technology itself. 

It's the point. And that's the problem. 

Just ask the techno messianists in baseball caps.
```

## Day 1543

2026-05-16 · Text, context, subtext

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/be1fa3d1-cb72-406c-a77c-5eb118f7a088_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 16, 2026)*

Kyiv, like certain beautiful women and certain unreliable relatives, rarely reveals its biography at first meeting. At first you think: ah, a handsome pink building with a whimsical spire. You rent a top-floor apartment because you are young enough to believe that climbing five flights of stairs every day is evidence of character rather than bad judgment. You open the window and see the chestnut tree flowering below, and you imagine that history, having already exhausted itself in this city, will politely remain in museums.

This is where I arrived—I’d spent months drifting through Belgrade and Budapest after leaving Minsk, burned out on foundation work, disappointed by indifference to outcomes. I was looking for something I couldn’t name. By the time I got to Kyiv, the United States was preparing to start bombing Yugoslavia. I had no way of knowing it then, but I’d arrived just in time to watch history decide it wasn’t finished with this part of the world after all.

Naturally, history laughs.

The house at *Будинок із вежею на Рейтарській* — also known as the Shlenzkevich House, and later, with proper Kyiv absurdity, as the House of Tarapunka’s Tower — seems to have been built precisely to mock the idea that buildings are passive things.

First it belonged to a noblewoman. Then to a cavalry captain. Then to a merchant of the first guild, which sounds less like a profession than a title in a Gogol story. Then to a man named Sokolnikov. Then, in 1912, it was purchased by the wife of a barrister, Hanna Shlenzkevich, who commissioned the architect Oleksandr Verbytskyi to build something suitably ambitious for the highest point of Old Kyiv.

And Verbytskyi, apparently in no mood for modesty, built a house that could not enter a room quietly.

It has a turret. It has a spire. It has mascarons — stone faces frozen in permanent astonishment, which is the correct expression for anyone living through Kyiv’s twentieth century. It has floral ornament, garlands, volutes, decorative vases, curving lines of late modernism and enough ornamental confidence to suggest that the Austro-Hungarian Empire may have sent emotional support from Vienna.

Then came revolution, civil war, Bolshevik nationalization, communal apartments, Soviet neglect, and the special brutality of “renovation,” in which officials improve a building by removing everything that made it worth preserving.

In apartment number 6, from 1915 through the 1930s, lived Igor Sikorsky — the architect’s own apartment, though Sikorsky was no architect but an engineer designing helicopters, which meant the building housed both the man who built it and the man who was learning to build things that flew[1](#footnote-1). (No relation, incidentally, to Radek Sikorski, Poland’s current foreign minister — just a coincidence of surnames.)

In apartment number 4, from 1914–1916, the editors of *Vestnik Magnetizma* produced a journal devoted to animal magnetism, hypnotism, and mediumism — the kind of popular science that seems quaint now but felt urgent then.

IIn apartment number 14, during the brief and feverish years of Ukrainian independence in 1917–1918, editors produced the satirical magazine *[Ґедз](https://kp.nlu.org.ua/item/1875) (The Gadfly)* — ten issues spanning October 1917 to July 1918, edited by Zakhar Biksky.[2](#footnote-2)

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a8c4d8aa-f74a-4ce0-834d-866e32015cbb_1023x1460.jpeg)  
*Ґедз (The Gadfly)*

It was one of three Ukrainian-language satirical journals that emerged during the Ukrainian Central Rada period, alongside *Budiak* and *Rep’iakhy*. The magazine carried more than two hundred caricatures and satirical illustrations by artists including Ivan Buryachok, Yuri Vovk, Hryhorii Zolotov, and Okhrim Sudomora. Rather than mere entertainment, these journals served as constructive opposition to the authorities, using wit and caricature to comment on the nation’s founding moments — the declaration of independence, failed negotiations with Russia, the succession of regimes. The artists understood something vital: that laughter could unite a fractured people, and that satire was a form of nation-building. In Kyiv’s chaos, where power changed hands repeatedly, *Ґедз* became a mirror in which Ukrainians could see themselves clearly, if darkly. Writers gathered there to mock power — always a dangerous profession in this region.

Decades later, comedian Yurii Tymoshenko lived there, and the tower acquired his nickname, as though the building had decided that surviving empire and ideology was not enough; it also wanted a career in comedy.

And then, many decades later, I arrived on the top floor.

History likes to introduce itself through dramatic gestures — murdered journalists like Heorhiy Gongadze, revolutions in orange scarves, presidents escaping in convoys of black cars. It prefers headlines because headlines are vain.

I chatted up Gongadze months before they killed him. He was running *Ukrainska Pravda* from somewhere in the city—an independent website republishing things the government didn't want reported. He was desperate, borderline incoherent, nervous in a way that people are when they understand exactly what unafraid can cost. The security services were already harassing his staff, showing up at their doors with questions about Chechen separatists and drug trafficking—the kind of questions that aren't really questions at all, just theater meant to intimidate. He'd written about it, complained to the Prosecutor General. He was trying to document his own persecution as though the record itself might save him, but you could hear the fear underneath it all—the understanding that he'd said hings that powerful people wanted unsaid, and that being right about corruption was not going to protect him.

Gongadze was a gadfly. That's what they killed him for. Not for anything he'd done, but for the simple act of biting—of being the irritant that makes power uncomfortable, that keeps it from sleeping.

[I kept writing about it](https://maidan.org.ua/arch/arch2003/1060931792.html)—the men who’d followed him, the Interior Ministry apparatus, the whole machinery of state violence. I reported on Oleh, an investigative journalist who’d also been tracking the case, and who paid a price for it: threatening calls, strip searches on trains, the State Security Service (run then by Russia) launching a criminal investigation into whether he’d published state secrets. The state’s message was clear: we know who’s asking questions, and we know how to make them stop. By then, the secret recordings had emerged—the Melnychenko tapes, Kuchma and his security chief Derkach discussing Gongadze’s disappearance in casual, profanity-laced tones. They were caught on tape, and they knew it. Which meant the machinery of denial had to work twice as hard, and twice as ruthlessly.

But real life is usually happening upstairs. Someone burns onions. Someone practices scales as an opera singer, hitting the high notes with heroic competence. Someone hauls groceries up stairs designed before elevators were considered a human right. Someone leans out a window in late spring and watches the chestnut tree bloom below, convinced for a moment that history has finally grown tired and gone elsewhere.

Naturally, this belief never lasts long in Kyiv.

This is where you would have noticed something important: an old building eventually becomes what all old buildings become if they’re lucky enough not to be demolished — a witness.

Its pink façade remains slightly theatrical. Its spire still points upward with unreasonable optimism. Beneath it passes all of modern Ukrainian history — empire, revolution, censorship, independence, betrayal, protest, invasion.

And the chestnut tree, indifferent but loyal, flowers on schedule. In Kyiv this passes for permanence.

“Under the spreading chestnut tree I sold you and you sold me:  
There lie they, and here lie we  
Under the spreading chestnut tree.”

―**George Orwell,[1984](https://www.goodreads.com/work/quotes/153313)**

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

Igor Ivanovich Sikorsky (1889–1972) was a Russian-American aviation pioneer born in Kyiv. He studied engineering at the Kyiv Polytechnic Institute and by the 1910s was designing fixed-wing aircraft and early helicopters in Russia. After the Bolshevik Revolution, he emigrated to the United States in 1919, where he eventually founded the Sikorsky Aero Engineering Corporation. He is best known for designing the VS-300, the first truly practical helicopter, which he piloted himself in 1939. His single-rotor design became the standard configuration for helicopters and remains dominant today — making him, in a manner of speaking, the great-great-grandfather of all modern vertical-lift aircraft, including the Ukrainian drones that now dominate the skies above Kyiv.

[2](#footnote-anchor-2)

For a detailed scholarly examination of *Ґедз* and its companion satirical journals (*Budiak* and *Rep’iakhy*) as historical sources on the Ukrainian Revolution of 1917–1921, see Svitlana Pankova, *[Teкст, контекст і підтекст](https://antikvar.ua/tekst-kontekst-i-pidtekst)* (Text, Context, and Subtext), . Pankova’s work recovers the identities of the artists and traces the political significance of satirical graphics during the Central Rada period, treating these magazines not merely as ephemeral publications but as instruments of nation-building during Ukraine’s founding moment.

## Day 1545

2026-05-18 · The gap between them

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5cf51934-12a1-4573-b700-a1d297b5a194_1844x853.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 16, 2026)*

In 1997, during the full collapse of Belarusian institutions, I made a simple argument in a newspaper interview: *principles do not depend on circumstances***[1](#footnote-1).**

Duties bind absolutely. Political chaos does not suspend truth-telling. Institutional weakness does not relieve moral obligation.

If corruption exists, you name it.

I no longer fully believe that argument in its pure deontological form. Over time, I moved toward utilitarianism. Consequences matter. Outcomes matter. Preventing suffering matters.

But here is what is striking about corruption during wartime: both frameworks lead to the same conclusion.

The deontological position says truth-telling is a duty.

The utilitarian position says exposing corruption prevents suffering.

In wartime procurement scandals, these are not competing moral systems. They converge.

Expose corruption. Force accountability. Prevent repetition.

Yet there is a recurring type of public figure who cannot tolerate this convergence.

They are often articulate critics of dysfunction. They can describe institutional rot with remarkable clarity: the Soviet management habits, the procurement failures, the vanity projects, the bureaucratic chaos, the systems that fail soldiers in predictable ways.

They understand exactly how corruption works.

But when specific evidence emerges—recordings, financial trails, procurement irregularities, insider favoritism—their certainty evaporates.

Suddenly they become proceduralists.

Let the courts decide.

Let investigators investigate.

We must wait for formal findings.

We should avoid premature judgment.

This would be defensible if these same people believed institutions functioned well.

They do not.

They openly acknowledge that courts are compromised, prosecutors are politically constrained, and powerful offices routinely make scandals disappear.

They know this.

And yet they retreat into procedural language precisely when procedural mechanisms are least trustworthy.

Why?

Because procedural deference offers something extremely valuable: moral distance.

It allows someone to preserve the appearance of principle while avoiding the risks that come with speaking plainly.

They can continue condemning corruption in theory while refusing to identify it in practice.

They can maintain reputations for seriousness without confronting power directly.

This is not neutrality.

It is moral evasion.

And the consequences are not abstract.

When wartime procurement fails, evacuation systems fail.

Medical supplies arrive late.

Equipment shortages compound.

Soldiers wait longer for help that should already exist.

Some die who did not need to die.

Meanwhile others profit from chaos.

This pattern survives because enough respectable people insist on waiting for institutions they know are unreliable.

And every time accountability fails, the system learns the same lesson:

wait long enough, and public outrage fades.

In actual institutional collapse, insisting on principles is difficult but necessary.

In partially functioning democracies, the temptation is different: outsourcing conscience to institutions that exist just enough to provide cover.

That may be the more sophisticated moral failure.

Not abandoning principle outright.

Not rejecting consequences outright.

But selectively invoking whichever framework demands less courage in the moment.

And that is how corruption survives war—protected not only by thieves, but by people who know better.

## Day 1546

2026-05-19 · The veal dinner

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/51b090af-7f88-4700-9e93-a27bfe1592fd_1074x719.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 16, 2026)*

We have long observed that there are two wars in Ukraine—or perhaps more accurately, two simultaneous interpretations of the same war. A paracosm, they call it in English: a detailed, complex imaginary world created in the mind, so internally consistent that it becomes real to those who inhabit it. The West has constructed such a world.

It is told by people who have visited Kyiv for a week, eaten at the InterContinental (which has a parking garage converted to a bomb shelter, a detail that somehow proves institutional competence), and spoken with officials who have been carefully selected by other officials to speak with them. In this world, Ukraine’s state capacity is crystallizing. Drones favor the defense. Palantir’s dashboards can see the entire conflict with the clarity of gods. Resilience will prevail. The narrative is clean. It has the shape of a story.

But there is another world—one that exists in parallel, often in the same rooms, sometimes in the same moments, in different heads.

In March of this year, the Defense Minister Umerov, a man of some importance, invited a procurement official named Zhumadilov to dinner. Not to his office—to his apartment. On Hrushevskogo Street. With another fellow, a businessman named Mindich, who had certain interests in defense contracts. They discussed body armor. Over veal, presumably. They did not announce this dinner. They did not hold a competitive bidding process. They simply had dinner, as men do, and discussed how the business of defending the nation might be arranged[1](#footnote-1).

By August, this same Mindich had offered to purchase half of Fire Point—a company already receiving major defense contracts—for approximately one billion dollars. The progression is rather transparent, you understand. Get to know the Minister. Gain access to contracts. Buy into the companies receiving those contracts. Become richer. It is, as we say, a formula.

Now, I watched a 8-minute video by a man named Nick Paton Walsh, a correspondent for CNN. He skipped along a road in eastern Ukraine called the Road of Life[2](#footnote-2). It took him five hours to cover a distance that should take one hour, because of the drones. Soldiers were sprinting between trees. There were burned-out vehicles. A young woman named Afina, twenty-five years old, said simply: “I didn’t expect anything like this.”

This seemed to me the truest thing I had heard about the war.

And the American analysts—they see the drones, the adaptation, the soldiers staying low and moving alone rather than in groups, and they conclude: institutional coherence is emerging[3](#footnote-3). Capacity is being built. But I ask myself: what is institutional coherence when the institutions are simultaneously being hollowed from within by their own administrators? What is capacity when it is being redirected through private apartments and billion-dollar stock purchases?

The soldiers on the Road of Life—exhausted, frail, their supplies carried by small robotic trucks—they are doing something extraordinary. They are surviving. They are adapting. This is true.

But their survival is being managed by people who are, at the very same moment, enriching themselves through the management of that survival.

This is not unique to Ukraine. This has been the eternal pattern. But it is peculiarly dangerous in a country that is dying to build something worth being.

I do not say Ukraine will lose. The evidence suggests otherwise. But I wonder—and I say this with the affection one feels for a cousin who is both brave and unfortunate—I wonder whether Ukraine will win *and* remain a place worth living in afterward.

This is the question that no Western op-ed addresses, because it is uncomfortable, and Americans prefer comfort in their narratives. They see soldiers adapting brilliantly and conclude the state is being competently rebuilt. They do not ask what happens when courage and corruption advance at the same pace. When survival and enrichment happen in the same apartment, sometimes in the same conversation.

The veal dinner at Hrushevskogo Street 9a: that is the future. That is what we are actually building, while the paracosm shows us something else entirely.

2026-05-20 · Café Riga

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f976d5f4-d7e5-4550-8c5d-a46cdf0cc799_1740x904.png)

The tights are a bold, avant-garde statement piece featuring a burgundy base with large, black oversized polka dots. The pattern creates a striking visual rhythm that anchors her entire look, especially when paired with her matching red heels. They have a semi-opaque finish that allows for a high-contrast, graphic effect, leaning into a sophisticated, retro-modern aesthetic, perfect for a café in Riga.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/006c2edd-2188-4315-8f6e-5b2dfadbcbc7_4032x3024.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 16, 2026)*

This guy obvi approves.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/07627c2f-6871-403a-8789-c321251f3502_774x248.png)  
*c/o Politico (May 20, 2026)*

There is something almost touching, in a metaphysical sense, about how the modern world has managed to conduct its disagreements. A Ukrainian drone, disoriented by Russian electronic wizardry, wanders into Estonian airspace like a confused guest at a party thrown by someone else. A Romanian fighter jet—stationed in Lithuania to prevent precisely this—must now apologize to its Ukrainian allies while simultaneously shooting them down. Everyone involved understands the script. Everyone insists they followed it correctly. This is what we call civilization.

I mention this because one of our founding members vacations in Latvia. He had planned to return next month. Now he finds himself in the peculiar position of hoping—sincerely—that Ukrainian drones remain sufficiently disoriented to avoid his favorite vaca hangouts, while simultaneously supporting Ukraine’s right to use any airspace necessary to strike Russian targets.

But there is more. [Z now warns](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/zelenskiy-says-russia-considering-plan-attack-nato-country-belarus-2026-05-15/) that Russia is considering plans to attack a NATO country *directly from Belarus*. So our founding member must now also hope that Russia does not successfully execute this plan, which would mean Article 5, which would mean NATO at war with Russia, which would mean Latvia is no longer merely a place where drones occasionally get lost but an actual theater of conventional warfare. The contradiction is no longer his alone. It is everyone’s.

Consider the architecture of the denials. [The Russians claim Ukraine plans to launch drones from Latvia.](https://en.interfax.com.ua/news/general/1169055.html) [The Latvians deny this.](https://www.reuters.com/world/russia-warns-latvia-against-letting-ukraine-launch-drones-threatens-retaliation-2026-05-19/) [Ukraine apologizes while maintaining its right to strike targets in Russia.](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/may/19/russian-jamming-blamed-nato-jet-downs-ukrainian-drone-estonia) Each statement is technically true. Each is also beside the point.

What strikes the observer is not the chaos but its *courtesy*. Everyone apologizes. No one admits to wanting any of this. Our founding member checks airline schedules. In Minsk, Lukashenko [launches drills involving Russian nuclear weapons](https://www.dw.com/en/belarus-launches-drills-involving-russian-nuclear-weapons/a-77204498).

## Day 1548

2026-05-21 · From one floor

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/808e6343-2b8c-43bf-943c-6f315112aa44_4192x1715.jpeg)  
*May 21, 2026 (Photo c/o abdymok )*

From the eighth floor, the sunrise behaves itself.  
It arrives modestly, like a guest who understands the limits of hospitality. The pink clouds gather at a polite angle; the light distributes itself with a certain civic fairness: a portion to the apartment blocks on the left, a portion to the villas below, and a diluted remainder to the distant high-rises.

Nothing argues. The world appears arranged.

From the twenty-first floor of the same building, the sunrise becomes something else entirely.  
The angle shifts, and with it the hierarchy of illumination. The pink clouds are no longer pink in the same way. What was soft sharpens; what was visible withdraws; what was distant advances. The same sun, encountering the same city, produces a different account of reality.

One begins to suspect that the sunrise is not a thing, but an agreement—fragile, conditional—between height and perception.

You are not seeing different sunrises.  
You are seeing the same event from different levels of description. And each level, with quiet stubbornness, insists on its own completeness.

This is the difficulty with the Ukraine debate.

Everyone is watching the same sunrise—the same war, the same May of 2026—but from different floors of the same slightly unsteady building. And because no one specifies their floor, each concludes that the others are either blind or acting in bad faith.

[Yesterday](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1547), in Latvia, we encountered what might be called the architecture of courtesy: drones losing their way with improbable consistency, air defenses responding with professionalism and apology, each side observing the forms while quietly disregarding the substance. Everything proceeded correctly, and almost nothing made sense.

Today, a less polite question suggests itself: what do we mean when we say Ukraine is winning?

---

##### Layers of Lunacy

Wars, like old cities, accumulate rather than resolve.  
Trypillian traces beneath Soviet concrete beneath glass towers reflecting a future no one entirely inhabits. Each layer remains, and each claims, with some justification, to be the real foundation.

Looking at Ukraine in May 2026, one begins to suspect that what analysts call “levels of description” are better understood as layers of managed contradiction—stacked carefully, like floors no one has recently inspected.

Philosophers will note, with some relief, that before asking whether a system has agency, one must specify the level at which the question is posed. A system may be rational at one level and incoherent at another. The answers do not contradict each other; they simply fail to meet.

So it is here.

---

##### Layer 1: Tactical (Where Reason Still Performs Its Duties)

At the tactical level, the war retains a certain sobriety.  
Drones arrive where they are sent. Refineries burn with geometric regularity. Attrition behaves, reassuringly, like arithmetic. Logistics—unimaginative but indispensable—continues to govern outcomes.

Here, the maps produce a coherent sentence: Ukraine adapts, strikes, learns. If one asks, without embellishment, “who is winning the drone war?” the answer, for now, is Ukraine.

On this floor, the sunrise remains orderly.

---

##### Layer 2: Strategic (Where Reason Becomes Self-Conscious)

Climb one level higher, and reason begins to hesitate, as if aware it is no longer entirely appropriate.

Victory, at this level, has already been redefined. It no longer means breakthrough or triumph, but endurance—the slow raising of the cost of war until it becomes politically intolerable for Russia.

In principle, this is achievable.  
In practice, it requires decisions that remain unmade.

Six hundred thousand additional soldiers are required—and are not mobilized, because mobilization is unpopular during an existential war. The state conducts not only a war, but a continuous referendum on its own survival.

It is not that the necessary actions are unknown.  
It is that they are deferred.

Here, the sunrise flickers.

---

##### Layer 3: Social (Where Sacrifice Is Carefully Distributed)

Higher still, and the tone changes again—not tragic, exactly, but arranged.

Society is invited—persistently, respectfully—to demonstrate virtue through sacrifice. Some accept, some resist, most endure. Meanwhile, above this arrangement, another one develops with less publicity.

In early 2022, while ordinary Ukrainians were deciding whether to stay or flee, certain plans were already advancing elsewhere: not shelters, but estates. Kozyn, with its discreet geometry—R1, R2, R3, R4—offered continuity of a different kind, financed through the quiet circulations of energy and defense.

The principle is simple enough:  
those who die will be honored; those who remain near the center will be accommodated.

Patriotism becomes, in this configuration, a system of allocation—dignity downward, comfort upward.

A society can sustain this—for a time.  
But not indefinitely.

Here, the sunrise is observed through well-insulated glass.

---

##### Layer 4: Nuclear (Where Reality Is Replaced by Announcement)

At the highest level, the structure no longer attempts coherence.

If victory at the strategic level depends on raising the cost of war, then the counter-move is equally clear: raise the stakes faster than the cost can accumulate.

Actors unable to secure immediate objectives speak with composure about ultimate ones. Nuclear weapons reappear—not as instruments of use, but as instruments of suggestion. Alongside them, another line of effort: the removal of uncertainty by removing the decision-maker.

A different negotiator, a different Ukraine—that, too, is a form of victory.

Here, the sunrise is no longer seen.  
It is declared.

---

##### The Real Question

So: is Ukraine winning?

The question does not fail; it disperses—unless one specifies the floor.

- **Tactical:** Ukraine is winning the drone war, the daily work of adaptation.
- **Strategic:** Ukraine is pursuing a winnable strategy—raising the cost of war—but without fully committing to the means required to sustain it.
- **Social:** Ukraine distributes sacrifice in ways that reveal the limits of its cohesion.
- **Nuclear:** The war expands upward into signaling, where outcomes are shaped by perception as much as force.

Victory is possible.  
But it is conditional.

It depends on two absences: that nuclear escalation remains theatrical, and that internal rupture does not occur.

One cannot win an attrition war below while losing coherence above. Russia, for its part, inverts the problem: losing tactically, it escalates vertically—nuclear signaling, informational pressure, and the persistent search for a political break inside Ukraine itself.

The contest is no longer horizontal.  
It is architectural.

Which layer gives way first?

Both systems exhibit strain. Neither maintains what might be called unified agency across its own structure. Victory, in its classical sense, requires alignment. What is visible instead is misalignment, carefully managed.

The building remains standing.  
But the floors have ceased to recognize one another.

## Day 1549

2026-05-22 · Five scenarios

A [fascinating collection](https://szru.gov.ua/news-media/news/putin-vymahaie-rozkhytaty-vnutrishnyu-sytuatsiyu-v-ukraini) of screen captures from online government agency sources on May 20. The urgency and directness of FISU’s [front page](https://szru.gov.ua/) is striking: there’s such pure logic in the stripped design. If you can keep your head while others, et cetera.

And it’s fun to remember how clueless and dotcomified Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service still was that day. You can practically see Oleksandr Litvinenko pacing around in Belgrade with the expression of a provincial bank manager discovering the auditors have arrived early. *If I return to Kyiv, will I still have an office? Will the parking pass work?*

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/494d5673-f4b2-450c-bd67-9aab6df60fc2_1676x874.png)  
*СЛУЖБА ЗОВНІШНЬОЇ РОЗВІДКИ УКРАЇНИ (May 20, 2026)*

[Is this the entire plan?](https://www.kyivpost.com/post/76567)

The communiqué has a touching informality. Lower-case abbreviations. Parenthetical whispers. Quotation marks scattered like ash on a ministry carpet. Not the language of intelligence work but the tone of a nervous uncle forwarding Telegram rumors after his third cognac.

Which raises the obvious question: if you truly possessed Kremlin materials, would you present them this way? Would actual intelligence officers write like district-level PR interns in an energy-drink emergency? Or would you quietly use the information for something useful?

But on May 21, the very next day, something interesting happened.

“Ukraine will send reinforcements to its northern regions and step up diplomatic pressure on Belarus to counter what Kyiv believes are Russian plans to launch a new offensive north of the capital,” [Zelenskyy announced](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/may/21/ukraine-war-briefing-fresh-threat-of-attack-from-belarus-front-warns-zelenskyy). “We analysed in detail the available data from our intelligence agencies on Russia’s planning of offensive operations in the Chernihiv-Kyiv direction.”

Kyiv knows of five scenarios Russia has drawn up. Yikes!

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/31b8fe69-b686-4454-ab79-00ff987bf35f_1043x695.jpeg)  
*c/o President’s Office (May 21, 2026)*

So FISU had real intelligence. Actionable intelligence. The kind that moves armies and changes deployment. And yet on May 20, when they addressed the public, what occupied their bandwidth? A lengthy statement about how Russian disinformation campaigns work—complete with lower-case abbreviations and nervous quotation marks.

The subtext becomes clear: while intelligence officers were presumably analyzing Belarusian attack vectors and Chernihiv logistics, someone was deciding they needed to issue a domestic political statement. About foreign interference. About why Ukrainians shouldn’t believe their own skepticism.

Once any uncomfortable question can be described as Russian orchestration, citizens are invited to choose between patriotism and eyesight.

The statement confirms what it denies. Yes, there is a campaign against Z and his circle. But—and here the anxious little quotation marks flutter around like frightened pigeons—Moscow is behind it. For people already skeptical of Z, this sounds less like refutation than confession: the intelligence apparatus entering domestic politics with all the elegance of a drunk traffic policeman directing tanks.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4f6385cd-02a0-47d2-bc7b-f2d1b1377cbc_1127x1395.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (May 22, 2026)*

Have a great weekend!

## Day 1553

2026-05-26 · The pavement

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/08cc0be7-43df-4ce6-92c2-94815296028d_1010x555.png)

A chunk of Russian bomb fell outside our office door on Sunday. Nobody noticed it immediately. For hours it just lay on the pavement—fragment of a cruise missile or anti-aircraft ordnance, still hot from being fired at the city—until the garbage truck picked it up. Just another piece of garbage. Just another fact of Kyiv in May 2026.

We pondered this situation on [Day 1545](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1545), where we argued that in wartime, deontological and utilitarian ethics converge. Truth-telling becomes both a duty and a practical necessity. And [the following day](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1546-c5b) we watched as this convergence broke down entirely, as respectable people retreated into procedural evasion precisely when procedure was least trustworthy.

But the bomb fragment on the pavement is the better illustration.

---

There is an argument that seems designed precisely for understanding what is happening in Ukraine right now. Supervenience does not imply reducibility. Yes, high-level facts supervene on low-level facts. Yes, everything about Ukrainian military adaptation and state capacity is necessarily determined by billions of low-level facts—individual decisions, resource flows, institutional choices. But supervenience doesn’t mean you can *explain* the high level by reducing it to the low level. The levels have “explanatory autonomy.”

[The Atlantic tells us](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/05/putin-lost-control-russia/687269/) that Russia is losing the war. [The Institute for the Study of War documents](https://understandingwar.org/research/russia-ukraine/russian-offensive-campaign-assessment-may-25-2026/) Ukraine’s military adaptation at scale. [TIME Magazine celebrates](https://time.com/article/2026/05/23/how-ukraine-found-the-cards-to-win-without-help-from-the-u-s-/) Ukrainian ingenuity and drone capability. All of this is true at the macro level. The strategic facts are real. Ukraine is finding asymmetric advantages. The drones are working.

But can you explain what is happening to Ukraine by reducing it to these high-level strategic facts? Can you derive the actual conditions of actual soldiers from the macro narrative? Can you *reduce* the experience of people trying to evacuate from Kostiantynivka to the statement “Ukraine is winning”?

No.

And that’s where the problem begins.

---

This is what it sounds like when a serious person operates entirely at the macro level.

Finland’s President Alexander Stubb recently [assessed](https://yle.fi/a/74-20227651/64-3-300219?utm_source=chatgpt.com) Ukraine’s military situation:

> “Nyt se on puhdasta matematiikkaa."

He noted that the casualty ratio is approximately one Ukrainian soldier for every eight Russian soldiers, and that support for the war is declining in Russia.

Pure mathematics, he said. One to eight. A ratio. This is not a lie. The casualty statistics are real. The trend is real. Ukraine is indeed in a stronger position than it has been.

But what is it *reducing*?

The mathematics supervenes on low-level facts. One Ukrainian soldier. Eight Russian soldiers. But what supervenes upward from those numbers? What does it mean to be that one Ukrainian soldier? What are they fighting for? Who is allocating their supplies? Who is enriching themselves through the management of their unit?

The macro-level assessment cannot answer these questions because it has evacuated the micro level. “Pure mathematics” is deliberately indifferent to the apartment dinner, to the procurement system, to what is actually happening at the level where soldiers live and die and where corruption advances at the same pace as adaptation.

This is not because Stubb is lying. It is because he is operating at a level of description where such things are invisible. Where you can celebrate a ratio while remaining entirely indifferent to whether the system producing that ratio is being hollowed from within.

And this is the problem with explanatory autonomy taken to its logical extreme: it permits you to tell a true story at one level while being completely oblivious to what is actually happening at another.

This matters for Ukraine because the country is being described at multiple levels simultaneously, and these descriptions are increasingly in tension.

**At the macro level:** Ukraine is adapting. Its drone program is devastating Russian infrastructure. The soldiers are surviving. The state is building capacity.

**At the micro level:** [A minister invites a procurement official to dinner in a private apartment.](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1546-c5b) A businessman interested in defense contracts is present. Months later, that businessman is purchasing stakes in companies receiving state contracts worth billions. The soldiers on the Road of Life are being managed by people who are simultaneously enriching themselves through that management.

The temptation is to say: the micro level is just “the way things work” in a stressed state. The macro level is what matters—Ukraine is winning, strategically speaking.

But our framework suggests this is precisely backwards. You cannot explain what is actually happening at the macro level by reducing it to strategic statements alone. The low-level facts—the apartment dinner, the billion-dollar stock purchase, the procurement system being hollowed from within—these supervene upward. They shape what “military adaptation” actually means when it is being managed by people with corrupting incentives.

---

The bomb fragment on the pavement is both.

At the macro level, it is nothing—one fragment among thousands. The war continues. Russia is losing. Ukraine adapts.

At the micro level, it is everything—it landed outside our door. It could have arrived through the window. It landed at a specific coordinate at a specific time and happened not to kill anyone this time.

You cannot derive one description from the other. The strategic truth does not make the tactical threat disappear. The tactical reality does not invalidate the strategic assessment. But they are incommensurable.

And the people making decisions about procurement, about resource allocation, about who gets what contract—they are choosing which level to inhabit. They are living at a level where strategic victory is compatible with personal enrichment. Where corruption can advance at the same pace as adaptation. Where an apartment dinner about body armor can coexist with celebrations of institutional coherence.

This is not because the low level reduces to the high level. It is precisely because it doesn’t. Because there is explanatory autonomy at each level. Because you can tell a true story at the macro level that completely elides what is happening at the micro level.

---

We are troubled less by the fact of corruption (that is eternal) than by the fact that respectable analysts can celebrate military adaptation while remaining entirely indifferent to the procurement system being hollowed from within. They are not lying. They are simply operating at one level and refusing to see what supervenes from below.

This is the sophisticated moral evasion: the understanding that high-level facts and low-level facts are autonomous enough that you never have to explain how they fit together. You can celebrate the drones while ignoring the dinner. You can praise institutional capacity while the institutions are being systematically compromised.

Our framework allows for this. It permits explanatory autonomy. But that autonomy also permits complicity.

The bomb fragment lay on the pavement for hours. Nobody thought it remarkable. It was just debris. Just one more fact among millions.

But it was real. And so was the dinner. And so was the billion-dollar purchase. And so was the soldier saying to the foreign correspondent: “I didn’t expect anything like this.”

All true. All autonomous. All impossible to reconcile without asking what we actually believe about what is happening.

## Day 1554

2026-05-27 · Signal and the noise

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fa89358e-6deb-4ee9-8852-c880e55be5cc_1672x941.png)

**Editor’s Note:** This analysis draws on material we have covered since before Russia’s full-scale invasion—particularly [Roman Chervinsky’s account of SBU operations and Yermak’s role in sabotaging intelligence work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EZ0a9lBO0RQ&t=416s). We wrote about these patterns as early as [Wagnergate in 2021](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/scale-free-wagner-pmc), through pieces like [Drones in My Bones](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/drones-in-my-bones) and [We Must Pull the Lever](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/ukraine-goes-coup-coup). When Chervinsky was arrested in April 2023, we noted—in [Day 426](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-426)—that Ukraine’s “greasy clowns” had jailed a career counterintelligence officer. By June we were writing about [kangaroo courts](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-481) and the impossibility of NATO membership for a country where courts function as instruments of patronage.

Most of these pieces are behind a paywall. Readers are welcome to subscribe. The woman resembling [KonMari](https://konmari.com/?srsltid=AfmBOop7imy-JDCOTUsdbOhFPQ3rzMnQRV72tGDVnwV4vM5koAoeQB3O) will be happy to make them available.

None of this is new. Chervinsky’s recent testimony merely supplied operational detail for what had long been visible to anyone willing to look directly at the mechanism.

---

There is a particular kind of theater that appears when a feudal system briefly loses its chief administrator. Not reform—that would imply the existence of institutions—but reassurance. Everyone must reassure everyone else that the hierarchy still functions, the extraction continues, the servants remain indoors, the street stays quiet. It is exhausting work, especially when nobody truly believes it.

So [on May 25, our president gathered the familiar faces](https://www.ukrayinska-pravda.com/). Officially, the meeting concerned legislation and creditors. In reality, it concerned panic. His former chief of staff had just posted bail, the machinery of control had jammed, and the oligarchs required confirmation that the house still had an owner.

So he performed consultation. Poroshenko. Tymoshenko. Opposition figures arranged like furniture in a provincial wedding hall. He spoke of unity, of the spirit of 2022, of six more months until Russian collapse—the phrases people repeat when the floor beneath them has already begun to shift.

The difficulty is that Andriy Yermak understood something his employer never fully grasped: in a feudal autocracy wearing democratic makeup, the important word is not democratic. It is feudal. Such systems are not reformed. They are managed. Milked carefully. Their subordinates reminded where they belong.

[The recordings made this almost embarrassingly clear.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQrnaTEzUpY&t=804s) Ten thousand dollars for an interview. Entrance fees for state positions. Corruption so open it had ceased even pretending to be embarrassed. But Western institutional fetishists still misunderstand the essential point. The system did not fail because Yermak was corrupt. Corruption is the operating system. The crisis began because Yermak was arrested.

Visibility, not corruption, is what threatens the arrangement.

Once the canary starts singing from inside the cage, the aristocrat suddenly finds himself standing in full light. Z must pretend he has governed all along. Parliament must pretend it is not merely a plumbing system for patronage. The oligarchs must pretend the patron still exists. Everyone performs stability for everyone else, and especially for the street.

Because the street is the only thing in this arrangement that actually matters. Not elections. Not committees. Not constitutional language lovingly translated for Brussels conferences. The street. The possibility that people may eventually stop pretending alongside the regime. That possibility alone imposes the faint outline of accountability.

---

Now consider what both regimes face in May 2026, which the macro analysts keep missing because they are too busy admiring their own abstractions.

[Russia is exhausted.](https://...) The war that was supposed to stabilize Putin’s system through patriotic intoxication has produced instead fatigue, resentment, and the dull silence of people who no longer believe but continue out of habit. The militarist narcotic has lost potency. Not casualties, not sanctions, but duration itself has broken the spell. The Kremlin threatens Kyiv with obliteration because it no longer knows what other lever still moves the machinery.

Ukraine is exhausted differently. Not with the war, but with the apparatus managing the war. A system capable of receiving American assistance to extract a witness to Russian war crimes, then sabotaging the operation for the sake of domestic prisoner-swap optics. A system where the president resembles an amiable provincial actor while the valet understands the mechanics of extraction.

[Europe, meanwhile, supports Ukraine qua state,](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/26/world/middleeast/iran-ukraine-wars-similarities.html) though increasingly not Ukraine qua Z. The distinction matters. Europe will finance the war because the alternative is worse. It will not reform the system. It will preserve a feudal arrangement while quietly hoping somebody else eventually cleans the stable. But preservation is not stabilization. It is merely the slowing of collapse into reorganization.

---

Ukraine can be described at many levels simultaneously. There is the level of drone statistics and artillery ratios - Stubb mathematics. The level of parliamentary theater and Telegram leaks. The level of oligarch bargaining, street psychology, European financing, Kremlin exhaustion. Each level contains immense detail. The mistake is believing that more detail necessarily produces more understanding.

It does not.

When we move from microscopic descriptions to macroscopic ones, we inevitably discard information. But the important point is that we do not do this merely because our brains are small or our computers slow. We do it for a principled reason. We coarse-grain reality in order to separate signal from noise.

A chemist does not track every individual molecule in a kettle in order to understand boiling water. A biologist does not describe a wolf pack through the quantum states of carbon atoms. The lower-level details are real, but many become irrelevant at higher scales of description. One extracts the pattern by discarding the chatter.

Politics works the same way.

At the microscopic level, the Ukrainian system contains endless noise: leaked recordings, procedural scandals, parliamentary quarrels, corrupt intermediaries collecting envelopes in dim restaurants while pretending to discuss patriotism. One can spend years cataloguing these details like an elderly aunt inventorying spoons after a funeral.

But coarse-graining reveals the actual structure beneath the commotion.

The pattern is feudal. Patronage flows downward, extraction flows upward, institutions function theatrically rather than substantively, and crises are managed through performance rather than reform. Chervinsky’s interview matters not because it revealed isolated corruption—everyone already understood corruption existed—but because it clarified the macro-pattern hiding underneath thousands of disconnected anecdotes.

More importantly, coarse-graining does not merely remove information. It changes the categories through which we understand reality.

At one descriptive level, Yermak appears as a uniquely corrupt official. At another, he becomes something more illuminating: a perfectly normal feudal administrator operating exactly as the system requires. At one level, Parliament appears dysfunctional. At another, it reveals itself as a mechanism for distributing patronage. At one level, Z appears weak. At another, he appears almost incidental—a symbolic figure floating atop deeper structural currents he neither controls nor fully comprehends.

And this is why the Chervinsky interview matters.

Not because of any single revelation. Not because one more scandal surfaced in a country already buried beneath scandals. But because, for ninety minutes, the system accidentally described itself at the correct level of abstraction.

The noise fell away. The pattern emerged.

Shared knowledge is what everybody inside the system already knows but politely leaves unspoken, like a family avoiding mention of the uncle who steals watches. Common knowledge is when everyone knows that everyone else knows. Once Chervinsky spoke publicly, the mechanism ceased to be deniable. The system can no longer convincingly pretend to be something other than a patronage structure managing a war.

And that is the real signal.

The system will not reform. It will reorganize. Yermak may disappear, but the logic he embodied—extraction, patronage, sabotage of inconvenient operations—remains intact. The canary sits in the cage, singing loudly, while the structure around him continues creaking forward.

The drones still fly. Militarily, Ukraine retains genuine advantages. But the apparatus managing those advantages is now visibly feudal in a way that can no longer be explained away with wartime sentimentality.

And feudal systems under sufficient stress do not evolve. They fracture.

So we arrive at the autumn window Z promised: six months until something breaks. Perhaps he is right, though not necessarily in the way he intended. The eurocrats depart for holiday. The Kremlin promises apocalypse with the weary monotony of a drunk uncle repeating himself at dinner. The patronage networks quietly reorganize behind closed doors while everyone publicly performs stability.

Only the street remains unpredictable.

Until it rises—or until it decides not to—we are left watching the performance continue: the canary in its cage, the showman pretending to govern, the entire feudal machinery grinding forward while everyone involved knows exactly what it is.

But once the canary has sung, the theater of stability can never quite recover its former credibility. The signal is now unmistakable to anyone willing to listen.
