## Day 1555

2026-05-28 · Too late

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a94c09b6-7ae0-449b-9f99-a11868114695_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok enchanted by AI illustration (May 28, 2026)*

The “ia” diphthong rendering is the tell. [ISW](https://understandingwar.org/research/russia-ukraine/russian-offensive-campaign-assessment-may-27-2026/) is using “Kosty-” which slides toward a softer, Russified-adjacent transliteration, when the Ukrainian standard calls for “Kostia” with that distinct “ia” break. Same goes for Zapsillya (sic) and Myropillya (sic), small flattened mistransliterated Ukrainian towns in northern Sumy region.

No one notices this. It is the kind of detail that only matters if you are looking directly at the mechanism. But it is the mechanism: the habit of rendering Ukrainian through a Russified filter, the unconscious drift toward Moscow’s phonetic gravity, the way language itself gets colonized before analysis even begins.

Late choice starts here. In the small decisions that accumulate. In the transliterations that slide. In the descriptors applied without examination. By the time you notice the pattern, the machinery has already been running for years.

[The Economist](https://www.economist.com/europe/2026/05/26/ukraines-latest-challenge-is-how-to-deal-with-hope) publishes on May 26 with the same information we have been circulating for years. Ukraine is winning militarily. Ukraine is losing institutionally. The paradox is real. The outcome is unknowable. All accurate. All incomplete.

Here is what separates their analysis from understanding: they see the problem as corruption within a democratic framework, when the framework itself is not democratic. They prescribe reform to institutions that were never institutions in the first place.

At one point, they describe the system around Z as “Byzantine.” This is revealing in exactly the same way as the transliteration errors are revealing.

---

*Sources cited:* [The Economist](https://www.economist.com) · [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com) · [Institute for the Study of War](https://isw.pub/UkraineConflictUpdatesISW)

---

Byzantine and feudal are not interchangeable words. Byzantine describes a style of governance: opaque court politics, intrigue, informal influence networks, decisions made through whispers and rivalries rather than transparent procedure. Feudal describes a structure of governance: vertical patronage relationships, extraction flowing upward, protection and resources flowing downward, loyalty maintained through dependency.

One is atmospheric. The other is architectural.

Calling the system Byzantine keeps the analysis at the level of personality and leadership style. It implies complexity, intrigue, perhaps excessive centralization, but ultimately something reformable. Calling it feudal names the underlying structure itself. And once you name the structure, a different set of conclusions follows.

The transliteration error performs the same operation linguistically. “Kosty-” instead of “Kostia.” Byzantine instead of feudal. In both cases, the descriptor quietly shifts the center of gravity eastward toward inherited imperial frameworks while preserving the illusion that nothing important has changed.

They write: “Ukraine will probably emerge as a damaged but functioning democracy and a new middle power: poorer, traumatised, but confident in its identity.”

This assumes that institutions can be reformed under wartime stress. It assumes that Yermak’s arrest signals accountability rather than reorganization. It assumes that the system contains within itself the seeds of its own democratization.

None of this is true.

The real problem is not with people trying to understand from inside the situation. It is conveying what is actually happening, or are compartmentalizing the information for future use, being oblivious to the feudal logic staring them in the face.

This is a familiar dynamic. A month ago we wrote about conversations that don’t happen—about analysts and historians who understand patterns clearly elsewhere but won’t apply them to Ukraine because naming those patterns late means admitting they chose not to see them, or chose not to say them. The same logic applies here. The pattern is visible. The cost of naming it is admitting late choice. So the naming doesn’t happen.

There’s nothing quite like having a polemic with oneself across a four year’s worth of dispatches. But the consistency is instructive.

This is the occupational hazard of liberal institutional analysis: it cannot conceive of a system that is fundamentally not liberal, so it treats every feudal mechanism as a temporary deviation that will eventually self-correct.

It will not.

There is, however, something new in the landscape that the Economist touches on without quite grasping its implications. Ukraine has developed asymmetric warfare innovations that the Pentagon now desperately wants. Drone technology. Dirt-cheap homemade interceptors. Tactics that make expensive military platforms obsolete. Z, having been told by Trump he had no cards, now holds a deck that matters strategically.

This does not reform the feudal system. But it changes the West’s tolerance for it.

Europe will back Ukraine qua state because Ukrainian sovereignty matters strategically. The Pentagon will back Ukraine qua innovation because drone warfare has become essential to American military doctrine. Neither will back Z qua democrat, because he is not one and never will be.

But that distinction—between backing the state and backing the person—means the feudal system can persist longer than its internal contradictions would normally allow. The street may remain quiescent because the West keeps funding the machinery. The oligarchs may maintain stability because external support buys time. The apparatus may reorganize smoothly enough that fracture can be deferred.

Not forever. But long enough.

There is, however, a pressure building on the other side that complicates this stability. Russia is losing nearly 35,000 soldiers monthly, more than the Kremlin can recruit. Continuing the war at its current pace will soon become untenable without forced mobilization—something Putin fears because it signals weakness and damaged his popularity the last time. So he faces a trap: admit defeat, mobilize and risk internal collapse, or escalate horizontally. Test NATO cohesion in the Baltics while Trump undermines European deterrence and far-right parties demand an end to Ukraine aid.

As one EU official noted, this is “a very dangerous point.” Putin will have to escalate in order to justify mobilization.

The signals are already visible. Russia has launched massive strikes on Kyiv, threatened “sustained” bombardment, and warned diplomats to leave. [But as the NYT reports](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/27/world/europe/russia-ukraine-kyiv-attacks.html), analysts believe the escalation rhetoric is partly directed at a domestic audience—Russia must show that its response is “not symbolic, but tough and systematic.” More importantly, Moscow is signaling to Washington: you cannot cool toward Ukraine without consequence. The Kremlin is effectively demanding that Trump re-engage in mediating a settlement, or face the possibility of further escalation, potentially including tactical nuclear weapons.

The stalemate may not hold. The feudal system may persist, but the arithmetic may force Putin’s hand toward expansion anyway.

Here is the cost of late choice: by the time the pattern becomes undeniable—by the analysis catches up to reality—the machinery has already calcified. The West has already decided to prop up the feudal system because it produces useful weapons. The oligarchs have already reorganized. The decisions that should have been made when the pattern was still deniable can no longer be made at all.

You can document everything. You can know the system inside out. But if you name it late, you name it when naming no longer changes anything.

That is the trap. And we are already in it.

## Day 1559

2026-06-01 · The same pipe

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c426dbb6-621d-4275-a724-f20294f57ff9_1536x1024.png)

There are performances in politics that resemble village weddings. Everyone knows why they have gathered, yet for a long time nobody mentions the bride.

Last week Mykyta Poturaiev, chairman of the parliamentary committee responsible for information policy, participated in such a performance on live television[1](#footnote-1). He was asked a simple question: among the nearly two hundred deputies who recently met with President Z, did anyone ask about the Dynasty compound near Kozyn? About the four mansions that appear in the NABU recordings? About the house designated R1, allegedly intended for a certain “Vova”?

A simple question is dangerous because it leaves little room for escape.

Poturaiev’s answer began not with the houses but with the pipes.

The deputies, he explained, were concerned with matters of genuine public importance: air defense, winter, energy infrastructure. Then he offered a memorable image. If frozen excrement begins flowing from Kyiv’s taps, he suggested, people will have little interest in discussing the affairs of Yermak, Mindich, or anyone else.

The image was so vivid that it seemed to consume the question itself.

This, apparently, is the official position regarding the possible fourth mansion: we were too busy worrying about the plumbing.

The difficulty is that the plumbing and the mansion may not be separate subjects. One does not need to be a prosecutor to understand the connection. If public money intended for infrastructure is diverted into private networks, then the frozen apartment and the luxury estate become two ends of the same pipe.

That is why Poturaiev’s answer was so revealing. He did not deny anything. He did not explain anything. He merely moved the conversation from one place to another. The house became the faucet. The accusation became winter. Accountability became a distraction from survival.

It is an old trick, though war gives it fresh strength.

A citizen who asks about corruption can be portrayed as a citizen who does not care about missiles. A journalist who asks about a mansion can be portrayed as a journalist who does not care whether people freeze. In this way the question itself becomes suspect.

Yet questions have an unfortunate tendency to survive.

The Dynasty compound existed before the invasion. It existed during the invasion. It continued to grow while ordinary Ukrainians endured blackouts, shortages, and uncertainty. Whatever investigators ultimately conclude, the timeline itself raises questions that cannot be answered by discussing pipes.

Western admirers of Z should pay attention to this distinction.

They were not wrong about everything. His conduct in the first days of the invasion mattered. His refusal to flee mattered. Those were real acts, and history will remember them.

But symbols are simpler than systems.

Many foreign observers saw the symbol and assumed the system behind it must be equally admirable. The Dynasty affair suggests something more familiar: that wartime patriotism and ordinary post-Soviet patronage may have been operating side by side all along.

The investigators are uninterested whether Z himself bears responsibility.

But Poturaiev’s performance told us something regardless. A government confident in its innocence usually welcomes a clear answer. A government that responds to a question about a mansion with a lecture about sewage has made a different calculation.

The calculation is that enough people, for long enough, will accept the substitution.

Perhaps they will.

But winter has a way of clarifying things. So do pipes.

And the more insistently officials speak about the faucet, the more people begin to wonder about the fourth mansion.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

**Host:** Did any of those 180–200 deputies ask the president about Mindichgate — about his possible role — given that a certain “Vova” was mentioned, and a mansion in Dynasty is apparently being built for some “Vova”? Was that raised?

**Poturaiev:** I was waiting for you to ask that. Fortunately we’re all sensible people, and we were interested not in what’s been chewed over for three weeks now and what the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office — the two bodies currently investigating the Mindich recordings and the Dynasty properties — are handling. Please. We were interested in questions of genuine public interest. What happens to the Bortnychi aeration station. Whether we’ll have PAC-3 missiles. That’s rather more global — so you’re not smiling this winter from some warm city in Zakarpattia.

**Poturaiev:** I don’t know where you’ll go. Listen to me carefully — if you’ll be leaving a studio where from the taps instead of drinking water comes frozen shit, I think you’ll have no time to re-chew the Yermak and Mindich questions. We were interested in genuine public interest questions: missiles, Patriots, air defense, cogeneration. We’ll laugh when *we*, not you, do something so the country doesn’t freeze and so that from Kyiv’s taps flows water, and not shit — not from the toilets, but from the taps. I understand it’s very, very satisfying right now to laugh at us, at the president, at our government, at our faction. You laugh only because you have that opportunity.

Compared with Swarmer's explosive ascent this may seem almost pedestrian, but most investors would gladly accept a 48% return in under three months, particularly from a company operating at the intersection of drones, defense, and a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

Pots of gold and the ends of rainbows have traditionally been regarded as imaginary destinations, suitable for children, poets, and other persons not yet initiated into the practical affairs of life. The modern investment community has improved upon this arrangement. It has discovered that a rainbow need not terminate in folklore. Given a sufficient quantity of Russian cruise missiles, Ukrainian drone sorties, Pentagon procurement officers, and speculative capital, the phenomenon may be made to terminate quite satisfactorily in a brokerage account. The old Irish peasant looked for his treasure at the end of a rainbow arching over a green field. His latter-day successor looks for it at the end of a rainbow arching over a smoking oil depot somewhere beyond Rostov.

The circumstance is not without its instructive features. The drone, having first converted fuel depots, command posts, and assorted military assets into debris, proceeds through the accustomed channels of modern finance to convert debris into revenue, revenue into earnings expectations, and earnings expectations into capital gains. The resulting increase in shareholder wealth is then received as evidence of industrial foresight and technological progress. By this ingenious mechanism the pecuniary culture succeeds in extracting a pot of gold from the end of a rainbow illuminated by distant fires, while preserving the agreeable conviction that the transaction is not merely profitable but morally elevating. Those who arrive first at the treasure naturally attribute their success to superior judgment and, with becoming magnanimity, invite the public to admire the view.

## Day 1562

2026-06-04 · Unorthogonal

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/03ccfaf3-1e9a-411d-9524-5bb71f816d0f_1535x1024.png)

Last week Edward Luce, writing in the [Financial Times](https://archive.ph/7tMnY), offered a diagnosis: both Putin and Trump gambled on weak adversaries, assumed quick victories, and have instead produced case studies in geopolitical self-harm. This week Jack Watling, in *[Foreign Affairs](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/ukraine/ukraine-turns-tide-cease-fire-jack-watling)*, adds the granular military argument — Russian combat performance is waning, Ukrainian tactical proficiency is quietly improving, and a cease-fire has moved from fantasy to realistic possibility.

The arguments are reasonable. They also are incomplete.

Its hidden assumption is that people eventually submit to reality. Reality arrives, presents its credentials, and is admitted indoors. The mistake lies in believing this always happens.

Consider Iran.

Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei is fifty-six years old. He did not inherit an ordinary state. He inherited an idea disguised as a state. The Islamic Republic is often described as a government with a foreign policy. In truth it resembles a foreign policy that acquired a government for administrative convenience.

Its central proposition is simple: America is the Great Satan, and accommodation is apostasy.

A man can retreat from a battlefield. He can retreat from a negotiating position. He can even retreat from a promise. But how does he retreat from the premise that gave meaning to his life?

If Trump’s terms are accepted — whatever those terms may be — something larger than a policy has failed. The foundation itself begins to crack.

Putin’s predicament differs in language but not in structure.

For more than twenty years he has told Russians — and, one suspects, himself — that Ukraine is not truly a nation, that its sovereignty is a historical misunderstanding, and that history itself was waiting patiently for correction. When a man spends enough years repeating a story, the story ceases to be propaganda. It becomes furniture. He begins bumping into it in the dark.

This is why it is not quite right to say Putin miscalculated the war. He miscalculated history. A military error can be corrected. A mistaken view of history is harder to amend because it has usually become part of the person holding it.

Z and Trump, both wreckers, are trapped as well, but theirs are more ordinary traps.

Their constraints depend on audiences, elections, approval ratings, headlines, donors, allies, and opponents. These are powerful forces, but they belong to circumstances. Circumstances change. A politician can discover a new argument, a new coalition, a new justification. Ego is remarkably flexible when survival requires flexibility.

The traps of Putin and Khamenei are different. Not external. Internal.

Ideology is not a prison wall surrounding the self. It is part of the self.

To admit defeat is not merely to lose. It is to become someone else.

And here the two kinds of traps intersect.

Z cannot end the war by satisfying Putin because what Putin requires is not a concession but a confirmation: Ukraine must cease to be fully Ukraine. Trump cannot settle matters with Iran by satisfying Khamenei because what Khamenei requires is not an agreement but a world from which American power has withdrawn.

The result is a curious mechanism. The rigid trap on one side makes the flexible trap on the other permanent. The more room Z or Trump have to maneuver, the less useful maneuver becomes.

One side cannot concede enough. The other cannot compromise enough.

The locks face in opposite directions. No one has the key.

This is why the assumption of eventual rationality deserves scrutiny.

Observers ask how the Kremlin will react once it recognizes that its prospects are worsening. But recognition is not a mechanical process. Human beings do not absorb unwelcome truths the way thermometers absorb temperature.

A man who believes he is correcting a historical injustice does not easily conclude that the injustice should remain uncorrected. More often he concludes that one final effort is required. One more offensive. One more winter. One more missile salvo.

Reality may indeed be winning its argument.

The question is whether the men losing that argument can afford to hear it.

## Day 1566

2026-06-08 · The bicycle problem

When two distinguished analysts arrive independently at identical conclusions, the reader is entitled to experience a certain relief. The matter appears settled. [Fareed Zakaria](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdtfJra3K6M), from his studio, and [Anne Applebaum](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/06/ukraine-war-momentum-shift/687444/), from her van, have both examined the war and reached the same verdict: momentum has shifted, drones are working, Europe has stepped up, Ukraine is not losing.

Most of this is true. The drones are working. Momentum has shifted. These developments are visible even from Kyiv, where some residents receive updates during the night.

What attracts attention is not what the two analyses contain but what they leave out. The omissions are remarkably similar. One hesitates to call this coordination. It is something more dependable.

Ukrainian resilience is real. Russian brutality is real. These facts present no difficulty. What presents difficulty is information suggesting that Z and several people around him have done rather well during the prolonged defense of the country they are defending.

The same difficulty appears in the treatment of Z’s recent open letter to Putin. Abroad it was received as a peace initiative. Closer to the scene, many regarded it as a carefully arranged provocation. The difference is less important than the fact that only one interpretation seems admissible.

Meanwhile, Putin’s system resembles a bicycle. It remains upright while moving and becomes unstable when stationary. This does not mean it is approaching collapse. It means only that stopping may be more dangerous than continuing.

For Europe, this creates an unusual strategic problem. Defeating Russia is one thing. Managing a Russia that cannot win and cannot stop is another. The regime’s remaining escalatory options — pressure on the Baltics, nuclear use, full mobilization of the economy — appear less decisive the more closely they are examined. Yet a government may continue for a long time on options that are self-destructive. History contains several examples.

These matters are absent from both the van piece and the studio piece. Not because they are secret. Not because they are unknown. They simply belong to a different category of information.

The young civil servant Applebaum quotes, grieving the loss of a flight to Barcelona, reads Ukrainian. She reads Russian as well.

She is familiar with the missing category.

## Day 1568

2026-06-10 · The cultivation problem

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f525fdd8-273d-4c25-8c57-6345b9392894_1600x942.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok*

There is a Ukrainian word, *vyroshchuvaty* (вирощувати) — to cultivate, to grow, as one grows vegetables or children — that Roman Chervinsky uses seven times in the space of thirty minutes. He uses it the way a farmer uses it, without drama, as a description of ordinary agricultural work. You plant a seed in the correct soil, you water it, you wait. Eventually it grows into whatever you needed it to grow into. The fact that the seed is a human being, and the soil is a Ukrainian intelligence agency, and what it grows into is an agent of a foreign power, does not, in Chervinsky’s telling, make the process less agricultural. It makes it more so.

Chervinsky is worth listening to. He was, until the state decided otherwise, the head of counterintelligence for Ukraine’s Security Service. He knows how these gardens work because he spent years tending one. He knows how they are infiltrated because he watched it happen. He knows the specific smell of a cultivated asset — the slightly-too-good results, the exchanges that succeed where others failed, the quiet accumulation of presidential trust — because he was trained to recognize it. And then, in a development that will surprise no one who has been paying attention, the state he served charged him with crimes and made him the subject of the very machinery he had once operated. He mentions this with the equanimity of a man who has had time to find it funny.

What follows is his chronology. I have translated it as faithfully as I can.

---

---

It begins, as so many Ukrainian stories begin, in 2019.

A man named Dmytro Shtanko is making recordings. He is recording Denys Yermak — the younger brother of Andriy Yermak, who will become the most powerful man in Ukraine — and Denys Yermak is explaining, with the candor available only to people who do not yet know they are being recorded, exactly how the new government will work.

“People were appointed to positions,” Chervinsky says, “so that they would do their jobs but remember who appointed them, and what their main tasks were. They were to form financial flows directed toward the new elite of the country.”

The new elite, Denys Yermak explains on the recording, is organized on a family principle. “Z-Yermak. Their fathers are friends too. They traveled to Tibet together.” And then, in September or October of 2019 — before Bohdan has been fired, before the Paris summit, before Oman — Denys Yermak says the following: *“Soon my brother will be head of the Presidential Office.”*

Dmytro Shtanko, who made these recordings, was subsequently sent to the front. He was placed on a forward observation post at Bakhmut — beyond Ukrainian lines, Chervinsky specifies, not at them — and he was kept there for a month. He did not survive the month.

Chervinsky mentions this without raising his voice.

---

The Paris summit of December 2019. Z meets Putin for the first time as president. The Normandy Format. Andriy Bohdan is in the delegation. Nothing is resolved. Something is, apparently, communicated — or rather, the absence of what was expected to be communicated is communicated.

What had been expected: a signing. Another negotiator — Surkov — had reportedly reached agreement with Z on a soft handover of the Donbas, the literal implementation of the Minsk accords. A fully agreed document was waiting. Merkel and Hollande were present as witnesses. Z flew from Kyiv to Paris to sign it.

Somewhere over Poland, he changed his mind. He understood that the moment of signing would be, upon his return to Kyiv, the first act of a civil war — and the last act of his own political career. So instead of signing, he told Putin, in front of Merkel and Hollande, why Putin was wrong.

Such things are not forgotten by anyone. They are especially not forgotten by people as easily wounded as Putin. He did not forget. He added to this war, among all its other dimensions, the character of a deep personal enmity. From that moment in Paris, Putin’s feelings toward Z could be described, borrowing from a Russian film, as a personal antipathy so intense he cannot eat.

“The conversation in France didn’t go the way Z wanted with Putin,” Chervinsky says — which is one way of putting it. “Apparently the promises weren’t kept — whatever Z had promised, whatever he’d envisioned about how he’d negotiate with Putin, what he’d talk about.”

Shortly after Paris, there is a trip to Oman. Yermak goes. Bohdan does not.

“What was in that Oman?” Chervinsky asks. “That’s the big question. And after this, Yermak is appointed head of the Presidential Office.”

His interpretation is precise: “In Oman, they most likely showed Z who should be head of the office — through whom there could be direct communication, communication that would lead to the results Z wanted at that time.”

Bohdan is fired shortly afterward. No explanation is given. He has been, in Chervinsky’s reconstruction, a normal chief of staff — organizing the president’s schedule, handling legal and economic matters, the things he was actually trained for. But this is not what the Presidential Office is needed for. “His main task and goal — he wanted to show himself as a talented diplomat from the people, who could negotiate with Russia and organize peace. Very quickly, unlike Poroshenko.” Bohdan cannot provide this. Yermak can. Or rather: Yermak is being grown to provide it.

---

The cultivation of Yermak proceeds through prisoner exchanges.

“Russia was cultivating its asset in the eyes of President Z himself,” Chervinsky says. “They showed Z that only this man could solve Ukraine’s most critical problems. And that’s how they installed him.”

The method is consistent. Identify an ambitious figure with access to the principal. Manufacture results. Allow him to succeed at things others have failed at. Watch him rise. Chervinsky traces this pattern across three generations of asset cultivation: Viktor Medvedchuk and his back-channel relationships, Volodymyr Ruban and his prisoner exchanges, and now, in what Chervinsky presents as the current live operation, HUR’s Dmytro Usov. “The same thing is happening in the HUR environment. They have this Dmytro Usov, who is also supposedly a talented negotiator and exchanger, together with Budanov. But I believe the Russians are again cultivating their asset in our corridors of power and intelligence agencies.”

*A note on names: Dmytro Usov — HUR deputy head and keeper of the direct back-channel to Russian Military Intelligence (GRU) General Alexander Zorin since March 2022 — should not be confused with Andriy Yusov, HUR’s representative for strategic communications and adviser to the Presidential Office. The Usov-Zorin channel, initially used only for prisoner and war dead exchanges, became the most stable line of communication between the two sides throughout the war; it was through this channel that the Azovstal surrender and release was negotiated in May 2022. When Budanov was elevated to Presidential Office chief in January 2026 and Oleh Ivashchenko installed as the new HUR head, Usov became the senior continuity figure in HUR’s Russia negotiations — his structural position quietly strengthened at precisely the moment Chervinsky’s warning about his cultivation was being recorded. As for Yusov: in February 2026, Ukrainian and Moldovan law enforcement disrupted a Russian-directed contract killing operation; Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko confirmed Yusov was among the intended targets. Different men, similar names, same building.*

There is, in the exchanges themselves, a specific example that Chervinsky presents not as interpretation but as documented fact. The exchange of Tsemakh — a witness in the MH17 investigation, handed to Russia in 2019 as part of the deal that returned the Kerch Strait sailors. The sailors were already coming back, Chervinsky says. The International Maritime Court had ruled. Sanctions for non-compliance were the next step. By including Tsemakh in the exchange, Z resolved Putin’s problem, not Ukraine’s. “Z solved more of Putin’s problems than Ukraine’s problems, because the guys were about to arrive in Ukraine anyway.”

---

The appointment of Oleksandr Lytvynenko as head of the Foreign Intelligence Service — the SZRU — comes in July 2021.

Chervinsky notes, as others have noted, that Lytvynenko studied at the FSB academy through 1994. He notes it without the outrage that a less experienced man might bring to it, the way a doctor notes a patient’s relevant history. What matters is not the academy. What matters is what happens in August.

In August 2021, one month after his appointment, Lytvynenko begins dissolving the SZRU’s department responsible for tracking Russia. This is the unit that has been reporting on troop buildups, axes of advance, invasion preparations. “He quietly disbanded the department,” Chervinsky says. “And by December it was gone.”

The documentary intelligence reports do not stop being produced. They stop being transmitted accurately. “These documentary reports, he simply didn’t take them into account, or even produced opposite reports — that there would be no war — and informed the president accordingly.”

Meanwhile, Z is telling the CIA that Ukrainian intelligence is superior and there will be no war. “He constantly boasted about his Ukrainian intelligence and informed the CIA representative that their intelligence was good, but ours was better, and there would be no war, everything would be fine.” The CIA representative was telling him otherwise. The Ukrainian intelligence agencies, penetrated and misdirected, were telling him to concentrate forces in the east. The northern approaches to Kyiv were demined. Defensive positions were removed. “The armed forces, the overwhelming majority of all efforts and forces, were moved predominantly there, to the east, to the JFO zone.”

On February 24, Russia came through the north. And through Chonhar, “where everything had been demined, defensive positions removed, the units that defended these positions removed.” Kyiv was held by one battalion of the 72nd Brigade, based at Bila Tserkva. “And fortunately, everyone who didn’t flee Kyiv, didn’t leave Kyiv — well, except women — took up weapons and went to show that they were ready to defend Kyiv.”

“The intelligence service,” Chervinsky says, “performed a destructive function — it put the existence of the entire country at risk.”

All of these people remain in their positions. “These intelligence officers are still in warm baths. They are not afraid to be here in Ukraine, even though they are effectively the guilty parties.”

Lytvynenko was not sent to Serbia. He was promoted. In March 2024, he was appointed Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council, replacing Oleksiy Danilov. He held that post until July 2025.

---

On the sanctions against Bohdan, Chervinsky is brief and surgical.

“Sanctions are the kind of thing you can impose, and then go ahead and prove you’re not guilty.” No criminal case has been opened. No charges filed. Four of the five people sanctioned in the same decree are Russians — providing legal camouflage for the real target. “He places Bohdan in the same row as them. This is already absurd and frankly funny.”

The purpose is not legal. The purpose is informational. “This is pure populism, aimed simply at changing the topic being discussed in society — especially in the more sober opposition part of society, where everyone clearly understands that the president’s inner circle was robbing the country during the most difficult period for our country.”

Bohdan, Chervinsky notes, has been abroad for at least three years. He has no media presence in Ukraine, no business interests, no mechanism of influence. “How can he cause harm to Ukraine if he has no influence, no business here? None. This is simply Z’s fear. This is paranoia.”

As for what Bohdan actually knows: “I hope Bohdan has enough insider information that he can communicate, and it can genuinely destroy Z’s authority and his image as a non-corrupt honest guy from the people who is trying to fight the system. Because Bohdan genuinely has enough information about how all of this began — where the money came from for all their processes, for the election campaign, and so on.”

Z, Chervinsky suggests, knows this too. He is hitting preemptively. If Bohdan speaks, it will be reframed: he is doing it for personal revenge, he has an axe to grind, he was fired and never forgave it. The sanctions create the narrative in advance.

---

On the Medvedchuk assets, Chervinsky permits himself one moment of controlled contempt.

Medvedchuk’s media empire. His fuel stations. His real estate. All confiscated under sanctions. “Where did it go, this empire? It dissolved into Yermak’s pockets. The stations were renamed and simply kept working. We don’t know who owns them and how all of this happened. There’s no transparency here.”

No public accounting. No court proceedings explaining the disposition of assets. The stations are operating under new names. Who owns them is not a question the state has found time to answer.

---

The closing argument is, in some ways, the most interesting one, because it is the argument that explains everything else.

The corruption exposés — the Mindich recordings, the Yermak wiretaps, the dynasty mansions, the drone procurement schemes — are not, in Chervinsky’s reading, simply journalism. They are leverage. “By means of these scandals, by means of this exposure of information about Z’s corrupt circle, they are trying to force him to sign a peace deal in the format that would suit Russia.”

Trump wants a quick signing. Russia wants specific terms. Z, weakened by the corruption of his own circle, weakened by the institutional damage done by the people he trusted and the people they installed, is being squeezed from both sides. “The president has seriously weakened. He has weakened himself through his own corrupt circle. And this gives external forces — in this case both the Russians and the Americans — the ability to put pressure on him and force him toward certain things.”

He resists. The state suffers.

“Our fighters on the front lines deserve this respect — from the whole world, from Europeans, from Americans, from ordinary citizens. And someone is destroying this respect with their corruption, with their arrogance, with their unwillingness to look honestly at what is actually happening in the country.”

---

The laboratory, as always, belongs to whoever owns the building.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7a8ad380-b6b3-4602-9af3-758ab8293164_1038x714.png)  
*c/o MinFin (June 11, 2026)*

The *New York Times* ran a piece [yesterday](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/10/world/europe/ukraine-midrange-logistics-strikes.html) about Ukraine’s “logistics lockdown”—the systematic drone campaign targeting Russian supply lines up to 100 miles from the front—and it is, in its way, an excellent piece of work. The photographs especially: Brendan Hoffman’s images of drones launched into bruised skies, soldiers scrawling messages of retribution on thermobaric wings, the dark silhouette of a Hornet against orange and blue at dusk. War as chiaroscuro. One looks at these photographs and feels, briefly, that the story is complete.

It is not complete. But let us not blame the photographs.

The article informs us that Ukraine now launches more than 5,000 mid- and deep-range strikes per month; that a single Ukrainian company has scaled its drone contract from 112 units in 2024 to 25,000 in the current cycle, that European nations have allocated $1.63 billion to Ukrainian drone production this year, more than in all of 2025. [The Institute for the Study of War](http://isw.org) calls it a turning point. Jack Watling, writing in *Foreign Affairs*, adds the military argument: Russian combat performance is waning, Ukrainian tactical proficiency is quietly improving, and a ceasefire has moved from fantasy into the realm of possibility. A Ukrainian commander whose call sign is Whale explains the objective succinctly: Russia must learn that distance provides no safety.

All of this may be true. None of it is, strictly speaking, the whole story.

[We explored the hidden assumption in Watling’s argument back on Day 1562](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1562?utm_source=publication-search). His diagnosis depends on the belief that people eventually submit to reality. The mistake lies in assuming this always happens.

This matters because the *Times* piece builds toward the suggestion that Ukraine’s logistics lockdown constitutes leverage toward an exit. Perhaps. But leverage requires a counterparty capable of receiving it.

There is also the question—which the *Times* piece, like most Western coverage, declines to ask—of what Ukraine exits the war with.

Last time I checked, Ukraine was functioning as a free R&D laboratory for Western defense industries, which have been capitalizing handsomely while Ukrainian producers wait. The $1.63 billion in European financing for drone production is presented as evidence of Ukrainian momentum. Financing, however, is not ownership. Nations allocating capital to Ukrainian drone production may also be acquiring production footholds, supply-chain relationships, and battlefield-tested intellectual property. They may be purchasing access rather than building sovereignty.

A craftsman who perfects a tool he does not own has performed a service. For whom, exactly, is a question the workshop does not answer.

The article mentions, in a subordinate clause that deserves a paragraph of its own, that Ukrainian companies have agreed to share technological and tactical advances “through a mechanism set up by the Ministry of Defense.” In a country whose state has not always distinguished reliably between defense procurement and asset distribution, one naturally wonders who controls the mechanism—and in which direction the learning flows.

Ukraine possesses genuine battlefield adaptability. The logistics lockdown is real. These facts coexist comfortably alongside another fact, one for which the *Times* piece has no framework: a leadership with structural incentives to manage the appearance of war’s end rather than its substance will always find a hopeful moment more useful than a reckoning over industrial sovereignty.

The drones are extraordinary. The photographs are beautiful.

The laboratory conditions remain excellent.

## Day 1570

2026-06-12 · Raddison Blu

Kyiv has become a city in which it is no longer possible to distinguish consultants, contractors, intelligence officers, journalists, procurement specialists, venture capitalists, and people merely trying to drink coffee. This may itself be a form of integration into the Western defense-technological ecosystem.

Fifteen minutes ago, three heavily tattooed men in khaki sat outside a café opposite the Radisson Blu on Yaroslaviv Val beneath an awning that read, with touching optimism, “Любов.” They were lounging with the particular stillness of people who have learned, professionally, not to fidget. They may have been discussing drone procurement. They may have been discussing the Knicks comeback in Game 4. The point is that one can no longer tell. The clientel of [Tootsie Club](https://en.tootsie.kiev.ua/) has matured.

---

Hal Brands is the Henry Kissinger Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins, which tells you almost everything you need to know about what kind of distinguished professor Hal Brands is. Kissinger, we recall, believed that large countries possess legitimate security interests in rearranging smaller ones, provided the paperwork is in order and the larger country has enough rockets.

He is a scholar of American grand strategy and Latin American Cold War history — which is to say, precisely the wrong preparation for writing about Ukraine.

What he has produced is the geopolitical equivalent of a weather report delivered by someone standing inside the building: Ukraine has drones, Russia has losses, the trajectory is encouraging, but optimism can give way to pessimism. This is true in the way that Wednesday follows Tuesday. It is analysis in the sense that a menu is a meal: five analytical dimensions, zero questions about who runs the kitchen. Brands is not an outlier. He is a genre.

The piece never asks — indeed, cannot ask, structurally — why Ukraine’s world-class drone program is being built by a government whose defense procurement network is under National Anti-corruption Bureau of Ukraine investigation, whose president’s chief of staff was [staffing ministries according to the celestial calculations of a Kyiv fortuneteller](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1541?utm_source=publication-search), and whose inner circle was simultaneously constructing a gated residential compound in Kozyn.

The laboratory produces extraordinary weapons. Management invoices separately.

"Ukraine can tie itself into the Western defense-technological ecosystem by selling drone and counter-drone technology." — [Hal Brands, Bloomberg Opinion, June 12, 2026](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-06-12/ukraine-s-drones-are-beating-russia-for-now-at-least)

He concludes that a conflict going better for “the good guys” may become more dangerous before it ends.

The good guys.

One appreciates the clarity. It saves time.

The ecosystem has been integrating Ukraine for some time now. So has the media.

My eyes glazed over reading Yermak’s 2,500-word [scream for attention](https://archive.ph/fbHV7) featured in [Time Magazine](https://time.com/).

Perhaps you share my reaction to self-aggrandizing bullshit: as soon as I see it, a filmy layer of distrust and seething hatred gets in the way, and I can’t think of anything other than some unshaven doucherocket receiving accolades for being ‘visionary’ and subsequently feeling on top of the world because he gnarled whatever wit and narrative grace his speechwriter could muster into the successful injection of the Ukraine brand into a media ecosystem that, milliseconds later, does not care.

## Day 1571

2026-06-13 · Housekeeping

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/44a50559-3518-4cd8-97c0-9d129832b6f0_1536x1024.png)

Four years of war, sorted by a machine into eight piles. The piles are approximate. The war was not.

These eight clusters represent a machine’s attempt to sort a sampling of 1,142 posts by resemblance, which is not the same as meaning, and the reader is advised to treat them accordingly.

What it found: that 2024 belonged to the grinding arithmetic of military analysis; that 2025 was consumed almost entirely by one man’s reappearance on the world stage; that 2026 has produced something the classifier cannot name, and so called it geopolitics.

What it missed: everything written between the lines, which is where most of the writing lives. The sample begins in February 2022 — the moment the subject became unavoidable, and the author, like everyone else, somewhat more serious.

## Day 1572

2026-06-14 · One post in six

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d116e8e9-608b-4950-9d56-b6ba13cd0174_1536x1024.png)

I spent the greater part of Sunday morning in the company of half a million words — my own words, which is perhaps the most uncomfortable company of all.

What I discovered, sifting through this archive, was not what I expected to find. The strongest trait of the work is not that it “called” particular events — as if a writer were some kind of fortuneteller at a provincial fair, reading palms for coins. No. What the archive reveals is something more stubborn and less glamorous: a repeated insistence on three structural realities, each of which had to wait some time before the respectable world consented to notice them.

First: that Russia’s all-out invasion would not be a clean blitzkrieg. History is rarely clean. Nor are the people who make it.

Second: that the war would be politically harder to end than it was militarily to begin. This is the oldest lesson in the world, and the world forgets it with impressive regularity. The parties of 1914 rushed toward the guns with considerably more enthusiasm than they would ever bring to the table.

Third: that information distortion inside institutions would come to matter as much as anything happening on the battlefield itself. A shell destroys what it hits. A lie destroys what it doesn’t. The pattern is recognizable across a century — from the professors of Kiel writing indignant letters to the newspaper desks of London running photographs that required a certain squinting, to the gentlemen of the Department of War who were not so much dishonest as genuinely unable to distinguish between their interests and the truth. The information environment of 1914 and the information environment of 2022 are separated by a century of technology and united by everything that matters.

The archive itself, exported in June of 2026, runs to 1,694 posts — 1,413 of them available only to paid subscribers, and 281 open to anyone who wanders past. Roughly five locked doors for every open one. One post in six freely readable, which is perhaps a reasonable ratio for a world that has never quite decided how much truth it actually wants.

“[Common Sense About the War](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/13635/13635-h/13635-h.htm)” reached millions through a newspaper supplement and was denounced by Christabel Pankhurst, Arnold Bennett, the editors of two continents, and one suspects the ghost of every military attaché who had ever been shown too much at Aldershot. The parallel is imperfect. But there is something recognizable in the experience of writing about a war in real time, for a dispersed audience, knowing that what is disregarded on Tuesday has a way of becoming conventional wisdom by Thursday, attributed to someone else.

A small technical note, offered in the spirit of honesty that the archive attempts to practice: the audience status of each post reflects its setting at the moment of export, not at the moment of original publication. A post that was later opened or later locked is counted as it stands now, not as it once was. Even the archive is subject to revision. The same was true of the White Papers and the Blue Books and all those diplomatic dispatches which, by the time they reached the public, had been selected, arranged, and in certain crucial passages quietly amended. History is always the export. The original files are always somewhere else.

## Day 1573

2026-06-15 · Cageside

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5737a6b6-f0da-4104-bc5c-79dcc4873479_1672x941.png)

There is something clarifying about the image. The president of the United States, white golf cap lettered USA, peers through a chain-link fence at sweaty men grappling on the White House lawn. This is the UFC. This is diplomacy. This is the arrangement.

Or consider another image. The same cap. The same fence. Behind it, Kyiv at dawn: apartment blocks, treelines, a construction crane, a sky the color of a bruise. The smoke is there if you know where to look.

When the United States was a young and culturally peripheral republic, Europe was producing people who worried about whether freedom could survive if detached from moral duty. They gathered in places like Jena and treated the question with great seriousness. The individual mattered, certainly. But so did obligation. So did other people. So did the larger world into which one happened to be born. They were mocked as dreamers, and perhaps they were.

What would they make of this morning?

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2f3221e4-96b0-4310-9f97-a710484a5072_1280x720.jpeg)  
*Firefighters work at a site of the Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra monastery, which burns after it was hit during Russian missile and drone strikes, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine June 15, 2026. ( Ukrainian Culture Ministry/Handout/Reuters)*

This was the second strike on the Lavra since the full-scale invasion began. The first, in January, damaged structures near the Far Caves and the Church of the Conception of St. Anne. The Lavra is a UNESCO World Heritage site. It is also, apparently, a target.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/9cb3bb51-9efc-4543-86d5-e830552796f1_1280x960.jpeg)

The State Service for Ethnopolitics and Freedom of Conscience issued a statement. Moscow’s invaders, it said, had spent centuries trying to erase the monastery from the face of the earth. Their descendants had shown their true face once again. For Russian terrorists, nothing is sacred: not human life, not faith, not temples, not history.

In Kharkiv, five State Emergency Service rescuers were killed in a double-tap strike. The second missile arrived when they reached the scene of the first. At least five more were wounded. In Kyiv, by morning, four people were dead and twenty-three wounded, among them a child and a pregnant woman. The attack was still ongoing.

It was, by coincidence or design, the president’s [80th birthday](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/06/14/europe/kyiv-pechersk-lavra-monastery-fire-russian-attack-intl-hnk). He spent part of it on the phone with Putin, who called to congratulate him. The conversation lasted just under an hour. Trump called for an end to the war. Putin suggested that if Z wanted a meeting, he should come to Moscow. They agreed that Witkoff and Kushner would visit Russia again soon. Later, Trump spoke with Z as well. “We discussed many key things,” Z said. “Peace, surely, was among them.” They agreed to talk more at the G7 in France. In Kyiv, the attack was still ongoing.

The thinkers in Jena worried about what would happen when everything became instrumental — when value was measured only by utility, when spectacle displaced meaning, when freedom detached itself from obligation. They did not imagine drones. They did not imagine social media. They certainly did not imagine cage fights on the White House lawn. But they would recognize the tendency.

A thousand-year-old monastery burns in one country. In another, the cameras pan toward the entertainment.

The man in the golf cap did not comment on the Lavra. He was watching the fight.

What has the world come to. It is not really a question. It is the sort of sentence one says aloud in an empty room, in a city where the air-raid alert has become ambient, where a thousand-year-old altar burns at one in the morning, and where the leader of the free world is cageside.

Two centuries later, the world’s most powerful democracy appears to have settled on a different answer to the question the Jena people were asking. Freedom without obligation. Spectacle without meaning. The self without the world.

They were not wrong to worry.

## Day 1574

2026-06-16 · The future of journalism

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/ea3dd772-1a33-4e86-8f92-46a046d88e1c_1086x1448.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (June 16, 2026)*

One of the first things I saw on social media yesterday was Z and the prime minister stumbling around on the roof of the Assumption Cathedral with a priest, surveying the damage.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b2e2391f-e621-4a97-bbc2-38f070801750_1200x675.jpeg)  
*Ukraine's president Z and Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko visit the Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, which was hit during Russian missile and drone strikes © Reuters (June 15, 2026)*

The algorithm, with its usual sense of timing, served up Caolan Robertson’s chat with Tim Miller on [The Bulwark](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iyQA71bLKZU&t=1007s) before I was fully conscious.

The interesting part comes around minute thirteen. Miller asks what one is supposed to do when the air raid sirens go off. Robertson explains that he goes out and films, “but that’s not advised, really.” He then produces a chunk of metal — a missile or drone fragment, “probably made in Ireland actually, with the aluminum,” he says, that landed on his roof the night before.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2d586252-febb-41b4-a911-70fc34a03c2e_1680x1050.png)

“So you went up to the roof to grab that?” Miller asks.

“Yeah. I heard a massive bang and then saw this land.”

Miller, doing his best impression of someone’s mother: “Shouldn’t you be going into a bunker rather than onto the roof when missiles are firing in?”

“I guess so,” Robertson says, “but I also want to show people what’s actually happening here.”

He lives, by his own account, on the top floor of the tallest residential building in Kyiv. Two of his windows blew out that night. He went up anyway, retrieved the debris, brought it down, and showed it to camera. This is an extraordinary way to live, and also a very particular kind of way to live — one in which the danger and the documentation of the danger have become slightly difficult to distinguish from each other.

Caolan really does have nice digs.

---

The last time I encountered him in person was in March, at Golden Gate, practicing stand-up[1](#footnote-1). He looked lonely. I remember thinking, with the mild dread of someone recognizing a pattern, that he would eventually go the way of Sarah Ashton-Cirillo.

For those who weren’t following Ukraine media in 2022 and 2023: Ashton-Cirillo was an American who arrived in Kharkiv that March, became a war correspondent for LGBTQ Nation, then a combat medic, then a Territorial Defense Forces spokesperson with a Twitter following Kyiv was happy to put to use. El País called her one of the most significant voices for Ukrainian propaganda. She was wounded by shelling in Donbas in February 2023, came back, kept going, and then — suspended in September 2023 over unspecified statements, discharged in February 2025. She has, I’m told, since started a Substack called *Political Tips* and joined a foreign UAV unit. She is, by any honest accounting, now a [former journalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Ashton-Cirillo).

I bring this up because at the time, watching Caolan, I genuinely imagined him as her heir — not in the specifics, which differ wildly, but in the genre: the foreigner who arrives, fuses with the cause so completely that the line between reporting it and performing it disappears, and is eventually consumed by the fusion. It is a genre with a fairly reliable shelf life.

But this is only the segue. The actual point of today’s post is the move Caolan will never make, and the reason he will never make it.

---

He has been, by my reading, anointed. The Honorary Ambassador of Ukraine Award for Digital Diplomacy, issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, supported by the president’s wife — this is not a journalist being covered by a government. This is a content creator being curated by one. And the curation comes with an unstated but perfectly clear condition: you may say anything about Russia. You may not say anything that complicates the picture of Ukraine itself.

Which means Caolan — sincere, brave in the physical sense, willing to climb onto a roof during a massive combined Russia air missile strike to retrieve evidence — will never make the observation that Operation Midas has made unavoidable for anyone actually paying attention: that the war has not displaced the patronage system that ran Ukraine before February 2022, it has simply been laundered through it. That Yermak’s circle was extracting value from defense procurement while soldiers were short of ammunition. That Z, the man whose roof tour he will dutifully amplify today, presides over a state that is simultaneously heroic and, in its administrative core, rotten.

This is not a contradiction Caolan is equipped to hold. It’s not that he’s stupid or cynical — by every account he isn’t. It’s that his entire genre depends on a single, uncomplicated moral current running in one direction. Introduce corruption into the frame and the frame itself stops working. The sirens, the roof, the fragment of Irish aluminum — all of it depends on Z remaining legible as simply the good man under bombardment, not also the man whose government has been quietly stealing from the war effort while asking the world to die for it, metaphorically and otherwise.

---

Caolan should meet Trey. I am confident they would hit it off.

Trey Yingst is Fox News’s chief correspondent in Ukraine. He [speaks zero Ukrainian, knows zero about Ukraine’s history, has never served in the military, and usually gets the story wrong](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1005?utm_source=publication-search) — this according to me, eighteen months ago, and I see no reason to revise the assessment. He suffers, by his own account, from PTSD triggered by the smell of barbecue. He has given two pieces of advice to the public on how he survives his job. The first, to [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-04-11/8-travel-tips-from-ukraine-war-journalist-trey-yingst-any-globetrotter-can-use): balance a camera battery on a water bottle against the hotel room door, so an intruder knocks it off and wakes him. The second, to [Men’s Health](https://www.menshealth.com/health/a45781351/trey-yingst-mental-health-war-israel-friday-sessions/): practice cold plunges in peacetime so you learn to control your breathing when your body wants to panic.

Neither tip is about Ukraine. Both are about Trey. This is, I think, the actual genre, stated as plainly as it is ever likely to be stated: a man teaching the audience how he, personally, manages the experience of being near a war, in lieu of teaching them anything about the war itself.

Caolan, climbing to his roof for the aluminum, narrating his own nervous system in real time, is doing the same exercise with a different aesthetic. Trey performs control. Caolan performs exposure. Both performances require the war to remain legible as backdrop — a place where brave, interesting things happen to the narrator — rather than as a country with its own administration, its own patronage networks, its own Yermaks and Mindiches, capable of disappointing the people currently building careers on its suffering.

---

The goat thief understood goat theft better than anyone alive and understood it less than almost anyone, because his understanding had become inseparable from his need to be against it. Caolan’s understanding of Ukraine has become inseparable from his need to be for it. Both states are, in their way, sincere. Neither one is curious.

What Z’s government is counting on — what every government counts on, when it can get away with it — is that the people best positioned to amplify the cause will never look too closely at the cause’s custodians. Caolan won’t, because looking closely would cost him the access, the award, the entire architecture of meaning he has built. Sarah didn’t either, until the system that built her up quietly set her down. The moral contrast holds only as long as nobody mentions the contrast running through Kyiv’s own government — and someone curating “digital diplomacy” awards understands that better than anyone.

## Day 1576

2026-06-18 · Wartime sketches

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/61ef5dd4-6a18-4635-8b0a-cadc1d3264f0_1536x1024.png)

Kyiv runs on a small number of rooms built for exactly one purpose: letting a muckraker, a case officer, and a man who introduces himself only as being “in logistics” share a bar without anyone having to admit which one he is.

Decadence on Rustaveli was one of these once. Opened in 2004 as an Italian restaurant by day and a disco on weekends — no signboard over the door, strict face control, curtained couch-zones for those who preferred their evenings unobserved — it ran for several years as the defining address for the city’s nightlife elite before closing around 2010. Many venues since have tried to fill the same room, and several have managed it, at least for a season. Decadence faded into oblivion rather than be switched off, which here counts as a dignified exit.

[Tootsie Club](https://uk.tootsie.kiev.ua/) did not get that courtesy. It was switched off, by force, in January of last year, when searches turned up rather more than dancers — an underground brothel, women coerced under threat, hidden cameras confirmed to have been filming guests for blackmail, and a quantity of drugs and weapons no theatre café should require. The premises sit inside a Neo-Renaissance monument from 1901, once a salon for the city’s literary intelligentsia, later a deli, then a casino, then Tootsie.

Kyiv’s rooms close for every reason except the one anyone admits to out loud — irrelevance, or eventually the goons — which is the local specialty: managing the appearance of an ending rather than its substance.

---

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2884ece9-fc78-4236-9f32-997d0dcf8dee_973x1231.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o Ruslan Lobanov ( Wartime Sketches )*

---

I was reminded of a particular kind of wartime sketch early this morning, when a founding member of this publication — an old friend and a veteran of many an evening at Tootsie in its heyday — sent me [a link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3njlIlPayYg&t=1954s) to a curious conversation, with no message attached beyond an unusual quantity of exclamation marks, which from him constitutes a full literary review.

Forty-five minutes of two middle-aged white American men talking the way men talk when they have already decided they agree: warmly, quickly, with the cadence of people building a case for the room rather than examining one. One had run operations against the Iranians for three decades. The other edits an investigative outlet. Between them sat a combined expertise spanning the Middle East, the Caucasus, and most of what used to be called the Near Abroad. Neither man has ever been within a thousand miles of Lake Baikal. Neither, I would wager what remains of my friend’s Tootsie tab, has ever gone in — not even to the ankle.

The trouble is not distance from the subject. The trouble is mistaking warmth for depth, the way a man in a sauna mistakes a temperature someone else set for a fact about his own body. And what these two gentlemen were warm about was Kyrylo Budanov, whom one described — not exaggerating — as “beloved.” The Jason Bourne of Ukraine, he called him, a phrase that sounds like a compliment until you remember that Jason Bourne is a deniable asset whose own employers were never quite sure who he was working for by the third act.

The case rested on three pillars, none of which would survive five minutes in a Kyiv kitchen with the lights on: that he was built into a unit assembled by people Langley trusted; that he is known “intimately” for “a decade,” as though intimacy were a vetting procedure rather than often its opposite; and that he has personally inconvenienced a great many Russians — true, admirable, and entirely beside the question of whether the man now sitting across a negotiating table on Ukraine’s behalf can be trusted with the rest of the country’s business.

None of the following made it into the forty-five minutes: that Budanov, a fortnight into his intelligence appointment, attributed a Ukrainian operation to the Russian Federal Security Service agent on camera, that he was found sharing an estate with the family of a deputy interior minister whose résumé includes a Rostov childhood and considerable proximity to the president, that the chair he now occupies was vacated by a man who had himself arranged for thirty-three mercenaries to land in the wrong country’s custody so as not to spoil a ceasefire announcement. The chair was not cleaned before the new man sat down. It was simply reupholstered, and the upholstery is doing a magnificent job.

There was also, earlier in those same forty-five minutes, a word offered as a compliment: a visiting officer, fresh from the field, had called the whole arrangement “a lab experiment.” This publication had occasion to use the same word twice in the preceding eight days, in neither case as a compliment — once to note that a country can supply battlefield adaptability and own none of the industry that results, and once to observe that the laboratory, as always, belongs to whoever owns the building. The two gentlemen were filing a confirmation report on an argument already on file. They had simply not been told which side of the glass they were standing on.

The two gentlemen moved on to discussing Cuba and what makes a good dive bar, on which subject I have no quarrel with them whatsoever. A man can be entirely wrong about Kyiv and still know his way to last call. I only wish that before the next forty-five minutes, someone would hand him a map of the lake.

## Day 1577

2026-06-19 · The door is currently closed

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8a0780ca-38f3-4d8a-a267-5002c158f9fa_1536x1024.png)

> Historians’ conversation, being unfettered and life-affirming, will usually cause other diners to fall silent, ashamed of their bourgeois values and enchanted by the exuberance of the ‘credentialed’. A kindly act is to draw them into your group by waving or going over to their tables, kneeling down before them and begging forgiveness in extravagant language. Try to sing the theme tunes from obscure Cossack ballads, quote from Ivan Ilyin, and – of course – lots and lots of regional accents and silly voices.  
> — “The Historiography of Lunch” ([Day 934](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-943?utm_source=publication-search))

It’s churlish to dwell on all that can go wrong with the professional historian. True, some aren’t completely annoying to be in the same room with, and some do [good work](https://web.archive.org/web/20011214052756/http://wwics.si.edu/kennan/), har har[1](#footnote-1). And you have to admire the tenacity to remain in a profession wherein rejection and slamming criticism are just the beginning. Gaping insecurity, white-hot neediness, gelatin bravado – there are worse characteristics to have.

All of which are savagely thrashed in a most welcome 4-year old post of “Cheap Caviar Comes With the Job,” written by the alter ego of someone resembling [Nigel Planer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Planer), whom you might recall as Neil the hippy on [The Young Ones](https://theyoungones.fandom.com/wiki/The_Young_Ones_Wiki).

> “It is relevant that he [Z] stayed and it’s relevant that the Ukrainian government stayed. But like that raises the final thing I want to talk about which is why it was so obvious to him that he should stay. And I think this has to do with Ukrainian civil society... He says I stayed because I knew it’s what the people expected of me. So like he sidelines the question of like are you so courageous and he says no I’m not so courageous. I stayed because that’s what people expected me to do.” — Timothy

Z’s self-deflation — “I’m not so courageous, I stayed because that’s what people expected me to do” — is the most interesting detail in the passage, and it’s the one that cuts against the heroic-communicator narrative that Snyder himself had just been building. It also sits in some tension with our treatment of Z — documenting governance failures. In February 2022 the same figure is doing something that Snyder, twenty years into studying Ukrainian civil society, describes as the inevitable expression of what Ukrainian horizontal networks of trust produce. The courage wasn’t personal — it was structural. Which is, interestingly, not so far from the feudal-autocracy thesis: the same structure that enables extraction also, under maximum pressure, produces a particular kind of accountability to popular expectation.

But I digress. The point here is that neither [Timothy nor Michael](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NPPDzVIKb3c) avail themselves of the opportunity to at least mention the historical fact that Z’s popularity in early 2022 was near zero, and that he and his top managers were building mansions in Kozyn instead of heeding months of detailed warnings that Russia intended to decapitate them.

---

A venue I neglected to mention in [yesterday’s survey](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1576) of Kyiv’s rooms: Doors (Двери), on Reitarska — the same Reitarska Street where, in October 2003, a Land Cruiser carrying Volodymyr Kysil blew up opposite No. 13, six people inside, the Gongadze case visibly eating its own witnesses. Doors was running at full capacity that autumn. It was always a rough crowd, in the specific sense that rough and credentialed were the *same* crowd: the room had a talent for producing evenings where a foreign emissary, deeply confused about the country he had just arrived to save, could be debriefed at length before anyone told him what year it was. I hosted a number of those sessions. The Orange Revolution, which set the stage for the Revolution of Dignity, which set the stage for everything else, was already audible in the walls if you knew what feedback sounds like before it peaks.

The venue is now called Zig Zag. [We noted its existence in September 2024.](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-943?utm_source=publication-search) I avoid it on principle. The door, as you can see, is currently closed.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/10206f47-c745-464b-a299-071faab848fa_4032x2268.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (June 19, 2026)*

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4b59c88a-a7e4-47b9-a2ab-7de8fd198cb6_1230x820.jpeg)

The event has been extensively memed.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/be63a0cf-c604-446c-8e3d-457bb2b57424_857x1280.jpeg)

The text reads “ми спалимо вас на%уй!” — “we’ll burn you the f\*\*k up!” — in the aggressive red Soviet-style lettering that Ukrainian meme culture has been cheerfully repurposing since 2022.

The refinery is so thoroughly on fire it has achieved the energy of a lit cigarette carelessly flicked, or possibly that the whole operation was that casual. Either way it has the specific Ukrainian wartime meme energy of treating catastrophic violence as an occasion for a cheerful selfie in a flower crown. Russia’s official response, so far, has been restrained and formulaic, with officials promising to continue bombing us into oblivion.

Wonderful.
