## Day 1581

2026-06-22 · Summer solstice

Sunday night into Monday morning. A Russian drone hit a private house in Zaporizhia. A woman died. Three people were injured, including an 11-year-old boy who is under medical supervision. Ivan Fedorov, head of the regional military administration, posted a photograph of the house. The photograph exists. The house is on fire in it.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d7697116-5813-42eb-a034-428514388710_1280x855.jpeg)

In the Black Sea, a Russian UAV struck the cargo vessel *Victress*, flying the flag of Panama, and set it on fire. Nine crew members — citizens of Egypt, Turkey, and India — were aboard. Ukrainian Navy boats conducted a rescue operation and evacuated the crew. One did not make it: a 58-year-old Egyptian cook. Eight sailors went into the water on a life raft. The vessel lost its seaworthiness. Deputy Prime Minister Kuleba called it a war crime and said it required a decisive response from the international community, which is the kind of sentence that has been said, in various forms, for 1,580 days.

Two other vessels were also struck overnight — one flying the flag of Palau, one flying the flag of Belize. Preliminary data showed no casualties. Both continued moving with damage. This detail, the vessels continuing to move with damage, is doing more work than it appears to.

Also Sunday evening: an Iskander ballistic missile hit an agricultural enterprise in Odesa district. One person killed, three injured. Vehicles, fuel tanks, a warehouse. A fire.

---

On Sunday, Zelensky told 1+1 TV that Ukrainian drones had struck oil refineries in Tyumen — 2,070 kilometers in a straight line, 2,500 by route. The next generation of drones will reach 3,000 kilometers and beyond. “We understand where all their military factories are, where their oil bases, gas storage facilities are,” he said. “We need tools for a longer distance for a longer time.”

Tyumen is in western Siberia. It is not a place that, on February 24, 2022, most people would have included in a map of this war.

The map keeps getting larger.

---

##### The map keeps getting larger

The archive contains 1,702 posts. Of these, 1,423 were published and 279 abandoned — drafted, reconsidered, and left in the condition of thoughts a man decides not to finish in front of witnesses. The published pieces total roughly 706,000 words across twelve years: about the combined length of *Journey to the End of the Night*, *The Unbearable Lightness of Being*, *Humboldt’s Gift*, and *Sometimes a Great Notion* — a novel about war, one about occupation, one about a poet destroyed by America, and one about people who refuse to quit when quitting is the only rational choice. As comparisons go, it is more honest than *War and Peace*.

Of those 706,000 words, 492,000 were written after February 24, 2022. Such is the arithmetic of full-scale invasion: eight years of intermittent observation compressed into a daily obligation. Between 2014 and 2021 there were 260 posts; from 2022 to mid-2026, 1,044. Nineteen exceed 2,000 words. Seventy-four contain fewer than 100. The longest runs to 5,787 words and concerns Vladimir Putin, Karl Popper, and the Russian Orthodox Church, which explains, without further comment, why 74 others are so short.

The subject is a country that, over twelve years, has been called a post-Soviet democracy, a failed state, a frontline civilization, a laboratory for Western defense technology, a feudal autocracy sustained by popular uprisings, and a living argument against the idea that history moves in one direction. Only one of these descriptions appears in the archive. The others belong to people writing at a comfortable distance, which is itself a useful fact. The archive disagrees with all of them on most days, without raising its voice.

This is not only a book about Ukraine. It is also about the problem of writing about Ukraine, which turns out to be, in large part, a problem of tools.

Long before the archive began, English-language commentary on this corner of the world suffered from two persistent ailments. The first was the conviction that every catastrophe somehow confirmed the perfection of the market, producing a steady supply of books praising economic self-surgery while cities were busy being shelled. The second was the habit of dressing up the latest internet gold rush in manifestos, slogans, and revolutionary iconography and calling it analysis. Neither inspired much editorial skepticism.

Writing around both required precision, which required decent instruments. A decade ago the author spent an unreasonable amount of time complaining that software for producing clean prose behaved like farm machinery repaired with string. Switching between formatted text and markup was harder than it ought to have been; formatting conversations resembled untangling barbed wire; every paragraph had to be inspected in a browser to make sure it had not quietly become ridiculous. As content management systems multiplied, writers did more podcasting and less page construction, which solved nothing.

Artificial intelligence has since relieved some of the drudgery. Flagging text is easier. The ideal application — one that moves effortlessly between elegant prose and structured markup without making the writer feel like a plumber — remains somewhere over the horizon. Still, the tools are better than they were.

The archive is partly evidence of that: 706,000 words produced from an apartment in Kyiv about a country most of the tools’ designers had scarcely considered. Whether the words justified the tools is another matter. That, after all, is what archives are for.

---

---

Graphic design is, in part, the construction of navigation systems: imposing visual structure on meaning, establishing hierarchies, placing elements in context — saying, look at this for a while, then look at that. Yet a great many professionals approach design as a switch with which to turn on experience, or complete the accessories of lifestyle. The distinction matters more than it sounds.

A long time ago, it occurred to me that the first year of a communication design education should not replicate kindergarten — now you are a tree, blowing in the wind — but should instead focus on nothing but maps. For a year, students would be dropped into utterly alien environments: Luhansk, say, or Millwood, New York, armed with whatever maps were available. The exercise would be to gauge how long it takes to get oriented using these baffling, arbitrary wayfinding systems, each one more chaotic than the last — and then, having survived that, go be a designer.

This project is, among other things, a map. Ukraine is among the more alien environments available to the Western reader: a country that has been mislocated, mislabeled, and misread for thirty years by people who were holding the wrong chart. What follows is one person’s attempt at orientation, conducted in real time, from inside the territory, over twelve years. The maps are imperfect. The environment kept changing. Neither of these things is unusual.

There is also a case to be made — not here, but somewhere — for reviving the pulp fiction tradition of putting maps on the back cover, so that a reader lost in a labyrinthine plot could simply turn the book over and find out where they were. The argument for it applies, with some force, to nonfiction about Eastern Europe.

## Day 1582

2026-06-23 · Bracketing the elephant

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/385986a7-ee54-4b82-ad30-09091ae620c0_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (June 23, 2026)*

*In the old parable, a group of blind men come upon an elephant, and each, touching only the part within reach, describes it faithfully. One feels the trunk and reports a snake. One feels the leg and reports a tree. One feels the ear and reports a fan. Each description is accurate. None of them is the elephant.*

It is a delicate craft, narrating a small nation’s war against a large one, and like all delicate crafts it rewards specialization[1](#footnote-1). The specialist learns early which parts of the animal are within reach, and reports those faithfully, at length, with real eloquence — and learns, just as early, which parts to leave for someone else’s hands. A man who stayed in his capital while missiles fell — that is the trunk, and a fine trunk it is, worth describing twice. A man’s approval rating in the weeks before that, hovering near the floor, for reasons having nothing to do with the missiles — that is somewhere further back, past the shoulder, and nobody’s hand happens to wander there.

One of our blind men is, at least, honest about his method. Before he even begins, he announces it: he is “*quite deliberately bracketing*“ the ethics and the law of the thing, he says, and will speak only of power. A reasonable enough discipline, and an admirable bit of housekeeping — name the part you’re not touching, so no one mistakes the trunk for the whole animal. He does this for the war he is angriest about. For the other war, the one he loves, no such announcement is made. The bracketing happens anyway — governance, patronage, the small mountain of birthdays and helicopters — but silently, as if the category itself had never occurred to him to name, let alone set aside. One omission is a method. The other is just an absence, dressed, by its tailoring, to look like one.

Our visiting historians, lovely people, deeply read, weep real tears for Mariupol and mean every one of them, arrive with frameworks sharpened on other people’s corruption — they can tell you, unprompted, how patronage calcifies into governance, how a circle of old friends becomes a budget line, how proximity launders itself into plausible ignorance over enough birthdays in enough mountains. They have written whole books describing exactly this part of exactly this animal, in other countries.

They simply find, this once, that their hands have wandered to the ear.

This is not dishonesty, properly speaking. Dishonesty would require noticing there’s a hindquarters at all. What we have instead is a kind of professional hygiene: a man stands in a dark room with an enormous animal and reports, with complete sincerity, the only shape his palm has found.

And it is not only the historians in the room. The official-turned-podcaster is there too, and he reaches for his own favorite part — the ingenuity, the feedback loops, the basements full of soldering irons — and tells, with visible pride, of the *“Ukraine technology sprint”* his own people fought the Pentagon for, the $1.5 billion they got into the country’s drone industry “by the end of ‘24,” seed money for a harvest, he says, beyond anything they could have imagined. All true. All the trunk. What goes unmentioned, by a man holding the very part of the animal closest to it, is which hands that seed money eventually passed through, and which of those hands now have a missile named, with the specific cruelty of the accurate, after a friend.

So the helicopter that flew friends to a birthday in November before the invasion does not make it into the podcast. Neither does the warehouse of vests cleared by “one phone call,” nor the missile the soldiers call by that friend’s name. What makes it into the podcast is not merely freedom *from* but freedom *to* — all true, all moving, all of it the trunk, none of it the elephant.

The animal, for its part, never asked to be described in parts. It simply stood there, whole, in the dark, while careful men took turns explaining it to each other.

---

**Addendum: A Man Who Has Already Touched the Whole Animal**

There is, it turns out, a man who does not need to feel around in the dark, because he used to run the department that turned the lights on for a living.

Colonel Roman Chervinsky spent years as head of the SBU’s counterintelligence directorate — the man who pulled Tsemakh out of Donetsk for the Hague, who built the operation against Wagner’s mercenaries in Belarus, who is named in Western reporting as the coordinator on the ground for Nord Stream. He has, in other words, held the trunk, the leg, the ear, and a few parts the parable doesn’t have words for. He is currently on trial himself, on charges he calls retaliation for refusing to stay quiet about what he saw — which means he has, in the most literal sense available to a human being, skin in this particular game, and his account should be weighed as such: not a disinterested seminar paper, but the testimony of a man currently being prosecuted by the system he is describing.

What he describes is not a missing trunk or a misplaced ear. It’s the suggestion that someone has been quietly walking the elephant out of the building since 2019 — that the corruption wasn’t a wartime lapse but the founding architecture, that the Wagner operation collapsed because someone with access to the timeline made sure it would, that a President’s Office could, while citizens were memorizing air-raid schedules, still find the staff and the patience to build four houses outside Kyiv. He goes further than the documents do, further than any court has ruled — he names the thing directly, treason, agentry, intention — and that further step is his own, not yet anyone’s verdict. But the documented scaffolding underneath it — the Dynasty case, the Tsemakh irregularities, the Wagner sabotage allegations, the elder Yermak’s reported trips east — is not something a credentialed visitor would need a source for. It’s been reported, for years, in the same country the seminar is praising for its candor.

None of this makes the rabbit’s old description of the trunk untrue. It makes it a description of one part, offered by men who had the choice of which part to touch, given by a man who has touched all of it and is currently paying for having said so out loud[2](#footnote-2).

## The Map Keeps Getting Larger

2026-06-23 · A Preamble to the ukraine@war Archive, 2021–2026

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5c523837-a28d-4f88-9cf7-757937e408bc_819x1231.png)

---

I should say at the outset that I am not an impartial witness. This seems obvious, but it is worth stating, because a great deal of writing about Ukraine has been produced by people who believed themselves to be impartial witnesses and were not, and the difference between knowing this about yourself and not knowing it turns out to matter considerably.

I have lived in Kyiv since 1999. Before that I spent years on a hill above Berlin — Teufelsberg, the devil’s mountain, a heap of rubble the size of a small Alp constructed from the wreckage of the Third Reich and topped with listening domes — intercepting Soviet and East German military communications. The job was to detect signals that the other side considered impossible to detect, to find the side-loop emissions from relay towers at distances the East had decided were beyond the range of such frequencies. That was their error. The signals were there. You simply had to know what you were listening for.

I mention this not as biography but as method. The hill does not leave you when you leave the hill. You carry forward a permanent suspicion of institutional assessments, a specific impatience with what intelligence analysts call “bounded rationality” — the assumption that adversaries will behave within the limits of what seems reasonable to the person doing the assuming. This assumption has cost more lives than most weapons. Putin, as I have noted here many times across many years, is not a bounded-rationality problem. He is a man who does what he says he will do. The only mystery is why this keeps surprising people.

\* \* \*

After Berlin, before Ukraine, there was Russia and Belarus, but that’s another story.

\* \* \*

The archive before you contains 1,029 posts across six years: 2021 through the third week of June 2026. Of these, roughly 750 were published and the rest abandoned — drafted, reconsidered, left in the condition of thoughts a man decides not to finish in front of witnesses. The published pieces total somewhere north of 400,000 words.

Of those words, the overwhelming majority were written after February 24, 2022. Such is the arithmetic of full-scale invasion: years of intermittent observation compressed into a daily obligation that has not yet ended. Between January 2021 and the morning the Russian army attempted to decapitate the capital, there were 42 posts. From that morning through the week before this preamble was written, there were nearly a thousand more. The longest concerns Vladimir Putin, Karl Popper, and the Russian Orthodox Church, which explains, without further comment, why so many others are so short.

The subject is a country that has been called, variously, a post-Soviet democracy, a failed state, a frontline civilization, a laboratory for Western defense technology, and a living argument against the idea that history moves in one direction. I have called it none of these things. The people who have are mostly writing from a comfortable distance, which is itself a useful fact about their descriptions.

\* \* \*

The governing method of this archive is conjecture and refutation — Popper’s phrase, adopted not as academic decoration but as operational discipline. You state what you believe to be true. You look for the evidence that would falsify it. You update when you find it. You do not protect your prior assessments by refusing to look.

This sounds simple. It is not simple. It is especially not simple when the thing you are trying to assess is also, intermittently, trying to kill you.

What it produced, across six years, is a record with a property I will describe plainly because there is no modest way to describe it: the predictions mostly held. Phase 3 of the war — the protracted slog of de-occupation — was named and described in May 2022 as the coming phase, the longest and most deadly, something that would last months or years. It has now lasted four years. The mobilization crisis was documented as a systemic failure before it was acknowledged as one. The fortification deficit was flagged before Avdiivka fell. The institutional rot — documented in the Wagnergate posts of early 2021, visible in the December 2019 transcript of officials trying to explain macroeconomics to a president who did not know the difference between a balance of payments and a balance of trade, traceable to every SBU scandal and parliamentary maneuver of the pre-invasion years — did not emerge from the war. The war revealed what was already there.

None of this is presented as clairvoyance. The archive contains wrong calls, dead ends, and positions later revised. What it does not contain is the retrospective adjustment of memory that afflicts most war commentary — the gradual rewriting of what one thought at the time into what one now believes one should have thought. The posts are timestamped, public, and unchanged. This is the only form of epistemic accountability available to a writer who does not work for an institution that can protect him from being wrong in public. I have been wrong in public. The record shows it. It also shows, I think, the more important thing.

\* \* \*

A word about voice, since readers sometimes ask.

I call Z “Ukraine’s moron president” in the first post of this archive, in January 2021, and continue doing so through posts that simultaneously document his government’s intelligence failures with granular sourcing, named sources, and classified testimony. Some readers find this inconsistent. It is not inconsistent. It is the specific position of someone who wanted the country to survive and watched its leadership make survival harder than it needed to be — someone who had, as described above, watched this particular dynamic operate before, in another capital, and knew how it tended to end when the institutions built to check executive power were systematically hollowed out before the crisis arrived.

The acid in the prose is not performance. It is the residue of watching things that could have been prevented not be prevented, and of writing about them in real time for an audience that could see the same evidence.

The treatment of the Western press — the ISW analysts with their bounded-rationality models, the correspondents who spent eight years calling Russian-directed fighters “rebels and separatists” and have since, in some cases, apologized, and in most cases not — is similarly specific. I tracked this not as sport but because the quality of Western analysis about Ukraine had direct consequences for the quality of Western policy, and the quality of Western policy was, from 2022 onward, a matter of life and death for people within earshot.

\* \* \*

The posts collected here begin in a city that was at peace, or what passed for peace in a country that had been at war in its east since 2014, and end in a city that has absorbed four years of bombardment and is still, against considerable evidence, standing.

The first year documents what the war would inherit. The second year documents the invasion itself, day by day, from this apartment, at the pace the days arrived. The years that followed document the long, grinding, expensive, partially preventable catastrophe of Phase 3, in which Ukraine demonstrated simultaneously, and in equal measure, its capacity for tactical improvisation and its incapacity for institutional reform.

Long before the archive began, it occurred to me that the first year of a design education should focus on nothing but maps. Students would be dropped into alien environments — Luhansk, say — armed with whatever maps were available, and required to figure out where they were. The point was not cartography. The point was to learn what a map actually does: not describe the territory but navigate it, imposing just enough structure on chaos to make movement possible.

This archive is a map of that kind. Ukraine is among the more alien environments available to the Western reader — a country that has been mislocated, mislabeled, and misread for thirty years by people holding the wrong chart. What follows is one attempt at orientation, conducted in real time, from inside the territory, over six years. The maps are imperfect. The environment kept changing.

What I can tell you is that the wolf they were looking for in the Botanical Garden on January 5, 2022 — trackers with heat-vision goggles, five in the morning, 117 hectares, no luck — was never found. Seven weeks later, Russia invaded. The wolf, presumably, is still out there.

\* \* \*

*Kyiv, June 2026*

#### A Reader’s Guide to the ukraine@war Archive, 2021–2026

---

There is a particular kind of boredom that comes from being right too early. It is not quite the same as ordinary boredom, which can be relieved by a walk or a glass of wine. It is closer to the boredom of a man who has already read the last page of the book and must now sit politely through the middle chapters while everyone else discovers what he has known for some time. I do not recommend it. But I have had considerable practice.

What follows is a guide to the posts in this archive that did the most work — not the most entertaining, not the most widely read, but the ones that named what was happening before it was comfortable to name it, and the ones whose predictions turned out to matter. I have tried to say, for each year, what the year was actually about, which is sometimes quite different from what it appeared to be about at the time.

\* \* \*

##### 2021: The Rot Was Already There

The year before the full-scale invasion is not, in retrospect, a prelude. It is an explanation. Everything that would fail in 2022, 2023, 2024, and beyond had already failed by the time this archive opened in January 2021. The question was not whether the institutions were compromised. The question was whether anyone in a position to do something about it was willing to look.

[SBU Goes Coup Coup](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/sbu-goes-coup-coup) (January 25) opens the record with the SBU — Ukraine’s State Security Service, the institution whose primary job was to detect and counter Russian intelligence operations — actively eating itself over control of contraband revenue. I made an observation then that seems worth repeating now: an institution fighting over illicit income is not, simultaneously, an institution capable of executing a sophisticated operation against Russian war criminals. These things are mutually exclusive not as a moral proposition but as a practical one. You cannot do both. The SBU had chosen.1

[Ukraine is Not a Piano](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/wagnergate) (February 28) and the Wagnergate series (March 3) document the fate of an operation that had taken years to build: a plan to lure Wagner PMC fighters — several of whom had shot down Ukrainian military aircraft and the MH17 airliner, killing 298 people — out of Russia and into Ukrainian custody. The operation was prepared brilliantly, down to the smallest detail, according to the man who authorized it. In the last hours before the arrests, information was leaked from the President’s Office to Moscow. The mercenaries went home. Andriy Yermak, head of that Office, said the entire affair was “a detective story made up from A to Z.” Several Ukrainian intelligence officers contradicted him under oath. Their testimony was classified. It remains classified.2

I want to be precise about what this means. This is not merely a story about a botched operation. It is a story about an institution — the presidency — that, when confronted with evidence of its own culpability in a catastrophic security failure, chose to lie, systematically, to the parliament, to the press, and to the Western partners who had cooperated on the operation. This choice was made in 2020. The same institution would be managing a full-scale war by February 2022.

[Operation Г](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/ukraines-plan-) (September 11) follows the parliamentary investigation into this affair — an investigation chaired by a doctor with no military or intelligence background, which produced a report raising more questions than it answered and was largely ignored.3 The Soviet comedy Operation Ы features a criminal who practices for a warehouse heist by placing a handkerchief over the nose of a ceramic cat. I had used this comparison once already. I would use it again.

[Z’s New Clothes](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/zelenskys-new-clothes) (November 30) introduces a distinction from game theory that proved useful throughout the following years: the difference between mutual knowledge — information that everyone knows — and common knowledge, which is not only information that everyone knows, but information that everyone knows that everyone else knows. The proposition that Z was unqualified to lead a country at war had been approaching mutual knowledge in Ukraine for some time. His five-and-a-half-hour press conference, in which he referred to himself in the third person and declared dozens of times that he was Ukraine’s president, began to move it toward common. The charade continued regardless. This, as it turned out, was the more important fact.4

\* \* \*

##### 2022: Day One, and What Came After

On January 5, 2022, I published a short post about a wolf running loose in Kyiv’s Botanical Garden. Trackers with heat-vision goggles had arrived at five in the morning. The garden is 117 hectares. They hadn’t found anything. They said they would keep looking.

Seven weeks later, Russia invaded.

[Day 1](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1) (February 24) was, I think, characteristically dry. I noted which media outlet had the best coverage on what I called “the jacket” — a term borrowed from print design, where the jacket is the thing that wraps the story. I noted a first Russian prisoner of war. I noted that Christopher Miller of Buzzfeed, who had spent eight years describing Russian-directed fighters in Donbas as “rebels” and “separatists,” was still describing them that way with what appeared to be the same expression. What the post did not contain was panic. I mention this not as a boast but as a data point: the invasion, when it came, was not a surprise to anyone who had been reading the signals.6

The first weeks of war I spent not catastrophizing but parsing. I watched the ISW maps and maintained what I hoped was a productive skepticism about their “bounded rationality” framework — the assumption that Putin would behave within the limits of what seemed strategically rational to an American analyst. I watched the 40-kilometer Russian convoy north of Kyiv stall and then disintegrate. I woke at 1:40 a.m. to four large explosions, stumbled around the apartment for twenty minutes, and went back to sleep. The methodology held. The city, for the moment, also held.

[Day 27, Phase 2](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-27-phase-2) (April 21) is where I named the framework that would structure everything that followed. Four phases: the failed attempt to decapitate Kyiv in February and March; the Russian pivot to Donbas in March and April; Phase 3, which was beginning now, which would be de-occupation, which would be the longest and most deadly part, which would last months, probably years; and Phase 4, which I described as a conflict that would never truly end. I made this prediction at Day 100 of the war. It has since been confirmed by 1,300 additional days of evidence.7

[Day 25, Phase 3](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-25-phase-3) (June 2) states it plainly: “We’re only in the beginning of Phase 3, which will last for months, maybe years. It will be the most deadly and depressing part.” I have quoted this line in several subsequent year-end assessments, not because I take pleasure in having been right, but because the prediction was made publicly and should be publicly acknowledged. It was right. It remains right.8

Ignore Analysts (June 18) is the methodological statement of the war period, and I think the clearest argument I have made in this archive for dismissing a certain kind of accredited expertise in favor of watching the thing directly. ISW’s December 2021 forecast — which assumed Putin would not invade because invasion was not rational — is the central exhibit. Bounded rationality assumes that your adversary shares your definition of rationality. Putin does not. He does what he says he will do. The only thing surprising about this, I wrote, was that it kept surprising people.9

[Day 22, Phase 3](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-22-phase-3) (December 28) closes the year by listing what I had taken to calling the gate scandals — Wagnergate, Chausgate, Semenchenkogate — as a single continuous thread: the President’s Office managing perception while the war managed the dead.10

\* \* \*

##### 2023: Positional Warfare, and the Problem of Being Right

[This is (still) ‘ukraine@war’](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/this-is-still-ukrainewar) (January 1) is a recommitment. Conjecture and refutation. The old tools. The bloody mess I hoped to survive.11

By November, General Zaluzhny would publish his famous essay describing the war as a World War I-style stalemate. I had been describing it that way since June 2022. I do not fault Zaluzhny for the timing. He was operating under constraints I was not. What I will say is that 2023 introduced me to a particular variety of frustration: the frustration of being right about things that do not improve because you are right about them.

[Day 499](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-499) (July 7) is simply a list. Three things I had asked for repeatedly, in various formulations, since the early days of the invasion: close the sky, authorize the Third Army Corps, send longer-range weapons. The format — numbered, uncommented — says everything I had to say about what it had been like to be asking.12

[Day 516](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-516) (July 24) names the journalists who spent eight years calling Russian-directed fighters in Donbas “rebels” and “separatists.” One had apologized by then. Most had not. The list of the unapologetic is long and includes correspondents from publications that have since received considerable praise for their Ukraine coverage. I do not find this surprising. Institutions that produce wrong analysis for eight years do not typically respond to being proven wrong by extensively reconsidering their methods. They respond by producing new analysis, in the same manner, about the next thing.13

[Day 673](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/pause-operationnelle) (December 28) ends the year with the observation that the gap between what Russia will accept and what Ukraine can agree to was not closing. It would not close in 2024. It has not closed since.14

\* \* \*

##### 2024: The Chair is Reupholstered, Not Cleaned

On the second anniversary of the full-scale invasion, [Day 730](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-730) (February 23) carried a number that required sitting with for a moment: 600,000. This was the figure Arakhamia presented to parliament — the number of ghost soldiers in the AFU’s rolls, men counted as present who had deserted, gone AWOL, or existed only on paper. The mobilization system, it turned out, was not failing at the margins. It was failing at its foundation.15

Three days later, [Day 733](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/coming-to-a-theater-near-you) (February 26), Zaluzhny was dismissed and replaced by Syrsky. The same week, the New York Times published a 6,000-word investigation into the CIA’s relationship with Ukrainian intelligence. It was the kind of article that required years of access and dozens of sources. It did not mention Wagnergate. The chair, I wrote, has been reupholstered. It has not been cleaned.16

[Day 748](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-748) (March 13): no demobilization until the war ends. No rotation plan. No exit date. One in ten soldiers AWOL, by the most conservative estimates available. I did not editorialize. The numbers did.17

By year’s end the archive’s tone had shifted in a way I recognized but could not quite name at the time. Less acid, more compression. The compression of someone who has been counting days in a city that is both standing and not standing, depending on the hour.18

\* \* \*

##### 2025: The Four Failures, Named

The year opened with the 155th Mechanized Brigade. France had trained and equipped it. Before it fired a single shot, 1,700 soldiers had gone AWOL. The brigade commander was dismissed immediately upon deployment. One of the senior officers responsible for its formation died of a heart attack. Yuriy Butusov, the most rigorous military journalist in Ukraine, was precise about what this was: not a crime of soldiers, a crime of leadership. [Day 1044](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1044) (January 2) carries his full assessment.19

[Day 1049](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1049) (January 7) is the post I would choose if I were permitted to choose only one from 2025. It lists four things: fortifications not built, forced conscription a systemic failure, new brigades a systemic failure, domestic production a systemic failure. Four hundred words. No commentary beyond the list. Every one of these failures had been documented in this archive for years before they were acknowledged anywhere else. None of them had been fixed.20

The mortar scandal ran through the middle of the year: $500 million in domestically produced shells that, upon being fired at the enemy, declined to explode. This was the moment at which domestic production was supposed to be reducing Ukraine’s dependence on Western supply chains. The shells did not explode. No one was held accountable in any way that mattered.21

[Day 1402](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1402) (December 26) closes 2025 with the negotiation gap. Russia’s position, Ukraine’s counter-position, the arithmetic of the distance between them. “Check for logic,” I wrote. “There isn’t any.”22

\* \* \*

##### 2026: The Barometer Does Not Cause the Weather

The year’s most useful post is also, structurally, the simplest. [Day 1409](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1409) (January 2) applies Judea Pearl’s framework for causal reasoning to Z’s New Year’s address. Z’s speech constructs a causal diagram in which presidential rhetoric produces hope, which produces peace. But the barometer does not cause the atmospheric pressure. You can move the needle on public morale without generating electricity or ending wars. What you produce, instead, is a society increasingly unable to receive accurate information about its own situation — which is, as I had occasion to note earlier in this archive, a familiar condition.23

[Day 1454](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1454) (February 16) is the parabiosis post — old blood, young blood, the research into whether you can reverse aging by mixing them. I found it a useful frame for the European diplomatic situation: Orbán as senescent cell, Medinsky at the Geneva negotiations as a séance, the entire Western response to the war as a gerontological problem. It is, I think, the funniest post in the archive about a situation that is not funny.24

Day 1524 (April 28) states plainly what this archive has maintained since January 2021 but rarely put so directly: military resilience is not the same thing as liberal democracy. Ukraine’s soldiers and its society performed something extraordinary in resisting the invasion. This is true and should be said clearly. It does not follow that the political leadership presiding over that resistance exemplified the highest standards of democratic governance. Power concentrated. Media consolidated. Parliamentary dissent narrowed. Courts were, in certain cases, convenient. I have held both of these things simultaneously because both are true, and because holding only one of them at a time produces a picture of Ukraine that is flattering but not accurate.25

[Day 1577](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1577) (June 19) — the last post before this guide was written — holds together two things that resist being held together. Timothy Snyder has observed that Z’s decision to remain in Kyiv after the invasion was structural rather than personal courage — the act of a president who understood what his departure would mean for the country’s survival. This is true. It is also true that this same president, before the invasion, had an approval rating approaching zero, was constructing a residence in Kozyn while ignoring five months of explicit, specific warnings that Russia would invade, and had presided over the cover-up of a security failure that cost Ukraine its best opportunity to arrest the men who would later help run the war against it. Both of these things are in the record. The record is public. I did not rewrite it.26

\* \* \*

##### A Note on Method

This archive does not retrospectively adjust what it said. The Phase 3 prediction from June 2022 is still there, in the form it was written. The Wagnergate posts from January 2021 are still there. The posts documenting Ukraine’s Defense Minister calling the invasion risk “low” five days before it arrived are still there.

Most commentary about Ukraine — from Western analysts, Kyiv correspondents, think tanks whose institutional positions required certain forms of optimism — has been quietly revised in memory if not in archive. What people thought at the time has been substantially rewritten to match what they now believe they should have thought. I have not done this. I cannot do it. The posts are dated, public, and unchanged.

I have been wrong in public. The record shows this too. What it does not show is the systematic conversion of prior errors into subsequent authority — the professional habit, common among analysts, of treating the last wrong prediction as the foundation for the next confident one.

The wolf in the Botanical Garden was never found. The trackers eventually went home. The garden is 117 hectares, which is a great deal of ground to cover with heat-vision goggles at five in the morning, and some things, it turns out, do not want to be found.

## Day 1583

2026-06-24 · The Eagle Is in the Mail

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/32014056-84a2-44fe-819a-0149191b3593_2865x4032.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (June 24, 2026)*

Standing this morning before our ambitious refrigerator, I found myself veering away from the usual disjointed bushwa about visible language and maps of the mind and centers that cannot hold toward a reiteration of thoughts from an [article](https://web.archive.org/web/20011204201032/http://www.alistapart.com/stories/readingdesign/) I read awhile ago, by that bright fellow Dean Allen.

It would be interesting to establish the point in history – no doubt somewhere in the ad-soaked marketing-mad Seventies – when function lost its lustre, when artistry became secondary to its presentation, when illustrators became entrepreneurs and the cult of haughty ego took hold.

In addition to the usual stint prattling on about magnet typography, a couple other upcoming things:

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7037ff49-d557-4fe2-87a4-8d44ec1c8e5a_905x1280.jpeg)

Coming up in a few weeks is the Feldman Sisters exhibition in New York City. This is part of the Design and Publishing Program, which is part of the Center for Studies in Exhibiting Art. If you add it all up you get DPP CSEA.

---

If you had taken the course in Kyiv you would have gotten four Tuesday evenings of faintly snarky but often informative hooey about text, the placement of imagery, the saving of text from brutalization, data, type, rare Replacements bootlegs, colorful concrete bombshelters in Odesa, what to read while reducing sauces and an awful lot about a duck-shaped restaurant.

Persons looking for a more immersive experience might consider attending their exhibition in Washington, DC, which will be at least three long days of hyperhyper design thinkin’ and moaning in the corner about hucksterism and the demise of Flash.

---

*Closer to home*, **The Conference That Will Definitely Take Place**

There is a conference scheduled for Gdansk on June 25th and 26th concerning the reconstruction of Ukraine, and it will definitely take place. This has been confirmed by Adam Szlapka, spokesperson for the Polish government, who wished also to confirm that he has no signs that Z will not be present, which is a subtly different thing from confirming that Z will be present, though in the language of diplomatic communications these distinctions are sometimes considered impolite to dwell upon.

Z himself has not yet provided an answer. His communications advisor Dmytro Lytvyn explained on Monday that they are still analyzing. As soon as a decision is made, he said, they will report immediately. This is reassuring. The conference starts tomorrow.

---

The immediate cause of the current unprecedented tension — the greatest in many years, as Szlapka described it, with the careful tone of a man who has lived through lesser tensions and is now, for the first time, genuinely impressed — requires a brief history.

On May 26th, Z signed [a decree](https://archive.ph/w9hEP) honoring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, known by its acronym UPA, a formation that fought against the Soviet Union during and after World War II, and that also, in 1943, conducted a campaign of ethnic cleansing against Polish civilians in what Poland remembers as the Volyn Genocide. Historians estimate the campaign killed approximately 80,000 Polish civilians. To Ukrainians, the UPA is remembered for its armed struggle against Moscow. To Poles, it is remembered for something else entirely. These two memories have coexisted uneasily for decades. Z’s decree made them less easy.

Poland’s President Nawrocki responded on June 19th by revoking the Order of the White Eagle — Poland’s highest state decoration, named after the bird on the Polish coat of arms, which has been white since the thirteenth century and shows no signs of reconsidering — that had been awarded to Z in 2023 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda. To strip someone of the Order of the White Eagle is to say, with the full ceremonial weight of the Polish state behind you, that you have changed your mind about this person. The Ukrainian government, having received this message, photographed the Order being packed into its presentation box in Kyiv and released the photograph to the press. The photograph has the quality of a statement.

Z said he would return it first. His chief of staff Budanov and Foreign Minister Sybiha returned their Polish state awards the same day. The following Saturday, former presidents Kuchma, Yushchenko, and Poroshenko announced they were returning theirs as well. The eagles were accumulating.

Former Foreign Minister Czaputowicz delivered perhaps the most honest Polish assessment of the situation: Poland did not win this exchange. Ukraine has not changed its stance. Poland’s international position has decreased, and will decrease further. He said this on a television program called *View of Szubartowicz*, which is either a very serious program or the name of a man who bought a television channel and named it after himself, and either way seemed an appropriate venue for this particular reckoning.

Tusk, meanwhile, said what everyone sensible was saying and nobody sufficiently powerful was hearing: “The conflict between Poland and Ukraine pleases Putin and shocks our allies. The front line is elsewhere.”

The far right disagreed. Sławomir Mentzen, whose Konfederacja party received fourteen percent of the vote in last year’s presidential election, wrote on Facebook that it was good the Ukrainians were giving back their awards, but that “it’s just a pity that we handed them out like candy in the first place.” He added that once they had returned all the awards, they could also return the money, weapons, ammunition, and everything else Poland had previously given them. This position has the virtue of consistency and the defect of arithmetic, since the removal of Polish transit routes for Western military aid to Ukraine would primarily affect the front line that Mentzen does not appear to have visited.

---

Nawrocki was not invited to the conference in Gdansk. This is because the conference was organized by Tusk, jointly with Z, and Tusk did not invite the President of Poland, because it is a government event, and the President is not the government. Szlapka pointed out, helpfully, that neither the German president nor the Italian president attended similar conferences in Berlin and Rome. “There is absolutely no malice here,” he added. When a spokesperson says there is absolutely no malice, the correct interpretive procedure is to note the word *absolutely* and continue.

Nawrocki’s office noted that the president had not been invited by Tusk or by Z, and therefore would not attend an event to which he had not been invited. This is the kind of statement that presents itself as obvious but rewards a second reading. It is, in the most precise sense, true.

---

There is also the matter of the canceled meetings. Marcin Przydacz, head of the International Policy Bureau at the Presidential Chancellery, explained that a phone call had been scheduled between Nawrocki and Z, and then canceled by the Ukrainian side. Then a visit to Warsaw was proposed, a date and time were established, and then, a day before the visit, Z declined, offering a different time. The Presidential Palace concluded that most likely the Ukrainian side was not interested in the conversation taking place at all.

Lytvyn denied this. “There were no dates agreed upon by both sides,” he said.

This is a dispute about whether dates were agreed upon. Both men have access to the same calendar. The calendar, presumably, knows what happened. The calendar is not talking.

---

The Polish Business Council, representing nine of the largest organizations of entrepreneurs and employers, has called for calm, on the grounds that hundreds of billions of euros in infrastructure, city reconstruction, digitalization, and energy investment flow somewhat less efficiently through a diplomatic crisis than through cordial relations. Marek Gora, President of the Lewiatan Confederation, put it plainly: it would be good if Polish firms, together with European partners, participated in this. *It would be good* is the business community’s version of *please stop.*

The Order of the White Eagle is in a box in Kyiv. Z is still analyzing. The conference will definitely take place.

The Polish Business Council would like everyone to calm down.

---

*Update, June 23:* Z has finished analyzing. He will not attend.

Szlapka had no signs of this. Lytvyn said they would report immediately when a decision was made, and they have, with two days to spare, which in the current circumstances counts as advance notice. The conference will still definitely take place. There will be Ukrainian representation, since it concerns the reconstruction of Ukraine. The practical dimension, Szlapka had said, is much more important than the political dimension.

The practical dimension is now also absent.

Nawrocki, who was not invited, will also not be there. This means that the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Gdansk will be attended by neither the President of Ukraine nor the President of Poland, which is one way to de-escalate tension, in the sense that it is difficult to have a diplomatic incident between two heads of state who are both somewhere else.

---

*Also June 23:* Poroshenko has issued a statement.

He explained that two weeks ago he had promised his colleagues at the conciliation council that he would return his eagle if they failed to convince Nawrocki not to strip Z of the award. They did not succeed. He is therefore returning it — a gesture of solidarity with Z that is notable because Poroshenko and Z have spent the better part of six years in a state of mutual political hostility that has occasionally resembled a second front. The eagle, it turns out, is a more powerful unifying force than most things that have been tried.

Poroshenko noted that Medvedev had already congratulated Nawrocki. Once you have noted that Moscow is applauding, further argument becomes somewhat awkward for the other side, since nobody, in the current climate, wishes to be the thing Moscow is applauding.

He quoted Tusk — “if we quarrel over the past, someone else will win the future” — and Sikorski — “only Moscow can emerge as the winner in the war over history and orders” — and said he agreed with both. This is the political equivalent of citing scripture: you have not made the argument yourself, but you have arranged for two senior Polish officials to make it for you, which is more efficient and considerably harder to rebut.

On the question of textbooks — always, in Polish-Ukrainian relations, the question of textbooks — Poroshenko was precise: he does not want Poles editing Ukrainian textbooks, and he does not claim that Ukrainians should adjust Polish textbooks, because otherwise, he noted, they will send a joint textbook from Moscow. This image — a jointly authored Russo-Polish-Ukrainian history textbook, arriving unannounced, explaining everything — is the most clarifying thing anyone has said about this crisis.

He invoked John Paul II. He invoked Rzeszów as a symbol of solidarity. He proposed that starting Monday, politicians should look for solutions.

Monday is tomorrow. The conference is also tomorrow.

The eagle is in the mail.

---

*Further update, same day:* The journalists have issued an appeal.

Twenty-six media organizations — Polish and Ukrainian, broadsheets and digital outlets, radio stations and press clubs, including the redoubtable Gazeta Wyborcza and the Kyiv Independent, who will also publish the appeal, a fact noted at the bottom of the document with the slight emphasis of an institution that wants you to know it is joining but did not organize — have released a joint statement calling on the politicians of both countries to demonstrate wisdom and reasonableness, seek understanding, and find a way out of the crisis.

This is what journalists do when the politicians have made such a thorough mess of things that the only remaining option is to publish a letter. It is a gesture of considerable dignity and complete powerlessness, and the twenty-six organizations who signed it deserve both acknowledgment and sympathy.

The appeal invokes a joint statement from 2013, in which former presidents Kuchma and Kwaśniewski — men who had presided over their respective countries in the 1990s and thus carried the particular authority of people who had watched things be much worse — wrote that the commemoration of the victims of past conflicts should not become an instrument for inflaming relations or squandering the gains of reconciliation. The appeal notes that this obligation now rests on all of us.

*All of us* is doing considerable work in that sentence. It encompasses Z, who is not going to Gdansk. It encompasses Nawrocki, who stripped the Order and was not invited. It encompasses Tusk, who organized the conference and did not invite the President of his own country. It encompasses the politicians, the media, civil society, and the citizens of both nations, which is a list comprehensive enough to include everyone and therefore, in the practical sense, no one in particular.

The time for serious conversations about the past, the appeal concludes, will come when Ukraine defeats the aggressor. This is a reasonable position. It is also, if one is being precise, a deferral. The Volyn massacre occurred in 1943. It has been deferred before. The victims, who have been waiting eighty-three years for the serious conversation, are not available for comment.

---

*Final update, also June 23:* Donald Tusk has spoken.

“Regardless of who spoils our work in Warsaw and Kyiv,” the Prime Minister announced from the Council of Ministers meeting, “the conference in Gdansk will take place, and we will do our job.”

Two hundred agreements and contracts between Polish and Ukrainian companies have been prepared for signing. Tusk has spent many hours working to minimize the costs and damages arising from the decisions of the presidents of Ukraine and Poland, which he described not as a diplomatic crisis or an unprecedented moment of tension but simply as *spoiling the work*, with the weary precision of a man who has organized a very large dinner party and is now watching two guests throw the crockery at each other in the foyer.

The practical dimension is arriving by train from Kyiv on Wednesday.

And then there is Z’s statement, which arrived late and which I have saved for last because it is, in its way, the most clarifying thing said by anyone in this entire affair. Z noted that the Order of the White Eagle is a symbol of trust of the Polish state and gratitude of the people, and that Ukraine respects Poland’s contribution to the common fight. And then he added — with the timing of a man who has been waiting several days to say this — that Ukraine will not dispute decisions on awards if such symbols remain with Catherine the Great, Benito Mussolini, and Gerhard Schroeder.

Catherine the Great. Benito Mussolini. Gerhard Schroeder.

This is not a diplomatic statement. It is a list. Each name carries its own considerable freight — an empress who partitioned Poland out of existence, a fascist who invaded it, a chancellor who built the pipeline that funded the army now bombing Ukraine — and the implication is that the Order of the White Eagle has, over the centuries, kept interesting company, and that its current symbolic weight might therefore be assessed accordingly.

The calendar knows what happened.

The conference will definitely take place.

Two hundred contracts are waiting in Gdansk.

And somewhere in the long, unresolved argument between Poland and Ukraine about what history means and who gets to say so, a jointly authored textbook from Moscow sits on a shelf, patient as only unread books can be, waiting for everyone to finish.

## Day 1584

2026-06-25 · Tears of Russian Fears

Ruslan Lobanov has museum editions of *[Wartime Sketches](https://www.ruslanlobanov.com/%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%B8%D1%8F-not-black-and-white-cinema-book?lightbox=dataItem-lhytsvei)* left. Three, he says. Selected, a new large-format book printed in Verona, is also out.

Both are about visualizing Ukraine’s victory.

We wrote about *Wartime Sketches* in January 2024, when it first appeared[1](#footnote-1). The book is about optimism. The photographs of fully naked women cannot be called excessively provocative, which is itself a kind of argument. A concept addressing the war directly would not have worked. We live in the modern world. Yes, Russian invaders are murdering people and dropping bombs in eastern Ukraine. *Wartime Sketches* makes no attempt to illustrate bloody disaster. It illustrates something else, which is harder.

The cover of *Selected* shows a woman pouring Tears of Russian Fears champagne into glasses at the celebration of Putin’s demise. I have not seen the prints inside. Yet. I suspect they are not about bloody disaster.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5ec0ce11-d346-491a-8532-0139d928e373_3024x3106.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (June 25, 2026)*

---

The news, meanwhile, arranges itself, accordingly.

Belarusian signal repeaters along the Ukrainian border reportedly went dark on June 22. Z had told Lukashenko to disable them by June 26 or Ukraine would strike the equipment. Lukashenko, characteristically, neither complied nor refused. The repeaters simply stopped. Whether they were dismantled or merely paused is, at this point, a Belarusian state secret, which is to say a Russian one.

The Kremlin is pressuring Lukashenko to let Russian forces launch drones from Belarusian territory and extend the frontline westward. A former Russian intelligence officer told the Wall Street Journal that Moscow is threatening to cut financial support if Minsk does not cooperate. Lukashenko has been resisting this particular demand since 2022. He continues to resist it. This is, by the standards of the neighborhood, statesmanship.

Medvedev dismissed Z’s legitimacy. Lavrov said Russia will not freeze the current frontline. Ryabkov invoked the Alaska Summit. Russian officials have been invoking the Alaska Summit regularly, citing an agreement that no one confirmed and no public statement followed. The Kremlin alleges agreement in order to assert that the US is not abiding by it. This is the negotiating equivalent of a receipt from a restaurant that does not exist.

In Moscow, gasoline is running short. The city removed permit requirements for fuel tankers to keep supply moving. Azimuth Airlines says Russia has reached a critical aviation fuel situation. Russia is negotiating with Kazakhstan for 50,000 tons of AI-92. Ukraine’s strike campaign against Russian refineries since March has been producing these results at a pace that is no longer being called surprising.

---

A hill that is not a hill is a tell. The Irish equivalent of a crannog.

People build a village. It burns down. Another village is built. That one burns too. Centuries pass. The same patch of ground accumulates houses, ovens, coins, bones, ash, broken cups, children’s toys. Eventually there is enough debris to create a rise in the landscape, and someone, seeing only the gentle slope, mistakes it for nature.

We know better.

Roman Chervinsky has appeared more than 230 times across over 100 posts in this archive. He arrived first as an arrested counterintelligence officer, then as Wagnergate’s inconvenient witness, then as an increasingly lonely custodian of institutional memory. Read chronologically, his appearances form less a biography than a stratigraphic column of the Ukrainian state’s arguments with itself.

His latest interviews are interesting not because they contain spectacular accusations — Ukraine has never lacked those — but because they attempt to connect the layers[2](#footnote-2). Oman ceases to be an isolated curiosity and becomes a foundation trench. Prisoner exchanges stop being humanitarian episodes and become methods of advancement. Tsemakh explains Wagnergate. Wagnergate explains the distrust inside the security services. The ignored invasion warnings explain February 24. The houses outside Kyiv cease to be vulgar corruption stories and become artifacts from the same settlement.

One need not accept every conclusion to appreciate the excavation.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/55a57eec-a9ec-4964-ba1a-e193884646db_1024x1486.png)

An archaeologist is allowed hypotheses. He may say this shard probably belonged to this pot, this wall probably supported this roof, this destruction layer probably corresponds to this invasion. Other archaeologists may disagree. What matters is that the pieces are finally being laid side by side instead of catalogued in separate drawers.

The alternative is journalism by surface inspection.

One writes about a mansion without asking who appointed the owner. One writes about a prisoner exchange without asking why the same negotiators always prosper. One writes about intelligence failures without asking who promoted the men who failed. Each article is accurate. None requires remembering the article before it.

The tell grows taller.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

[Day 702](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-702?utm_source=publication-search). *The Weapon of Art* (January 26, 2024)

[2](#footnote-anchor-2)

Roman Chervinsky. Planted in 2019 (YouTube [interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gMkqe2DNcSg&t=1212s) from June 22, 2026)

It’s been disgusting to learn about the Trumps’ drone and scorched earth raw minerals Dominari gouge, but [this](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/28/world/europe/trump-lutnick-sons-kazakhstan.html) takes the cake.

> After Mr. Trump returned to the White House, Dominari hired Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump as paid advisers, [giving them](https://app.quotemedia.com/data/downloadFiling?webmasterId=102691&ref=320096268&type=HTML&symbol=DOMH&cdn=94260f7c5554dbc15ecb4cf545352d3d&companyName=Dominari+Holdings+Inc.&formType=SCHEDULE+13G&formDescription=Statement+of+acquisition+of+beneficial+ownership+by+individuals&dateFiled=2026-06-01) stock [now worth](https://app.quotemedia.com/data/downloadFiling?webmasterId=102691&ref=320096269&type=HTML&symbol=DOMH&cdn=c9ee67a0a2b9fee6e74a69c2ce8a3e61&companyName=Dominari+Holdings+Inc.&formType=SCHEDULE+13G&formDescription=Statement+of+acquisition+of+beneficial+ownership+by+individuals&dateFiled=2026-06-01) about $7 million, representing about 10 percent of the company’s total shares. The firm launched an explicit effort to invest in companies aligned with the president’s agenda, ranging from [military drones](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1956955/000168316824008413/umac_s1.htm#:~:text=Dominari%20Securities%20LLC%20(2,J.%20Trump%20Jr.%20(6)) to critical minerals. - [Trump Cut a Billion-Dollar Mining Deal](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/28/world/europe/trump-lutnick-sons-kazakhstan.html). [His Sons Stand to Profit](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/28/world/europe/trump-lutnick-sons-kazakhstan.html). *An agreement between the U.S. and Kazakhstan has given a group of American investors with ties to the president and the commerce secretary access to one of the world’s largest untapped reserves of tungsten* ([The New York Times](http://nyt.com), June 28, 2026)

---

On June 28, Vladimir Putin addressed the United Russia Party Congress to explain that everything is going very well. Ukraine is retreating along the entire frontline. The West cannot win. Russia is strong, united, and has always been strong and united, which is why it always wins.

Russia is also, simultaneously, going through a “difficult” and “fateful” time. Putin mentioned this too, in the same speech, without apparent embarrassment. The Kremlin is aware of all the problems and responding appropriately. Russia will fulfill all its social obligations. The gasoline shortages — nationwide, visible from space — went unmentioned, as did the Ukrainian drones that have been burning Russian oil infrastructure with the quiet diligence of a very motivated seasonal worker.

The United Russia Party announced that it is officially Putin’s party, the first time it has said so since 2007. Its campaign poster features his face and the slogan: *United Russia is the president’s party. Being for Putin is the bare minimum.* The letter Z appears in the design, because it would be a shame to waste a good war.

Medvedev unveiled the party’s top five candidates for the September Duma elections: a foreign minister, a mayor, a milblogger, a children’s rights commissioner under ICC indictment, and a seventeen-year-old boy named Vladislav who runs something called Yunarmia. The list, we are told, represents people Russians know for their “strong patriotism.” The bar for the other qualities was not disclosed.

Meanwhile the frontline moved slightly near Kupiansk, which is the military equivalent of adjusting a picture frame during a house fire. Russia launched 142 drones and six ballistic missiles at Ukraine overnight. Ukraine struck Russian oil refineries. Everyone is continuing.

The question everyone is discussing — in think tanks, in cafés, in the kind of Telegram channels that claim to know things — is what Putin does next, now that each thing Europe does goes unanswered, and each non-answer quietly expands what Europe believes is permitted. The Venezuelan tanker precedent. The shadow-fleet seizures. The gradual drift of the frontier of the possible.

The honest answer is: nobody knows. The optimists say the ceiling is real. The pessimists say we are measuring the ceiling while standing on a rising floor. Putin, for his part, is preparing for the September elections by putting his face on a poster with a war symbol and calling it a party.

## Day 1589

2026-06-30 · The whiz and the sandwich

It seems that Caolan and Z have independently converged on the same register. Z learned, fifteen deadlines into this war, that verified fact and emotional crescendo travel further stapled together. Caolan learned the same lesson from the other direction: drone footage plus “the myth is cracking” travels further than either alone.

It’s useful to identify the point where something vague becomes definite. An adult male living alone stops being vaguely tragicomic once he is simultaneously taking a whiz and eating a sandwich. At that point the condition is no longer speculative.

Caolan crosses his own dividing line on a rooftop in Kyiv, [ten minutes into this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oxbBEsVPi3c), when he suggests that the quiet sky might mean Belarus has stopped helping guide drones into the capital out of fear. Not as a sourced hypothesis, but as a hunch — delivered with the cadence of revelation, to an audience that will receive it as fact by morning. He has discovered that uncertainty, properly lit, performs exactly as well as knowledge.

That is the whiz and the sandwich. Caolan does not lie. He escalates. Every observable fact — a drone strike, a fuel queue, a quiet sky — passes through the same machine and emerges as victory.

We heard this register in the summer of 2023. Coffee in Yalta — occupied and unreachable, which was rather the point, wherever you sat to drink your coffee. The peninsula was about to become reachable, the war’s shape was about to change decisively, any week now. The register was victory-shaped months before the facts on the ground had earned it, and stayed victory-shaped well after the facts had stopped cooperating.

Eleven seasons further along, the register doesn’t belong to one side. Putin uses it too — “we are advancing virtually everywhere,” delivered with the same cadence of inevitability, while people who actually check the map find four percent of a town where he claimed nearly all of it. He escalates a captured outskirts into a captured province the same way Caolan escalates a quiet sky into a collapsing empire, the same way Z escalates a fuel queue into Putin’s demise. Three men, three positions in this war, one register among them — because the register is the only thing that performs.

---

Mykola the Pork Chop [gets the kosh](https://english.nv.ua/nation/ukrainian-lawmaker-named-suspect-in-corruption-case-by-nabu-50620150.html), finally.

Remember Mykola, a.k.a. Kolya Obolonsky?

He built a body for television and a reputation for rackets, and for a while these were mistaken for the same achievement. He became *kum* to Yermak, which in this country passes for a constitution.

He was, briefly, a regional overseer, until Zakarpattia overseered him out.

In the third year of the war, while the capital performed its grief correctly, he went to Thailand to swim. This was his only honest act.

After that he hunted call centers for tribute, investigating nothing, collecting everything.

In the end it was not the rackets or the extortion that finished him, but a piece of paper: a gift from his wife that was never given. He signed his own indictment and then, needing a witness, signed hers too.

Mykola is survived by a declaration, a former wife, and the general principle that greed, when it runs out of other people’s money, starts spending family.

## Day 1590

2026-07-01 · Under the Heat Dome

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/45e6f27e-d733-4327-a113-9a439ba529dc_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok*

On [the twenty-fifth of June](https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/06/25/8041138/), Z approved something called an influence operation. Forty days, he said, though he did not say what would fill them. This is a very Ukrainian kind of precision: an exact number attached to unspecified content, like a wedding invitation announcing the date but not the couple.

I have counted, because someone has to. Today is the seventh day. Thirty-three remain, assuming the operation survives its own naming, which is not guaranteed. Wars produce many things, including bird nests, faster than they produce forty consecutive days of anything.

What has happened in these seven days is this: nothing has happened that was not already happening. The State Security Service of Ukraine struck the Dubna communications center for the second time, which is impressive and also, if we are honest, a continuation of a sentence that began before Z sat down with General Khmara and decided the sentence needed a title. The refinery outside Moscow that supplies forty percent of the region’s fuel remains, according to reports, out of commission through the end of the year. This too predates the operation.

Meanwhile, [Phillips O’Brien, writing for a magazine that specializes in the discovery of patterns](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/06/moscow-ukraine-drone-attacks/687745/), discovered a pattern. I do not begrudge him this. Discovering patterns is a livelihood like any other. The pattern he found — pressure on money, pressure on command, pressure on the fiction that Moscow is safe — is a real pattern. I only note that its load-bearing evidence was gathered before the pattern was given a name and a countdown.

Meanwhile in Russia, a different pattern is being managed, and managed well. [The Times sent a correspondent](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/29/world/europe/russia-ukraine-rhetoric.html) to ask why nobody in Lyubertsy would say where the bomb shelters were, and the answer, delivered with the calm of a man explaining that the sky is up, was that the country is not officially at war, shelters are for wartime, and therefore there are no shelters, only PDFs. Bashkortostan has decided sirens cause more depression than drones.

This is not a society approaching the limits of self-deception. It is a society that has found an economical relationship with the truth: enough to keep the trucks running, not enough to cause anyone to ask why the trucks keep not arriving. Arkhipova, who studies such things professionally, calls it a performance of obedience. I think she is exactly right.

I want to be fair to Z. A president cannot announce, “We will continue doing what we have been doing, at approximately the same pace, for an indeterminate period.” This is true, but it is also not a speech. Somebody in the room will have argued that a number creates momentum, that a countdown is a promise the enemy can be made to fear even if the promiser has not yet decided what precisely is being promised.

It is a fairly ordinary piece of statecraft, and there is a reasonable chance the audience is not the Kremlin, which has not dignified the operation with comment, but Washington. [If the Kyiv Independent’s super-secret source is to be believed](https://kyivindependent.com/ukraines-sbu-to-wage-40-day-pressure-campaign-against-russia-zelensky-says/), the White House wanted boldness. If that is the audience, the operation is already succeeding. A man who tells his boss he has forty days to fix something has purchased forty days in which the boss stops asking whether it can be fixed at all.

I have been reading, in the meantime, a young Irishman named Caolan, who [returned from Venice and Ireland this week](https://ukrainetoday.org/this-is-the-hardest-moment-of-putins-life/) and announced, with the sincerity of a man who has just gotten off the train, that the air in Ukraine felt different.

He does not mention that the air, in the most literal sense available to a thermometer, was in fact different across much of Europe. He landed in the middle of [a heat dome that spent a week moving east](https://www.mappr.co/europe-heatwave-map/), breaking records in Germany, Poland, and Slovenia before settling over Kyiv, where [people were cooling off in the Dnipro](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/29/nx-s1-5872293/record-breaking-heatwave-moves-east-engulfing-more-of-europe) because it was, for entirely mundane meteorological reasons, extremely hot.

I believe Caolan felt something. I believe he felt something roughly forty degrees Celsius.

I am less certain the feeling is evidence of anything beyond the fact that a person who has spent two weeks abroad will, upon returning to a country at war during a historic heatwave, feel that something has shifted. Something always has shifted. War and weather are both reliably shifting conditions, and a man fresh off a train is poorly positioned to say which one he is describing.

[Being present where it is hard to be present](https://universitytimes.ie/2026/05/the-kilkenny-lad-russia-wants-to-arrest-caolan-robertson-is-still-in-kyiv/) is Trey Yingst’s kind of journalism: proximity offered up as its own species of evidence, with no standards desk, no editor whose job is to ask whether “the shortest vampire” is really the phrase he wants in a dispatch about potato planting.

[The Institute for the Study of War](https://www.kyivpost.com/post/79237), working through the same seven days with a map and a percentage sign, found that Russian and Ukrainian forces made no confirmed advances on the twenty-ninth of June. No shift in the air registers on their instruments. This does not mean Caolan’s air was imaginary. It means he and ISW are measuring different things, and only one of them intends to be measuring anything at all.

So: Day Seven. The war continues at the pace it was continuing before it received a title. Moscow manages its citizens’ understanding of their own fuel lines with a discipline that would be admirable in any other context. Z’s *boldness* appears to have received a press release. And a young man from Kilkenny has told his subscribers that something is different now, which is either the truest sentence anyone has written this week or simply the sentence a returning traveller always writes, regardless of what he finds when climbs up to the roof.

Thirty-three days to go. I will count the rest.

## Day 1591

2026-07-02 · Under the waning Strawberry moon

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7f74302b-81d2-4ded-95d2-a5ccf119bbd7_1981x793.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 2, 2026)*

Day 8 of Z's influence operation against Putin. No clouds, lots of smoke, at least a dozen dead by morning, twenty-eight locations across the capital hit by Russian drones and missiles.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d6436b3d-82b5-458d-aa17-60cd57ea9e03_2560x1755.jpeg)

They came, as they always come now, in a manner that had long since stopped surprising anyone and had not yet started to feel survivable — up to six hundred of the buzzing things, Gerans and Gerberas and their cousins, a very large number of them jet-propelled now. Behind them, up to twenty-five Iskander-M ballistic missiles lifting off from Bryansk and Kursk, launched, one assumes, by men who believe in the necessity of their labor, up to thirty Kh-101 cruise missiles crossing out of Vologda airspace, patient and low and old-fashioned in their way, and, almost as an afterthought, about eight Kalibrs from the direction of Novorossiysk.

Of the newest and proudest children, little can honestly be reported, since eyewitness accounts of hypersonic Zircon arrivals are thin — they are faster than their own sound. The city hears the missile’s wake before it hears the missile, a boom that announces an object already past, followed a beat later by the sound of that object detonating. It arrives having already announced its own arrival, from the future, so to speak, of its own flight path.

Preliminary damage report:

- Obolonsky district: A major fire broke out in warehouse facilities in an industrial zone.
- Darnytsky district: A 9-story residential building partially collapsed — destruction from the 1st to the 6th floor.
- Pechersk: Strikes recorded in the courtyards of the Frantsuzkyi Kvartal, Bulvar Fontaniv, and Trinity residential complexes. Dozens of cars destroyed or damaged; a private clinic destroyed.
- Desniansky district: An apartment building damaged; people remain trapped under the rubble.
- Shevchenkivsky district: Residential buildings, a hotel, and a medical facility damaged. Medical workers were among the injured; one paramedic is in extremely critical condition.
- Podilsky district: Residential buildings in the Dibrova Park complex damaged.

I checked in on Caolan, who increasingly reminds me of [Sarah](https://x.com/AshtonCirillo) and [Trey](https://x.com/TreyYingst). And, no, billions of people don’t live in Kyiv.

Maybe they’ll team up and serve together in the same Ukrainian military unit some day.
