## Day 1593

2026-07-06 · Compaction, not collapse

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/e8c113cf-695f-4135-89a3-98077605729f_2560x1755.jpeg)

Scenes of death and destruction not unlike last week. The pattern this morning was the same. First ballistic missiles, then jet-propelled Kamikaze drones, followed by cruise missiles and more drones. At least 11 reported dead and dozens injured as of this writing.

Kyiv is the main target not by accident. Z warns people in advance, as he did before last week’s strike, telling them to be careful, to heed the sirens, because intelligence suggested something large is coming. The population, dutifully, obeys — packs into the metro with fresh foam mats, sleeping bags, does what a warned population is supposed to do. And in the morning the death toll is announced anyway. The warning system functions perfectly, and it changes almost nothing, and everyone involved — the mayor, the air force spokesman, the woman being pulled from the rubble of a nine-story building she was told to shelter from — understands this and continues anyway, because the alternative to the ritual is no ritual at all, which is worse.

Russian missiles are not aimed at military installations, which are hundreds of kilometers away. What gets hit here is an apartment block in Podil, a hotel, an ambulance station, a monastery with a UNESCO plaque — an inventory of things that have no front line to speak of. The message, if we’re going to be honest about there being one, is addressed elsewhere: to the people of this city, who are meant to understand that warning is not the same as safety, and being warned changes nothing about who gets carried out on a stretcher. And it’s addressed to the people who keep being asked for more interceptors and keep sending fewer than asked: a Patriot battery without enough missiles is worthless. It is not a demonstration anymore, in the sense of a single dramatic gesture. It’s a rehearsal that has been running long enough to become policy, performed for an audience that keeps watching and keeps not quite doing the one thing that would end the performance.

---

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/316dc89e-2a62-43ad-b48a-7e2adee8810c_1086x1448.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 5, 2026)*

A day earlier, Z dressed the Motherland Monument up in red, white and blue.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/3609046e-a282-44bf-a11c-7e9f7270f93d_836x1115.jpeg)  
*c/o Z (July 4, 2026)*

---

In other news, heavy rains washed out hundreds of newly dug graves at the National Military Memorial Cemetery near Vita-Poshtova in the Hatne community of Kyiv region, thirty minutes south of the capital. The cemetery’s administration moved quickly to correct the record: [this was natural soil compaction in burial places,](https://sud.ua/en/news/ukraine/365766-u-natsionalnomu-viiskovomu-memorialnomu-kladovyshchi-poiasnyly-poiavu-provaliv-pislia-zlyv) not the washing away of graves or the influence of groundwater. Compaction, not collapse. A process, not an event.

What the statement declined to mention — because statements like this never mention it, that’s the whole genre — is that the site was contested well before the first grave was dug. Hydrologists and ecologists **had warned for years** that the chosen location sat on nature-reserve land with a high water table, unsuited to burials at scale. A district administrative court had apparently ruled the land’s use for a cemetery unlawful, a ruling the Verkhovna Rada is said to have legislated around with 267 votes; and the contractor entangled in the construction is linked, to a sanctioned businessman more recently in the news for an alleged assassination attempt in Monaco. Whether all of that survives scrutiny is a separate question from whether it’s the kind of thing anyone wants to believe, and in Ukraine those two questions rarely get to stay separate for long.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/88aa4e14-3b63-4304-ac7f-59632ff268a3_768x560.webp)  
*Photo c/o Novynarnia (July 5, 2026)*

This is the feudal autocracy running its most efficient process of all: the conversion of consequence into vocabulary. Land-use law inconvenient to Z and his top managers gets a legislative workaround. Warnings from people who actually understand water tables get filed under noise, the same folder Z kept Western intelligence’s invasion warnings in back when the state was busy prioritizing the May holidays over the border. And when the mud finally, predictably, arrives — not as tragedy but as the fully anticipated output of a fully anticipated failure — the state doesn’t apologize for the decision. It apologizes for the footage.

Sorry for your concern, not sorry for the swamp.

Here is the arrangement in its complete, closed form: the state that cannot keep the front line supplied without laundering procurement contracts through Miami real estate is the same state that cannot bury its dead without laundering hydrology through a press release. Nothing has been built here — not the drones, not the cemetery — that will still exist once the money and the war both stop being useful reasons not to ask who built it and on whose water table. The soldiers get the compaction. Somebody else, eventually, gets the audit. The families get told, in the meantime, to trust the state’s account of the ground over the state’s own photographs of the ground opening.

## Day 1594

2026-07-07 · Durable until Tuesday

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4e3751ea-8192-47ef-b726-cdd50bc6212d_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o 1+1 (July 6, 2026)*

Vonnegut’s answer to trauma was to abandon linear narration. In *Slaughterhouse-Five*, Billy Pilgrim becomes unstuck in time because chronology can no longer contain Dresden. “So it goes” is less a catchphrase than emotional flatline: the only response left when horror has exhausted description.

Welcome to Vyshneve.

Houses burned to their foundations. So it goes.

Entire micro-districts treated simultaneously as crime scenes and cemeteries, pending confirmation of which. So it goes.

Six hundred evacuated. Fifty more by armored transport because the roads themselves had become targets. Five hundred relocated “temporarily,” a word that now means only *later*. So it goes.

The detonations continue at irregular intervals, as though the war has forgotten to turn itself off. Officials promise replacement passports within days—an admirable administrative reflex applied to a settlement with too few intact buildings left to issue them. So it goes.

This is not damage. Damage implies something remains against which loss can be measured. This is a village being informed, street by street, that it used to exist. Billy Pilgrim would recognize the tense.

Hours later, Z [sits down](https://archive.ph/jbqM9#selection-1765.0-2041.90) with a Tralfamadorian from *The* *Financial Times* and describes a war entering its decisive phase in the air. The land front is largely static. Russia has been denied the sea. The remaining contest is overhead, where, he argues, Ukraine’s principal weakness remains air defense. During Monday’s attack—the same attack that devastated Vyshneve—not one of the twenty-nine ballistic missiles was intercepted. Patriot interceptors, he says, sometimes arrive only a day before the barrage they are meant to stop.

Vyshneve is that sentence made concrete. So it goes.

A military analyst would make the same point more coldly. Patriots and SAMP/T batteries exist in meaningful numbers around Kyiv and almost nowhere else—not Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv or Sumy. Perfect air defense exists nowhere.

Billy Pilgrim and Z share the affliction, not the response. Billy drifts through catastrophe because sequence has ceased to matter. Z, briefed every thirty minutes as the war jumps from Kyiv rooftops to Omsk refineries to NATO summits without transition, refuses that passivity. His nightly address is not a shrug but an argument that the chaos still has shape—that it bends toward air defense, production lines, diplomacy, tomorrow.

Putin “vanquished” ordinary apartment blocks—Z’s word, repeated with the flat consistency of someone who has exhausted synonyms. Sixty-eight missiles. More than 350 drones. Twenty-two dead. Ninety injured. Kyiv again.

So it goes.

Vyshneve receives one clause in the speech: *“The situation is difficult... because of secondary detonation.”* The bureaucratic register compresses into twelve words what the smoking streets had already said all morning. The speech and the wreckage describe the same event from different altitudes.

Z [says](https://t.me/V_Zelenskiy_official/19817) he wants the Security Service to report what happened. Of course he already knows. Klymenko briefs him every half hour: fires, rubble, rescue. The Cabinet will release emergency funds because Vyshneve no longer possesses the resources to repair what was done to it overnight.

He thanks the rescuers, the mayors, the businesses, the partners.

So it goes.

---

Something that’s been bugging me lately are the [center-of-gravity arguments](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/2023-military-campaign-propects?utm_source=substack&utm_campaign=post_embed&utm_medium=web) of bona fide experts. A friend of mine, a deputy battalion commander on the zero line for more four years, put it to me in June with great tenderness: we have reached, he said, a durable balance. Modus vivendi.

I believed him for about three weeks, which is roughly how long it takes Moscow to reload.

Because here is the trouble with balance, durable or otherwise: it assumes both parties are weighing the same thing on the same scale. One side is counting kilometers. The other is counting how many Patriot interceptors the enemy has left, and when the answer is not enough, the correct military term for what follows is not “stalemate” — it is “Tuesday.” Twenty-nine ballistic missiles arrive over Kyiv in a single night, unintercepted, and somewhere a spokesman explains, patiently, like a doctor delivering a diagnosis to a child, that only American systems can catch these, and America’s next delivery is scheduled for 2027, which is to say: after the patient has already been discharged, in several senses of the word.

Meanwhile the same capital that cannot always intercept a missile aimed at itself managed, the same week, to set fire to a refinery two and a half thousand kilometers away — a small, embarrassing miracle that the Kremlin’s own television was instructed not to mention, on the theory that the Russian viewer should hear only about the missiles that land, never the drones that do. This is the durable balance we have reached: one side can reach Omsk, the other side can reach the fifth floor of an apartment building on any given night it feels like proving a point before a summit. A balance, yes. Durable, no. A seesaw is also, briefly, level — right before someone gets off.

So my friend is not wrong that the war has answered its two big questions, about whether Ukraine exists and whether Russia will collapse. He is only wrong about what comes next being arithmetic. It is not a ledger. It is a country waiting to see whether the world remembers, at the summit, that a balance held up entirely by someone else’s missiles is not a balance at all — it is a favor, renewed nightly, at the at the pleasure of western leaders whose convictions have the shelf life of a news cycle.

## Day 1595

2026-07-08 · State of Exception

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/980476c2-37f5-485b-8b3a-d69becc01751_1536x1024.png)

Five stories from this week. Separate on the surface. One mechanism underneath, if you know where to look: the extraordinary measure, invoked as necessity, that quietly becomes the ordinary way of doing business.

**1. The Monaco hitwoman**  
([Interfax-Ukraine, July 7](https://interfax.com.ua) / [ZN.ua](https://zn.ua/ukr/UKRAINE/pidozrjuvanu-u-zamakhu-na-jermolajeva-znajshli-mertvoju-bilja-kijeva-zmi.html))

June 29: an explosion in Monaco critically injures sanctioned Dnipro businessman Vadym Yermolaiev, his companion, and his 13-year-old son.

Interpol identifies the suspect: Anastasiia Berezovska, a Ukrainian citizen reportedly traveling disguised as a man. She re-enters Ukraine on July 1.

By July 3, Ukraine’s Prosecutor General opens a case, attempted contract murder of multiple victims. Investigators follow her contacts after her return: family, and two men, one a former law enforcement officer, the other a serving officer in Defense Intelligence (HUR). Both had transferred her money, via crypto and bank, enough to put them on the radar.

Under questioning, the HUR officer confesses: he killed her, together with the other man. He claims he acted alone, no orders, no reporting up the chain, no authorization for the contact, the payments, or the killing itself.

A search of the former officer’s home finds a basement room resembling a torture chamber. A reconstruction leads to her body: gunshot wounds to the head, shell casings recovered.

Both men are charged with premeditated murder by a group acting in concert. The SBU confirms the account. Prosecutors say Monaco has been fully briefed. The original заказчик, the one who sent her, remains unknown.

In plain terms: a state security officer carried out an extrajudicial killing, entirely outside his chain of command, inside a case his own government had just opened. The exception, here, isn’t the murder. It’s that no ordinary process, no order, no oversight, no authorization, was apparently required for a servant of the state to decide a woman should die before she could talk.

**2. The gag order**  
([Radio Svoboda, July 7](https://www.radiosvoboda.org/a/news-rozsliduvannia-sukhachov-cpk-sud/33798487.html))

Journalists spend months documenting 143 properties linked to the brother of the head of Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation, the agency meant to investigate official corruption.

The story never runs.

Instead, the brother’s company sues. A Kyiv court bans publication outright, preemptively, before a single line appears.

In plain terms: prior restraint, a legal instrument meant for genuine, provable, irreversible harm, deployed here against a story that hadn’t even been published. The exception swallows the rule it was carved out from.

**3. The explosion no one owns**  
([YouTube, July 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BX6rd0tY_8c))

A blast at a munitions depot in Vyshneve, near Kyiv. The footage suggests multiple stockpiled explosives detonating together, not a single strike.

The obvious questions: why was a major ammo depot placed in a residential area, and why was so much concentrated in one location?

Instead of answers, the president goes on camera asking his own security services to investigate, publicly outsourcing responsibility to the same system responsible for making sure stockpiles of explosive materials are not stored in the middle of a populated area.

In plain terms: the ordinary machinery of accountability, an investigation, is invoked here as a way to defer accountability rather than deliver it. Asking the question in public substitutes for answering it.

**4. Sanctioning a critic**  
([Interfax-Ukraine, July 7](https://interfax.com.ua/news/general/1182801.html))

Z signs a sanctions package: Russian propagandists, a Moscow official, companies feeding Russia’s missile industry. Standard, justified.

Folded into the same decree, alongside fourteen Russians, is one Ukrainian: Boryslav Bereza, former MP and government critic.

Bereza’s response: being sanctioned by both Putin and Z is “bingo.” He’s not wrong.

In plain terms: sanctions are, by design, an emergency power, no trial, no charge, no right of appeal, justified only by wartime necessity. That is precisely what makes the instrument attractive for uses a courtroom would never permit. The exception was built for the enemy. It gets used on whoever is inconvenient.

**5. The drone maker raid**  
([Kyiv Independent, July 8](https://kyivindependent.com/top-ukrainian-drone-ceo-searched-by-law-enforcement/))

July 7: the SBI conducts roughly 70 searches targeting Vyriy Industries, offices, contractors, even the CEO’s family homes.

Vyriy produces roughly a quarter of Ukraine’s FPV drones, at prices low enough to disrupt the market. The allegation: price inflation on about $157 million in state contracts, use of shell companies, and nearly $900,000 in undeclared cash on site.

No charges yet. CEO Oleksii Babenko says he is a witness, not a suspect. The cash, he says, is payroll, withdrawn the way Ukrainian firms often operate. The accusation, he says, makes no economic sense.

Industry reaction is telling. Concern isn’t about compliance, it’s about motive. One veteran-led initiative warns this could mark the start of something broader: corporate raiding, political pressure, or a reshaping of the market. Another source puts it more bluntly: the real question is not the producer, but who upstream benefits from removing a cheap, high-output competitor.

In plain terms: a search-and-seizure regime built for wartime urgency lands on the cheapest, most productive contractor in the sector, while costlier, better-connected ones proceed untouched. The emergency justifies the raid. It does not explain the target.

A killing with no order behind it.  
A gag order with no publication to justify it.  
An investigation that exists to avoid a finding.  
A sanction that requires no proof.  
A raid that requires no charge.

Ukraine is fighting two wars. One is against an invading army. The other is against the normalization of the exception, the wartime logic holding that due process, a free press, and reasoned prosecution are luxuries for peacetime, and that whoever controls the emergency measure gets to decide who it applies to.

Each of these five stories is the same discovery, made separately: that the extraordinary tool, once available, gets reached for on whoever is inconvenient, not only whoever is dangerous. Parliament cannot investigate who failed to prepare the country for invasion, or who has profited since, because the people empowered to authorize that investigation are the same people who would be its subject.

Russia never needed perfect spies. It needed something simpler: people positioned inside the right systems, security services, courts, procurement, who found it convenient to be useful, and profitable to stay so.

That arrangement does not disappear when the war starts. It adapts, and it learns to wear the emergency’s own clothing.

The exception was supposed to be temporary. Increasingly, it is just how the state now operates, and it keeps getting the last word, after the facts are fixed, after the witness is gone, after the story is stopped before it runs.

## Day 1596

2026-07-09 · The License

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/3dfb69d9-4aed-4599-a336-bda969fd5c46_1537x1023.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 9, 2026)*

Trump told Z yesterday, at the NATO summit in Ankara, that *a little birdie* had whispered in his ear: perhaps Ukraine should get the license to build interceptors for its own Patriot batteries.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/817cbca2-b395-4506-a3ed-abd46e283d5b_1536x1024.png)

Ukraine is good at snapping stuff together. But assembling hundreds of interceptor rockets — seekers included — is a different order of task, and it will likely take a couple of years before Ukrainian engineers can do it at scale. By then, with any luck, neither man will still hold public office. And we won't be dead.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/ef40d12d-5c03-4f5e-96f6-4e489961b30d_1280x853.jpeg)  
*Z and Trump (Ankara, July 8, 2026, Photo c/o Z )*

Photos of Vyshneve, the village one mile south of Kyiv that was incinerated on July 6, have started popping up on the internet.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fc3051b1-7ab9-4ab7-9b50-cff3bdfcf1c4_1280x720.jpeg)  
*Vyshneve (Photo c/o Микола Калашник . Libkos has a bunch of photos of the aftermath here )*

Most of the 100 or so houses in the village were vaporized in secondary explosions, the cause of which no one wants to talk about publicly. Prime Minister Svyrydenko [said](https://kyiv.tsn.ua/en/kyiv/worst-destruction-since-the-war-began-svyrydenko-reveals-shocking-scale-of-overnight-strike-on-vyshneve-3122084.html) the tragedly illustrates “the most extensive destruction to the residential sector since the start of the full-scale invasion.”

---

Listened to an unsatisfying podcast w/ Z stenographer Simon Shuster.

Sigh.

It occurred to me that postliteracy arrived in Ukraine before the Americans found a word for it. In 2019 the candidate did not debate, did not read, did not need to. He governed by clip, the way a comedian governs a room — not by argument but by rhythm. The résumé was retired; only the face remained, warm and unaccountable. Z!Team supplied the punchlines, Z supplied the smile, and the electorate, starved of Hegel, voted for the closest thing to a laugh track.

It is not that reasoning failed. It is that reasoning was never on the ballot.

Seven years on, Simon’s magazine [explains](https://archive.ph/hJRqc#selection-761.0-1805.227) that television made politics into entertainment, and entertainment cannot be cross-examined. Kyiv already knew. We had merely mistaken the diagnosis for a punchline of our own — pink unicorns, 47 seconds, the war reduced to a demo reel. The dialectic did not lose the argument. It was never invited.

I listened to Shuster’s podcast hoping for a plan. Four and a half years into the largest land war in Europe since 1945, someone who has spent more time in the presidential bunker than any other Western journalist ought to know whether the man running the country has a theory of how it ends. Shuster came close. He built forty minutes of scaffolding toward the question — Z’s endgame, the privacy of his own mind — and then, right at the threshold, the podcast asked its listeners to subscribe. The answer to “does Z have a plan” was itself paywalled.

What Shuster gives us for free is not a plan but stagecraft. Z’s team, we’re told, worked hard — deliberately, consciously — to preserve the Churchillian image manufactured in the invasion’s first days, particularly for audiences abroad too far away to see the seams. The nightly address is not governance; it’s a running production. The bunker gym, the ping-pong table, the disciplined diet — Z himself understands physical fitness as part of the image. Even his health is cast, not lived. The Trump courtship followed the same logic: not “how do we end the war” but “how do we avoid being blamed for its continuation.” A positioning exercise, not a peace plan. Z hoped his own outsider-comedian-turned-president arc would resonate with Trump’s — casting, again, not statecraft.

So it goes: a license to build interceptors, a couple of years off, timed to outlast whoever’s still in office to take credit or blame. A village vaporized, folded into the same feed as the summit handshake. Z is not waiting for victory or negotiating toward peace. He is performing continuity — competent, disciplined, camera-ready continuity — until some other force, battlefield or ballot box or mortality, writes the ending for him. So it goes[1](#footnote-1).

## Day 1597

2026-07-10 · 25 Days Left to Fix It

Z announced the influence operation against Putin on June 25 with a stated 40-day span. So today, running the count forward, we’re wrapping up the second week of the adventure.

The op itself, as we framed it back on [Day 1590](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1590), is a number attached to no declared content — a countdown offered less to Moscow, which hasn’t dignified it with comment, than to Trump, who reportedly enjoys boldness. Forty days bought is forty days he stops asking whether the underlying problem is fixable at all.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/77b5e3d7-c510-4a00-8e84-904482d66f02_1536x1024.png)

The munitions depot in Vyshneve, in Kyiv region, belonged to one of the enterprises of [Ukroboronprom](https://ukroboronprom.com.ua/). On 6 July, during a massive Russian strike, it caught fire, then began detonating, in that order, as such things do. Nine people died. This is a fact, and facts, in this country, tend to arrive well after the funerals they describe.

Z was asked about it on July 9. [He answered by voice message](https://interfax.com.ua/news/general/1183781.html), which is itself a small monument to the age. There is a criminal case, he said. Guilty parties will be held responsible. There will, without doubt, be dismissals at Ukroboronprom, since the depot belonged to one of its enterprises. The sentence has the shape of accountability without containing any.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/9333d9ac-5f0e-495b-9d6c-3d834fac2bff_1554x1012.png)  
*Ukroboronprom HQ is up the street from Lukyanivka, which was obliterated before Z announced his 40-day plan (Photo c/o abdymok , June 14, 2026)*

The strike itself came the night before, on July 6, and the explosions that followed were not modest. The Kyiv Regional Military Administration counted nine dead. A spokeswoman for the State Emergency Service reported that rescuers were still working through the aftermath at thirty-five separate locations, which is the kind of number that tells you more than any statement does.

The Ministry for Communities and Territories Development counted 280 damaged residential buildings — 253 private houses, 27 apartment blocks. The government will send more than UAH 3 billion (about $67 million) from the state budget’s reserve fund to deal with the consequences. Reserve funds, in Ukraine, are where consequences go to be paid for after the fact.

Andriy Lykhoviy, spokesman for the General Staff, told [Interfax-Ukraine](https://interfax.com.ua/news/general/1183781.html) this week that the site where the explosions occurred does not belong to the Armed Forces’ sphere of management and is not subordinate to them. A useful sentence, in its way — it draws a boundary around responsibility with great precision, right at the moment responsibility might otherwise have had somewhere to land.

---

**Ukrainian Words of the Week**

- **Вечорниці (vechornytsi)** — Not “party.” Youth gathered in the evenings to sing, embroider, joke, smoke pot, court each other, and dance — a single word doing the work of an entire social institution, one that happened to also produce a fair number of marriages.
- **Рушник (rushnyk)** — Not “towel,” or only barely. An embroidered ritual cloth that accompanies a person from birth through marriage to burial — the thing a couple stands on during a wedding, the thing used to bless children, the thing that greets honored guests bearing bread and salt. Every pattern and color carries meaning most people quietly know and never explain. Untranslated into other languages for the same reason a word for a specific bone in the body doesn’t translate as “bone.”
- **Щем (shchem)** — Maybe the hardest of the three. A single feeling that braids together a light ache, nostalgia, tenderness, longing, and warm memory all at once — the emotional equivalent of a chord rather than a note. Other languages can hit individual overtones. None has one word for the whole chord.

Have a great weekend!

## Day 1601

2026-07-13 · The Chair and the Table

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/07371951-fe51-461c-bc69-7e040d1dfac6_2172x724.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 10, 2026)*

It’s Day 19 of 40 — [assuming June 25th counts as day one](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1590) — of Z’s influence campaign against Russia. He arrives in Paris today, on the eve of the midway mark, for a Coalition of the Willing meeting chasing the thing Ukraine actually needs: Patriot interceptors, and a seat at Europe’s slow-motion effort to build an anti-ballistic air defense system of its own.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/9782d5a0-2379-4c9a-82b3-3b0047bb7d3c_1188x1324.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 10, 2026)*

Somewhere in the same frame of city as all this, a woman on Friday evening walked down a central Kyiv street with a champagne bottle already popped, cork gone, foam still finding its way down the neck. Nobody told her the government would fall over the weekend. She would not organize her weekend around it if they had. Just a woman who bought champagne and was drinking it on the way to wherever she was going, and cabinet reshuffles proceeding on a separate, parallel clock that occasionally intersects with hers as an air raid siren and otherwise does not.

There is a detail worth pausing on: the ambassadorial reshuffle in Washington seems to have driven the cabinet reshuffle in Kyiv — a diplomatic vacancy mattering more to Z than the head of government did. We read this as evidence of the government’s secondariness. It is better described as its whole biography. A government assembled by an office rather than a coalition was never going to behave otherwise. You cannot accuse a chair of failing to be a table.

The result is more foam — in Kyiv, at least. Ukraine has hit ninety Russian oil tankers in the Sea of Azov since July 6, and Russian milbloggers are doing something Kyiv’s commentariat rarely bothers with anymore: admitting, in public, that their system is broken, too.

The woman with the champagne, for what it’s worth, is hung over.

## Day 1602

2026-07-14 · Constant Choreography

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/807e6527-ce34-4c53-8c81-f76c8a7ab522_1536x1024.png)

Cosmologists have a name for the laziest possible theory: the cosmological constant. A single number stapled onto Einstein’s equations that explains why the universe accelerates—and asks nothing further of you. It fits the data beautifully and is, by design, completely uninteresting: a number with no story behind it.

Ukrainian governance has had its own cosmological constant since roughly forever. The ongoing theoretical fuss about replacing that constant with something dynamical increasingly reads like Bankova with the names filed off.

The constant, in one line: a primitive post-Soviet patronage system that survives by rearranging personnel, never its physics.

Everything else—the ministers, the “programs,” the solemn Telegram choreography—is quintessence: a scalar field, slowly rolling, creating the appearance of motion while the underlying vacuum energy remains exactly still.

Countries are ruled by their diagnoses. The diagnosis here hasn’t changed. It isn’t corruption—that’s a symptom. It’s a management system with no legal mechanism for rotating power short of collapse.

Formally, dismissing a government is parliament’s prerogative. In practice, deputies learn of it from rival factions before their own leadership tells them, and are then asked to ratify a decision made fifteen minutes earlier on Bankova. The vote is less a check than a formality—with a price attached: a case dropped here, an appointment or embassy dangled there.

So: Svyrydenko out after eleven months—before even reaching her first anniversary—thanked, and floated for Washington as ambassador. A posting that remains, for now, a promise rather than an agrément: Washington hasn’t signed off.

The seat is open because her predecessor, Olha Stefanyshina, is being quietly unwound ahead of a reported second NABU suspicion—this time for illicit enrichment—layered atop an older case from a Yanukovych-era justice ministry program, involving roughly 2.5 million hryvnias that never quite adapted anything to European legislation, plus a Kyiv apartment reportedly purchased well below market.

By some accounts, it was Washington itself that nudged the process—preferring a quiet rotation to the embarrassment of a sitting ambassador under formal suspicion.

Svyrydenko, installed as Yermak’s executor, repledged herself to the palace the moment the alignment shifted, with the same fluency. The coupling constant doesn’t care which particle it attaches to—only that the attachment holds.

Along the way, she reportedly drew over three million hryvnias teaching at a university run by a serial state-board veteran, without ever specifying how many hours she taught. A parliamentary inquiry circled back empty—ministry to university and back again—the kind of paper trail that generates its own criminal referral.

Koretsky in: a plausible technocrat, a workaholic, not a politician—which, after three failed premierships, now counts as a credential.

The only question that matters is whether he arrives with a field of his own, or as a lone particle dropped into an otherwise unchanged system. Early signals suggest the latter: most ministers remain, merely reshuffled between portfolios.

Possibly Fedorov out of Defense—not demoted so much as reclassified: deputy prime minister without portfolio, the standard resting state for a rival whose approval ratings begin to rhyme with the president’s.

Zaluzhny, in London, is rumored for the same kind of “rotation”—the polite word for removing a man from a post that was itself the polite word for exile.

This is the coincidence problem in local form.

Why, of all epochs, do we observe dark energy and matter density at comparable scales? Kyiv’s version: why does each reshuffle land precisely when a corruption exposure becomes undeniable—often abroad before it is at home?

Last July: Chernyshov, pulled back under suspicion.  
This July: Stefanyshina.  
Right on schedule, the system produces a replacement already legible to Washington.

A coincidence that repeats on schedule isn’t one. It’s a coupling nobody writes down, fitted after the fact and called something else.

And the result, after every dynamical model gets its turn—tracker fields, phantom energy, modified gravity—is the same: none of it solves the problem it was built to solve.

Swapping the field doesn’t touch the constant. It just layers a new unnaturalness on top of the old one.

The unequipped version is simpler: stop grading surnames. Watch the program. Check back in three months.

Nothing will have moved.

The honest prediction—the one the smart money still holds:

**w = −1.**

Everything else is well-funded motion against a fixed background.

---

Last night Kyiv was again hit by something that gives almost no warning.

Not Iskanders. Not cruise missiles. Russia appears to have fired six to eight modified S-400 air-defense missiles in their secondary role as short-range ballistic missiles. They are among the nastiest weapons in Moscow’s inventory because they reach the city in little more than a minute from launch sites across the border. Several of us heard the explosion before our phones even finished announcing the air raid.

That isn’t a glitch. It’s physics.

Designed to shoot down aircraft, S-400 missiles can also be fired at ground targets.

Unfortunately, we’re out of Patriot PAC-3s.

The strikes set warehouse facilities ablaze in Holosiivsky district. Falling debris ignited cars in Darnytsky. We heard around eight explosions in rapid succession.

The point isn’t merely to destroy buildings.

It’s to compress the time between ordinary life and war until they become almost indistinguishable.

## Day 1603

2026-07-15 · Two Floors Above

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d1b8e049-f636-44b5-a47e-cb35a19453e4_1536x1024.png)

The poster was torn down minutes after I took this picture. Someone had given Parliament Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk horns, wedged a megaphone in a glass box between his hands, and declared Draft Civil Code No. 15150 a threat to freedom of speech and journalistic investigations — an unusual accusation to level at a civil code, the driest branch of law ever invented, the one concerned with contracts, property and who inherits your dacha. Strangeness has never been an obstacle to political advertising here. By the time I’d looked back, someone else was already peeling it off the wall.

The new Civil Code has acquired the familiar dignity of every grand legal reform: everyone agrees Ukraine needs one, and almost everyone dislikes it for a different reason. It is said to be too European, too academic, too theoretical, too liberal, too cautious, too long, too complicated and, perhaps most unforgivably, too optimistic about the amount of free time available to Ukrainian judges. Family lawyers fear it swallows the Family Code. Business lawyers complain it leaves too much uncertainty. Human-rights advocates find gaps where they expected guarantees. Technologists see yesterday’s answers to tomorrow’s questions.

And hanging over all of it is the oldest Ukrainian objection of all: before rebuilding the house, perhaps we should first make sure the roof has stopped exploding.

So the Code is controversial, and almost nobody likes Stefanchuk.

But he is the wrong villain for this particular week.

The poster made him look like the architect of the country’s troubles. He isn’t.

Horns painted on the man rewriting inheritance law is the sort of scandal a country produces when the real architecture of power is operating exactly as designed.

**That architecture has an address.**

**It is two floors above the President’s Office.**

Start with the arithmetic, because it is the least controversial part.

Z has never really had a chief of staff. The formal post has long functioned as the centre of executive power itself, with appointments, budgets, judges and political discipline flowing through a single office that exists largely outside **a constitution on pause**.

"Усі ті права, які гарантує Конституція України, для нас із вами зараз особисто як для представників нашої держави – вони на паузі". - [Z](https://www.president.gov.ua/news/shodnya-vi-mayete-vidchuvati-sho-vid-vashoyi-roboti-zalezhit-80041) (December 23, 2022)

Over time, the judiciary acquired a reputation for responding less to statute than to informal pressure, while lawyers learned there were clients best left unrepresented if they valued their future careers. Whatever one calls it — state capture, informal governance or simply survival — it is difficult to describe it as an independent rule of law.

Members of parliament elected in 2019 remained remarkably disciplined for years. **Only after the envelopes stopped arriving did they rediscover independent judgment.** New parliamentary groupings are now forming, but this looks less like a democratic awakening than a change of landlord.

Not incompetence.

Policy.

**Ukraine’s tragedy is not simply corruption. It is a state that reallocates its enemies rather than defeats them.**

That is why Mykhailo Fedorov’s predicament matters.

The Economist’s [profile](https://www.economist.com/europe/2026/07/13/ukraines-reforming-defence-minister-is-under-fire) this week is sympathetic, yet inadvertently describes the structural trap facing anyone who threatens an entrenched revenue stream without possessing an independent political base. Fedorov introduced competitive procurement and reportedly reduced artillery-shell prices by sixteen percent almost immediately.

**The saving tells us less about Fedorov than about the system that preceded him.**

He has no faction.

No institutional base.

No independent constituency.

One patron.

Fedorov himself has spoken publicly about pressure from corruption networks surrounding defence procurement. **Yet many of those associated with the old system remain among the president’s most trusted advisers. There has been no public accounting. Only continuity.**

That is the mechanism in miniature.

Failure is rarely punished.

It is redistributed.

The pattern appears elsewhere. A senior general dismisses criticism by asking whether passengers would board an aircraft flown by a shopkeeper. Contempt substitutes for argument. Senior officers delayed manpower reforms for months before finally accepting them. Delay itself becomes a political instrument.

Fedorov’s vulnerability is therefore structural, not personal. His problem is not a lack of military credentials. It is that he is attempting to reform institutions whose defenders remain politically entrenched while possessing little protection beyond Z’s favour, at precisely the moment that favour appears least capable of enforcing itself.

---

Which reminds me of Yuriy Shchyhol.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5004b49b-7a33-43fc-887b-3b544bc0ee4d_1656x488.jpeg)

> There are different ways of understanding the above transaction. Some UAH one (1) million in UAH 500 notes weighs approximately 2.3 kg. If a pack of UAH 6.4 million were all 500 UAH, then it would weigh 14.8 kilos. Obviously, most of them were UAH bills, which, as we know, are more popular than UAH 500 bills for cash payments in heavy satchels.

Last time I checked (this morning), no verdict, case still pretrial and reportedly weakening on procedural grounds, and he's back in uniform rather than in prison. Dismissed, detained, bailed, stalled, and quietly reabsorbed into the security apparatus while his case drags into my thesis better than a clean conviction would have[1](#footnote-1).

## Day 1604

2026-07-16 · High-T, Low Trust

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fb309ee8-18cf-4514-a0d9-15d43e788ebe_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 16, 2026)*

The Telegram message from Ukraine’s former defense minister [reads](https://t.me/zedigital/6882):

**What didn’t work out:**

1. Completing the organizational transformation of the Ministry of Defense according to NATO standards and common sense. The new structure was launched, many people were let go, many processes were begun. But we needed to be more decisive in dismissing people who were slowing down the changes.
2. Moving absolutely all procurement to a tender system.
3. Building a culture of accountability for decisions made. I believe that it is precisely the heroic Ukrainian people who will shape this institutional culture.

Thank you to everyone, men and women alike, who is defending Ukraine and working toward victory.

Thank you to my entire team for their effective 24/7 service.  
I especially thank my family for their patience.

Thank you all for your support!

I will continue working toward the mission I came to the Ministry of Defense with in the first place — to defeat the enemy through asymmetry, speed of innovation, and organizational strength.

---

Read plainly, it is a confession. Three admissions of insufficient decisiveness, from the man readers of [The Economist](https://archive.ph/tjTtC) would have named the most decisive person in the building. Which tells you less about Fedorov’s nerve than how little of the political apparatus around him was built to reward using it.

Z’s replacement is [Ihor Klymenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ihor_Klymenko), the nation’s top cop, a man whose formative organizational experience appears to have been perfecting hospital corners in a barracks somewhere in Zhytomyr after the Soviet Union imploded. I hadn’t clocked that he’s still young enough for that biography to be true.

As we tried to argue [yesterday](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1603), none of this changes very much. The ministry gets a new occupant. The building keeps its architecture. The Rada will presumably wave it all through today, hours after this goes out, in whatever theatrical register these confirmations get performed in — and none of the spectacle will touch the arithmetic underneath it.

Which brings us back to the general we left last night weighing his own alleged haul in kilograms. Nearly three years after Yuriy Shchyhol’s office was cleared out over sixty-two million hryvnia in software procurement — a case adjacent to, but distinct from, the drone-pricing scandal that also carries his name — the file has produced no verdict. It has produced seven separate attempts to open a preparatory hearing, and, this week, a finding from the High Anti-Corruption Court that the very technical documents prosecutors called improperly classified were in fact legitimately secret all along, which is not the sort of ruling that strengthens a corruption case. Meanwhile the general who was found, at his arrest, sitting on a small currency exhibition of euros and dollars is back in uniform, brigadier general rank intact, serving in military intelligence while his case loses altitude on procedural grounds rather than merit.

This is what accountability looks like inside a procurement system too byzantine to convict anyone in real time: the money gets weighed, the suspect gets detained for a night, bail gets posted, and then the file simply outlives everyone’s attention span. Nobody is acquitted. Nobody is convicted. People just change desks until the scandal ages out of memory. Shchyhol didn’t beat his case. He’s outlasting it.

In this photo I’m looking due west - again in the direction of Vyshneve — at a cloud of smoke from a ballistic missile strike early this morning on a warehouse in Sviatoshinsky district. At least two people dead.

In other news, [Hegseth plans to screen all US troops, including women, for low Testosterone](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/15/us/politics/hegseth-troops-testosterone.html).

Every American service member over thirty will be screened annually for low testosterone. Women included, treatment optional. The branding, naturally, was not optional: a “High-T Department of War.” Add it to the pile. Transgender troops banned. Women’s promotions blocked after the selection boards had already approved them. Beards gone. The flu vaccine mandate gone too, until an outbreak at basic training killed a recruit and the mandate came quietly back. This is a defense secretary curating virility for a force that, at the moment, is not fighting anyone.

So: one military stages a toughness it does not need, screening healthy men for a deficiency in order to sell them a drug and a slogan. The other has toughness on constant, involuntary demand, and a rising share of its draft-age men are removing fingers, forging documents, or swimming rivers to get out from under it. Hegseth’s manosphere is theatre. Ukraine’s is a court filing nobody wanted to make, from a state that ran out of volunteers years ago and still hasn’t found an honest way to ask for the rest.

## Day 1605

2026-07-17 · Who is Vova

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b05efd01-32a2-468a-b9b6-4adf85439738_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 17, 2026)*

Fedorov’s [exit briefing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g-7UA-eDDuo) names everyone except the one person who matters.

Asked how many foreign governments called about his dismissal, he doesn’t answer. He tells a story instead: Pistorius as a new Churchill, Karp calling with urgency, Fedorov politely deferring. Whether it happened that way is beside the point. The names do the boasting. A phone call stands in for an answer.

Twenty minutes later, same move with sharper edges. Who bought Trukha? Who’s behind the Telegram pile-on? Thrown into the room, never resolved. He built that ecosystem himself in 2019. Telegram was a campaign weapon before it turned on him. He noticed it only when it became personal.

Outside, near Franko, people did what they do here when institutions don’t hold: they showed up. But read the signs closely and the target isn’t Fedorov’s reinstatement — it’s commander-in-chief Syrsky. The last cardboard protest was aimed at a policy nobody could put a face to. This one has a face, and it isn’t the man who lost his job. It’s the general who kept his.

Fedorov himself was a reshuffle accident — one draw in a chain no one planned. The same lottery removed Zaluzhny, with no protest at all. Good draw, bad draw. Same dice.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8bff1fd6-64d3-435a-823c-6d4f93ac6c1e_1536x1024.png)

Fifty-five minutes of questions, and no one asked the one that mattered: who is Vova.

Not an abstraction. A man who, with friends, has been building a mansion complex outside Kyiv — before the invasion, during it, after it. The referent behind last year’s “golden toilet mafia.” Others get named to their faces. Vova gets the unwritten rule: investigate the court, never the king, especially while the house is still going up.

Call it what [Day 1546](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1546-c5b) called it: two wars running in parallel, sometimes in the same room. Abroad, this is filed as institutional churn — a reformer, a general, a system finding its footing. The version outsiders need.

The mechanism is simpler. A minister, an apartment, a stranger who turns out to own half the defense economy, dinner over veal, no minutes taken. Different address, same blueprint. The mansion outside Kyiv and the apartment on Hrushevskoho are the same structure at different heights.

Small footnote, same calendar: [Halushchenko moved into the Justice Ministry — the seat that decides who gets prosecuted — on July 17, 2025. Not because of scandal. He was already in the chair months before anyone was raided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Galushchenko).

The forecasting question didn’t stay rhetorical for long.

Last night Vova named Yevhen Khmara, acting head of the Security Service, acting defense minister. Not a politician. The justification was his record — long-range strikes, Alpha, High-T. Then the phrase that matters: control over the internal situation. Control is the point. Internal is the tell.

Parliament will confirm him later, after “procedures.” In the meantime, “acting” governs. A familiar maneuver — widely understood, rarely stopped.

By morning Andy [runs the reshuffle](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/16/world/europe/ukraine-military-defense-minister-drones.html), quotes the line: the situation is what it is, someone has to choose. What it doesn’t run is why the choice sits where it does, or what “internal intelligence” means in practice — the Security Service, and within it, Alpha. Corruption appears once, sourced to Fedorov, as contractor complaints. It isn’t followed up the org chart to the mansion complex outside Kyiv.

So the next minister wasn’t drawn.

He was installed. Same evening. From the one institution built to watch everyone else.

## Day 1608

2026-07-20 · Dialogue police

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/11c34b96-a792-47fe-9dfa-9594c6906815_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 18, 2026)*

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/cc4f6e09-7ec1-4417-b03c-a2cb9c774d28_1449x1085.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 18, 2026)*

There were many more people on Saturday afternoon at the Missing in Action rally on Independence Square than a block away at Ivan Franko Square protesting Z’s decision to sack Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

One crowd was searching for sons, husbands and fathers swallowed by Russia’s war. The other was trying to make sense of a political system that suddenly seemed to be talking to itself.

A few hours later, Russia settled the argument in its customary way. Ballistic missiles pounded Kyiv for hours. Fires broke out across the city. The entrance to Lukianivska metro station, where generations of Kyivans have sheltered from Russian air raids, was itself shattered by the blast wave.

Wars have a way of restoring perspective. They also expose whether a political system can still hear itself think.

The most revealing sentence of the week came not from the protesters but from Z himself.

“Without me,” he told reporters, “they don’t sit down together.”

He wasn’t speaking metaphorically. Ukraine’s defense minister and commander-in-chief had stopped talking to one another. Messages passed through the president.

It reminded me of something I wrote years ago about corruption. Corruption wasn’t the disease. It was the thermometer. The disease was a political system that had stopped correcting itself.

The *Financial Times* [reports](https://www.ft.com/content/1b34caa6-d909-4df8-a90f-b928f2199261?syn-25a6b1a6=1) that Z is now weighing Syrsky’s dismissal after firing Fedorov. The headlines are about personalities. The more interesting story is about feedback.

Every institution depends on disagreement. Engineers argue with engineers. Generals argue with civilians. The argument isn’t the malfunction. It’s the repair mechanism.

Russia long ago found a different repair mechanism. It doesn’t correct mistakes. It consumes the people who point them out. For more than a century the Kremlin has devoured its own prodigal children. Ukraine has always been noisier. People argue, protest, resign, leak, complain. That noise is not a defect. It is often the sound of a society correcting itself.

Which is why the danger isn’t that Ukrainians gathered in Franko Square to criticize their government. The danger is if, somewhere behind the walls of Bankova, disagreement no longer circulates unless it passes through a single office.

From the outside, everything still looks normal. Orders are issued. Press conferences are held. The machinery keeps running.

Only the feedback has been disconnected.

Sunday’s missile barrage answered none of the questions raised in Franko Square. It merely reminded everyone that Russia gets a vote.

Wars are won not only by courage or technology, but by institutions capable of hearing bad news before the enemy delivers worse.

Last week, the quietest sentence was also the loudest.

“Without me they don’t sit down together.”

Everything else followed from that.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/bbbd6e3a-d94f-4c83-95e4-8025c7f651fa_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 18, 2026)*

## Day 1609

2026-07-21 · The direction of travel

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c4707d40-9a54-45f9-80f1-f14bc51ebfff_1536x1024.png)

When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, almost everyone thought they already knew how the story would end. Ukraine was expected to lose before anyone had time to become tired of reading about it. That did not happen.

Instead, something stranger happened. The front moved less than people expected. The missiles moved more.

Russia began the war convinced that only Ukrainian cities would live under this particular weather. Moscow was somewhere missiles departed from, not somewhere they arrived. In those first months Ukraine possessed almost nothing capable of reaching deep into Russia. There were the Neptune missiles, intended for ships rather than cities. One of them found the *Moskva*. Otherwise, Ukraine watched while Russian missiles crossed the sky in the opposite direction.

The arrangement seemed permanent. Nothing ages faster than a permanent arrangement.

For months now Ukrainian drones have been appearing over Moscow and St. Petersburg. People gradually became accustomed to them, which is one of humanity’s more unsettling talents. Ballistic missiles are harder to become accustomed to.

Last week Ukraine’s [outgoing defense minister said the country had successfully tested one](https://euromaidanpress.com/2026/07/16/symbolically-says-ukraines-departing-defense-minister-new-ballistic-missile-was-tested-on-day-government-resigned/). Two weeks earlier, [Russian sources quietly reported intercepting](https://defence-blog.com/russia-confirms-intercept-of-new-ukrainian-ballistic-missile/) what they described as a Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile over Moscow Oblast.

If the reports describe the same event, Moscow has entered a different chapter of the war.

#### An old comparison

People have begun comparing it with the Iran-Iraq War. The comparison is not exact. History rarely bothers with exact copies. It prefers family resemblance. During the 1980s neither Iran nor Iraq could defeat the other, so they began shooting missiles at each other’s cities instead. The newspapers eventually gave it a simple name: the War of the Cities. Simple names usually belong to complicated tragedies.

Readers with improbably good memories may recall that we wandered into the same neighborhood three years ago, in [“2023 Military Campaign Prospects.”](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/2023-military-campaign-propects) The argument then was less about missiles than about geometry. The authors identify Russia’s center of gravity: its monopoly on long-range strike. Not territory. Not manpower. Not Crimea. Long-range strike.

Three years later, the front has moved less than many expected. The mental map has moved rather farther.

#### Three roads

Ukraine now appears to be approaching the same destination by three different roads.

**The first road belongs to the state.** The old Sapsan program, abandoned and revived often enough to resemble an orchard rather than a weapons project, appears to be alive again. Much of what is known comes from Defense\_SCM’s *[The War Russia Fears](https://defensescm.substack.com/p/the-war-russia-fears)*. It is an unusual essay — rich in detail, poor in footnotes. Some of its claims can be checked independently, others cannot.

**The second road belongs to private industry, propped up by the state.** Fire Point first became known for drones. Now it speaks increasingly about ballistic and antiballistic missiles. [Joshua Yaffa, writing in The New Yorker](https://nationalsecurityjournal.org/ukraines-most-revered-general-has-a-warning-about-the-deep-strike-campaign-russia-can-strike-back-with-equal-or-greater-force/), watches the consequences. Oil depots burn. Airfields fall silent. Fear migrates eastward. *(Links to coverage of the July 15, 2026 New Yorker piece; the New Yorker article itself couldn’t be fetched directly.)*

[Simon Shuster, in The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/national-security/2026/07/ukraine-denys-shtilerman-drone-missile/687931/), walks through the workshop. He returns smelling faintly of epoxy and carbon fiber while his host points from drones to cruise missiles to whatever comes next.

Neither man is wrong. They are simply standing in different places.

[Z promised three thousand missiles and missile-drones in a year](https://kyivindependent.com/zelensky-missiles-drones/). A factory owner speaks of hundreds of drones every ten days and a handful of missiles each afternoon. The numbers refuse to agree. Numbers often behave like relatives. They share a family name while declining to share an inheritance.

Perhaps there are factories nobody has mentioned. Perhaps “missile” has acquired cousins. Perhaps wartime arithmetic follows rules unknown to accountants. Factories, however, are stubborn creatures. They eventually settle every argument.

**The third road** runs through Britain, which is working with Ukraine on a longer-range missile expected to enter production over the next several years.

#### The direction of travel

Three roads. Different travelers. The same destination.

The direction of travel has changed. Russia invaded believing that distance was one of its allies. Distance has an awkward habit. Once technology notices it, it begins to disappear.

Fire Point is plainly building things. Russian oil depots testify to that often enough. Whether it will someday build ballistic missiles in the quantities people now imagine remains an open question. Reality has the irritating habit of publishing its own corrections. Factories answer such questions more honestly than interviews.

Russia entered this war believing missiles traveled in one direction. Technology, unfortunately for Russia, has never been especially sentimental about permanent arrangements.

History rarely invents new jokes. It prefers to tell the old ones to someone else.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/128d52a9-9598-4259-a88d-cb0899dcce76_1042x695.jpeg)  
*c/o President’s Office (July 20, 2026)*

\* Distance disappearing is not, it turns out, a courtesy extended in one direction only. [A recent CSIS analysis](https://www.csis.org/analysis/tale-two-strategic-attacks-race-end-war-ukraine) counts the numbers on the other side of the ledger — Russian ballistic missile launches up roughly ***sevenfold*** since 2023, Ukraine's interception rate now down to about ten percent. The war has become two punishment campaigns running at once, each side betting its exhaustion will arrive first. Russia's escalation, at least, comes with footnotes. Ukraine's still mostly comes with bullshit.

## Day 1610

2026-07-22 · One Year Later

Today is the exact one-year anniversary of the day Z signed the law gutting the independence of the country’s anti-corruption agencies — triggering the biggest wartime protests Ukraine had seen, until this week.

Not one of the outlets covering Tuesday’s reshuffle seems to have noticed the date.

We did, at the time, in a [dispatch](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1246?utm_source=publication-search) now tucked behind a paywall that was considerably less composed about it than we’re managing to be now.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b1cede78-c11a-41d2-9ff4-b66610d3ed0d_1536x1024.png)

With less than two weeks left in Z’s 40-day influence campaign against Russia, he has named a new commander-in-chief.

This is not the same as appointing one.

The distinction is doing a great deal of quiet work.

After several days of protest in Kyiv and elsewhere, Z announced that Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapaty, commander of the Joint Forces, would take over from Oleksandr Syrsky.

He asked Syrsky, with the courtesy one extends to a man being removed, to hand over his affairs to his successor in a civilized manner.

It was a gracious sentence built around an event that has not happened.

Here is how it read from Washington, in the Institute for the Study of War’s nightly assessment:

Z “dismissed ... Syrsky and appointed ... Drapaty as his replacement late on July 21.” — I[nstitute for the Study of War](https://understandingwar.org/research/russia-ukraine/russian-offensive-campaign-assessment-july-21-2026/), July 21, 2026

Note the tense.

Not designated.

Appointed.

Full stop. Past and completed. The way an institute of record has to write it when choosing between the categories available and none of them is:

**“Pending a signature that depends on a minister who does not yet exist.”**

That is not a criticism of the institute.

It is a comment on how much information a clean sentence can lose.

Ukrainian procedure requires a sitting defense minister to submit the candidacy of a new commander-in-chief before the president can appoint one.

Ukraine does not currently have a sitting defense minister.

It has an acting one, Yevhen Khmara, who is expected in time to be confirmed by the Rada. After that, he will formally propose the man everyone has already been told is the new commander-in-chief.

Pavlo Palisa is understood to be the next chief of the general staff.

None of this is official.

All of it is settled.

The country has become fluent in the grammar of the fait accompli.

What it has not become fluent in is patience with the one demand the protests actually made: the reinstatement of Mykhailo Fedorov to the defense ministry he was pushed out of.

That will not happen.

Z has offered him, by his own description, a worthy post overseeing the state’s technological development — worthy, but not the ministry, and not adjacent to it.

So the arithmetic of the week is this:

The commander everyone objected to is gone.

The minister whose return everyone demanded is not coming back.

And the crowds that produced both outcomes are left to work out for themselves which of their two grievances was actually addressed.

A protest can be satisfied without being answered.

This appears to be such a case.

Syrsky, for what it’s worth, has not conceded anything.

The day before this designation, he wrote that he had no intention of resigning.

A general who intends to fight for his position does not necessarily change his intentions because the position has been given, on paper that isn’t yet paper, to someone else.

His response to his own removal, whenever it arrives, will tell us more about how settled this settlement is than anything Z’s office has announced so far.

The shake-up arrives on the anniversary of the crowds that forced Z, eventually, to abandon the law folding the country’s anti-corruption agencies into a structure he controlled.

The comparison is obvious enough that it’s already being made.

What’s less obvious is whether it holds.

The timeline is worth getting right before deciding.

Franko worked because the thing the crowd wanted was simple and binary:

Kill the bill or don’t.

But “worked” took longer than the shorthand suggests.

Z signed the original law.

Protests erupted the same day.

It was two days before he proposed reversing it and more than a week before parliament actually passed the reversal.

This week’s crowd wanted two things and got a partial and an ambiguity within roughly the same span.

Syrsky is gone in substance but not yet in paper.

Fedorov is not coming back, in any form the protesters would recognize as the demand being met.

So before anyone files this alongside last July as a second instance of the street functioning as an unelected fourth branch of government, it’s worth asking the plainer question:

Did it actually work?

Or did it merely look, for one news cycle, like the same trick performed twice?

So:

A commander has been named, not installed.

A minister has been designated, not confirmed.

A dismissed reformer has been offered a consolation that isn’t the thing he was promised he’d get back.

A general who was supposedly eased out with civility hasn’t said he’s leaving.

Four sentences.

Four different tenses.

None of them finished.

## Public Service Announcement

2026-07-22 · I gave 700,000 words to Gemini.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8a549626-c762-408e-8d44-eaf2990bc5d7_1672x941.png)

A brief note to anyone arriving here for the first time: I plan to start corresponding with people again once I get over feeling guilty about not corresponding with people for the last several years.

Call it a Samsa moment. I went to sleep as someone who got away with pretending the rest of the world didn’t exist, and woke up as someone who could not.

For years, I have been trying to work out what to do with [ukraine@war](https://abdymok.substack.com).

It has grown into something rather larger than the website on which it appears: more than 1,700 posts, roughly 700,000 words, and twelve years of trying to make sense of what has happened in Ukraine, what I thought was happening at the time, and the way the war looks from Kyiv.

A normal archive lets you find things.

A search engine lets you search for things.

I wanted something that would let people ask questions of the archive.

Not just:

Find every mention of Fire Point.

But:

When did Fire Point first appear in ukraine@war, what did I think the company was doing at the time, and how did that understanding change over the following three years?

Or:

What did ukraine@war get right before it became conventional wisdom?

Or:

What has ukraine@war written about running long distances in Kyiv?[1](#footnote-1)

I did not expect a machine to notice that the running and the writing are the same argument.

So I donated the archive to Gemini.

Google has just renamed NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook. Apparently, the world did not yet have enough things called Gemini.

The archive itself is a separate PHP/MySQL project, built specifically for searching and interrogating the text of the posts. It isn’t simply this website with an AI bolted onto the side.

Run entirely through the browser—no FTP mucky-muck—it is intended to make it possible to interrogate the archive and quickly obtain detailed information about the war, the people and institutions involved in it, and the way all of this has looked from Kyiv.

**[INTERROGATE THE UKRAINE@WAR ARCHIVE](https://notebooklm.google.com/notebook/0c30d4e5-3bba-4d3c-a488-01ee2444e3bd).** It’s free. It’s fun!

The current archive covers the period from mid-2021 through the end of June 2026.

I have forgotten a great deal of what I wrote.

The words have not.

**What it’s supposed to do**

You can ask it to:

Find every prediction made in the archive about the future of the war. Which predictions were correct, which were wrong and which remain unresolved?

I am particularly interested in the last category.

It is always comforting to discover that one was neither right nor wrong.

One is merely awaiting further developments.

You can ask:

Which people, weapons, companies and ideas were once discussed frequently in ukraine@war but have since disappeared?

Or:

Find stories that seemed minor when they were written but later became historically important.

Or:

Which people first appeared as minor figures and later became important?

Or perhaps:

What is the central question ukraine@war has been trying to answer since 2014, even when the author did not know he was asking it?

You can ask what the archive says about the weather in Kyiv for the past five years.

**The experiment**

The point is not to ask the AI to summarize ukraine@war. That would be boring.

The point is to interrogate the archive.

Ask it what disappeared. Ask it what I got wrong. Ask it which arguments survived twelve years of war — and which ones should have been taken out behind the shed and quietly disposed of.

Go ahead. Ask it anything.

Ask it something you have always wondered about the war.

Ask it something you remember reading here years ago.

Ask it to find a person, an idea, a prediction or a story.

Then ask it what happened next.

And if you find something interesting, send it to me.

**There is one important thing to know about the archive.**

It does not have the photographs, maps, illustrations, screen grabs of leaked recordings, bad drawings or satellite imagery that accompany the posts.

And those are half the weight of the archive.

They have recorded what the war looked like from where I happened to be standing: Kyiv under attack, smoke on the horizon, blackouts, the metro, ruined buildings, soldiers, streets, sunsets, breakfasts and all the strange, stubborn fragments of ordinary life that continue even when Russia is trying very hard to make ordinary life impossible.

Many of the photographs have become wildly popular with readers.

Some have been viewed more often than the posts they accompanied.

The AI, at least, can tell you what I wrote about.

**Subscribers can see and hear what I’m talking about.**

If you are already a subscriber, thank you. You have helped keep *ukraine@war* alive—and helped finance the ongoing attempt to understand the horrible bloody mess we are all currently living through.

If you are not a subscriber, you are welcome to rummage through the archive.

If you enjoy the experiment, consider subscribing.

You will get the continuing dispatches.

You will get the photographs.

**And you will help keep me alive for whatever comes next.**

**[UKRAINE@WAR](https://abdymok.substack.com)**

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

I asked it that question myself, expecting a joke about mileage. Instead it came back with a small chart: the 6-minute mile as a running measure of maintained capacity, the anandamide sermons, shoes patched with bicycle brake pads and Hercul glue, a club with an unprintable name I invented purely as intimidation through radical honesty. It reached, unprompted, for something close to Popper — the running and the writing as one long experiment in conjecture and refutation, a way of finding out what a person is made of without an audience. It did not, however, produce maps of the running routes indicating where GPS spoofers are located in the capital.

## Day 1611

2026-07-23 · Lindsey and Laura

Funeral services for the late [Sen. Lindsey Graham](https://time.com/article/2026/07/12/the-world-pays-tribute-to-sen-lindsey-graham/) will take place on July 28 and 29 in both the nation’s capital and the Republican’s home state of South Carolina. Graham died on July 11 after a trip to Kyiv.

“I’ve never been more optimistic than I am today. We have a magic moment in time here.” - Lindsey Graham, [Kyiv](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o3n2mWvtOcA), July 10, 2026

Lindsey died coming back from Kyiv. Days later, Laura arrived by train. Ick.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/677ae768-73c3-4bd1-8c9e-09eb7efc4292_1535x1024.png)

They were the same species of Ukraine lover, just at opposite ends of the food chain — he supplied gravitas, [she pumped out selfies](https://united24media.com/war-in-ukraine/maga-commentator-laura-loomer-visits-kyiv-after-years-of-echoing-kremlin-narratives-what-changed-20990). Yesterday the deputy PM and deputy head of the president’s office [took her for a stroll](https://x.com/BerezhnaT/status/2080020056931442905) around Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.

Z might crash Lindsey’s funeral later this week at the Washington National Cathedral.

> “The arrangements have been complicated by the fact that so many global leaders would like to attend. And so the process of figuring out when the National Cathedral would be made available at the exact same time that the global leadership would want to come, and all the other national leaders who will be there, that has made it a little more difficult to get it done this week.” - South Carolina Senator Tim Scott (R), [The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/5980028-senator-graham-memorial-services/), July 17, 2026

Maybe Laura will hitch a ride back home with Ukraine’s president.

Lindsey and Laura were not chummy.

Graham called her “toxic” to her face, more or less — told a reporter last September that whatever policy disagreements existed, “the history of this person is just really toxic,” citing the incident where she’d suggested a political rival’s teenage daughter should hang herself. Loomer’s response was not measured. She spent the following days on X informing Graham he was “gay,” repeatedly, festively, as though it were an argument rather than an insult, and reminding her followers that he’d once been booed off a stage at a Trump rally in his own state — proof, in her taxonomy, of disloyalty rather than merely proof that South Carolina crowds get bored.

None of this makes her wrong about Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra being worth a stroll. It only makes it stranger that the deputy PM gave her the tour.

The through-line, for anyone who read the Times [profile](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/08/us/politics/laura-loomer-trump.html) from last summer, is that Loomer’s currency was never friendship — it was fear. She doesn’t do warmth. She does “scalps,” her own word for the officials she gets fired by being a heat-seaking missile for Trump’s ass. Graham was one of the very few Republicans willing to say the emperor’s new adviser had no clothes, and he paid for it in gay-panic memes rather than policy rebuttal, which tells you what register the argument was actually being fought in.

So no: not chummy. And a woman who plays, by her own account, for an audience of exactly one, is not going to make an exception for a man’s funeral just because he happened to die well.

---

On the war jacket, you can’t out-appoint a war this politically strangled.

In feudal Ukraine, when somone gets sacked, people first check whether it was fate or theft — and only much later, if ever, do they bother asking which. Watching [Bessmertny](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2g4ScSfV5C8&t=4728s) and [Butusov](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ho_H8qfkjA) work through the same week of upheaval — Z sacking Syrsky, sidelining Fedorov, installing Drapaty and Khmara — one senses two men circling the same goat, each certain the other has missed the horns.

Bessmertny plays the tragedian. For him this is theater with a hidden author. He walks the audience through Fedorov’s ultimatum — the minister refusing every consolation prize Bankova offered, insisting his goal was never simply to hold a ministerial title for its own sake — and reads it as proof that the real fight isn’t personnel, it’s power itself, with Andriy Yermak’s uninvited shadow stretching across a frontline command post where, by rights, a man under investigation has no business standing. Bessmertny keeps returning to Valeriy Zaluzhny’s [old warning](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/11/29/how-to-defeat-putin-and-build-a-better-ukraine/), unfashionable until now: **that no reshuffling of surnames fixes a war being choked by political meddling from Kyiv**.

Butusov is the accountant among the mystics. He wants ledgers, not omens. His sharpest insight is the coldest one: Hungary lifted its veto on the EUR 90 billion defense credit in May, and within weeks — before the money could touch a ministry account — the minister most likely to control its distribution was gone. Not exile as tragedy, in his telling, but exile as bookkeeping. He’s equally unsentimental about the army itself, noting that no after-action review was ever done on Syrsky’s tenure, no diagnosis handed to his successor — just a man swapped for a man, which he calls, not unkindly, a kind of messianism: the peasant faith that changing the icon changes the harvest. And he lands his real blow on procurement, describing tenders written so vaguely — “characteristics,” never brand or maker — that a single firm can absorb an order for 250,000 fiber-optic drone spools no single firm could actually spool, which he treats less as scandal than as the honest signature of the system’s design.

What both men arrive at, from opposite temperaments, is the same joke told two ways: a state that cannot explain its own decisions to itself will always look, from a distance, like either a conspiracy or a shakedown — and it is usually both, taking turns. Bessmertny hears the shadow footsteps of Yermak, Butusov hears the quieter click of a ledger closing early. Neither is wrong. In a house without walls, everyone claims to have heard the thief, because everyone did — they just heard him from different rooms.
