## Day 1612

2026-07-24 · From Heel to Toe

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/25b3ed9a-e6d1-437e-8554-f3ddd864c2cc_1402x1122.png)

A sketch of a photograph I took on the steps of my house near the western border of the Cherkasy region. In 2008? It was summer. I had just picked a bunch of berries and was sitting down for breakfast.

The piece of metal on the right is the heel of a broken scythe. I replaced it successfully later that morning.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/fb85a0b9-e90d-4d15-81b2-6bbc833e0ccd_1535x1025.png)  
*Kvotsovik (far left) is the heel and nosok (far right) is the toe.*

**Yesterday I wrote about Laura Loomer.**

*The hot-girls-wear-sunglasses-and-eat-shashlyk part of today’s post follows. The* [story](https://puck.news/laura-loomers-stunning-reversal-on-ukraine/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) *has, predictably, been covered by* [The Financial Times](https://archive.ph/QYzhM?utm_source=chatgpt.com) *as well, although* [Caolan](https://www.facebook.com/CaolanRobertson/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) *hasn't touched it yet.*

Today, I [read](https://x.com/petereharrell/status/2080365980841038103) that her conversion to the Ukrainian cause is “a powerful reminder of the importance of being open to engaging with people you might profoundly disagree with today.”

This is probably true.

It is also exactly the sort of thing I would now like to ask the [archive](https://notebooklm.google.com/notebook/0c30d4e5-3bba-4d3c-a488-01ee2444e3bd) about.

What did I write about Laura before she came around on Ukraine?

The answer, as it turns out, is nothing.

I had never written about Laura Loomer.

But I had written quite a lot about people who changed their minds—and about the difference between a change of position and a change of heart.

The archive reminded me that I had described *ukraine@war* as containing “wrong calls, dead ends, and positions later revised,” arguing that this is the only form of **epistemic accountability available to a writer**: leaving the record of what you once believed where somebody can find it later.

I contrasted this with institutional analysts who “systematically convert prior errors into subsequent authority.”

Ask the archive about the author of the *Financial Times* piece about Loomer.

It will bring him up.

Not because I wrote about Laura.

I didn’t.

But because I wrote about Miller’s earlier reporting, his later admissions about “the signs we missed,” and what I called his “autohagiography.”

The archive, in other words, had been thinking about Laura Loomer before I had ever heard of Laura Loomer.

Or rather: it had been thinking about the problem she now represents.

**When somebody changes a position, what exactly has changed?**

The conclusion?

The evidence?

The people they trust?

The political incentives?

**KonMari will sort everything out, eventually.**

Will Z visit America next week? I don’t know. After chatting up Laura, anything is possible.

## Day 1613

2026-07-25 · Rave on

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b9b8d107-71d7-4ed4-950f-9639864a41cc_1088x1445.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (July 25, 2026)*

Things no longer feel quite as static as they did a year ago.

That’s because it’s now a war against the rear — a war of rear-ends, Z’s and Laura’s, as it were.

The thought occurred to me this morning looking across the courtyard at a hollowed-out building advertising a film called Rave On, starring Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Laura Loomer, hanging from a crane hook above a doorway whose elevator hasn’t worked in years — the kind of image that makes you suspect the city itself is doing the editorializing.

Thanks to Laura, the war has also moved into MAGA world. The woman who not long ago told her audience that Ukraine was run by Nazis, then by jihadi apologists, and called its president more dictator than elected leader took the thirty-hour train from Poland — there is no other way in now — and came back with a cruddy film.

They deserve each other, frankly — two people who have never once let the facts on the ground interrupt a good performance.

She toured the ruins near the Lukyanivka McDonald’s, watched children walk dogs past a crater, and decided this wasn’t quite what she’d been told. Whether that’s conversion or good television remains disputed. One camp calls it edgelord diplomacy, a bid to outflank a rival influencer rather than a genuine change of heart. Caolan other shrugs and says a keyboard warrior humbled by an air raid beats one who never left the patio. Both are probably true at once, which is usually how these things go.

Ukraine’s real service to Washington was never sentimental. It was structural: a wall built and staffed at no cost to the country it was protecting, standing in the way of a specific ambition to reconstitute something like the old empire. That transaction, stated plainly rather than left to subtext, is the whole logic behind a rehabilitated MAGA influencer now doing more diplomatic work than that jackass Elbridge Colby.

Some of that work looked like this:

> **Loomer:** Would you be willing to sign a peace agreement with Russia in the Oval Office?
>
> **Z:** Yes, I’m ready. I’ve always told President Trump I’m ready to come to the United States, to the Oval Office, or to Mar-a-Lago. It depends on what you prefer.
>
> **Loomer:** That’s very beautiful. Have you ever been to Palm Beach?

A wartime president offers to fly anywhere to end a four-year war. The follow-up question is about the club.

Laura, for her part, was elsewhere entirely this morning — woken by a siren, heart racing, genuinely rattled, and moved to [post about it](https://x.com/LauraLoomer/status/2080787840376401963), eight hours before I took the photo: this can’t be healthy for anyone’s nervous system, every night, for years. Fair point, sincerely made, not a wrong one. It also happened several kilometers from a rooftop full of people demanding Z get his shit together. No sign she’d noticed that either.

By hour three she’d moved on to better news: the President had reposted her interview, and she was [thanking him for it](https://x.com/LauraLoomer/status/2080866141367419387), tucking in that the White House meeting was now set for July 28 — delivered with the brisk satisfaction of someone who’s just watched her own segment get picked up by the biggest possible viewer. Between the siren and the retweet, she does not appear to have slept, and does not appear to have needed to. The news cycle she’s starring in runs on a different clock from the one on the rooftop, and it was never going to pause for a placard.

At 10:02 a.m., Kyiv time — presumably we’re both in the same city — the picture underneath all this: the front itself is essentially frozen. Four years in, drones have made large infantry advances so costly that even a successful push barely registers. But the war didn’t stop. It moved — into a rear with no real edges: refineries, fuel depots, drone expo centers, shipping routes, the warehouses of the adversary’s biggest online retailer. A country can tell itself it isn’t really at war so long as the packages keep arriving; hitting the warehouse is also a way of making that point stick.

The other thread worth keeping is about advantages, and how thoroughly they’ve flipped. The larger side spent years perfecting exactly the tools that turned out not to matter here: mass, armor, manpower, the reassuring math of nine times the budget. By the time that machine reached full strength, the war had already relocated somewhere it couldn’t follow. What matters now is control of the layer that lets a drone be steered precisely — and there, the larger power spent two years simply borrowing its opponent’s satellite service, only building one of its own once that access was cut off.

The bigger side never had to solve its technological gap. It just kept paying to cover for it, the way a Soviet factory got refunded for output nobody bought. Ukraine never had that luxury — the absence of a safety net is what forced the drone-and-network war into existence in the first place.

The blitz failed. The slower grind it fell back on is failing too, since costs are climbing faster than the front is moving, with no sign of the other side hitting its limit first.

A settlement has even been sketched out loud, mostly as a thought experiment: Crimea formally ceded, everything else vacated, special status for the two contested provinces, some reparations from oil revenue, sanctions eased — generous enough that both sides could plausibly call it something other than defeat. But the one man who’d need to sign it is the least likely to. It would mean admitting, out loud, that the whole thing was a mistake he cannot afford to have made.

And underneath it all, the part that lingers: a Ukrainian president who can’t show strength at home travels abroad — to Washington, DC — to look for somewhere else to show it. While he was packing, several hundred people were gathering on the rooftop across from his own office, having given him until the end of the day to reverse a defense-ministry firing that struck most of them as inexplicable on any grounds except the usual ones. The dismissed minister had become inconveniently good at making procurement transparent. Whoever inherits the job will spend months just learning where the light switches are. The front does not have months.

Defense is not a normal cabinet post here. It controls a trillion-hryvnia budget, the entire pipeline of allied money and weapons, and the only formal mechanism by which a civilian can ask the military why it needs what it’s asking for. Replace the person holding that particular door and the question stops being asked for months — exactly the gap the war doesn’t currently have room for.

No tents were pitched. It’s a rolling ultimatum rather than an encampment. The going theory is that someone’s circle finds a functioning, well-connected minister harder to work around than a decorative one — and that partners abroad, the ones quietly slowing disbursements on contested loans, the ones who say only that they “don’t understand Z’s decision,” which in that dialect means they warned him beforehand and were ignored anyway.

The hope, presumably, was that Z’s trip to Washington would let the misunderstanding dissolve in his absence.

Placards reading SHAME don’t dissolve.

They wait.

## Day 1615

2026-07-27 · Quorum sensing

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/cd26650e-a002-4b2b-9754-19e7aa23daa9_1672x941.png)

We wrote at the start of running season this year about [parabiosis](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1454?utm_source=publication-search) — old blood and young blood sharing one circulatory system, the old mouse barely helped, the young one aged twice as fast.[1](#footnote-1) Putin the old mouse, Z the young one, the war the shared vein between them. That was the science of decline. There’s a companion science of assembly worth setting beside it.

A single bacterium can’t do much. It’s too small to matter, too weak to overwhelm anything on its own. What it can do is leak a little chemical into its surroundings and wait. More cells, more chemical, until the concentration crosses some threshold — and then, with no boss cell issuing orders, they all switch behavior at once. Toxins released in unison overwhelm an immune system that a lone bacterium never could. This is [quorum sensing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quorum_sensing): cells counting their neighbors by smell, and only acting once they know there are enough of them to matter.

It’s tempting to read the last two years this way. No single warehouse fire, no single refinery strike, changes anything — the ledger of the war doesn’t move on any one of them. What moves it is density: enough strikes, close enough together, and the rear stops absorbing the damage quietly and starts visibly buckling. Same logic on the other side of the ledger: no single influencer conversion, no single senator’s deathbed consistency, no single sanctions bill matters on its own. But enough of them clustered in the same six weeks — Loomer, [the comedian with the MAGA audience](https://apnews.com/article/laura-loomer-trump-ukraine-russia-interview-101852f6deab17e1d8d215fdde675ee5), Trump’s Truth Social post, the [Ossoff evisceration](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JMFw71IV5oQ) — and something that looked frozen for years quietly crosses a threshold and the tone in the room changes, the way it’s supposed to.

“Laura Loomer is doing a great job in Ukraine. Her interview with President Zelenskyy was very interesting and informative. She has really changed her mind on Ukraine, and I think that is a good thing. Congratulations Laura!” - Trump, [Truth Social](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/116972245395063508), July 23, 2026.

The uncomfortable part of the metaphor is the eavesdropping. Bacteria aren’t the only ones who count signals — the viruses that infect them do too, sitting dormant inside a host cell until they sense enough other hosts nearby to make it worth bursting out and killing this one. They wait for someone else’s quorum to ripen before cashing in on it. Watch who in this story seems to be doing that.

## Day 1616

2026-07-28 · Sit on my lap, I'll give you a ride

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/34380c2f-8b1c-4295-a452-e562ae6900f8_1536x1024.png)

I finished Sunday’s run after reaching the top of the hill, then walked about a kilometer back home — hair a mess, drenched in sweat, probably looking like I was about to pass out, the way I usually do after a long run in the heat. As I passed the hospital — which last year added a clinic to fit and install prostheses — I saw two in wheelchairs, both missing their left legs above the knee, rolling toward the adjacent Fora supermarket. One turned to me and said something I couldn’t hear because I was listening to music. Thinking he wanted help getting to the store, I pulled out my earbuds and asked, “What did you say? Do you need a push?”

“No,” he laughed. “I said sit on my lap and I’ll give *you* a ride.”

Two strangers who couldn’t hear each other over the noise still landed the joke together. We wrote yesterday about bacteria doing something similar — counting their neighbors by smell, waiting for the chemical concentration to cross some threshold before switching behavior all at once. Watch the last 48 hours. It happened again, and this time the signal wasn’t military. It was mood.

Kim Barker and Ken Bensinger, [in the Times this morning](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/28/world/europe/zelensky-trump-meeting-ukraine-war-russia.html), report the room has changed temperature: “**better chemistry now**,” an Odesa academic tells them, before both men fly to Washington for Tuesday’s meeting — Z also stopping for Lindsey Graham’s funeral, the senator having died hours after his last Kyiv visit. One analyst’s read is unsentimental: each man needs the other to validate himself at home. That’s not romance. That’s two organisms sensing the same threshold and deciding, independently, that it’s finally safe to bloom.

[Politico’s four-byline account](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/27/ukraine-is-embracing-maga-its-not-clear-if-maga-is-hugging-back-01013312) of the courtship is less romantic still — Loomer says it was Z who reached out to her, not the reverse, which makes the whole conversion look less like sensing and more like inoculation. Kurt Volker, who once ran U.S.-Ukraine negotiations for this same administration, gives the metaphor its cleanest gloss yet, calling Ankara’s tone “a signal to the MAGA world that it’s OK to support Ukraine.” A quorum, once declared, doesn’t need to be true. It just needs someone senior enough to announce that the threshold’s been crossed.

Everyone else seems to have smelled it too, on schedule. Terekh [tells the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/27/fire-point-ukraine-cruise-missiles-russia), on the record and in hard numbers, that Fire Point is back to a hundred Flamingos a month after the EU-lending pause — Cheboksary hit at over a thousand miles, refineries down a fifth, Patriot production worldwide barely covering two weeks of the Middle East’s appetite. Shtilerman [tells Gordon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S3nHlc1oP68) something wilder and unhedged: autumn strikes on Moscow, Wildberries and Ozon next, Russia’s whole geography curdled from asset to liability. Chervinsky, freshly un-silent after Fedorov, [tells a YouTube stream](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ch4LtOLbPJ4&t=3873s) that the war’s entire architecture — Yermak, Budanov, a compromised counterintelligence chief with in-laws in Urengoy — is one Russian-run body finally being smelled out by a public that’s counted enough corpses to cross its own threshold. Bezsmertny, [elsewhere](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mP0061bjMVM), smells oil money instead of treason: Chevron’s tanker complaint as the real agenda item in the Oval Office, dressed as diplomacy.

None of these five is talking to the others. None of their thresholds are the same chemical. And yet they’re all reporting the identical event — something has tipped — at exactly the moment the room in Washington also tips. That’s either confirmation the signal is real, or proof that a quorum, once it exists, gets smelled by everyone with a reason to smell it, true or not.

Which returns us to the eavesdroppers. A virus doesn’t create the quorum. It waits inside the host, dormant, until enough neighboring cells ripen for bursting to be worth it. Trump gets to look like a peacemaker without spending anything. Shtilerman gets to be the man Ukraine can’t do without, weeks after a corruption scandal nearly swallowed his own company whole. Loomer gets a redemption arc in a war zone. Yermak, if Chervinsky’s right, gets to keep running things from behind a curtain precisely because the public quorum is busy sensing Syrsky instead of him. Everyone here is a virus who found the concentration convenient.

On the war jacket: Russia fired 117 ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities this month, almost a monthly record, while all of the above was busy smelling chemistry in a different room.

## Day 1617

2026-07-29 · Keeping up appearances

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/e748bec9-b6ec-4c08-aaea-a6911c19a273_1086x1448.png)

In 1997 it was audits. Not indictments—audits. Tax inspectors, fire marshals, and sanitary inspectors would arrive at the same NGOs within days of one another, citing different regulations while serving the same political purpose. Lukashenko didn’t need to outlaw independent civil society. He only had to make compliance impossible and let bureaucracy accomplish what repression would have announced more loudly. We wrote about this then.¹

**The same administrative instinct is increasingly visible in Kyiv.**

Lukashenko’s real innovation wasn’t ideological. Belarus in the 1990s had very little ideology worth exporting. It was administrative. The important decisions quietly migrated out of institutions and into an informal circle around the president. Parliament continued to meet. Courts continued to function. Ministries continued to exist. Increasingly, however, they existed to formalize decisions already made elsewhere.

Bankova now operates in much the same way. The archive has documented the gradual transfer of authority into Z’s inner circle² and the parallel evolution of the security services into instruments of that circle rather than independent institutions.³ Parliament still votes. It mostly ratifies.

The legal mechanism differs, but the logic is familiar. Lukashenko used constitutional referendums to normalize permanent presidential authority. Ukraine doesn’t require referendums. War performs the same function. “Wartime necessity” has gradually replaced anti-corruption reform as the universal justification for concentrating power, while courts increasingly endorse those decisions rather than independently review them.⁴⁵

The institutions remain standing, but much of their load-bearing function has been removed. Independent oversight bodies need not be abolished if they can be weakened, restaffed, or deprived of meaningful authority. That is precisely what has happened to Ukraine’s anti-corruption architecture through the campaign against its agencies’ independence.⁶

The same migration is visible in procurement. Decisions that should pass through transparent institutions increasingly emerge from private networks instead. Multi-billion-dollar defense contracts are discussed in apartments rather than boardrooms. The roles now under investigation involving figures such as Mindich and Yermak illustrate how political authority migrates into relationships that exist largely outside formal accountability.⁷

The pattern extends to the press. Modern authoritarian systems rarely require overt censorship. Prior restraint is quieter and far more effective: legal pressure, confidential court orders, and informal warnings ensure that stories disappear before publication, leaving no visible act of censorship to protest. The tactics now facing investigative journalists in Kyiv bear a striking resemblance to those used against independent reporting in Minsk decades earlier.⁸

---

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8dcd6493-dd81-434b-a2f5-e77d19c936b5_1536x1024.png)  
*The photograph is about appearance. This post is about governance. (Photo c/o Z , July 28, 2026)*

---

Appearances matter. So do institutions. They are not always telling the same story.

Meanwhile, in Washington, Trump smiles beside Z. Sanctions advance. Republicans again speak openly about helping Ukraine win. Those developments matter. They may prove consequential.

They are also largely disconnected from the institutional trajectory inside Ukraine.

NABU. SAPO. Mindich. Yermak. Vova.

Those belong to a different conversation altogether.

One country. Two narratives. They increasingly pass one another without making contact.

Washington has understandable reasons for emphasizing battlefield success over constitutional architecture. Wars are measured in territory gained, sanctions imposed, weapons delivered, alliances reaffirmed. Institutions are slower. Administrative decay rarely photographs well.

That is what Belarus demonstrated three decades ago. Democratic backsliding seldom begins with tanks outside parliament. It begins when institutions continue to function in public while decisions quietly migrate elsewhere.

None of this requires Ukraine to imitate Belarus. Post-Soviet presidential systems drift toward the same equilibrium when institutions cease restraining power. Lukashenko justified it through constitutional engineering. Z justifies it through wartime necessity.

Keeping up appearances is easy. Keeping institutions independent is harder.

I was listening to Fedorov’s 96-minute exit interview for the second time at 2 in the morning, when no one yet knew the trajectory of the 50 or so cruise missiles crossing the border. *Vision. Plan. Structure.* Those words came up again and again. Antiballistics did not come up once — not even in passing — despite being the single word Z used most insistently [with Sky News the same week](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-HypRv9GHuI&t=23s), his one unambiguous ask of Washington and London. Yermak’s name surfaced, arms-lobby names surfaced — but 96 minutes in, nobody asked the one question that would have actually mattered:

Who is “Vova”?

Fedorov, for his part, offers his own tidy account of why he was really sacked — procurement reform, wounded interests, a system that couldn’t tolerate transparency. [It is not the account of Z,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-HypRv9GHuI&t=23s)  who stayed entirely upstream of all that: two institutions failing to coordinate, a president forced to choose. Two men, two stories, and neither one touches the name that would make either version legible.

Which reminds me of the disbandment of Det A.

Substack subscribers know that I’ve been following the “Lighting up the Battlefield” saga since before 1984, when Detachment A was [disbanded](https://detachment-a.org/), and at least as doggedly for the now [deactivated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymmetric_Warfare_Group) Asymmetric Warfare Group. It’s all been hush, hush, hush, but that’s why the story remains so interesting and relevant, now with crypto twists and beer from Lida. — [Day 41, Phase 2](https://abdymok.substack.com/publish/posts/detail/53500960/share-center?alreadyPublished=true). *Ruska Lozova op begins* (May 5, 2022)

On the war jacket, we’re sitting ducks.

I’ve updated the markdown file for 2026 posts and asked [Gemini](https://notebook.google.com/notebook/0c30d4e5-3bba-4d3c-a488-01ee2444e3bd) to forecast what we can expect.

**Strategic Forecast: Ukraine Operations and Political Stability (August–September 2026)**

**1. The Air Defense Gap: Urban Survival and Interceptor Attrition**

As of Q3 2026, the Ukrainian theater is defined by the critical exhaustion of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors. This inventory depletion has effectively created an unshielded environment for major urban centers, coinciding with the Russian Federation’s intensified deployment of high-velocity munitions.

**Technical Challenges of Hypersonic Interception** Operational data from early 2026 (Days 1416 and 1430) highlights the deployment of the Oreshnik IRBM and Zircon missiles. While source data suggests velocities of Mach 10 (erroneously cited as 13,000 km/sec), the strategic reality is a catastrophic compression of the ODA (Observe-Orient-Decide-Act) loop. Regardless of precise physics, these weapon systems exceed the engagement parameters of current Western defensive arrays. Consequently, “urbicide” has shifted from a kinetic byproduct to a population displacement tool, designed to force a winter exodus toward the European Union and strain the social cohesion of the remaining state structure.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b6f0a0dc-9deb-492c-bd4c-7548fb1e9dd4_605x557.png)

---

**2. Operational Trajectory: The “Autumn Strike” Campaign**

The strategic posture for late 2026 marks a transition from urban defensive survival to an offensive interdiction campaign. Following a 40-day influence operation, Kyiv has prioritized the systematic targeting of Russian logistics and the domestic energy sector to generate economic parity.

**Deep-Strike Capabilities and the “Flamingo” Project** The “Flamingo” cruise missile project, once dismissed as a non-viable resource drain, has been re-integrated as the centerpiece of indigenous deep-strike capability. By bypassing Western restrictions on weapon usage, the “Autumn Strike” seeks to establish an autonomous deterrent. The strategy recognizes that “Reflexive Control” is no longer mitigated by Western diplomatic “pauses”—such as President Trump’s failed one-week moratorium request—but only by credible kinetic threats to Russian revenue streams.

**Primary Objectives of the Autumn Strike Campaign**

- **Logistics Disruption:** Disabling railway junctions and transshipment hubs within the 100-200km zone to starve Russian front-line units during the high-demand seasonal transition.
- **Economic Asymmetry:** Focused strikes against Russian oil refineries and energy export infrastructure, intended to inflate the domestic cost of the war for the Kremlin.
- **Reflexive Control Mitigation:** Forcing the redeployment of Russian S-400 units from the front lines to protect internal industrial assets, thereby diluting Russian air superiority over the Donbas.

---

**3. Leadership Stability: The Drapaty-Khmara Administration**

The current military-political tandem of Commander-in-Chief (CiC) Drapaty and Defense Minister Khmara follows the failed interim appointments of Mykhailo Fedorov and Kyrylo Budanov. The Fedorov/Budanov shift was characterized as a “Kvartal 95” patronage attempt that collapsed under the weight of Budanov’s stained political record (Wagnergate) and institutional friction.

**Loyalty vs. Competence** The “Drapaty-Khmara” integration represents a retreat toward military traditionalism after the OP’s failed attempts to manage the battlefield via loyalist “silos.” Institutional stability remains compromised by “Strategic Autophagy”—the internal consumption of the state by entrenched corruption networks. The fallout from **Operation Midas** provides the most damning data: **$100 million** was siphoned through shell companies in Anguilla and the Seychelles via “The Professor” and “Karlsson” (Timur Mindich), while funds intended for the hardening of the Trypilska and CHP-5 power plants were diverted into commission structures.

**Institutional Assessment (Q3 2026):** The relationship between the Presidential Office (OP) and the military command is characterized by extreme siloing. Following the SBU raid on General Zaluzhny’s command center and his subsequent London exile, the military command has adopted a detached operational stance, insulating tactical decision-making from the OP’s narrative-driven interference.

---

**4. Geopolitical Fallout: The Trump-Z Dialogue and “Donnyland”**

The late-July dialogues between President Zelenskyy and President Trump resulted in the “Donnyland” proposal—a framework predicated on the exchange of Donbas territory for conditional security guarantees.

**The “Donnyland” Proposal: Stated Terms vs. Legal/Strategic Hurdles**

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/17aa82ab-c53f-47e2-9ba7-a1db55b0a944_601x410.png)

**Operational Risk:** Active combat and the destruction of the energy grid prevent large-scale resource extraction or ROI for US investors.

The “Trump Stalling Strategy” has treated Ukrainian sovereignty as a “timeshare presentation,” forcing European “variable geometry” coalitions to surge support. However, as the US executive branch describes the situation as “fluid” (referencing 72-hour negotiation windows), the actual kinetic environment remains static and lethal.

---

**5. Strategic Synthesis and Systemic Vulnerabilities**

Ukraine enters late 2026 as a “hollow structure.” The state maintains a polished diplomatic facade, but its load-bearing institutions—demographics, energy, and military command—are under terminal duress.

**Critical Systemic Risks**

- **Parabiosis of Conflict:** A systemic “parabiosis” has occurred where the old, toxic blood of the Putin regime is hollowing out the younger Ukrainian organism. Instead of rejuvenation, the shared circulatory system of a 13-year war has accelerated the decay of Ukrainian institutions.
- **Demographic Collapse:** National deaths exceed births by **2.9 times**. In contested regions, this ratio has cratered to **11:1**, threatening the long-term viability of the labor force and military reserve.
- **Energy Fragility:** The administration celebrates a “nine-megawatt victory”—a capacity gain worth less than a **Tesla Model 3 per hour (€765/hr)**. This is a PR substitute for the structural hardening lost to the Midas scandal.

**Final Assessment** External diplomats continue to apply a “Design Stance,” treating Ukraine as a system to be managed or a “72-hour fluid window.” This fails to account for the “Intentional Stance”—the agency and internal “Will to Fight” of the Ukrainian population. Observation is not intervention. The risk for late 2026 is that external “designers” will attempt to impose a settlement on a hollowed-out state, ignoring the reality that a corrupted interior cannot support a forced diplomatic ceiling.

## Day 1623

2026-08-04 · Redundancy, sold by a monopoly

The same week Ukraine’s ambassadors were told to start tracking Patriot stock levels in their host countries and moving interceptors off warehouse shelves, Denys Shtilerman published [an op-ed in The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/08/03/ukraine-shows-war-how-build-modern-defense-industry/) arguing that modern war punishes single points of failure — a single supplier, a single factory, a single political decision — and rewards redundant, networked, auditable ecosystems. He is right about the argument.

He is, at the moment, the least credible messenger available to make it.

Shtilerman is the founder of Fire Point, the company behind Ukraine’s FP-1 strike drones and the Flamingo cruise missile, and by his own account soon to be a manufacturer of ballistic-missile interceptors and a ballistic missile of its own. Fire Point is also the company that received roughly **billions ($)** in state contracts while operating, essentially, as Ukraine’s only domestic producer of long-range strike systems — the closest thing the war effort has to the single-manufacturer dependency Shtilerman spent his op-ed warning against. Ukraine’s Antimonopoly Committee has been asked, more than once, why that concentration was allowed to happen. Fire Point’s own chief technology officer has given contradictory answers about whether a proposed foreign partnership even passed antitrust review.

Then there is the matter of who almost bought half the company. Shtilerman told a parliamentary investigative commission in May that Z’s former business partner, Tymur Mindich — the sanctioned businessman at the center of the corruption case implicating the president and his top managers — negotiated for a fifty-percent stake in Fire Point from 2024 into 2025, with an offer eventually reaching a billion dollars. The deal collapsed, Shtilerman says, over his own insistence on “clean” financing and a legal firewall against toxic shareholders. Perhaps. The recordings that triggered the wider Mindich scandal include Mindich speaking to the then-defense minister, **Rustem Umerov**, in terms that anti-corruption investigators read as those of an owner discussing his asset, not a rejected suitor. Fire Point calls this a smear campaign by jealous competitors. It may also simply be the going register of Ukrainian defense procurement as we approach year 13 of the war.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8a6cd33d-5cf6-4e5d-891b-7acdf766d277_1562x1007.png)  
*Ukrainian rocket men: Denys Shtilerman and Rustem Umerov*

There is a third thread, pettier but not irrelevant: an aviation engineer testifying before the same commission called Fire Point’s claimed capacity — thousands of ballistic missiles a year — a technical absurdity, the kind of number that exists to secure the next contract rather than to describe an assembly line. And the Anti-Corruption Center (anTAC) has spent the spring pressing Shtilerman on an old Russian court filing under a different surname, seeking to restore a citizenship he says he no longer holds. None of this makes the Freyja consortium a bad idea. Distributed production, IP escrow, independent audit — the architecture Shtilerman describes in the Post is the correct answer to the Patriot shortage, and Europe is right to build it.

But the op-ed asks readers to trust the diagnosis of monopoly dependency from a man whose own company is the case study, and to admire the audit provisions of Freyja from a founder whose own books have become the subject of a parliamentary commission. Ukraine did not build a fast, adaptive defense industry by accident, as he says. It built one fast enough that nobody had time to ask who owned it until the money was already spent.

##### Addendum: the domino, not the design

Rustem Umerov appears in this story twice — as the defense minister Mindich allegedly courted on those recordings, and, as of this week, as the man Z has just installed atop foreign intelligence, where his stated brief includes closing drone deals. It’s worth asking how he got there, Spoiler: not by selection, but by elimination.

Trace it forward. Umerov left Defense, so Denys Shmyhal — the former prime minister, whose own removal from that post was never explained — was installed in his place. Shmyhal then had to be pulled out again to cover a hole at the Energy Ministry, so Mykhailo Fedorov, until then the digitalization minister and a Z loyalist of long standing, moved into Defense by default. When Fedorov’s arrangement with the Presidential Office or the military command stopped working, Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko was floated to replace him — until public reaction made that untenable, and Klymenko was rerouted instead to the now-vacant secretaryship of the security council. That left Umerov holding no portfolio at all, which is how a man just removed from one security post arrives at the top of foreign intelligence. Every step in the chain was forced by the step before it. None of it was chosen for the job it produced.

This is the same failure mode Shtilerman’s op-ed diagnoses in defense procurement, one level up. **A system with no bench, run by one point of trust, will keep producing exactly the kind of concentrated, unaccountable dependency he says Ukraine’s drone industry has learned to avoid.** It hasn’t avoided it. It has simply relocated it — from a single company to a single man, currently sitting in the chair from which Fire Point’s own patron once tried to buy his way into ownership.

## Day 1624

2026-08-05 · I stumbled on Lukashenko

More than a dozen dead, scores wounded, in Kyiv and the surrounding region this morning.

On Saturday I wrote that the capital’s residents had become sitting ducks[1](#footnote-1).

Nobody needed today’s attack to confirm it—least of all Z and his senior managers, who will again tell us:

“*Well, we don’t have enough Patriot missiles, so what can we do? Everyone’s on their own now. Things are going to be bad.”*

To me, that’s a sign of incompetence, unprofessionalism, and an unwillingness to do anything.

Picture water coming through the ceiling. Option A: empty the bucket, faster than the water fills it, for as long as you can stand there. Option B: go upstairs and turn off the tap. Ukraine currently owns several excellent buckets, refuses to go upstairs, and calls the resulting posture a strategy.

The Iskander systems and the other launchers firing at us sit close to the border, in fixed and known positions. Nothing prevents striking them—not distance, not a shortage of means. Drones will do it. The same Flamingo F5 missiles built to hit Moscow work equally well pointed at a launch site forty kilometers from Kharkiv.

No launch battery can be guarded everywhere, all the time, with total security. There are several ways to reduce the number of ballistic missiles reaching this Kyiv. All of them share a premise: if the missile cannot be caught in flight, it must never leave the ground. That premise requires a system, a plan, and people whose job is to execute it rather than complain about not having enough interceptors.

Yesterday's meeting between Lukashenko and his flunkies, discussing the creation of an "academy of the future," grabbed my attention for the same reason. It is the same style of governance long practiced in Moscow, and increasingly here. Like Belarus and Russia, Ukraine has no independent parliament and no functioning judiciary, and independent media have been largely marginalized—Z doesn't take questions from them either. The result, in both capitals, is ritualized obeisance, Telegram bot armies, and the kind of cringing sycophancy on display in the video clip below. A government staffed by people whose job is agreement doesn't just fail to go upstairs and find the tap. It stops being able to conceive that upstairs exists.

**EXCLUSIVE:** [Fire Point targets first interception by mid-2027.](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukraines-fire-point-starts-integrate-european-tech-into-missile-defence-system-2026-08-04/)

Really? At least we’re no longer looking at PowerPoint slides.

Ten months is an abstraction until you sit with what’s happening in the meantime. Kyiv no longer enjoys anything resembling dependable protection against ballistic missiles. The sirens, when they sound at all, increasingly go off after the explosions, because a ballistic missile’s flight time is shorter than the interval needed to detect it and push a warning to your phone. The advice that circulates, when officials bother to give any, amounts to this: be fast. Keep your shelter route memorized. Physical fitness is, for now, a substitute for air defense.

This is the texture of the “winter humanitarian crisis” Z himself has been warning about—a phrase that sounds like boilerplate until you notice Russian strikes are landing on energy and logistics infrastructure roughly every two or three days, aimed at leaving Ukrainians without heat and light before the cold sets in. It is also, not incidentally, the backdrop to Z’s own offer to negotiate an energy truce directly with Putin: not a sign of confidence, but a request for time the missiles aren’t giving him.

The numbers bear this out district by district. Compiled from Kyiv Military State Administration/Kyiv City State Administration Telegram channels and open-source reporting, recorded strike hits across Kyiv since February 24, 2022 range from 38 in Pecherskyi to 104 in Shevchenkivsky—and in most districts, a disproportionate share of that total has landed in the last two years alone.

None of this is happening because the danger is ambiguous. It is happening in plain view, on television, discussed by talk-show hosts and their guests with the flat fluency of people describing weather. That fluency is its own symptom: when the discussion of no available interceptors settles into the same register as advice about running shoes, the sycophancy described above has done its work twice over—once on the institutions, and once on how ordinary catastrophe gets talked about.

Which brings us back to Minsk. Lukashenko’s “academy of the future” is a small, almost decorative example of the same disease—officials competing to flatter a man who has already decided what he wants to hear, in a room where no one present has the standing, or the nerve, to tell him otherwise. Kyiv’s version is less cartoonish but not structurally different. It just wears black miltech pajamas and calls itself wartime necessity.

Fire Point sits slightly outside this culture of political theater, which is precisely why it's worth paying attention to. (Reuters reported August 4 that Fire Point has begun integrating European tech into its missile defense system—reason enough to withhold judgment on the company for now, rather than take the announcement at face value)[2](#footnote-2).

An interceptor either works or it doesn’t. It won’t be moved by a flattering seating chart, and it can’t be summoned into existence by a presidential administration deciding not to take questions. If Ukraine gets through this winter, it will be despite the governing style described above, not because of it—on the strength of engineers who answer to physics rather than to Bankova, working against a deadline that has nothing to do with anyone’s approval ratings.

The state doesn’t need to lie to you outright. It only needs to keep handing you small, dignified rituals to perform—running drills, positive symptoms, academies of the future—while the actual protection against the actual threat remains however many months away it will turn out to be once this deadline, too, has come and gone.

In the meantime, be fast, keep your shelter route memorized, and try not to notice how familiar all of this has started to feel.

## Day 1625

2026-08-06 · The remainder

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/cf5b25e0-15ad-437b-aada-3e8ef53a764d_1536x1024.png)

Yesterday's post put words in Z's mouth before he'd said them: no interceptors, everyone's on their own, things will be bad. It looked like a rhetorical flourish. A few hours later it became the headline.¹

### [Ukraine fails to halt Russian barrage as Z blames partners for ‘horrific casualties’](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/08/05/ukraine-fails-stop-russian-missile-barrage-after-zelensky-says-interceptors-gone/)

*U.S.-made systems are Kyiv’s only means to shoot down ballistic missiles, and Ukraine says it has run out of interceptors. Seventeen Ukrainians died overnight. - [The Washington Post](http://wapo.com), August 6, 2026*

Z’s actual language, after the August 1 strike, was that partners needed to understand anti-ballistic systems aren’t meant to sit in warehouses. By evening he was demanding “real answers” to what he called Russian terror. Four days later nothing had changed except the casualty count. Yesterday’s barrage killed seventeen and wounded dozens. Kyiv’s depleted air defenses failed to stop a single incoming missile, and Z went back to Telegram to blame everyone except the people whose job it is to prepare for exactly this.

The appeal abroad has become the policy. Everything else now follows it around carrying the bags.

Kyiv did not become collateral in the forty-day campaign by accident, and it did not become collateral without warning. The cost of answering escalation with escalation was calculable before the campaign began because Russia had very few ways left to raise the stakes. One of them was always obvious.

Russia banks part of its ballistic inventory for winter. It still intends to freeze Ukraine again, and that requires a reserve. The missiles left over are divided between military targets and Kyiv. Kyiv is the one asymmetric answer available to a country that cannot yet strike Russia in kind with ballistic weapons. This isn’t mysterious. It’s bookkeeping. Kyiv is simply where the remainder gets entered.

The problem was never dependence on partners. The problem was turning the partners’ delivery schedule into the strategy instead of treating it as something a strategy should gradually make less decisive.

What’s worth noticing isn’t that Z repeats himself. Politicians do that. It’s that responsibility keeps migrating away from him.

On Monday, before this latest strike, he was talking about seventeen companies exploiting sanctions loopholes to keep producing the missiles landing in Kyiv. That is a real problem. It is also an unusually convenient one because sanctions are enforced by somebody else’s government in somebody else’s capital. Trump, meanwhile, had spent the previous week retreating from his own promise on domestic Patriot production, providing another convenient somebody else right on cue.

There is another story running underneath this one, and it is aimed not at foreign governments but at Ukrainians.

Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries and logistics are presented as precise military operations bringing peace closer. Russia’s strikes on Ukraine are presented as something that exists outside cause and effect, as though describing them as retaliation would somehow justify them. Both stories lean in the same direction. Ukrainian strikes are real. Russian strikes are real. Both shape the battlefield. Both alter the next day’s decisions.

Yet a population that increasingly wants the war to end is being sold not the end of the war but its next chapter, wrapped in the language of peace.

None of this requires unusual insight. It requires only paying attention to four years of these posts,² where every major strike follows the same sequence: casualties, appeal abroad, responsibility reassigned to whoever is least able to answer back.

A pattern this stable isn’t prediction. It’s arithmetic. You don’t predict the answer to two plus two.

You already know it.

Nobody upstairs has gone to turn off the tap.

Zero of the missiles fired at Kyiv on Wednesday were intercepted. On Saturday it was one out of twenty-seven.

Progress, if you’re grading on the wrong curve.

The same abdication scales down as easily as it scales up. In Kherson, Russian drone operators have spent weeks hunting civilians one at a time, a slower and more personal cruelty than a ballistic barrage but the same permission structure underneath it — nobody upstream decided [this](https://archive.ph/8JtWx#selection-613.0-898.0) was worth stopping, so somebody with a drone and no oversight decided what came next.

## Day 1629

2026-08-10 · Why Umerov keeps getting promoted

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4b32d3d7-b089-4e5e-a7d2-dadc7fd1182f_1536x1024.png)  
*Glasses are fixed. UAH 600, the equivalent of about $13.*

We wrote about the consolidation of Ukraine’s ultra-competitive arms-procurement system under the Office of the President — via Rustem Umerov — in the last days of January 2025, Day 1060-something of this newsletter, right around the time Donald installed Pete and announced the dawn of a new Golden Age of America. That was the same year Fire Point, the murky missile-and-drone manufacturer, began pulling in the billions it was given to build Ukraine a domestic ballistic-missile system. Eighteen months on, the Atlantic filed two dispatches on Ukraine within forty-eight hours of each other last week, and between them they managed to describe two different countries, neither of which mentions Umerov, Zhumadilov, or Fire Point by name. Michael Weiss’s was [the “model ally”](https://www.theatlantic.com/international/2026/08/ukraine-ally-trump-patriot-missile/688226/) — ten million drones a year against America’s hundred thousand, oil terminals burning in Siberia, a CIA director charming Trump on the golf course with casualty figures, a Patriot license practically signed. [Missy Ryan and Simon Shuster’s](https://www.theatlantic.com/national-security/2026/08/ukraine-war-zelensky-trump/688203/), filed two days earlier, was the retraction nobody announced as a retraction: the license quietly walked back, the Starlink favor still refused, a defense minister fired to street protests, an ambassador resigned and then charged with enrichment. Both pieces are competently reported. Neither one is wrong, exactly. But read together they describe a correspondent corps still filing on the assumption that the war is a story about what Washington decides to give Kyiv, when the more interesting story — the one we’ve been tracking since those last days of January 2025, and the one that actually explains why ministers get fired and who gets promoted afterward — is happening entirely inside Bankova, in a language the Atlantic doesn’t file dispatches in.

By any Western accounting Umerov should be a liability by now. He left the defense ministry trailing his own procurement scandals on top of Reznikov’s — nine-hryvnia eggs, mysterious NABU wiretaps, a starring role in the Mindich tapes. By the logic of “model ally,” a man like this gets quietly retired. Instead he has been floated for Washington ambassador, installed as secretary of the RNBO — Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council, the body that coordinates the war effort across the security services — and is now running Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, having never produced a day of intelligence work in his life. The Atlantic doesn’t ask why. We do, and the dates, once you lay them out, tell you the answer is not really a scandal — it’s a job description.

On January 23, 2025, the supervisory board of the Defense Procurement Agency — the body built after Reznikov specifically to take weapons purchasing out of the minister’s hands — voted unanimously to extend the contract of its director, Maryna Bezrukova, an anti-corruption reformer who’d cut intermediary involvement in arms deals from eighty-two percent to twelve. Umerov overruled the board the next day, January 24, refusing to renew her contract and, in the same order, dismissing the two state representatives who’d voted for her — Taras Chmut of the Come Back Alive foundation and Yuriy Dzhyhyr, a former deputy finance minister — for the crime of ignoring the ministry’s preference. He named Arsen Zhumadilov, then head of the separate non-lethal procurement body, as her replacement. NABU opened a criminal probe into Umerov on January 28 for abuse of office. It went nowhere, as these things do. By March 6 Zhumadilov held the DPA seat formally.

The merger is the part that matters more than the purge. Umerov had been pushing since 2024 to fold the two procurement agencies — lethal and non-lethal, roughly a trillion hryvnia a year between them — into a single body under Zhumadilov, over NATO’s own objections that consolidation should wait until after the war. He didn’t live to finish it in office: it was his successor, Denys Shmyhal, who announced on December 3, 2025 that the merger would take effect January 1, 2026, and it did. But Zhumadilov ran the reorganization commission throughout, under both ministers, and Zhumadilov is Umerov’s man. The upshot is that the entire architecture of Ukrainian arms procurement — everything the state buys, lethal and otherwise — now sits inside one agency, run by one loyalist, installed by the minister who broke the law to install him and kept there by the one who followed. Whoever holds the title of defense minister, or RNBO secretary, or head of foreign intelligence, the purchasing itself answers to the same chain regardless. That’s what the promotions were for.

That is the entire Umerov story, and it is also the entire Ukrainian governance story, the one I’ve been filing from this address since long before the war made it fashionable to notice: institutions here are not weak so much as provisional, tolerated only until someone with the president’s ear decides they’re inconvenient, at which point they’re merged, gutted, or handed to a loyalist. Umerov isn’t surviving corruption allegations. He’s being promoted for having ended an experiment in independent oversight and delivered its remains to Bankova gift-wrapped. Loyalty, not competence, is the currency — a Ukrainian commentator said as much bluntly this week, and he wasn’t being cynical, he was describing the org chart.

The same week’s talk-show circuit filled in the rest of the reshuffle in similar terms. Davyd Arakhamia is accused, on leaked NABU audio, of running financed cells of ten to fifteen loyal MPs inside his own faction. Yermak’s circle — Vereshchuk, Shurma, Smirnov, Tatarov — gets described not as corrupt so much as constitutionally foreign, “little Russians” building, in one host’s phrase, a small Russia inside Ukraine while Putin builds the large one; the charge is credited, with visible relish, to Oleksiy Arestovych, which ought to tell you something about the durability of anyone’s reputation here.

We worked out the mechanics of the reshuffle itself [last week](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1623), and it’s worth restating because nobody else has bothered to trace it. Umerov left Defense, so Denys Shmyhal — the former prime minister, whose own ouster from that post was never explained — was installed in his place. Shmyhal then had to be pulled back out to cover a hole at Energy, so Fedorov, until then the digitalization minister, moved into Defense by default. When Fedorov’s arrangement with the Presidential Office stopped working, Klymenko was floated to replace him at Defense — until the street protests made that toxic, and Klymenko got rerouted instead to the vacant RNBO secretaryship. That left Umerov holding no portfolio at all, which is how a man just removed from one security post arrives running foreign intelligence. Every step was forced by the one before it. Nobody chose Umerov for that chair; elimination did.

There’s a further irony worth pulling forward, courtesy of Denys Shtilerman, founder of Fire Point, the drone-and-missile manufacturer that has absorbed most of the money once destined for a Ukrainian Patriot analog. Shtilerman published [an op-ed in the Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/08/03/ukraine-shows-war-how-build-modern-defense-industry/) arguing that modern war punishes single points of failure and rewards redundant, auditable supply chains — a fair argument, undercut by the fact that his own company is the closest thing this war has to the dependency he was warning about, and that Tymur Mindich, the sanctioned businessman at the center of the president’s own corruption case, reportedly spent 2024 and into 2025 trying to buy half of it, with recordings that read, to investigators, less like a rejected suitor than an owner discussing his asset. Umerov surfaces there too, on the other end of those calls, back when he still ran Defense. The reshuffle and the procurement story are not two separate scandals. They’re the same failure mode at two altitudes: a system built, on paper, for redundancy — competing agencies, supervisory boards, alternate ministers waiting in the wings — that keeps collapsing back onto a single point of trust, whether that point is a company or a man.

None of this is verified to Atlantic standards, and some of it — the ethnography of Yermak’s inner circle especially — tells you more about the domestic opposition’s own instincts than about the men it describes. But it explains the mechanism where Weiss and even Ryan and Shuster only describe the weather. “Model ally” is a real category, and Ukraine has earned a version of it on the battlefield, with drones and Delta and the Highway of Death. It is not a category that extends to Bankova’s cadre policy, which still runs on the oldest rule in this country’s politics — the one the Soviets called krysha, the roof: you don’t ask whether the tenant is honest, you ask who’s covering him. Umerov built Bankova a roof over its own procurement. That’s the whole appointment.

## Day 1630

2026-08-11 · Who is in charge?

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/704cd7b9-d44e-4fed-b1c3-ffdf827d6879_1536x1024.png)

The interesting thing about four recent conversations on Ukraine is not what they say about the war. It is what they say about who is actually building the country that fights it.

Fiona Hill supplies the thesis, in passing, on a Prof G Pod episode with Anne Applebaum.[1](#user-content-fn-1) Ukraine’s wartime innovation, she says, comes from society compensating for a state notorious for cycling through corrupt or incompetent leadership. The state doesn’t fix itself. Society routes around it. Call this what it is: not resilience, the character trait Western commentary likes to award small brave nations, but a structural fact. The state is the part of the building that keeps failing inspection. People stopped waiting for the repair.

Radek Sikorski, on The Long Game, checks how far the compensation has gone.[2](#user-content-fn-2) He hedges properly — a draw at sea, a draw in the air, ground still contested — but the claim underneath the hedging is that Ukraine now inflicts losses faster than Russia can replace them, and that Gulf states court Ukrainian drone expertise rather than the reverse. A state that had actually organized this would be taking the credit. It didn’t, and isn’t.

Illya Sekirin explains the mechanism.[3](#user-content-fn-3) Something near ninety-five percent of casualties and matériel losses now come from drones, which has inverted the old arithmetic of offense and defense. Soldiers hold one foxhole for fifty, a hundred days, resupplied by ground robot instead of convoy. None of it was ministry work. Hundreds of small companies and units built it faster than anyone assigned to coordinate them could keep up.

Which is the altitude of Yuriy Lutsenko, talking to Ihor Lapin the night before last.[4](#user-content-fn-4) His story predates the invasion by three years. It’s the origin document for everything above it.

Summer 2019. Lutsenko, a few months into Z’s presidency, still prosecutor general, is summoned over the fate of Volodymyr Tsemakh — the separatist commander in custody as the one material witness willing to place a regular Russian officer at the MH17 launch site, at a moment when Europe still doubted Moscow’s direct hand in it. Moscow wants him back. Lutsenko refuses to sign off. He’s told, more or less, that his job is one phone call from someone else’s. He doesn’t preempt it by resigning. The cabinet is reshuffled at the end of August, he’s out, and within the week Tsemakh is on a plane to Russia as part of the exchange.

It’s also where he first meets the aide at Z’s shoulder — not yet head of the President’s Office, just a young man with opinions about why Ukraine doesn’t need Europe and should deal directly with Moscow. Lutsenko tells him that kind of talk put Yanukovych on a plane out of the country. The aide is Andriy Yermak.

Seven years on — five of them under full-scale invasion — Ukraine has built an entire war economy on the lesson of that room: the state will trade away its own witness for comfort with Moscow, so don’t build anything load-bearing that depends on the state behaving otherwise. Drones are what that lesson produced. They are cheap, dispersed, replaceable, and owned by nobody the state can discipline into cutting a deal.

Which is exactly what nags at me lately, watching Fire Point market Freyja. You cannot crowdsource a ballistic missile shield. The whole model that produced Ukrainian drone supremacy — thousands of small actors, no single point of failure, nothing important enough to trade away in a back room — is structurally the wrong model for interception. Interceptors need integration: shared radar, a command architecture, guidance seekers sourced from German manufacturers on their timeline, not Ukraine’s. Fire Point’s own numbers say the first successful intercept is scheduled for mid-2027, and the company has had to publicly deny, this month, that it can “close the skies” by any date sooner.[5](#user-content-fn-5) That denial is itself worth sitting with. It means someone upstream found it useful to let people believe otherwise, for a while.

The society-compensates-for-the-state model works when the thing being built is small, distributed, and forgiving of individual failure. A drone that gets shot down is a bad Tuesday. An antiballistic missile shield that doesn’t exist yet, marketed as though it might, is a state deciding what its people are owed the truth about, and choosing comfort instead.

---

1. Anne Applebaum and Fiona Hill, on [The Prof G Pod with Scott Galloway](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nto5huujAhA).
2. Radek Sikorski, with Jake Sullivan and John Finer, on [The Long Game](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IYDfiio-hhg).
3. Illya Sekirin, with Dominik, on [drone warfare](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDD6cvHhNeU).
4. Yuriy Lutsenko and Ihor Lapin, on [Lapin from Ukraine](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QgTeHCF-axk).
5. On the Fire Point/Freyja timeline and messaging, see [reporting flagged here](https://x.com/front_ukrainian/status/2085328642809245891), confirmed independently by RBC-Ukraine and UA.News coverage of Fire Point’s mid-2027 first-intercept target and its denial of “close the skies” claims.

## Day 1631

2026-08-12 · Russia fires, Ukraine counts (and vice versa)

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/bfb21861-4362-42f6-810d-946165c4d5e5_1672x941.png)

At 05:53 this morning, Telegram lit up: “Two Zircons in the direction of Kyiv.” Two more Russian missiles headed our way before most of us had found our glasses.

Night became morning the way it has for months now — the internet thick with messages insisting that incoming projectiles had [disappeared over Chernihiv region](https://t.me/c/2004671103/74673).

Maybe.

After four and a half years of full-blown war, [the arithmetic is getting hard to ignore](https://apnews.com/projects/russia-ukraine-war-striking-russia-cards/).

Russia is leaning harder on ballistic missiles. In July, according to Ukrainian Air Force data cited by the [ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data)](https://acleddata.com/monitor/ukraine-conflict-monitor), Russia fired 198 of them at Ukrainian targets — a record monthly barrage. Ukrainian officials and Western analysts put Moscow’s production capacity at roughly 70 ballistic missiles a month.

Ukraine’s problem was never knowing what’s coming. It’s having something that can stop it.

Patriot remains Ukraine’s only reliably effective defence against ballistic missiles, and its stock of PAC-3 interceptors is dangerously low. The July 6 attack made the problem brutal and literal: Ukraine’s air defences intercepted none of the 23 ballistic missiles launched that night[1](#footnote-1).

Russia isn’t being subtle about targets — kindergartens, hospitals, transport hubs, energy and water infrastructure. It wants to make the country unlivable. Kyiv is the test case.

The West has known this for a while. [The Financial Times](https://archive.ph/HscUr#selection-1431.0-1857.284) is now arguing that Europe needs to hand over more Patriot interceptors, speed up SAMP/T NG deliveries, and expand production — and that longer term, Ukraine and its allies should bring defence start-ups into the business of building cheaper interceptors.

All sensible. There’s a catch.

Ukraine has learned to build a remarkable amount without the state — drones, boats, software, electronic warfare, ground robots. The genius of that system is its fragmentation: thousands of small actors experimenting, failing, adapting, trying again.

Antiballistic missiles defense doesn’t work that way.

You can crowdsource the missile. You cannot crowdsource the Ka-band radar seeker. A ballistic shield needs radar, tracking, command architecture, communications, guidance, seekers, launchers, software — and enough interceptors to make the arithmetic hold.

Ukraine is building its own answer in Freyja. Good luck.

Until then, the arithmetic stays what it is. Russia fires. Ukraine counts. And Kyiv waits to see which number runs out first — the missiles in Russia’s magazine, or the interceptors in ours.

You can route around a broken state. You cannot route around a ballistic missile.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

[Day 1594](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1596). *Durable until Tuesday* (July 7, 2026)

## Day 1632

2026-08-13 · Plumbing with epistles

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/3cb0dba7-1542-4850-9545-f1eb1b76c6af_1402x1122.png)  
*CNN , August 12, 2026*

Every civilization without a written account of its own beginnings invented one. Myths of origin are not lies. They are what grows where evidence should be. We still do this. We have historians now, and journalists, and podcast hosts with ring lights. The evidence is not scarce. The myth wins anyway.

Z has become an origin myth with unusually good video coverage.

Politician, wartime leader, hero, symbol. At each stage the man loses a little and the sentiment gains it. By the symbol stage you are not describing a person. You are maintaining an installation. The maintenance crew gets nervous when someone points at the plumbing.

Twenty-five narrators, five trades: witnesses, interpreters, celebrities, insiders, legitimizers. I saw him. I know what it means. Feel this. I knew him from inside. He belongs among statesmen. None of them need agree. None of them need know each other. The jobs converge on the same figure without coordination, the way ants build a structure none of them designed.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8df80a19-2eb7-4e46-943f-06275e336c71_1536x1024.png)

Almost all of them are foreigners. Two exceptions: Yuliia Mendel, Oleksiy Arestovych. The Ukrainian journalists who cover Z tend to be less comfortable in his presence than that. Yuriy Butusov’s 2021 quarrel with him is the specimen to keep on the shelf: no heroic interpretation offered, just a politician being made to answer for himself.

The foreign narrator meets the symbol. The Ukrainian journalist meets the administration. Symbols have one advantage administrations don’t: they never have to explain themselves.

Here is the mechanism, caught mid-operation. An outside expert is asked about the latest defense minister fired amid corruption allegations. The answer arrives in two parts. Part one: Z inherited a system rotten with Soviet residue, didn’t build it, has spent the war managing it. Fine. Part two: Z protects the rot and removes whoever threatens it. These cannot both be true at full strength. If the rot explains the firing, Z is a man fighting the system. If Z’s choice explains the firing, the rot stopped being the subject three sentences ago. Nobody notices the furniture has moved.

That’s what myth is for. It absorbs contradictions that would break an ordinary argument. The payment comes in the oldest currency there is: absolve the founder, blame the rot. The rot is ancient, structural, Soviet, someone else’s fault by definition. The founder stays exceptional. What goes missing is the one specific Tuesday when one specific man made one specific decision.

Patterns are less trouble than myths. Watch what happens when a subordinate gets a source of power that doesn’t run through the Presidential Office. Zaluzhny. Fedorov. Whoever’s next. No curse required. Just attention.

The machinery that turns a wartime president into a symbol was never his alone. It belongs to everyone standing around him with a camera or a memoir contract, narrating him upward, one testimonial at a time, until the symbol is finished and they’ve become its unpaid staff.

Spend enough time maintaining a symbol and the plumbing starts to look like sabotage.

## Day 1633

2026-08-14 · Funny numbers

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c2171123-225b-4722-b502-7a7ee24187c9_1672x941.png)  
*The 8th floor balcony*

Ukraine has a funny way with numbers.

America does too.

The trouble begins when the two countries use the same number to describe entirely different things.

Ukraine, according to Z, has about 1 percent of the ballistic-missile interceptors it needs.

The United States, he says, could give Ukraine 5 percent of its Patriot missiles. Or perhaps 10 percent.

Five percent sounds like a lot more than one percent. It isn’t necessarily.

The great thing about percentages is that they are meaningless without a denominator.

And the denominators in this case are doing almost all the work.

Ukraine’s number is:

`Ukraine’s missiles ÷ Ukraine’s requirement = 1%`

America’s number is:

`U.S. contribution ÷ U.S. stockpile = 5% or 10%`

Those numbers cannot simply be added together, compared side by side, or turned into some reassuring calculation about how much closer Ukraine is to solving its air-defense problem.

They are funny numbers.

Consider the Patriot arithmetic.

A Russian attack involving 20 to 30 ballistic missiles is not an especially large Russian missile attack by the standards of the war. But if the assumption is that two PAC-3 interceptors are required for every ballistic missile, then the arithmetic becomes rather less funny.

Twenty ballistic missiles require 40 interceptors.

Thirty ballistic missiles require 60.

At approximately $4 million per PAC-3 MSE interceptor, that gives us:

`40 × $4 million = $160 million`

and

`60 × $4 million = $240 million.`

So, under those assumptions, defending against one such attack costs somewhere between $160 million and $240 million in interceptors alone.

One night.

One attack.

And that is before we start counting launchers, radar, command-and-control, personnel, maintenance, reloads, logistics and everything else required to make a Patriot battery actually function.

This is the arithmetic that tends to disappear when politicians start talking about percentages.

Because now comes the interesting question.

What exactly does America’s 5 percent mean?

Five percent of what?

Five percent of the missiles the United States currently has available for transfer?

Five percent of the American stockpile?

Five percent of some larger inventory that includes missiles that are already committed, deployed, reserved for other contingencies, awaiting refurbishment or otherwise unavailable?

And what does 10 percent mean?

Ten percent of the same thing?

Or ten percent of something else?

Without the denominator, the number is political decoration.

And there is another number floating around: Ukraine’s 1 percent.

One percent of what?

According to the formulation, it is one percent of what Ukraine says it needs.

That is a completely different proposition.

If Ukraine says it needs 1,000 interceptors and possesses 10, then Ukraine has 1 percent of its requirement.

If America has 1,000 missiles and gives Ukraine 50, America has given Ukraine 5 percent of its stockpile.

Ukraine could therefore go from 1 percent of its requirement to 6 percent of its requirement — if those 50 missiles were actually suitable for the requirement being discussed.

Or it could go to 5 percent.

Or 3 percent.

Or something else.

It depends on the denominator.

This is not a pedantic point. It is the entire point.

Funny numbers are not a bug in Ukrainian politics. They are a feature.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/8465ba7e-2728-4173-98fa-beb6fa8c1010_1672x940.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (August 14, 2026)*

Governments here have long understood that a number sounds like a fact the moment someone reads it aloud with enough confidence. A minister stands up, recites a column of figures, and the figures acquire the appearance of truth. But numbers aren’t facts merely because they are numbers.

They are arguments waiting for a denominator.[1](#footnote-1)

We have arrived at a similar problem now, except that the numbers are attached to Patriot interceptors and Russian ballistic missiles instead of inflation and GDP.

And the stakes are considerably higher.

There is another number that makes the arithmetic considerably less funny.

Z says that this year Ukraine has two and a half times fewer interceptors than it had in 2025.

In other words, if it had 100 before, it now has 40.

He also says Russia is firing twice as many ballistic missiles per month as it did before.

If both numbers are correct, the problem is not simply that Ukraine has fewer interceptors.

The numerator is shrinking.

The denominator is growing.

Imagine, for the sake of arithmetic, that Ukraine had 100 interceptors available against 100 incoming ballistic missiles.

Now reduce the interceptors by two and a half.

Forty.

Double the ballistic missiles.

Two hundred.

Ukraine has gone from 100 interceptors for 100 missiles to 40 interceptors for 200 missiles.

The ratio has deteriorated from one interceptor per incoming missile to one interceptor for every five.

That is an 80 percent collapse in interceptor coverage.

Or, looked at another way, the ratio has deteriorated fivefold.

This is why the percentages are so slippery.

Ukraine’s 1 percent is a percentage of a requirement.

America’s 5 percent is a percentage of a stockpile.

And the requirement itself is moving.

Russia is firing more ballistic missiles.

Ukraine has fewer interceptors.

So when somebody says that 5 percent of an American stockpile will get Ukraine through the winter, the obvious question is not merely:

Five percent of what?

It is also:

Five percent against what?

Because the target isn’t standing still.

The great thing about numbers is that eventually they have to meet reality.

And reality is very good at arithmetic.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

[Funny Numbers](https://sites.google.com/site/abdymok/articles/funny-numbers?authuser=0), October 2009
