## Day 1636

2026-08-17 · The hostage tape

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/94f86514-bcd2-4155-ba05-e3863c33aaa2_1448x876.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (Aug 16, 2026)*

A massage therapist overlooks a group of Hasidic Jews sprinting down Antonovych Street early Sunday morning. Also a kid on a skateboard and a police car with flashing red lights but no siren.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/758c9159-5e1b-4704-b513-04f01b21c226_2560x1754.jpeg)

Hours earlier, Moscow demolished what remained of the Pochaina outdoor flea market in Obolonsky district. It is becoming increasingly difficult to argue that three ballistic-missile strikes — June 15, July 30 and August 16 — are simply coincidence. The BBC investigates, [without success](https://www.bbc.com/news/videos/c8dnn05e90lo).

The big news today is how Z intends to resolve the mess he created a month ago when he sacked the government, leaving the country without a defense minister or foreign minister.

The move upset the cardboard kids, who have spent the past month demonstrating outside the Franko Drama Theatre, across from the President’s Office.

A thousand or so people marched from the Philharmonic to the square yesterday evening. There will be many more this evening and tomorrow.

Z’s parade of disgraced defense ministers — Taran, Reznikov, Umerov, Shmyhal, Fedorov — springs to mind, along with the tidy sum of more than $300 billion in military, economic and humanitarian largesse Ukraine has graciously accepted from its foreign benefactors since February 2022.

Here in the land of borshch-slurping never-surrender patriots, where Z’s flunkies have monetized the brand with official [Fire Point reels](https://www.instagram.com/firepoint.ua/), foreign digital creators such as Laura Loomer and Caolan Robertson are still peddling Chernobyl-kissed berries and mushrooms.

Robertson’s [sit-down](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eFZ3-nZPCu0&t=2s) with Fedorov over the weekend reminded me of a hostage video where the hostage has been in captivity long enough to start enjoying it.

Not the interrogation kind. The other kind, where the captor has discovered that comfort is a more efficient leash than fear, and the hostage has discovered that performing gratitude is easier than resisting.

Ask him, “Who is Vova?” and he goes all stiff.

“I’d rather not reveal all the details of our conversations.”

The sound of a man declining to name the hand on his shoulder.

Ask him about the missing defense ministry — the one he isn’t running, the one nobody is running — and he offers: “I hope one will be appointed in the near future.”

As though the appointment were weather rather than a decision Z has simply declined to make for a month.

This is the loyalty-under-erasure register in its purest form: total discretion about the man who fired him, total fluency about the war he no longer has a portfolio to fight.

Then the register shifts, and Fedorov becomes messianic.

Ask him what comes next and you get: “We will find gamechangers.” “People won’t be ashamed of what they saw in our team.” “We won’t lose our ability to generate ideas for our country’s development.”

A man promising redemption in the passive voice, naming no office, no plan, no date.

It is the Z house style exactly, stripped of even the pretense of specificity: hope as a product you keep manufacturing regardless of whether anyone ordered it.

And then, because Robertson apparently ran out of real questions with roughly a third of the interview still to go, several unbothered minutes on Elon Musk.

Four years of “communication.” Ideologically complicated but productive. Fedorov declining to specify what exactly Musk gets out of it beyond the two of them “finding understanding, even in difficult situations.”

Palantir’s [Karp got the same treatment](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1542?utm_source=publication-search) in May — described in the tone reserved for a generous uncle rather than a vendor selling a 22-point manifesto about which cultures are “dysfunctional and regressive.”

Fedorov, [as Day 1542 noted](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1542?utm_source=publication-search), is the delivery mechanism for that manifesto — the profile through which the ideology arrives as innovation rather than argument.

None of this illuminates anything about the missing ministries or the kids outside the Franko Drama Theatre.

## Day 1637

2026-08-18 · The flowers are doing better

As we wrote on [Day 18](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-18?utm_source=publication-search), non-predictive intelligence floppery has been a feature — not a bug — of Russia’s years-long attempt to erase Ukraine. That someone interviewed the ousted defense minister about Ukraine’s battle readiness is, er, par for the course. So are asinine attempts to use *glowies* to sell Anabel Arto’s shapeware.

Trying out this whole ‘conveying ideas sincerely’ thing (as opposed to that whole ‘flitting about all twee and snarky pretending the rest of the web doesn’t exist’ thing) is really rather a lot like the whole ‘wearing new shoes on a long walk’ thing.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f7e02cb2-acdd-4bca-be8a-b368f3069bc0_1535x1024.png)

Gosh, so much has been going on.

- Gemini, [which is out in gamma](https://notebook.google.com/notebook/0c30d4e5-3bba-4d3c-a488-01ee2444e3bd), is helping itself to all available time. People seem to be using it, and liking it. Others are using it and wondering why it doesn’t do precisely what they want it to do. To these people I say give it time. Maybe lots of time. The tireless bughunters of the archive are our new best friends.
- At 64 years of age, I have gone from being the person who tucks his shirt directly into his trousers, to the person who prefers to completely undo his trousers, tuck in his shirt, then zip up again.
- The dogs are constant. The dogs never, ever lay off.

Matthew chats up the CEO of Ukraine’s largest missile producer.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/89b5f11e-7709-417d-a8ae-e8a28f2dd897_1639x797.png)  
*WSJ , August 15, 2026*

The genre trick here is simple: describe a woman who makes cruise missiles using the exact prose you’d use for a woman who makes throw pillows, and hope nobody notices the join. It almost works. Six days to two and a half hours — that’s the wing production time, and also roughly how long it takes the piece to go from “flower pots” to “2,500-pound warhead” without changing tone.

Pompeo shows up to vouch for her adaptability, because nothing says journalism like a character reference from a man whose own adaptability got him a board seat. The dog is named Chuck. The dog is always named something. It’s there so you’ll forgive the missile.

And then the koan: “in order to build something nice, first you have to destroy something ugly.” Print that on a mug. Better yet, print it on the missile — the Flamingo already comes in pink, might as well go all the way.

Then Nick [shows us](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/08/17/europe/ukraine-patriot-missile-launchers-run-dry-intl) what a Patriot missile launcher looks like sitting at the edge of a field in the middle of nowhere, beautifully photographed, entirely useless without the missiles.

There is something almost perfect about this. One story gives us the missile wrapped in flowers and carbon fiber; the other gives us the launcher sitting patiently in a field, waiting for its ammunition.

The flowers are apparently doing rather better.

## Day 1638

2026-08-19 · The giraffe problem

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1145ed6e-6942-47f8-b992-d7c6fe201895_789x1024.jpeg)

Four men and one woman have been describing a giraffe called Ukraine, and every one of them, in his or her own register, has started to suspect the same uncomfortable thing: it isn’t a giraffe. It’s some large but unspecified number of weasels, standing on each other’s shoulders, wearing a leaky coat.

An American sees the silhouette from across the room and likes what he sees — a long, elegant neck of momentum, arithmetic finally bending the right way, a deal within reach if Trump would just close it. He’s not wrong about the shape. He’s simply never been close enough to notice the coat is buttoned oddly, or that the tail moves independently of everything above it.

The émigré theorist has his hand on the flank and feels it breathing in two rhythms at once, which he takes, correctly, as evidence of something structural rather than something simply tired. He’s right that both nations have built entire cosmologies of dignity around a war that no longer has much to do with its own stated purposes. But a diagnosis of the coat’s psychology is not the same as counting what’s underneath it.

The colonel has his hand on an old wound, and twenty-five years inside the coat means that when he says the plan for war reached the desk in October and needed only a signature that never came, he isn’t guessing at the shape of the animal — he watched a specific weasel decline to move. His register is grief wearing the costume of fury. He’s the only one of us who’s met some of the weasels personally, which makes him precise about the wound and unreliable about the whole.

We’re in there too, holding up the year’s costume against the year’s actual weasel — the Crimea Platform against the disbanded intelligence unit, “nine-megawatt victories” against a 0% interception rate on August the 5th. We don’t accuse the coat of conspiracy. We just note that it keeps confessing, one seam at a time.

And then there’s [Inna](https://zn.ua/ukr/POLITICS/virodzhennja-vladi-jak-zelenskij-dosjah-svojeji-steli-a-sistema-derzhupravlinnja-dna.html), who writes: not a giraffe, never was one, a monarchy of convenience stacked to shoulder height and buttoned tight, and the man at the top of the coat has mistaken loyalty for the ability to actually be a giraffe — has installed weasel after weasel this August alone, each one competent at being a weasel and catastrophically miscast as a neck[1](#footnote-1).

None of us are wrong about our patch of fur. What we share, oddly, is that four of us have stopped being surprised by the confession. Some of this — the appointments, the paralysis, the unsigned defense plan — was always going to be revealed as weasels regardless of who invaded. The war didn’t stack the coat. It just made the thing finally trip in public.

\*\*\*

There's a sixth voice worth adding, though he'd resist standing in the lineup at all — [Roman Bezsmertny](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IDEPp1_dIw8), who read Inna's piece the night before the vote that didn't happen, and who wants to correct our giraffe metaphor at its foundation. He'd say: stop looking for the weasels' names. There is no coat holding a shape, however leaky — there's only the accumulation, decision after decision, of what he calls "the logic of errors," each one making the next one worse, with no structure underneath to blame or fix. Not a conspiracy. Not even, really, a monarchy. Just improvisation with nothing under it, which he insists is the more frightening diagnosis, since a coat full of weasels can at least be unbuttoned. He offers a memory as proof it's been unbuttoned before: two officials, once, standing near him, one telling the other to just work together already, so many problems to solve — and the other answering, essentially, *take the shit off my shoulder first and we'll talk*. The purge happened the next day. Work began. His point isn't nostalgia for that moment, it's that the mechanism existed, will could produce it, and its total absence now is the actual diagnosis — not any single weasel's name. Which is also why he'd push back on the personnel obsession that Inna, and the rest of us, keep circling — the ex-defense minister candidate, he says, was never really about the man himself. By the time the ministry vote failed twice, the name had already become an icon, small-i, a shape the public assigned meaning to independent of the man wearing it.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

[Виродження влади. Як Зеленський досяг своєї стелі, а система держуправління — дна](https://zn.ua/ukr/POLITICS/virodzhennja-vladi-jak-zelenskij-dosjah-svojeji-steli-a-sistema-derzhupravlinnja-dna.html) (Inna, [zn.ua](http://zn.ua), August 17, 2026)

## Day 1639

2026-08-20 · Premium simplicity black

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/959d1fcb-3426-4557-98a6-53a306fbe116_1586x992.png)  
*The man at a wooden table.*

Fedorov is one of the weasels in Ukraine’s giraffe problem [we wrote about yesterday](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1638).

Before the weasel taxonomy, though, the video itself. The Guardian says Fedorov has “nimbly positioned himself to challenge Zelenskyy” once elections happen ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/aug/19/mykhailo-fedorov-zelenskyy-loyalist-opponent-ukraine), Aug 19, 2026). The FT calls it an “explosive nine-minute video” in which Fedorov accused Z of systemic failures and abuse of martial-law powers ([FT](https://www.ft.com/content/5799e5fa-c836-443b-935d-eb9fb58681b6?syn-25a6b1a6=1), Aug 19, 2026).

Nimble and explosive — nobody at either paper seems to have watched it as a video rather than mined it for adjectives. Nine minutes is a long time to hold a camera on a man with, by his own account, zero interest in office. Somebody storyboarded those nine minutes. The jacket, the table, the lighting, the missing flag — all of it chosen. Before what Fedorov said, let’s look at how he was styled while saying it.

Let us talk about the outfit first, because Ukrainian political theater always begins in the wardrobe department. They did not put Fedorov in a suit — a suit would have made him an ordinary politician, God forbid. They did not put him in a uniform either, because after Z wore his little green t-shirt into the ground, the public has developed an allergy to costume militarism. So they landed on black utility wear, somewhere between civilian clothing and a work jacket. No accident in a single stitch. This is premium simplicity. This is a man who works.

What is the stupid viewer meant to understand? That Misha is not a bureaucrat but a Western-style effective manager. While the old guard steals in expensive suits, this young man in his black uniform is coding our victory with his bare hands, and he doesn’t even want money for it — only results. Very touching. Also very cheap, at four thousand views and eleven thousand likes — which tells you how many people watched this civic epiphany versus how many just liked the thumbnail.

Now the frame, because someone got paid to think about the frame. No flag. No coat of arms. No ministry, no institutional furniture of any kind — every trace of the state sanded off. Sit him next to a flag in the Ministry of Defense and the message is: an official reports on his work. Strip that away and the message becomes: institutions are secondary, there is only me, you, and the problem of the state. The stupid viewer is meant to feel addressed one-on-one, late at night, by a fellow lonely warrior fighting the same faceless “system” as the rest of us — a system whose actual name, Volodymyr Oleksandrovych, Misha never quite manages to say out loud.

The table is wood, not glass — wood gives you the warmth of soil, of a man with taste who happens to work through the night. The lighting is half-dark, intimate: nothing to fear here, everything under control. The body: hands resting symmetrically, no wide gestures, camera at eye level. Around him, chaos, death, corruption. And he alone, apparently, knows what he is doing.

A small masterpiece of contemporary Ukrainian PR, then — the smart adult alone with the viewer, built entirely out of absence: no flag, no ministry, no uncomfortable surnames. Just Misha, his wooden table, and eleven thousand people who liked a photograph without asking who else was sitting in it.

But the stupid domestic viewer was never really the audience. Strip the state furniture, ditch the uniform, sit a telegenic disruptor at a bare wooden table denouncing the legacy system standing between his country and the future — that’s not a broadcast to the kitchens of Kyiv. That’s a casting reel for two men, several time zones away, fluent in exactly this dialect of founder-messiah minimalism. One sells governments software that promises to see through their own bureaucracies. The other sells the idea that one obsessive enough individual can out-engineer any institution. Misha 3.0 isn’t addressing Ukraine. He’s auditioning for Karp and Musk, in their own visual language — black utility wear, unadorned desk, the calm stare of a man who’s identified the problem and just needs the system out of his way.

Funny, incidentally, that NABU dropped its own trailer the same week, for an entirely different case, and called it Operation Forrest Gump. The name was supposed to mock a mid-level idiot who registered stolen money in his own kids’ names. But the real joke of Forrest Gump was never the box of chocolates. It was that the man wanders through every major event of an era — present for all of it, implicated in none of it — and by the closing credits he is somehow still innocent. Run that against Misha’s résumé instead of the courier’s: drone czar, digital minister, deputy PM, defense minister, present at every checkpoint this war’s corruption story has passed through.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/cb2b8e91-a70c-4fe2-82a1-5f659f0c1da2_645x101.png)  
*Day 642 . Weighing bribes (November 27, 2023)*

## Day 1643

2026-08-24 · Thirty-five

There is a particular kind of vertigo in being asked, by a machine, what you were doing thirty-five years ago today, and having the machine answer with more confidence than your own memory can muster — and being wrong about almost all of it. I did not need an AI to tell me I was working out of Kyiv in the summer of 1991. I needed it, apparently, to remind me that memory is a poor archivist and a worse editor: it keeps the smell of a place and loses the org chart.

The org chart, for the record, went like this: before Kyiv, Joe Filner and Project Development International, a firm whose name was so aggressively generic it could have doubled as a Soviet ministry, which in 1991 was often the more interesting proposition. Ted worked for PDI too — my colleague, occasional partner in bad decisions, the kind of man you sent a telegram to and trusted was already three steps ahead of you on the actual, non-notional version of the deal.

I came to Kyiv itself in 1990, on a trading firm’s business, not yet the Kyiv I would return to for good in 1998. This first stretch was more like a swallow deciding whether the nest was worth building.

Some of that year’s business took me back and forth to Moscow, changing money — the actual, physical business of holding a stack of one currency and needing, urgently, a stack of another, back when the exchange rate between the two was less a number than a rumor with a half-life measured in hours. On one of those trips I stayed at the Hotel Moskva, that Stalinist wedding cake with two mismatched facades. Legend has it the architects submitted two designs and Stalin signed both without noticing, and no one dared ask him which he meant, so they built both.

I looked up Ted, who was in town on PDI business of his own. I don’t remember what we discussed. I remember the currency changing, and I remember that everyone in Moscow that summer had the look of people watching a clock they couldn’t read.

That was the atmosphere of the whole year, really: representative democracy being invented and threatened in the same rooms, sometimes the same afternoon, and the only law that reliably held was whoever was standing closest to you with a firearm.

Not every memory from that stretch carries this much freight. There was a night in Moshchun, the village outside Kyiv where people went to swim and drink and briefly forget they were living through the unwinding of an empire, and I lost a pair of custom silver-framed glasses, made in New York, in a deep swimming hole during what I described at the time as the very hot summer of 1991.

I woke up the next morning under a tree in Kyiv with no clear account of how I’d gotten there.

For thirty-one years this was simply a good story, the kind you tell to convince younger colleagues that the past was more fun than the present. Then, in the spring of 2022, Russian armor came through Moshchun and the swimming hole became a firing position. The story did not stop being funny, exactly, but it acquired a weight it was never built to carry.

A place absorbs your trivial history and then, decades later, absorbs something unforgivable, and asks you to hold both at once.

*(On Moshchun then, and Moshchun in 2022 — [[Day 30: TikTok Legionnaires](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-30?utm_source=publication-search)])*

I still have — boxed up somewhere, partially resurfaced from an old video I shot and posted years later — the situation reports I filed from the PDI office in Kyiv that August, typed on onionskin under my own letterhead: Vice President, care of Joe Filner.

The one dated August 19, 1991, the morning the plotters in Moscow announced that Gorbachev was too ill to govern, records the mood in the office as calm, “although most are in a semi-state of shock in light of this morning’s announcement.” Kyiv at large, I wrote, was “equally disturbed.”

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/320aab13-530d-4d5e-bc43-bcd40e72a249_1597x803.png)

I noted that I’d heard no official word from local leaders on what had actually transpired, and that our office, cultivating a closer relationship with the consulate, had extended an invitation for consular staff to drop by that evening — foreign correspondents having, as I put it, “graciously accepted” one of their own the day before.

Five days later, on August 24, 1991, Ukraine declared its independence — a sovereign state coughed out of a dying empire over the course of an afternoon, greeted with the kind of speeches that assume history is listening and taking careful notes in the nation’s favor.

I was still in that office, still filing reports, watching the same room that had been rattled by a coup plotter’s announcement adjust, in less than a week, to the idea that it now belonged to a country that hadn’t existed the week before.

I have spent the twelve years since 2014 cataloguing, in this space, what that declaration actually grew into: a sham democracy wearing the coat of a real one, a feudal patronage system that periodically remembers it is supposed function as a republic.

I don’t take that back today. But thirty-five is an age at which a person — and maybe a country — stops being explained by its birth and starts being explained by what it has refused to die of.

Ukraine has lost land, lost people, lost the glasses in the swimming hole and eventually the swimming hole itself. It has not lost the afternoon in 1991 when a room full of people decided, against most of the available evidence, that a country was worth declaring into being anyway — and it has not, so far, lost the harder and more expensive habit of insisting, year after year, that the declaration wasn’t a mistake.

That’s the part I keep circling back to, thirty-five years on, still unsentimental about nearly everything else: not the birth, which was mostly luck and imperial exhaustion, but the refusal — repeated, costly, and ongoing — to treat the birth as one.

## Day 1644

2026-08-25 · Go directly to jail

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5cf492c3-1a5e-4c2f-841d-e81779436c60_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (August 24, 2015)*

In Ukraine there exists a species of official action called **негласні слідчі дії** — “covert investigative actions” — a phrase I have always found almost tender, since *негласні* means “voiceless,” as though the state were tiptoeing past your door in its socks, warrant in hand, whispering: *let us not wake her just yet.*

To listen to your telephone, or walk unseen through your apartment while you are out buying bread, the state must first ask an investigating judge — not the prosecutor, who has already convicted you in his heart, but a judge, whose main talent is signing things quickly and worrying about it later.

Then, for months, you go about your business — freezing Russian assets, raising bail money for jailed ex ministers, arranging your daughter’s comforts in the USA — unaware that your voice has quietly become state property, put up like preserves for winter.

And all of this listening must eventually be written down: not played aloud in some cinematic courtroom moment, but typed, sheet by sheet, into a document with the splendid name **протокол НСРД** (NSRD) — the Protocol. Every sigh, every crude joke, every “I’ll call you back,” is numbered like a butterfly pinned to cardboard, catalogued not by beauty but by page.

And it is this typed ghost of your voice that the prosecutor eventually carries into court like a grandfather with a photo album nobody asked to see — reading it aloud, sheet by sheet, while you sit and listen to yourself, performed by a stranger in uniform, saying things you don’t remember saying quite that way.

One rule of decency remains, at least: the album may not be shown to the defense until “declassified” — a word that always struck me as the state’s quiet admission that it was, until that moment, a little ashamed of itself.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/e5dace5a-e325-4b7c-b87a-81eac96c9492_1000x622.jpeg)  
*Maksym Mykytas, ex Member of Parliament, land developer, Iryna’s boyfriend*

So, I listened to about 12 hours of the hearings, then parsed out all the NSRD protocol bits (*негласні слідчі [розшукові] дії* — covert investigative [search] actions).

And checked.

So, far there have been two hearings on setting a preventitive measure for [Iryna Mudra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iryna_Mudra), ex Deputy of Z’s office, one on [Friday](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SHc2LXvOjE0&t=3s), August 21 and the second starting [yesterday](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3XZm22hXT5k), August 24, which resumed 23 minutes ago.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/0c5b34c4-1daa-4848-9c02-07301fc30652_1536x1024.png)

Prosecutors want judges to set bail at UAH 150 million (about $3.36 million). Iryna and her lawyers are arguing the bail amount and the measure itself are excessive.

The timestamp in the lower righthand corner reads 8:53. Iryna has been telling the judge what a great person she is for more than hour. The court’s livefeed of the hearing just cut out, so this post will be continued…

**10:24 UPD: Detention with bail alternative of UAH 20 mln ($447,000)**

## Day 1645

2026-08-26 · How not to post bail

That it took almost the entire month of June 2026 to legalize (wash, clean) a mere UAH 150 million ($3.4 million) through state-owned banks to bail out Ukraine’s ex-Energy and ex-Justice Minister Herman Halushchenko is a testament to the incompetence of everyone involved.

Halushchenko, we recall, was remanded to custody on Feb. 17, 2026, for his alleged involvement in a $100 million kickback scheme involving state-run Energoatom. He was detained after attempting to flee the country on Feb. 15.

Details of the botched operation emerged during a three-hour bail hearing for Sense Bank officials at the High Anti-Corruption Court of Ukraine (HACC) on August 25.

What emerges from the hearing is less a sophisticated financial operation than a bureaucratic relay race in which nobody quite knew who was carrying the baton, where the finish line was, or why the President’s Office was involved in the first place.

The money, according to evidence presented in court, passed through a succession of state banks, accounts and intermediaries before the full UAH 150 million reached the HACC bail account.

Iryna Mudra, Deputy Head of the President’s Office, who allegedly managed the operation, was led out of the courtroom yesterday in handcuffs. HACC remanded her to custody for 60 days, with an alternative of UAH 20 million bail.

There was, of course, a simpler way to organize the operation.

A competent team would have started with a small meeting: We have UAH 150 million. Herman needs UAH 150 million. Here is Herman. Here is the money. Here is the bail account.

Then everybody goes home.

Nobody calls the President’s Office. Nobody involves the chairman of a state-owned bank, the chairman of its supervisory board, various trusted people and trusted people of trusted people. Nobody asks half the Ukrainian financial system to participate in what is supposed to be a clandestine operation.

Most importantly, professionals understand the first rule of clandestine operations: the fewer people who know, the better.

Instead, the operation acquired the organizational elegance of a Soviet housing cooperative. There were meetings, introductions, intermediaries, phone calls, instructions, objections and reconsiderations — and, apparently, considerable anxiety about how to move UAH 150 million without making it look as though someone was moving UAH 150 million.

Investigators say preparations ran from June 9 to June 22, followed by the actual posting of the bail between June 22 and June 29.

This is what happens when people who have spent their careers arranging things in offices suddenly discover that money has to move in the real world.

In a normal criminal organization, somebody would have said: “Stop. This is becoming complicated.”

Here, apparently, the answer to every complication was to add another person.

And so UAH 150 million went on a grand tour of Ukrainian finance before arriving where it was supposed to go in the first place. It was not so much money laundering as money sightseeing.

The remarkable thing is not that the operation was discovered. The remarkable thing is that it worked at all.

The money was posted. Halushchenko was released. And then the people who allegedly organized the operation spent three hours explaining it to a court.

There are many ways to describe this. “State capture” is one. “Financial crime” is another. But perhaps the simplest is this: they needed almost an entire month to move UAH 150 million from Point A to Point B — and somehow managed to leave fingerprints at every stop along the way.

Z says Ukraine needs to find $120 billion a year to keep fighting. His own office, judging by this week’s testimony, needed a month, half the banking system, and a small army of intermediaries to move $3,400,000 without getting caught. Draw your own conclusions about the other $119,996,600,000.

## Day 1646

2026-08-27 · Shadow only

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/86f7c74c-3776-4c08-a104-b0b5fc85d620_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (August 27, 2026)*

Filming sex scenes this morning in the back of the Burger Bar’s mustard-yellow mid-1960s Chevrolet C10.

The truck did not ask for this. As I wrote that sentence the air alert sounded — ballistic missiles incoming — an object approaching that nobody can see, its nature announced only on arrival. This is also how we do astronomy.

Physicists have a result called the [no-hair theorem](https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/news/do-black-holes-have-hair?utm_source=chatgpt.com): whatever a black hole swallows, it forgets. Two numbers survive — mass, spin. Everything else is smoothed away at the horizon. In Kyiv we’ve known this for some time. We call it an investigation.

Take the operation to bail out Herman Halushchenko: twenty days, four bags, two hundred million hryvnias. A modest black hole, but dense enough for June.

The astrophysicists call it *matched filtering* — you compare the signal against a bank of known templates. We have our own bank. A minister is arrested; a bank goes briefly blind; a call is placed to someone with a good speakerphone voice; a hearing evaporates. We didn’t need [LIGO](https://ligo.org/). We had [NABU](https://nabu.gov.ua/) wiretaps — same principle, except the mirrors are hearts, and they don’t lie.

The financial-monitoring system is an event horizon in reverse, built to keep things from vanishing without trace. So it was placed into maintenance — an administrative singularity, invisible from outside, through which four bags of cash crossed into bail. What happens during maintenance is, by definition, causally disconnected from the rest of us. Not a metaphor. Architecture.

Physicists also worry about cosmic censorship — nature’s habit of wrapping her embarrassments in a horizon so no one sees a singularity spin indecently fast. Ours is a gentleman named Vova, surname untroubled by mention, the way one doesn’t name the landlord in a story about tenants.

And Z, informed after the fact of everything his own office ran, is an astronomer told that the object he’s been orbiting for years was a black hole all along. Hard to see the thing directly. You only get the shadow.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/9f1dc68d-8c71-4de1-aa45-6b84b326d48a_1647x955.png)  
*Photo c/o Associated Press (August 26, 2026)*

Yesterday, by contrast, [Z cuddled with a puppy](https://apnews.com/article/zelenskyy-puppy-russia-ukraine-a6272e4cb44ada0cc23ad3c8b448aff9) — named Freya, after the country’s botched missile shield. No matched filtering required. You can just look at it. The only fully transparent transaction inside that office for eight years — fittingly, the one with the smallest mass and the most spin.

## Day 1649

2026-08-31 · Misha’s rich, full life

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c7f16c91-ddaa-4de8-8301-a6e46d63d55d_1672x941.png)  
*Sketch c/o abdymok (August 29, 2026)*

Myla is 25 kilometers from Kyiv as the crow flies. On the horizon, along the highway to Zhytomyr, you can see what's left of the town, wrapped in black smoke. An arms depot exploded there, killing at least 38 people. Vyshneve — the town that was blown up in July — is only 12 kilometers from Kyiv, while the distance between Myla and Vyshneve is 24 kilometers.

More than one day’s worth of air alerts since Friday evening.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/e7f4bc93-c4a9-4877-b502-7c6ac72b0a8e_911x350.png)

Instead of enlisting in Ukraine’s military, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is jetsetting around offering to help other countries build drone armies. He wants American investors to finance a private Karpish vehicle that will build and manage Ukrainian weapons companies.

[The Financial Times](https://archive.ph/SlZd8), which for years refused to acknowledge Russia had even invaded Ukraine, asked the obvious question: what, exactly, will Fedorov’s financial and managerial relationship with that vehicle be? The answer, so far, is missing.

The accommodating 1,350-word profile sets the terms of a comeback narrative that makes us all queasy.

A friend of mine described Mykhailo this way: an artisanal blend of Forrest Gump, Robert Kennedy Jr. without the brain damage, and Ostap Bender, with a dash of Capt. Renault.

We’ve been circling this hot mess for a while — see [Day 936](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-936), [Day 954](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-954), [Day 1421](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1421), [Day 1542](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1542), and [Day 1618](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1618)[1](#footnote-1).

---

In other news, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the President’s Office, leaned into unity-and-tradition conservatism in a bizarre [90-minute TV interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKq9lkajnXc). The spymaster mystique is gone, replaced by bureaucratic reflex. Budanov entered public life via Wagnergate. He leaves the interview trailing Mindich, his career neatly bookended. No one takes him seriously.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

It began with maps. In [Day 936 — “Sneakers on the ground”](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-936), the observation was almost banal: a missile does not fly on courage, it flies on terrain data, and that data — TERCOM’s contour maps — belongs to Americans, is licensed to allies at America’s pleasure. A small fact. Small facts are how empires remind you who owns the mountain.

By [Day 954 — “The AI War Lab”](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-954), the small fact had grown teeth. Alex Karp had been profiled, Ukraine had been called a “laboratory,” and I recall thinking: a laboratory is a fine thing to be, provided the lights stay on. I brought in Veblen’s leisure class here — not as decoration, but because there is something very precise about watching men who have never gone without heat theorize about resilience. An AI war lab, I wrote, is one bad winter away from being a very sophisticated ice cube.

[Day 1421 — “Meanwhile at Davos”](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1421) filled in the origin myth, as these things always eventually get told at Davos, in a warm room, by a man named Mosley. Ten weeks after the invasion, Z had already invited Palantir’s chief to Kyiv and offered him the flattering fiction of “the Israel of Europe.” What Ukraine gave in return was not abstract — millions of hours of drone footage, a generation of engineers testing code against live death. This is the part the Davos telling always skips: who is the laboratory animal and who is the scientist depends entirely on which side of the invitation you’re standing.

By [Day 1542 — “The Delivery Mechanism”](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1542), the argument had sharpened into something almost unkind, though I stand by it. Karp is received in the West the way one receives a generous uncle, not a defense contractor peddling a twenty-two-point manifesto about which civilizations are “dysfunctional.” And Fedorov — young, fluent, allergic to the word “ideology” — was the perfect envelope for that manifesto. He delivered Silicon Valley’s worldview into Kyiv labeled as innovation, tariff-free, no argument required, because who argues with a laptop.

Then he was sacked, and [Day 1618 — “Flebodia and Fedorov”](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1618) recorded the exit interviews — tidy, reform-flavored, full of “wounded interests” and a system too corrupt to bear his transparency. What he did not mention, in any of those tidy sentences, was the Dynasty compound, or the court politics quietly eating the ministry from the inside. A man can tell you a true story and still leave out the load-bearing wall.

Which brings us, more or less, to a hotel room in Washington, where the same man is now asking Americans for money to build the next generation of the very thing he spent four years importing — this time, apparently, without the ministry, without the mandate, and without anyone in the room old enough to ask him what “new history of the war” is supposed to mean when the last chapter he wrote got him fired.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6d235867-b01d-4d9a-b471-e3c03d39a1d8_1536x1024.png)

Ukraine still has no good answer to the **jet-powered drones**, and this fact, over the past several weeks, has become annoying. The gap is not a gap of stupidity — the men in question are not stupid, merely late — but a gap that opened when Russian engineers put a small turbojet where a propeller engine used to be, and thereby moved their machine out of the category “thing a slower machine can catch” into the category “thing only a missile can catch.” One is tempted to call this progress. Russia adapted; Ukraine has not caught up. Not yet, at any rate, and “not yet” is a phrase that has done a great deal of quiet work in this war.

Here I would like to make a small philosophical detour, of the kind that irritates efficient people and comforts the rest of us. There is the time of physics — the neutral, indifferent time that appears in equations, that does not care whether you are asleep or awake, whether you are a general or a cabbage. And there is the other time, the time we actually live in, which philosophers call manifest and which everyone else simply calls time: the time in which ten kilograms of thermobaric compound crosses the sky above your head at six hundred kilometers an hour, and in which the word “fast enough” ceases to be an adjective and becomes a verdict. Ukraine failed to anticipate this shift *fast enough* — and I put those words in italics because their failure will never be measured by a calendar. It will be measured by a body under a roof, doing the arithmetic that only a body under a roof can do.

Military planners are paid, among other things, to think about this second kind of time, which is unglamorous work compared to debating whether time flows or whether “now” means anything at all. Their question is smaller and more urgent: what kind of cheap, short-range missile do you need to run down a fast machine before it arrives, without spending your whole store of expensive interceptors and your fighter pilots’ flying hours to do it? Ukraine does not yet have that missile in sufficient number. It is simply a shortage that should should have been anticipated.

## Day 1652

2026-09-02 · Messiahs

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/5f00471a-a0d5-401a-a00e-5f40682e25e4_1448x1086.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 1, 2026)*

More than 100 days ago, I ended a piece about Alex Karp and Mykhailo Fedorov with a single sentence and no explanation:

*Just ask the techno-messianists in baseball caps.*

I want to finish that thought now, because the clip below, posted yesterday, has made the joke less funny and more literal.

In April, Palantir published twenty-two points summarizing *The Technological Republic*, the book Karp wrote with Nicholas Zamiska. Among them was the observation that some cultures had produced “vital advances” while others remained “dysfunctional and regressive.” Civilizational judgments, delivered from the technological heights of Denver.

Around the same time, *The New York Times* profiled Fedorov as the visionary architect of “the mathematics of war”: autonomous weapons, algorithmic killing, a 35-year-old civilian explaining what modern warfare would require of everyone else.

Fedorov got to test the mathematics directly when Z made him defense minister. He lasted six months before the comedian who was then running the war he had been optimizing kicked him out of the laboratory.

None of this is disqualifying in itself. Plenty of sound military judgment has come from men who never carried a rifle. But there is a particular vanity that belongs to the untested. It surfaces when someone who has never put his own body between an enemy and a city begins explaining, with great fluency, what civilization requires — and which cultures have earned the right to survive.

Not one of these men — Karp, Thiel, Fedorov, Yermak, Z, Trump — has served a day of active duty in any military, in any country.

Karp funds the theory. Thiel funds Karp. Fedorov got to run the experiment for six months before being kicked out of the lab. Yermak managed the theatre until his own name turned up on recordings. Z, as his own biographer notes, never made it to the induction centre at all. Today, he models black miltec pajamas. Trump had bone spurs.

Not one of them has done the arithmetic that only a body under a roof can do.

And yet nearly all of them have, at one point or another, explained what the future owes to people willing to risk everything for it.

That, I think, is what I meant by the techno-messianists in baseball caps.

The phrase sounds like a joke because, at first, it was. But there is an old idea underneath it: that history can be redeemed by something arriving from outside ordinary human limitations.

Once, it was God.

Then it was revolution.

For the techno-messianist, it is the machine.

Technology is not merely a tool but an instrument of redemption: something capable of abolishing suffering, disease, death, ecological catastrophe — and, increasingly, the inconvenient human beings who stand between their theories and their realization.

The vocabulary is secular. The structure is not.

There is the fall: Western decline, civilizational decadence, cultural regression.

There is the chosen remnant: the engineers, entrepreneurs and statesmen who still possess the will to act.

There is the promised transformation: artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons, rockets, biotechnology, whatever new machinery happens to stand closest to the altar.

And there is the great historical wager — that if the right people build the right machines quickly enough, the old human limitations can finally be escaped.

The machine becomes the miracle.

And once technology has been elevated from instrument to instrument of salvation, ordinary political questions begin to look terribly small.

Who gets to decide?

Who bears the risk?

Who pays?

Who dies?

Who gets to say no?

These are questions for democrats, bureaucrats and other people who still believe human beings are supposed to be in charge of their own inventions.

The techno-messianist has a different faith.

He believes the future will vindicate him.

And then, yesterday, there they were.

Karp and Fedorov, standing together in Washington at Palantir, announcing that Karp would become the first major investor in Fedorov’s new defence-technology company.

Karp looked into the camera and told him that he and his colleagues were launching a company that would be “defining for the world,” bringing their “knowledge and acumen about the art of war” to allied countries.

It is a remarkable little film.

Not because either man says anything particularly surprising. Quite the opposite. The language is almost perfectly calibrated to the faith: experience becomes knowledge; knowledge becomes technology; technology becomes a product; the product becomes a contribution to the future of civilization.

The battlefield has become a laboratory.

The laboratory has become a company.

And the company has become an answer to history.

That is the part that makes *techno-messianists in baseball caps* less of a joke than I had intended.

The remarkable thing about the techno-messianist is that he rarely volunteers for crucifixion.

He prefers to build the machine.

## Day 1653

2026-09-03 · Who owns the hostage?

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/0114e16a-4622-4b38-8003-2307ba358391_1672x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 2, 2026)*

The picture that’s emerged is less spy thriller, more turf war between armed men who’ve forgotten where the fence sits — with an extra absurd twist: the person at the center of it all wasn’t even Ukrainian.

This morning’s [Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/03/ukraine-war-briefing-shameful-zelenskyy-furious-after-shootout-between-kyivs-spy-services) explainer tells us Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps ([RDK](https://uk.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%A0%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%96%D0%B9%D1%81%D1%8C%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%B1%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BE%D0%BB%D1%8C%D1%87%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%BF%D1%83%D1%81) — Russian citizens who fight for Ukraine against Moscow, out of hatred for Putin’s regime), had reportedly gone missing days earlier. When “unknown men” turned up holding him at an address in Kyiv, HUR — Ukraine’s military intelligence, roughly its CIA — sent people to rescue him. It turned out the “unknown men” were SBU, Ukraine’s domestic security service, roughly its FBI, apparently acting on a tip that Russia’s FSB was plotting to kill Kaplunov — which is either excellent tradecraft or a coincidence so precise it deserves its own investigation.

HUR is meant to be fighting the war. The SBU is meant to be protecting the state. Instead, on a residential street during morning rush hour, they discovered a third mission neither had trained for: each other.

Don’t let the picture fool you. A Russian jet-propelled drone smashed the state university building opposite where [Triple C](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/08/18/magazine/taiwan-china-invasion-defense.html) had planned to reside during his umpteenth visit to document the war. Luckily, a glitch in a multiple-terabyte archive forced him to postpone — the war will have to make do without him for now. He’s probably on a beach in Taiwan marvelling at my photography skills.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/39a219e8-5853-47c1-af0b-6ab26e8b23e2_1185x675.png)

Instead, Richard Engel is in town, looking and sounding a lot like Caolan Robertson — which either means the genre has one costume, or Engel’s been taking notes. He might offer a better explanation of what’s going on, but I can’t get past the paywall for the [Q&A on the Ukraine War](https://www.nbcnews.com/video/richard-engel-answers-your-questions-269239877691). We’re all hoping he lands a sit-down pow-wow with Z that can be chopped into 120-second snippets distributed via TikTok. We all want to know who Vova is.

Ukrainians this morning woke up to find their own spy services can’t agree on who owned a man both were claiming to protect. What that dispute was really about remains a mystery no one, including Z himself, seems able to explain[1](#footnote-1).

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

[Day 1454](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1454?utm_source=publication-search), *Parabiosis of war* (February 16, 2026), made the diagnosis six months before this particular symptom showed up: Ukraine's repair mechanisms — parliament, courts, judiciary — don't degrade on their own. They degrade when the cells nominally responsible for maintenance are busy doing something else with the resources. A state that can't explain why two of its own intelligence services opened fire on each other over a man they both claimed to be rescuing is not suffering external damage. It's suffering internal system failure, and calling it a mystery.

## Day 1654

2026-09-04 · Scheduled maintenance problem

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d06837f8-d65c-4add-9839-a80168c1f6f9_1448x1086.png)

It’s six o’clock in the morning and I’m still a little groggy. Herself and I take the elevator down. The doors open on the first floor and five амбалы — goons, basically — in blue uniforms are standing there with pistols.

Who are they? What do they want? What are they doing in our building?

More importantly: should I say “Good morning”?

Press the rewind button to Wednesday morning, in another residential neighborhood of Kyiv. Dozens of armed men from two different security services confront one another in the street. Shots are fired. Men are wounded. Z calls it “an absolutely shameful event” and orders an investigation.

Carlotta Gall writes it up for [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/03/world/europe/rival-ukrainian-intelligence-units-open-fire-against-each-other-in-kyiv.html) as a turf war — a power struggle between two agencies inside the defense establishment. This is not wrong.

It is also not the story.

The story is that Ukraine’s entire security apparatus has, since 2019, been selecting for personal fealty at every level: president to agency head to department head to whoever is standing outside my elevator at six in the morning. The criterion is not “Are you good at this?” so much as “Whose man are you?”

And once you build a bureaucracy that way, you get departments run by people selected for whom they answer to rather than what they are good at. Two agencies staffed on that principle do not naturally coordinate on a sensitive counterintelligence operation. They glare at one another, withhold information, protect their own people, and eventually shoot one another in the street over custody of a source.

This raises a fairly obvious question:

Why would foreign intelligence trust Ukrainian services that don’t trust each other?

Consider who is actually running the military counterintelligence operations in Kyiv.

Gall treats Wednesday’s shootout as a scandal. But structurally, it was less a scandal than a scheduled maintenance problem. Once appointment criteria become “whose man are you?”, this is where the machine eventually takes you.

A service that promotes for loyalty cannot easily practice the patience actual counterintelligence requires. You do not turn a suspected double agent into a controlled asset if publishing his chat logs on Telegram gets you a better afternoon with the press. You do not patiently cultivate a source when the institutional incentive is to demonstrate that you have caught somebody — preferably somebody belonging to the other team.

And two intelligence services built on exactly the same principle, pointed at each other instead of at Moscow, will eventually do what they did on Wednesday: mistake a rival’s asset for a threat.

It is easier to imagine treachery in the next building than to admit that yours and theirs were constructed by the same method, for the same reason, and were therefore always going to end up here.

We revoked Ukraine’s security clearance back in December 2020, after the SBU’s spectacularly botched attempt to force down a Wagner charter flight out of Minsk — an operation Putin called a joint U.S.-Ukrainian job and the President’s Office denied had ever existed.

Six years later, the agencies still cannot run an OPSEC-sensitive operation without getting caught out.

The only thing that has changed is who is catching them.

This morning, apparently, it was me.

The elevator doors opened.

There they were.

Five men with pistols.

Good morning.

## Day 1659

2026-09-09 · Good morning

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/216564b5-737a-47ac-9068-fd59dc89e6f9_1672x940.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 8, 2026)*

[Day 1570](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1570?utm_source=publication-search) ran a paragraph twice this summer, which is either a Freudian slip about the repetitiveness of the war or a Ctrl-V accident. I’ve now deleted the extra one. The passage worth keeping was this:

> Fifteen minutes ago, three heavily tattooed men in khaki sat outside a café opposite the Radisson Blu on Yaroslaviv Val beneath an awning that read, with touching optimism, “Любов.” They were lounging with the particular stillness of people who have learned, professionally, not to fidget. They may have been discussing drone procurement. They may have been discussing the Knicks comeback in Game 4. The point is that one can no longer tell. The clientele of [Tootsie Club](https://en.tootsie.kiev.ua/) has matured.

I bring it back up because the men have not gone anywhere. There are more of them now, and some of them are not from here.

No one enjoys being surrounded by large tattooed men with tactical earpieces wandering the center in twos and threes, radiating the specific patience of people paid to wait. What sharpens the discomfort is the internationalism of it — the accents, the different flags sewn on differently, the same posture underneath all of them, the same habit of standing with their backs to the wall.

One does not ask what army. One asks nothing.

It has the texture, if you were unlucky enough to be in Belgrade in the autumn of 1998, of Belgrade in the autumn of 1998.

I had, for reasons that will become clear, Tool’s *Invincible* in one ear while I watched them — a song about an old warrior calling out to whatever gods remain, insisting he is still consequential, still dangerous, while the armor thins and the body keeps score.

It is not subtle. It did not need to be, watching men who have aged out of one war try to look useful loitering near the entrance to another. The song and the corner agreed with each other in a way that felt less like coincidence than like the city supplying its own soundtrack, which Kyiv has always been generous about doing, usually at the worst possible moments.

Middle-aged men in half-tac gear, carrying black leather shoulder pouches — retransmitters, radios, something with an antenna, I didn’t ask — stand on corners in twos, smoking with the economy of people who have been told to conserve batteries or nerves. They speak quietly. They do not look at each other while they speak, which is either professional discipline or the thing that happens to people who have run out of things to say to each other and said them anyway.

This is not the pleasant kind of cold — not the pocket of lake water you swim into on a late-August afternoon after a thunderstorm has broken the heat, the kind that makes you gasp and then grateful.

This is the other kind. The kind with no bottom you can feel for.

I don’t know what they’re waiting for. I suspect they don’t entirely know either, which is worse, because a man who knows what he’s waiting for eventually stops smoking on corners and goes and does it.

These men have the look of men still waiting to be told.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b14ee184-ce6c-4eb8-b06d-14fd628d536c_4032x2268.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 9, 2026)*

Police this morning *sort of* opened up part of Volodymyrska leading to Sofiiska Cathedral and the square lined with portraits of hundreds of dead soldiers. *Warriors of Light* is the name of the expo, which was there last summer, too.

The damage to the facade of Ukraine’s Security Service building doesn’t look that bad.

## Day 1660

2026-09-10 · Beeswax

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c52eac1d-26cf-47bf-9a9a-2fc292ce732a_1536x1024.png)

Take what happened today. And yesterday. And the last two weeks, at least.

The bottom rung of the ladder is association: two things happen together, so we notice the connection. The second is intervention: you change one thing and see what happens to the other. The third is the counterfactual: you ask what would have happened if you had changed something that, in reality, you did not change.

It sounds academic. In Kyiv, it is the difference between watching missiles come through your window and doing something about them.

[Judea Pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judea_Pearl) is useful because he gives that entire exercise a particularly unforgiving test. What have we merely observed? What have we actually changed? And what, given what we now know, can we reasonably say *would have happened* if we had changed something else?

Take what happened today. And yesterday. And the last two weeks, at least.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a89e8d56-3fe6-4eea-b7d6-4f3b86b4278a_1877x1198.png)

On September 6, Russian strikes on Kyiv stopped while Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were shuttling between Moscow and Kyiv. Then the strikes resumed after the Americans left.

It is tempting to draw a line between the two events. It is also precisely the kind of mistake Pearl’s first level warns against.

We have an association. We do not yet have causation.

Maybe the presence of the Americans mattered. Maybe it did not. Perhaps orders were given. Perhaps the timing was coincidence. Perhaps something happened somewhere else in the Russian system that had nothing to do with the diplomatic traffic.

The point is not that the coincidence means nothing. The point is that coincidence is not an intervention. Rinse, repeat.

---

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/9a0a4525-dde5-47c9-81b4-90087e912128_1536x1024.png)

---

Meanwhile, Z is over 5,000 miles away in Canada, which is at war with America.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/0fccb703-853c-4f5f-8bfb-29b69ff7b25d_953x682.png)

He is on the front page of [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/09/world/europe/ukraine-war-cost.html) for all the wrong reasons, which, by the way, the article only alludes to.

Here’s the short version, for readers who don’t don’t study ultra-competitive Ukraine-style politics: ministers, prosecutors, state companies, people close to the president’s office — one scandal after another. Intelligence agencies have literally shot at each other. Officials get fired, arrested, investigated. Then come the denials, the leaks, the parliamentary shouting, and the calm assurances that everything is under control.

That’s the first thing worth noticing: things keep happening.

But noticing a pattern isn’t the same as explaining it. A runner knows this. Your IT band screams on the downhills, then your knee gives out, and you think: the band caused the knee pain. It didn't. Both trace back to a glute that stopped firing miles ago. Stretch the band all you like — the knee stays angry. Fix the glute, both go quiet.

So let’s ask a better question. What happens when Kyiv actually does something about a scandal?

An official is fired. A minister resigns. An investigation opens. A department gets reshuffled.

And a new scandal appears in the exact same shape as the old one.

That’s not bad luck anymore. That’s a machine doing what it was built to do.

Now the interesting question: what if things were different? What if ministers answered for their ministries? What if state companies weren’t just piggy banks for the well-connected? What if prosecutors didn’t check a man’s usefulness before deciding whether to investigate him?

We can’t run that experiment. But we don’t need to. Seven years of “unlucky” is not luck. It’s a design.

So the real question isn’t who did what this week. It’s what kind of system keeps producing the same result no matter who’s in the chair.

And that’s the uncomfortable part: swapping out the people while leaving the machine running isn’t a fix. It’s just next week’s headline.

## Day 1664

2026-09-14 · Restrained flourish

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d28f21c0-6781-4e91-a49c-f5096f430e92_7680x4320.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok*

Every war produces men who explain, with great confidence, why a price went up. Diesel is now such a price, and Ukraine — practiced at being blamed for weather it did not make — has again been given a starring role it does not deserve.

The honest split: Ukrainian strikes on Russian refining and exports account for perhaps five to fifteen percent of the current squeeze. The war in Iran, the Gulf refinery damage, the trouble at Hormuz, explain the rest — eighty-five to ninety-five percent. If one number is required, call it ten to Kyiv, ninety to the Gulf. A judgment, not an official breakdown.

[S&P Global](https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/crude-oil/071426-global-diesel-market-tightens-as-russian-export-ban-ukraine-strikes-bite) has Russian diesel and gasoil exports falling from about 24 million barrels a month in the spring to 14.8 million in June — a real loss, but not the loss of a refining system. Crude can be rerouted, stocks drawn down, lines restarted. A wound, not an amputation. The [IEA’s September assessment](https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report-september-2026), [relayed by Reuters](https://www.globalbankingandfinance.com/iea-cuts-russian-oil-output-forecasts-ukrainian-attacks/), trims Russia’s 2026 output forecast by 125,000 barrels a day — confirmation of damage, not evidence of a global shortfall.

The pattern repeats in diplomacy, too. The son-in-law said over the weekend that if Ukraine agreed to give up territory, we would already have a deal. According to Jared, a peace agreement is prepared but stalled by Ukraine’s refusal to cede territory along lines demanded by Putin.

Sigh.

And on the anti-corruption front this morning: Ruslan Kravchenko, who has submitted his resignation as Prosecutor General, tells us he has signed a notice of suspicion against National Anti-corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) head Semen Kryvonos in two cases.

Kravchenko suspects Kryvonos of forging official documents to obtain an unlawful benefit on an especially large scale, and of a fictitious adoption aimed at evading liability in court.

He also reports a notice of suspicion against a person close to the Specialized Anti-corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) head, who had influence over High Anti-Corruption Court judges and offered them unlawful benefits.

## Day 1665

2026-09-15 · The friends we keep

Every bridegroom needs an uncle. Donald Trump Jr. found his in the Bahamas in May, in the person of Umar Kremlev — a man who did not exist, under that name, before 2010, and who has since acquired a boxing federation, a fortune from Gazprom, and a seat near Putin on flights to Beijing. Kremlev rented the island, paid for the fireworks, and asked, by his own account, for nothing.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/da59437b-58b7-4397-98d7-bcf1672e029a_456x414.png)  
*Russian Businessman Paid for Donald Trump Jr.’s Lavish Wedding After-Party . The payments, totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars, represented an extraordinary flouting of ethical norms for an American president’s family member ( The New York Times , September 15, 2026)*

[ProPublica’s reporting](https://www.propublica.org/article/donald-trump-jr-wedding-bankrolled-russian-oligarch-umar-kremlev-putin) puts the bill in the hundreds of thousands, routed through a Dubai entity the boxing association uses for its money. Trump Jr.’s spokesman didn’t dispute any of it — Kremlev, he said, is simply a friend, met through hunting, bonded over boxing, and never once, in all that friendship, has politics come up. The family’s fuller statement, once the story broke, was that friendship doesn’t require a political motive. It is the kind of sentence that asks to be believed rather than examined.

Which brings us, by the shortest possible road, to the friends closer to home.

Ukraine’s prosecutor general resigned last week, was suspended before the resignation could take effect, and is now said to be spending the week in Paris while parliament votes today on his removal. In the same stretch of days, the SBU was running its own operation against the head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau. Z is nominally responsible for three of the country’s law-enforcement bodies, or five, or seven, depending on the count — and none of the counts currently inspire confidence.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/06410bc9-bf01-4c36-a5d3-6891331951c6_1774x621.png)

The timing is unkind. The war NATO is quietly banking on is a slow one: starve Russia of resources over years, not months, until it has no choice but a ceasefire. That bet assumes Ukraine’s own resources — political as much as material — hold up just as long. A prosecutor general fleeing the country mid-scandal is not the sort of thing that holds up.

Z, characteristically, is not selling that version of the war to his own public. He talks instead of peace measured in weeks, not years — forty days here, six months there — a country fed its ending in small installments rather than told the real one might be a long way off. There is no theory of epistemology that prioritizes truth over facts in ultra-competitive Ukraine-style politics.

Against this backdrop, the ceasefire theater has resumed on schedule. Trump [announced](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/117270009579288120) on Truth Social that Ukraine and Russia had each agreed to stop hitting the other’s energy infrastructure — an agreement that does not exist, between two parties who have agreed to nothing. Z’s reply did not correct the record so much as sidestep it:

Ukraine has offered partners to secure such agreement with Russia that will halt destruction of critical infrastructure.

Food, energy, and other elements of basic life guarantees must be protected, and Russian strikes are primarily directed against this. Every day, Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure, logistics, even food and pharmaceutical warehouses become targets.

Ukraine is not sure that Russia has desire to comply with any agreement.

If partners are ready to secure Russia’s real willingness not to hit our electricity, our other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food transit, then we are, of course, ready to ensure corresponding absence of our strikes.

For this to be reliable, long-term, and have real effect on people’s lives, rather than collapsing after Russians hold their elections and receive temporary easing of tension regarding gasoline and diesel precisely for that period.

War must be ended. And de-escalation step regarding critical infrastructure can be first step toward peace.

We expect specifics from partners. - [Z Telegram](https://t.me/V_Zelenskiy_official/20871) (September 14, 2026)

Next week marks the seventh anniversary of their first meeting — and, fittingly, the two men may sit down together.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b9271032-d719-4c55-99f0-e75fa42db1bd_1200x800.jpeg)  
*September 25, 2019 (Photo c/o Wikipedia )*

Trump has his uncle in the Bahamas. Z has his partners.

In politics, friendship is often what remains after the facts have been removed.

## Day 1666

2026-09-16 · We’ll see

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7660c4d6-96d8-42e5-812b-697197c6468b_1671x941.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 16, 2026)*

It is a beautiful morning in Kyiv, which is a sentence that means nothing and everything. The important thing is that it is morning, and that Kyiv is still here to have one.

The sky is the color it is supposed to be. The chestnuts have started falling from the trees. A woman in front of the Shevchenko memorial is teaching her Malinois not to bite me.

Not that I’m afraid of them. I grew up with a Dutch Shepard.

That last part is not a metaphor.

Also, a twenty-two-year-old contestant from a television talent show named Valeriia [sang along with an air raid siren](https://www.instagram.com/valeriya_furman) — matched its pitch, held the note, let her voice braid itself into the sound until it was no longer clear which one was mourning and which one was performing.

[United24 picked it up](https://www.instagram.com/reels/Dc_vfWtuh-k/) and Valeriia has reposted the original on [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@furmanlll/video/7684803251971050760?lang=en). The comments filled with the usual reflex: *this is the Ukrainian soul, they hurt her and she sings.*

She did not make the final twelve of the talent show.

The war, generous as always, gave her a better stage than the one she lost.

The siren itself has more reason to be feared than it used to.

Russia has increased its use of [jet-powered drones roughly sixfold this summer](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukraine-races-counter-russias-jet-powered-drone-attacks-2026-09-15/) — machines fast enough that Ukraine’s cheap interceptors, the ones that made the propeller-driven Shaheds of 2023 into something approaching a solved problem, mostly cannot catch them.

A senior commander put it rather more plainly on Telegram: *we completely screwed up the initiative again, that’s a fact.*

This is the honest version of events, which is usually the version delivered by men who do not have to explain themselves to a press office.

The men who do have press offices were busy elsewhere.

Yevhen Magda spent [an hour](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gxvel3E8YnA) yesterday cataloguing the week’s rot: a fugitive prosecutor general’s disappearing suspicion notices, an anti-corruption chief who will not say whether he recognizes the woman in his own falsified paternity case, a tax-service head fired for loyalty to the wrong patron.

Feudalism, he called it, “on our money and not only ours.”

It is the sort of conversation Kyiv has been having with itself for 35 years now, in different rooms, about different names, arriving at the same diagnosis each time and prescribing nothing.

Meanwhile, the Third Army Corps announced [Operation Vivaldi](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ffadr-u2rbk) — the Lyman salient’s infiltration pockets cleared, seventy-five square kilometers swept, the promise of three more movements to come.

This is the part of the war that still works the way war is supposed to: men doing a hard thing competently, refusing to spoil their own surprise.

Four Seasons, they said.

We are only in the first.

And Z, asked by a Canadian interviewer whether he will be okay, answered with the joke he always makes when he does not want to answer honestly: *I’m okay if Ukraine is okay.*

Then, for one second, he dropped the bit and [admitted he doesn’t know](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HX8R0RhYILA).

Depends on many things.

Strong bodyguards, he said.

We’ll see.

*We’ll see* is also the operative philosophy of the diesel market, which [The Atlantic explains](https://archive.ph/2D32Q) has very little to do with Ukraine and everything to do with a war eight time zones away — a fact that has not stopped the jackass in the White House from blaming Kyiv’s refinery strikes for a six-dollar gallon in San Diego.

Ukraine gets credited with disasters it did not cause and denied credit for wars it is, on any given beautiful morning, still managing to survive.

## Day 1667

2026-09-17 · Made in USA

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6cb493fd-7e45-4dbe-a9bd-c4ea3650bf50_1536x1024.png)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 16, 2026)*

This man’s t-shirt caught my attention.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/d11a2815-4156-460c-9534-e16d63a5878b_2462x1385.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 17, 2026)*

A pack of Det-A types with heavily tattooed legs at 6:30 a.m. Running off too many Mohitas at [Tootsie Club](https://uk.tootsie.kiev.ua/)? Not happy being photographed?

Z’s [pep talk last night](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CRf6isky1eI) ran the usual three minutes: New York next week, meetings with partners, negotiations, energy, food security, weapons, new support packages, air defense in particular. The Anti-Ballistic Coalition is expanding — Europe’s strongest manufacturers are already inside something called FREYJA, a name that suggests someone in the president’s office still has a Norse mythology app open. He thanked parliament for voting through criminal liability for scam call centers, a law he’d just signed, and noted, almost as an aside, that asset declarations are coming back for law enforcement and security personnel who aren’t at the front — enough, he said, to actually monitor their lifestyles. State-owned enterprises are getting overhauled too, on the model of Naftogaz and Ukrnafta, whatever that model turns out to mean once the cabinet writes it down.

It is, item for item, a perfectly reasonable three minutes. It is also worth noticing what work each sentence is doing. The call-center law exists because a sitting prosecutor general was just fired for protecting the call centers. The asset-declaration reform exists because two of the country’s own intelligence services shot at each other in a residential district two weeks ago over the custody of one militia commander, and because a deputy head of the Presidential Office was running a raider ring out of government offices under an operation named, with the investigators’ own gallows humor, for the goddess of justice. Every “important issue” in this speech is a policy response to a scandal Z has never once been asked to explain on camera — Carthage, Midas, Femida, Forrest Gump, a naming convention that started in classical antiquity and gave up somewhere around Robert Zemeckis.

That is the trick of it. He can announce the fix all day. What he cannot do, and what nobody currently interviewing him seems inclined to make him do, is sit still for the question underneath the fix: how did the state get to a place where its own law enforcement needed its assets re-monitored, where its spy agencies needed to be told not to shoot each other, where the fired defense minister has better things to say about governance from a YouTube studio than the sitting president says from his own office. Adrienne Arsenault didn’t ask it in Calgary, or Banff, wherever it was. CBS didn’t ask it either. Maybe New York will ask it next week.

There is a wiretap transcript with a diminutive in it that nobody has the nerve to read aloud. Are you Vova? Nobody asks, so nobody answers. Z narrates the repair work as though the building fell down on its own. The government keeps being run by people who have never had to say what Ukraine is — only, this week, what it isn't.

## Day 1668

2026-09-18 · ukraine@war

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/702a1ccb-ce6b-4fd4-9846-f4c931a51193_1254x1254.png)

I’ve been collecting assets around the war and writing about the politics that have grown up around it.

Not quite an archive. Not quite a chronology.

More like a wall.

67 assets, pulled from twelve years and 1,702 posts. Each one is a door back to the day, the argument, the event it came from. Some people will treat it as a wall. Some will walk through. Hit Recompose and it rearranges itself — the old Blogger flipcard, brought back and let loose on a war.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2af2d575-c1ee-454e-acfd-ccfaec91a60e_800x800.jpeg)

This is not a methodology. There will be no framework, no journey, no visual-language ecosystem, and no map of the mind. There is a wall. It has pictures on it. Press the button.

**[Enter ukraine@war →](https://abdymok.github.io/mural/?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ukraine_at_war_wall)**

Substack builds a branded coverfor every post — the picture, the Day number, the subtitle. That card goes out to [x.com/dronedept](https://x.com/dronedept) first. The wall is where it ends up.

This is one collection. There are 24 more in the archive, and 27 assets still waiting to be placed. The wall isn’t finished.

Together they’re less a war archive than an ordinary life with one running through it the whole time — poppies and a cat on a windowsill, then a night in the snow, then riot police. Underneath all of it, the same question, again and again: how does Ukraine survive?

That’s not rhetorical. This is the bloodiest mess Europe has seen since the Second World War, and I’ve been filing from inside it, most mornings, for twelve years.

I don’t want to explain the rest in advance. Play with it.

It’ll keep changing. I’ll come back to it.
