## Day 1671

2026-09-21 · The 41st square

No transcript today. The video runs 12 seconds and ends with the last stanza of Miłosz’s [You Who Wronged](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/49482/you-who-wronged). The only sound — the approach of a Shahed drone and anti-aircraft fire — comes at the 12th second.

Not because it speaks for Ukrainians. Because it speaks for this project: write down the deed and the date, and let the record outlive the man.

One square, the 41st, is wired to appear 3% of the time. The rest, minus two, point to ukraine@war posts going back to 2019. The [40-square mural](https://abdymok.github.io/40/) is the thing itself.

Gemini picked the sample from 1,700 posts. It picked well enough. There is little time in Kyiv for curation.

The text is free, in the notebook, with no pictures. The pictures are the point, and they cost money.

We use pictures and sound as much as words. A century ago this year, Bernard Shaw refused his Nobel Prize money. This is no Project Gutenberg #13635 — that was Shaw’s war, bound and numbered before anyone knew how it would end. Ours keeps recomposing.

His reason, in the form most often attributed to him — which happens to be French: *Le prix Nobel, c’est une bouée de sauvetage lancée à un nageur qui a déjà atteint la rive.* A lifebelt thrown to a swimmer who has already reached the shore.

He spoke the language badly.[1](#user-content-fn-1) The line survives in French anyway — outliving him in a tongue he never quite had, the way a record is supposed to outlive the man who made it.

Words were never the thing.

---

1. Shaw himself admitted he spoke French poorly; a contemporary wrote that he “does not speak French well; but he expresses himself with such violence that he imposes himself.” [Source.](https://ia600102.us.archive.org/17/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.238203/2015.238203.Bernard-Shaw_text.pdf)

## Day 1672

2026-09-22 · Just a question of time

No one liked yesterday’s video post much. Or maybe subscribers just don’t like video posts?

That’s okay.

I loved making it. 40 was fun — and still is. It’s the little interactive archive of my Ukraine@war pictures and posts, and the [41st square](https://abdymok.github.io/40/) was an experiment inside it.

I learned a lot about Google Analytics, GitHub and how HTML works, or doesn’t work. I think we ironed out most of the glitches on Monday morning.

The bulk of the work was done over the weekend, when Russia was trying to kill us with jet-powered drones.

This morning the page in front of me looks like this.

Malevich. A cat. Kyiv metro. The 41st square and pliers.

It all makes perfect sense.

Or at least it did after coffee.

I was thinking about Bakhtin on my walk yesterday morning.

Three words came to mind:

*dialogue*, *carnival*, *chronotope*.

The dialogue is today.

Z and Trump meet in New York. They will presumably talk about the war, Russia, Ukraine, oil, peace, whatever is currently occupying the diplomatic universe.

They may even agree about something.

But I have a feeling they will mostly be talking past one another.

That is dialogue, too.

The carnival is everything swirling around them.

And the chronotope is the stubborn part: time and place. Geography that refuses to move simply because history has become bored with it.

Brett McGurk is writing about Europe preparing for the possibility that Russia’s war against Ukraine could widen into a broader confrontation, including the Suwałki Gap and the possibility of Russian testing of NATO. [McGurk on Europe preparing for a wider conflict](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/09/21/politics/nato-prepares-russia-widen-ukraine-war-mcgurk)

Vladimir Pastukhov, writing yesterday, makes a related argument in a very different register: the war is fundamentally a war Russia is waging against Europe, with Ukraine as the immediate battlefield. [Pastukhov’s strategic picture of the war](https://vladimirbpastukhov.substack.com/p/putin-strategic-picture-of-the-war?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

And Shaun Walker has spent much of this year going back through the warnings that preceded the full-scale invasion — who knew what, when they knew it and why so many people failed to believe them. [Shaun Walker on the warnings before the war](https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-interactive/2026/feb/20/a-war-foretold-cia-mi6-putin-ukraine-plans-russia?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

Three different people. Three different registers.

More or less the same geography.

I was at Teufelsberg 35 years ago. People were worrying about the Suwałki Gap then.

The Gap hasn’t closed. It’s as wide as ever.

That’s the chronotope.

Everything else is carnivalesque.

Which brings me to Oleshky.

Here’s where Oleshky is, so you can find it on a map.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/51987b58-54a4-4a77-939c-aa4e5880c189_1613x798.png)  
*Map c/o DeepState (September 22, 2026)*

Before the full-scale invasion, about 24,000 people lived there. Ukrainian officials now put the number at about 2,000, including roughly 50 children. There is no electricity or gas. Food and medicine have been severely restricted, and evacuation has not happened.

**People have been eating purslane.**

Anyone who has seen The Road will understand the atmosphere.

But here is the thing that bothers me.

Oleshky is not some isolated dot of misery that appeared last week because the United Nations General Assembly opened.

Ukrainian officials were raising the situation months ago. There were evacuation discussions in May. The UN human-rights monitoring mission reported in June that no food deliveries had reached Oleshky since May 26. Now the issue is being taken to the General Assembly.

Good.

About time.

But the people eating purslane did not suddenly become hungry because the General Assembly opened.

And Oleshky is not the only place on the map.

Kreminna. Debaltseve. Soledar. Popasna. Marinka. Krasnohorivka. Novohrodivka. Selydove. Ukrainsk. Vuhledar. Kurakhove. Polohy. Vasylivka. Kamianka-Dniprova. Hola Prystan. Kakhovka.

Cities.

Not villages on some abstract military map.

Cities with populations in the tens of thousands before the war. Places with schools and pharmacies and apartment blocks and bus stations and people who knew where to buy decent bread.

Some have been occupied for years. Some were occupied much more recently.

Their stories are not identical. Oleshky’s present catastrophe should not be flattened into a generic list.

But the map does something useful.

It restores the scale.

Oleshky is not the story.

Oleshky is a window.

And perhaps that is why the sudden attention to it feels so strange. The horror is real. The international attention is necessary. But the chronology is real too.

It is a chronicle of impotence.

JD Vance says the war will eventually be resolved.

> “Just a question of time.”

I suppose that is one way of looking at time.

Bakhtin might have had another.

Somewhere between Bakhtin and the Gap, I started thinking about complexity.

Vitebsk. The old journal. The carnivalesque.

Then Chara.

I went there in 1993, by helicopter from Chita, then the capital of Chitinskaya Oblast.

Chara is still there. It just isn’t in Chitinskaya Oblast anymore. Today it’s in Zabaykalsky Krai, whose capital is still Chita.

Same place. Different name.

I was leaving Moscow for Minsk.

Lukashenko had just been elected.

What a drag.

Thirty-two years later, Trump wants to buy Belarusian potash for the United States at a price he says would be substantially lower than what the U.S. currently pays Canada.

Last week Belarus released 25 political prisoners in exchange for U.S. sanctions relief.

And yesterday Trump put the potash version of the arrangement on Truth Social:

> “The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said yesterday that Belarus has little potash available for the United States this year because its 2026 output is already under contract.

The carnival continues.

The places remain where they were.

And then there is diesel.

Trump: stop hitting the refineries.

Fire Point: we’re hitting the refineries.

Moscow refinery: actually stopped.

The SBU said Ukrainian forces struck the Moscow refinery on September 20. Fire Point said its FP-1 drones were involved; Reuters reported that both primary crude-distillation units caught fire and that repairs could take several weeks.

According to the Financial Times, “diesel” came up repeatedly in Trump’s call with Zelenskyy on Sunday: “diesel, diesel ... diesel.”

Then Trump posted his own diagnosis on Truth Social:

“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine.”

So there we are.

Fire Point is hitting Russian oil infrastructure.

Trump is worrying about diesel.

And the Moscow refinery actually stopped.

Russia is losing refining capacity.

America is looking for cheaper Belarusian potash.

Lukashenko is releasing prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief.

Zelenskyy is meeting Trump in New York.

Oleshky is eating purslane.

And somewhere in the background the Suwałki Gap is sitting exactly where it was 35 years ago.

Dialogue. Carnival. Chronotope.[1](#footnote-1)

Sometimes I think subscribers just want my pano pictures and things exploding in the sky.

Fair enough.

On Sunday evening I took pictures from Shevchenkivsky Park.

One of the tiny red things in the corner of one panorama is not a light.

It’s a fireball.

Something was falling out of the sky.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6dd8d318-03c0-4192-beb1-0b030628b7a7_16380x3822.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 21, 2026)*

The other panorama looks almost exactly the same, but backwards. I was simply turning around.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/7024050f-0644-4630-961c-c955dff2085c_16382x3628.jpeg)  
*Photo c/o abdymok (September 21, 2026)*

Same city.

Different moment.

That’s the chronotope again.

And somewhere between the Gap, Oleshky, New York, Vitebsk and my Balush beside a Malevich book, the carnival continues.

Tuesday morning in Kyiv.

Again.

[1](#footnote-anchor-1)

Bakhtin’s dialogue is about voices meeting; carnival about the temporary collapse of the usual order; chronotope about time and place becoming one. I’m using all three rather freely. That’s part of the carnival.

[Dialogue and carnival](https://academic.oup.com/edinburgh-scholarship-online/book/33837/chapter-abstract/288638798?utm_source=chatgpt.com) · [Chronotope](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.14318/hau6.1.019?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## Day 1674

2026-09-24 · Between 1 and 1,000

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/e8cbbfa6-1a42-44d5-b569-a875303243af_1536x1024.png)

I left work early Wednesday evening after the air alert so I could save UAH 30 and get a free metro ride. The time was 20:40.

I had spent the afternoon trying to establish that the Parkovy data center had been hit once.

As I walked to the metro, I heard a swoosh above me that sounded a lot like the jet-propelled drones I’d been watching from my apartment balcony over the weekend. Seconds later: explosion.

By the time I got home, Telegram was telling me the Parkovy data center had been hit again.

I had spent the afternoon trying to establish that it had been hit once. I had just become a witness to it being hit again[1](#footnote-1).

This reminded me of something I wrote in *[Target practice](https://abdymok.substack.com/p/day-1008?utm_source=publication-search)* on Day 1008, back in November 2024:

> *Basically we’re target practice for the maniacs next door until Donald gets his shit together, or doesn’t.*

---

There’s a trap in numbers.

One is small; a thousand is large, so we imagine the road from one to a thousand as just a longer version of the road from zero to one.

It isn’t.

That’s roughly the point Oleksiy Babenko makes in his [long interview with Bihus.Info](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6W3R5Q9Hd24) about Ukraine’s struggle to intercept Russia’s new jet-powered Shaheds.

The new drones aren’t quite the same problem as the old ones. They’re faster, which shrinks the window between spotting a target and having something in position to shoot it down. A system built around slower drones discovers that time itself has turned into an enemy.

But Babenko’s sharper point comes after that.

Ukraine had already seen jet-powered drones intercepted — successful tests, even successful combat kills. That produced a comforting conclusion: the problem was being solved.

Except one successful interception isn’t a defense system.

Babenko says manufacturers, his own company included, believed for too long that they’d found the answer. Some of the early successes were flukes — tied to specific conditions, or to flaws in the attacking drone itself.

Somewhere along the way, “we managed to do this once” quietly became “we know how to do this.”

A large transformation disguised as a small sentence.

Then comes the second problem: production.

A prototype needs one clever engineer. A thousand machines need engineers, suppliers, testing, quality control, money, logistics, and people who know how to turn the first working unit into the thousandth — without discovering that some crucial part only exists in batches of fifty.

Babenko keeps returning to this gap: grant money isn’t production money, a successful flight isn’t deployment at scale, and a small team that can invent something isn’t automatically a team that can manufacture it at scale.

He’s blunt that Ukraine’s real shortage isn’t cash but engineers — and beyond that, people who’ve actually made the leap from one unit to thousands before. Because that leap brings its own unfamiliar failures.

Modern war is an exam in arithmetic.

The attacker doesn’t need one brilliant machine. It needs enough machines, made fast enough and often enough, to turn a momentary weakness into a permanent one.

The defender has to answer in the same currency, on the same clock.

So the real distance was never zero to one.

It’s one to a thousand — and then, worse, from today’s thousand to tomorrow’s, while the problem itself keeps changing shape underneath you.

That’s the part no demonstration flight, however successful, can settle.

---

**Poem of the Day — The Remainder**

There is always something left over.

A sentence.  
A photograph.  
A person standing at the edge of the frame.  
A day after you said the last day was finished.

The other day I put 41 into the middle of the forty.

It didn’t improve the number.  
It didn’t complete the archive.

It did something more irritating.

It kept it open.

Perhaps that is what an archive is for.

Not to finish the past.

Just to make sure the remainder has somewhere to go.

## Day 1678

2026-09-28 · The drone that brings a friend

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/88345bdf-a84b-4bf1-b7df-4893ce683dd7_1536x1024.png)

There is something almost old-fashioned about the Russian drone attack on the Inkom building in Kyiv on Friday.

Not the drone itself. The arrangement.

According to [Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash](https://t.me/serhii_flash/7775?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the Russians sent two jet-powered drones into Kyiv. One was a Geran-5, the attacking vehicle. The other was a Geran-4, flying at around three kilometres over the target. It acted as a MESH radio relay for the Geran-5 while simultaneously filming the attack and transmitting the pictures back. Afterward, Flash says, the Geran-4 flew beyond Kyiv and attacked a logistics facility.

At first this was one man’s reconstruction of what had happened.

Now the Russians appear to be providing their own visual corroboration.

The Varyag Telegram channel has published a 2½-minute video showing strike sequences against a series of Ukrainian data-center and network facilities, including the Inkom/Datagroup site. The video identifies eleven targets, among them De Novo, PrivatBank, Kyivstar, United DC, Cosmonova, G50/NEWTELCO, Inter Cars, BeMobile, Datagroup, Parkovy and Volia.

I have been keeping the data-center part of this story in a [running chronology](https://abdymok.github.io/40/articles/data-center-damage.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com). It began simply as a record of attacks on Kyiv’s data centers and network infrastructure. But as the pattern has become clearer, it has become difficult to look at those attacks in isolation.

The Varyag video does not, by itself, prove every detail of Flash’s reconstruction, particularly the relay function of the Geran-4. But it does something unusual. The attackers themselves are publishing pictures of the attacks that Flash was trying to explain.

The video shows the strike being filmed from the air. Flash’s account provides the explanation of how he believes that was done. Taken together, they describe a rather different kind of drone operation.

This is not entirely new.

For roughly the past month, the same family of jet-powered Gerans has been appearing around rather different kinds of targets. Trains have been among them, including trains carrying Western visitors leaving Ukraine for Europe. There have also been attacks on the SBU director’s office and other targets whose identities are less clear.

On September 4, Russian forces struck the SBU headquarters in Kyiv. Ukrainian officials said the office of SBU head Oleksandr Poklad was specifically targeted. Flash said the drone was remotely controlled and that a MESH-network repeater was involved.

The significance of the Inkom attack is therefore not simply that another building was hit.

It is the division of labour.

One drone carries the weapon.

The other brings the eyes — and, apparently, the telephone.

Flash has been warning about this development for weeks. He has described Russian use of jet-powered Gerans with MESH networking and argued that the technology is allowing operators to maintain control over drones at increasing distances.

And then there are the targets that become personal by accident.

The building hit in Pechersk on Friday was not some abstract piece of Kyiv geography. I lived there for four years. It was part of the ordinary map of my life, until suddenly it became part of another map.

There is a peculiar moment in this war when geography turns into literature all by itself.

For the last 72 hours, Kyiv has spent **almost 36 hours under air alert**.

So perhaps this is the part worth remembering.

The new danger is not simply that the drones are faster.

It is that they have begun to work in pairs.

One carries the bomb.

The other brings a friend.

## Day 1679

2026-09-29 · Ukraine is not Z, and neither are the ducks

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a297b469-652a-4fe5-939b-087f08d45034_1536x1024.png)  
*Reuters (Kyiv, September 28, 2026)*

A country does not become real because its president embodies it. And it does not become unreal because he does not.

That’s my beef with historian Tim Snyder’s [meditation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TKwfEs71VQI&t=2062s) over our current situation.

Snyder’s argument is that Z represents something Putin cannot accept: the idea that Ukraine is a real country, with its own history, interests and values. In Snyder’s telling, Z becomes almost a personification of Ukrainian sovereignty.

But there is an awkward question here.

Does Z actually deserve to represent all that?

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/3f2e8121-ac49-4767-8c29-041303f99280_1774x887.png)

Snyder is asking what Z represents. The timeline asks what Z did.

Those are not necessarily the same thing.

And then there is the phrase “Putin hates Z.”

Perhaps. But turning the war into a story about Putin and Z — two men who dislike each other — is precisely the framing Trump uses repeatedly. It makes a war against Ukraine sound like a personal quarrel that might be settled if only the two principals could get along.

But Ukraine is not Z.

And Z is not Ukraine.

That distinction seems rather important to me.

A country can be real while its president is disappointing, foolish, compromised or simply wrong.

Indeed, perhaps that is the point.

The country does not need its president to embody it.

---

There is a joke here that has been running longer than I would like. In January 2024, I wrote that Kyiv was “not a punching bag.”¹ Three months later we were “sitting ducks.”² By November, I had upgraded the zoology: “Target practice,” with the memorable diagnosis that Ukraine had become drone bait.³ In January of this year, I wrote about unmentioned urbicide, the crime under the Geneva Conventions, the Hague Convention, and the Rome Statute, and contrasted the physical reality of winter missile strikes on Kyiv with the absence of the word from the geopolitical yap sessions at Davos.⁴ Then, in July, Kyiv became a clay pigeon again for modified S-400s and ballistic missiles.⁵ In August, the ducks were still sitting.⁶ In September, after another exhausting procession of air alerts, we wrote: “more target practice. And we’re the targets.”⁷

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/9c60639c-2b55-444e-8b75-da92568c2a71_2170x725.png)

Perhaps “sitting duck” has outlived its usefulness. A duck at least has somewhere to go. The metaphors have stopped keeping pace with the news. We wait for Crotale NG VT-1 interceptors while ballistic missiles and jet-propelled drones practice their aim, and on Monday they hit the Academy of Sciences.

The same afternoon, a Russian drone also smashed into a hospital across the street from Ukraine’s Constitutional Court.

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f791a744-7585-475d-abbe-7cdda4cede78_1280x960.jpeg)  
*Ukrainian Emergency Service (Kyiv, September 28, 2026)*

The guy on the ledge survived. The building did not.

[Reuters](http://reuters.com) has its office next door, and [their photographers took lots of pictures](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/kyiv-science-academy-hit-russian-jet-drones-strike-across-ukraine-2026-09-28/). The New York Times [produced](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/world/europe/urkaine-drone-attack-kyiv-academy-sciences.html) a photo gallery of the damage.


```
You can kill one, but another is born.
```

Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published

```
The words are written down, the deed, the date.
```

Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published

```
And you’d have done better with a winter dawn,
```

Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published

```
A rope, and a branch bowed beneath your weight.
```

Czesław Miłosz, “[You Who Wronged](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/49482/you-who-wronged),” trans. Richard Lourie, *The Collected Poems: 1931–1987* (Ecco Press, 1988).
